en: Taittirīya Saṃhitā, Kāṇḍa 1–4; Taittirīya Saṃhitā, Kāṇḍa 5. Prapāṭhaka 5.1, Anuvāka 1.1: A description of the oblation to Savitṛ and the taking up of the *abhri* (wooden spade).
He offers the oblations to Savitṛ.
He offers with four ladlings for the sake of procreation;
cattle have four feet.
Verily, he wins cattle;
there are four quarters;
verily, he finds firm support in the quarters.
The *chandases* departed from the gods,
saying, "We will not carry the oblation for you unless it is shared with us.
For them, they set aside this fourfold-drawn portion.
In that he offers the fourfold-drawn portion for the invitatory verse (*puro'nuvākyā*), the offering verse (*yājyā*), the deity, and the *vaṣaṭ*-call, he thereby gratifies the meters;
these meters, being gratified, carry his oblation to the gods.
If one should desire,
"May he become worse off," one should offer for him one oblation at a time;
by means of the oblations, one seizes hold of him, and he becomes worse off.
If he should desire, "May he become more prosperous," he should offer all [the formulas] for him after reciting them in succession.
By means of the oblation itself, he causes him to advance; he becomes more prosperous.
Moreover, this is the overcoming of the sacrifice itself.
He indeed departs from the prosperity at the beginning of the sacrifice who departs from Agni as the deity.
There are eight of these Savitṛ verses.
The Gāyatrī has eight syllables; Agni is of the Gāyatrī nature.
By that very means, through prosperity from the mouth of the sacrifice, he does not depart from Agni, the deity.
There are eight oblations for Savitṛ, and the ninth is an offering; thus he extends the threefold sacrifice at its very beginning.
If he should desire,
"May I endow the meters with the glory of the sacrifice," he should make the *ṛc* the final one;
thus he endows the meters themselves with the glory of the sacrifice.
If he should desire,
"May I endow the sacrificer with the glory of the sacrifice," he should make the *yajus* the final element;
thus he endows the sacrificer himself with the glory of the sacrifice.
"Complete the hymn with the verse," he says,
for the sake of success.
He takes up the spade with four [verses]; there are four meters; [he does so] by means of the meters themselves.
"By the impulse of the god Savitṛ," he says for the sake of impulsion.
Agni hid himself from the gods.
He entered the bamboo;
he moved along this form, namely the hollow of the bamboo.
Therefore, the spade has a hollow; it is for the sake of common origin.
Wherever he dwelt, that place became black; it becomes speckled for the sake of the perfection of form.
It is sharp on both sides.
And for this reason, it is a fathom in measure, for the sake of securing the sun from here and from there;
for this much indeed is the vigor in a man.
It is commensurate with vigor;
it becomes immeasurable for the sake of attaining the immeasurable.
That among the trees which bears fruit is the most vigorous of them; the bamboo bears fruit.
It is made of bamboo for the attainment of vigor.
5.1.2 Anuvāka 2: Treading upon the earth with the horse, preceded by digging for the clay and proceeding toward it.
That which is performed in the sacrifice without a sacrificial formula (yajus) is indeed unsuccessful.
With the mantra, "They have grasped this rein of Order," he takes up the horse's halter.
For the sake of performing the *yajus* and for the prosperity of the sacrifice,
he places [the stone] upon the horse with the words, "O steed, run forward!"—
he thus proclaims its form and its greatness.
With the words, "Yoke the donkey, you two," he establishes the donkey upon the very non-existent;
therefore, the donkey is more non-existent than the horse.
"In every yoga, [we choose] the most powerful one," he says.
"In every yoga he yokes him; 'In every contest we invoke him,' he says. Contest (vāja) is indeed food."
Verily, he wins food; "Friends, for aid to Indra," he says;
verily, he wins power.
Agni hid himself away from the gods;
Prajāpati found him;
the horse belongs to Prajāpati.
He gathers [the materials] with a horse for the sake of finding [the goal].
Indeed, a state of inferiority is created when those who are superior and those who are inferior perform the same work together; [then] the inferior one [prevails].
For the donkey is inferior to the horse;
they lead the horse first to avoid the inversion of superior and inferior;
therefore, the inferior follows behind the superior.
One's rival is indeed many;
for he who piles the fire-altar becomes, as it were, like a horse, which is a thunderbolt.
"Advancing, come hither, trampling down those who curse," he says;
verily by means of the thunderbolt he tramples down his evil rival.
"From the lordship of Rudra," he says.
Animals indeed belong to Rudra; having begged the animals from Rudra himself, he performs the ritual act for himself.
"With Pūṣan as his companion," he says.
Pūṣan is indeed the gatherer of paths for the sake of attainment; for this Agni has the loose soil as his abode.
"The Aṅgirases first gathered this Agni Purīṣya among the deities from the seat of the earth; 'Come hither like an Aṅgiras,' he says;
thus he gathers him together with the deities in his own abode."
"We approach Agni Purīṣya in the manner of the Aṅgirases," he says; by this, he appropriates the prize of victory belonging to him.
"Having announced it to Prajāpati, Agni is to be gathered," they say.
This earth indeed is Prajāpati;
the anthill is its ear.
"May we carry Agni Purīṣya like Aṅgiras," with these words he approaches the anthill; having thus directly informed Prajāpati, he collects the fire.
"We carry Agni Purīṣya like Aṅgiras," he says.
"By which he gathers the prize; verily, he appropriates his prize.
"Agni has looked along the forefront of the dawns," he says.
"For the sake of manifestation.
"Having come, O prize-winner, from the path; having stepped upon the earth, O prize-winner," he says.
He indeed desires him with the former [verse] and finds him with the latter.
He strides with two verses for the sake of stability;
with two verses that are similar in form.
Therefore, suitable offspring are born.
"The sky is your back, the earth your seat," he says;
for from these worlds Prajāpati indeed impelled him forth.
He thus proclaims this very greatness of his form;
for the horse is indeed a thunderbolt.
It has more teeth than those with teeth on one side, and more hair than those with teeth on both sides.
Whomever one hates, one should meditate upon him as being underfoot;
thus one strikes him down with the thunderbolt itself.
5.1.3 Anuvāka 3: Description of the purification of the ground preceded by the treading of the horse.
With the two verses beginning "He has stepped out" and "He has stepped forth," he causes [the horse] to step out for the sake of firm establishment.
By means of two that are suitable;
therefore, suitable offspring are born.
He pours out water.
Wherever the waters go, there the plants take root;
as the plants take root, the animals take root after them; after the animals, the sacrifice takes root.
The sacrificer [offers] the sacrifice;

the offspring [follow] the sacrificer. Therefore, he pours out water for the sake of stability. If the Adhvaryu were to offer an oblation in that which is not fire, the Adhvaryu would become blind, and the Rakṣases would destroy the sacrifice.
Having placed the gold down, he offers the oblation.
He offers it indeed over fire;
the Adhvaryu does not become blind, and the Rakṣases do not destroy the sacrifice.
"I sprinkle Agni with mind and with ghee," he says;
for by means of the mind a person approaches the sacrifice.
"Him who looks toward all beings," he says.
"For he dwells facing all directions,
broad, transverse, and great"— thus he says;
for though born small, he is great.
"It becomes most wide-reaching food, impetuous and piercing," he says;
verily, he makes the food palatable for him.
"Everything is palatable to him who knows thus.
"I sprinkle you with speech and with ghee," he says; therefore, whatever a person conceives in his mind, that he speaks with his voice.
"Without a Rakṣas," he says, for the purpose of driving away the Rakṣases;
"Agni, whose color mortals desire," he says.
He bestows honor upon him;
he who knows thus becomes possessed of honor.

One ought indeed to attain with the mind that offering which the Adhvaryu offers into what is not fire; he offers with two verses containing the word "mind" (manasvatī) for the attainment of the two offerings.
With two [verses] it is for stability;
for at each opening of the sacrifice, when it is being performed, the Rakṣases seek to destroy the sacrifice.
Indeed, this is truly the mouth of the sacrifice: when the oblation reaches it,
he draws lines around it for the purpose of driving away the Rakṣases.
He draws around it with three [lines];
for Agni is threefold. As great as Agni is, from him he thus drives away the Rakṣases.
He traces around with the Gāyatrī;
the Gāyatrī is indeed splendor;
verily by means of splendor he encloses it.
He traces around with a Triṣṭubh verse; power indeed is the Triṣṭubh, and by means of power he thus encloses him.
He draws around with the *anuṣṭubh* verse;
the *anuṣṭubh* encompasses all meters for the sake of complete attainment;
he does so with the *anuṣṭubh* in the middle.
Speech indeed is in the middle; therefore we speak with speech from the middle. He draws the line around it first with a *gāyatrī*, then with an *anuṣṭubh*, and then with a *triṣṭubh*.
The Gāyatrī is indeed splendor, and the Anuṣṭubh is the sacrifice; with both splendor and sensory power, he thus encompasses the sacrifice on both sides.
5.1.4 Anuvāka 4: The Collection of Clay and Leather before Digging "By the impulse of the god Savitṛ," with these words he digs, for the sake of impulsion; moreover, by this he generates smoke.
"Thee, O Agni, full of light, of fair countenance," he says; by this he generates light.
That fire, once born, afflicted the creatures with distress; the gods pacified it with a half-verse.
"Auspicious to the creatures, not harming," he says; thus he pacifies it for the sake of the creatures.
He digs with two [verses] for the sake of stability.
With the words, "Thou art the back of the waters," he brings the lotus leaf;

for this lotus leaf is indeed the back of the waters. He brings it with its own form, and he gathers [the fire-wood] together with the lotus leaf; for the lotus leaf is the womb of Agni; thus he gathers Agni together with his own womb.
He collects [the materials] upon a black antelope skin; for the black antelope skin is the sacrifice; verily, by means of the sacrifice he collects the sacrifice.
If he were to collect upon the skin of domestic animals, he would afflict the domestic animals with pain. He collects upon a black antelope skin; thus he afflicts only the wild animals with pain.

Therefore, among domestic animals that are being born, the wild animals are fewer, for they are struck by sorrow. He gathers [the hair] from the hairy side, for it is from that side that it is pure for sacrifice.

He spreads out both the black antelope skin and the lotus leaf; the black antelope skin is this [earth], and the lotus leaf is yonder [sky]. Verily, by means of these two, he encloses him on both sides.
Agni hid himself from the gods; Atharvan perceived him.
"Atharvan was the first to churn you forth, O Agni," he says;
by means of him who indeed perceived him, he thus gathers him together.

"From the lotus, O Agni," he says; for he found him resting upon a lotus leaf. "And thee, the seer Dadhyañc," he says; for Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa was full of splendor; verily, he bestows splendor upon him. "And thee, Pāthya Vṛṣan," he says; he praises with a later verse that which has already been proclaimed earlier.
He brings it together with four [verses]; there are four meters; thus he does so by means of the meters.
With Gāyatrī verses for a Brāhmaṇa, for the Brāhmaṇa is connected with the Gāyatrī; with Triṣṭubh verses for a Rājanya, for the Rājanya is connected with the Triṣṭubh.
If he should desire, "May he become more prosperous," he should collect [the materials] for him with both sets [of verses]. Thus he bestows upon him brilliance and power in a unified manner.
He collects them with eight verses; the Gāyatrī has eight syllables, and Agni is of the nature of the Gāyatrī. As great as Agni is, so much of him he collects.
"Sit down, O Hotṛ! he says; thus he establishes the deities for him.

"Be present," he says for men; "sit down together," for birds; "be born, O conqueror, at the beginning of days," he says; thus he causes gods and men to be born after having been seated together for him.
5.1.5 Anuvāka 5: The gathering of the collected earth on the sacrificial ground.
"Verily, he does something cruel to her when he digs;
he pours water upon it."
The waters are indeed peaceful; with these peaceful ones he pacifies her affliction.
"May Vāyu Mātariśvan bestow [strength] upon you," he says.
Vāyu is indeed breath; by means of breath he unites her breath;
"May Vāyu unite with thee," he says.
"Therefore, the rain driven by the wind from heaven flows forth;
to him and to you, O Goddess, let there be *vaṣaṭ*!"— thus he says.
There are six seasons;
he thus places rain within the seasons,
and therefore it rains during all the seasons.
If he were to utter "vaṣaṭ," the Rakṣases would destroy the sacrifice;
he says "vaṭ," for thus he utters the vaṣaṭ-call in a cryptic manner.
His *vaṣaṭ*-call does not become exhausted, nor do the *rakṣas* strike down his sacrifice;
"Well-born together with light," he says, and binds [the horse] with an *anuṣṭubh* verse.
It is the *anuṣṭubh*.
All the meters are indeed the dear body of Agni;
verily, he encloses him with his own dear body.
He who knows thus becomes possessed of a dwelling. Agni, when bound, belongs to Varuṇa.
With two verses addressed to Savitṛ—"Arise, O performer of the fair sacrifice! and "Upright indeed for our protection!"—he rises up.
Thus, impelled by Savitṛ, he releases his upright wrath toward Varuṇa.
By means of two [feet] for stability;
once born, you are the embryo.
"Of the two worlds," he says;
these indeed are the two worlds, and Agni is their embryo.
Therefore he says thus: "O Agni, thou art beautiful, distributed among the plants," for when they distribute him, he then becomes more beautiful.
"He goes forth bellowing from his mothers," he says;
the plants indeed are his mothers;
it is from them that he causes him to move forth.
With the words, "Be firm, O solid-limbed one," he places the donkey down.
He binds him together with this [verse] for the sake of stability;
he gathers [the materials] with a donkey, therefore the donkey is the best bearer of burdens among animals.
He gathers together with a donkey;
therefore, even though the donkey is devoid of essence, it fattens more than other animals,
for with it they gather the food, the *arka*.
He gathers with a donkey;
therefore, the donkey, though possessing double seed, is born as the smallest among animals,
for fire consumes its source.
He has now indeed mounted upon the creatures.
"That Lord, burning the creatures with grief— 'Be auspicious to the creatures,' he says;
verily, he pacifies him for the sake of the creatures."
"O Aṅgiras, [protect] you from human women," he says, for offspring are of human origin.
"May you not burn against heaven and earth, nor the intermediate space, nor the trees," he says.
He pacifies him from these very worlds; "Let the prize-winner go forth, neighing," he says, for he is indeed a prize-winner.
"The braying donkey has fallen," so he said;
for the seers called it "donkey."
"Bearing Agni Purīṣya," he says;
for he indeed bears Agni.
"May I not fall before my full span of life," he says.
Verily, he bestows life upon him; therefore the donkey reaches its full span of life,
and therefore people are afraid when a donkey dies before its natural term.
"Bearing the bull Agni, the bull," he says,
for Agni is indeed a bull.
"The embryo of the waters, born of the ocean," he says;
for Agni is indeed the embryo of the waters.
"O Agni, come for the feast"— with these words these two worlds separated; when he says, "O Agni,
come for the feast," it is for the separation of these two worlds.
He has indeed fallen from his abode and has not yet reached a firm foundation;
at this moment, he meditates upon both the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer.
"The Law, the Truth," he says.
This [earth] is indeed *ṛta* and that [heaven] is *satya*;
verily, he establishes him upon these two; neither the *adhvaryu* nor the sacrificer comes to ruin.
Verily, this Agni, when bound, approaches the sacrificer as Varuṇa;
"O plants, receive this Agni," he says for the sake of pacification.
"Driving away all foolishnesses and hostilities," he says for the sake of striking down the *rakṣases*.
"Sitting down, may he strike away our ill-will," he says.
For stability:
"O plants, rejoice together!"
"He says, 'this one'";
the plants are indeed the portion of Agni;
by means of them, he causes him to prosper.
"Rich in flowers, with goodly fruit," he says; therefore the plants bear fruit.
"This germ of yours, born in due season, has sat down in its ancient dwelling-place," he says.
From whichever [deities] he causes him to move away, into those very ones he establishes him; with two verses he brings it down for the sake of stability.
5.1.6 Anuvāka 6: The Construction of the Fire-pan.
Agni, when bound, belongs to Varuṇa.
With the verse, "By his power," he loosens [the pan].
Impelled by Savitṛ, he releases Varuṇa’s wrath in all directions;
he pours out water. Water, indeed, is peaceful.
With peaceful verses alone he pacifies his grief;
he offers three oblations, for Agni is indeed threefold.
"To whatever extent Agni exists, he pacifies its impurity," he says, "Mitra, having united with the earth. Mitra is indeed the auspicious one among the gods;
by him alone he unites him.
For the sake of pacification,
if he were to mix it with the potsherds of domestic vessels, he would deliver the domestic vessels over to affliction.
He mixes it with potsherds from a ruined dwelling.
These indeed are things not fit for subsistence;
he consigns them to sorrow,
mixing them with gravel.
For steadfastness,
and also for peace;
he mixes it with goat's wool.
The goat is indeed the beloved body of Agni;
he unites him with his own beloved body, and also with splendor,
by means of the hair of the black antelope skin.
The black antelope skin is indeed the sacrifice;
by means of the sacrifice itself, he unites the sacrifice.
"The Rudras, having gathered together the earth," he says.
These deities indeed first brought him together;
with them alone he now brings him together.
"You are the head of Makha," he says;
Makha is indeed the sacrifice, and this fire-pan is its head.
Therefore he says thus:
"You two are at the feet of the sacrifice," for these two are indeed the feet of the sacrifice.
For the sake of a firm footing and stability,
he restrains himself with some [verses] and recites others in succession.
He makes it three-layered for the sake of pairing; these worlds are three, [he does so] for the attainment of these worlds;
he makes it with the meters.
The meters are indeed vigor;
he thus makes it with vigor.
He makes the hollow with a Yajus formula.
For the sake of distinction,
he makes it this large,
commensurate with Prajāpati as the mouth of the sacrifice.
He makes it two-teated for the milking of heaven and earth;
he makes it four-teated.
He makes [the cow] have eight udders for the milking of cattle; he makes her have eight teats for the milking of the meters.
One performing malevolent magic should make it nine-edged;
having thus prepared the threefold thunderbolt, he hurls it at his rival for the purpose of striking him down.
Having made the earth into a cauldron, he sets it down with the words "thus";
he thereby establishes it among the deities.
5.1.7 Anuvāka 7: The Preparation of the Fire-pan (Ukhā). He fumigates it with seven [substances]; for there are indeed seven vital breaths in the head.
The fire-pan (ukhā) is the head of the sacrifice;
verily, he places the vital breaths in the head of the sacrifice; therefore there are seven vital breaths in the head.
He fumigates with horse-dung; the horse belongs to Prajāpati, for the sake of common origin.

"Aditi [is] you," he says. This earth, indeed, is Aditi. By means of Aditi, he digs into the earth, so that there may be no injury to her; for one does not harm oneself. "The wives of the gods [are] you," he says. For the wives of the gods fashioned this [earth] first.
With those very [verses] he establishes it;
"The Dhiṣaṇās, you! he says, for the Dhiṣaṇās are indeed the sciences (vidyās).
Verily, he kindles her with the sciences;
"The women," he says, for the meters are indeed the women.
He cooks it with the very meters;
"O protectors," he says,
for the Hotṛ-priests are indeed the protectors.
"With the oblations of the Hotṛs he cooks her," he says; for she is indeed the wives of the gods. "O women," he says.
He generates her by means of those very [verses] and cooks her with six [verses].
There are six seasons; verily by means of the seasons he cooks it. "Let them cook it twice," he says.
Therefore, twice a year the crop ripens;
the cauldron, heated by Varuṇa,
he approaches with one belonging to Mitra.
"For peace, may the god Savitṛ dig you up," he says;
thus, impelled by Savitṛ, he digs her up with the sacred word (brahman) and with the deities.
Spreading out, O Earth, fill the regions and the quarters.
Thus he says: "Therefore Agni shines throughout all the quarters.
"Arise, become great; stand upright, you who are steadfast," thus he says.
For the sake of stability;
he smears the un-smeared vessel belonging to the Asuras, thereby making it belong to the gods.
He sprinkles it with goat's milk;
for goat's milk is the supreme milk,
and thus he sprinkles it with the supreme milk.
He covers it with the Yajus for the sake of distinction, and with the meters he seals it.
This [altar] is indeed constructed with the meters;
by means of the meters itself, one fastens the meters together.
5.1.8 Anuvāka 8: The Animal Victims for the Fire.
With twenty-one beans he approaches the human head.
Beans are indeed impure, and the human head is impure.
Having removed the impurity from it by means of the impure substances themselves and having made it pure, he carries it away.
There are twenty-one [pieces]; for man is indeed twenty-onefold.
The human head is indeed unsuccessful and impure with respect to the vital breaths, for it was severed from the man;
he places it upon an anthill mound that has been split into seven parts.

There are indeed seven vital breaths in the head; verily, he endows it with those very breaths for the sake of its sacrificial purity. As many as are the kinsmen of death, over them Yama has attained sovereignty.
He chants around it with the Yamagāthās; verily, he excludes it from Yama.
He chants around it with three verses.
There are these three worlds; he deprives him of these very worlds.
Therefore, one should not give to a singer.
For the verse takes that away. He offers animals to the fires;
the fires are indeed desires (kāma); verily he wins desires. If he were not to offer animals, they would not be won by him.

The animals would be [left incomplete]. If he were to release them after they have been carried around the fire, he would cause a disturbance of the sacrifice. If he were to complete the ritual, their heads would become exhausted.
In that he immolates the animals, by that very act he wins the cattle; in that he releases them after they have been carried around the fire, it is for the sake of the non-exhaustion of their heads;
he concludes with the one belonging to Prajāpati; Prajāpati is indeed the sacrifice; thus he establishes the sacrifice within the sacrifice itself.
Prajāpati created living beings; feeling himself emptied,
he perceived these Āprī verses.
With these indeed he gratified himself from the mouth;
that is why these are called the Āprīs.
The sacrifice is indeed Prajāpati;
by means of these [verses], he gratifies the sacrifice itself at its very beginning.
They consist of an unlimited number of meters.
Immeasurable is Prajāpati;
[it serves] for the attainment of Prajāpati.
The deficient and the redundant are a pair.
This metre is indeed named Lomaśa for the sake of procreation; the cattle of Prajāpati are hairy.
Verily, he wins cattle;
for these are all forms,
and all forms are employed in the piling of the fire-altar.
Therefore, these [verses] belong to the piled fire-altar;
he recites twenty-one *sāmidhenī* verses.
Or [the hymn] is twenty-one-fold; verily he goes to splendor, and also to a firm foundation, for the twenty-one-fold is indeed a firm foundation.
He recites twenty-four verses.
Twenty-four half-months make a year;
the year is Agni Vaiśvānara;
verily, he directly wins Vaiśvānara.
He recites [the verses] directed away,
for the world of heaven is, as it were, turned away;
"May the seasons, O Agni, strengthen thee," he says.
He increases the fire with equal [verses] alone.
"By means of the seasons, [illuminate] the year;
illumine all the quarters of the earth," he says;
therefore Agni shines forth across all the directions.
"The Aśvins have driven death away from him," he says;
verily, he drives death away from him. "We have risen up out of the darkness," he says.
Darkness is indeed evil; he thus strikes away evil from him.
"We have gone to the highest light," he says.
Yonder sun, indeed, is the highest light;
he attains union with the sun itself.
Neither the year remains [in its course] nor does his prosperity remain for him by whom these [rites] are performed.
He recites the *jyotiṣmatī* as the last;
verily, he places light above him for the illumination of the world of heaven.
5.1.9 Anuvāka 9: The Birth of the Ukhya Fire. He consecrates [the sacrificer] with six [verses]; for there are six seasons.
Verily, he consecrates him by means of the seasons;
he consecrates him with seven,
for there are seven meters.
He consecrates him by means of the meters;
with the verse "All [the works] of the god, the leader," ending in the Anuṣṭubh, he offers an oblation; for speech is indeed the Anuṣṭubh.
Therefore, speech is the highest among the vital breaths.
The first foot [of the Gāyatrī] has not attained one syllable;
therefore, humans subsist on that which speech has not attained.
He offers with a full [ladle],
for Prajāpati is, as it were, full.
He offers with a deficient [verse] belonging to Prajāpati, for from what was deficient Prajāpati created offspring.
If he were to pour it onto the flame for the sake of creating progeny, he would obtain what has already come to be; if onto the embers, what is yet to be.
He throws [the seed] onto the embers; thus he secures the future,
for the future is more than the past.
He separates them with two [verses]; the sacrificer has two feet, for the sake of stability.
This fire-pan (ukhā) was indeed prepared by Brahmā with a sacrificial formula (yajuṣ);
if it were to break, the sacrificer would meet with calamity and his sacrifice would be destroyed.
"O Mitra, heat this fire-pan," he says; for Mitra is indeed the Brahman.
Verily, by means of the Brahman, he establishes it.
The sacrificer does not come to ruin, nor is his sacrifice destroyed;
if [the vessel] should break, he should join it back together with those very same potsherds— that indeed is the expiation for that.
One who has attained prosperity should pour [the remainder] into that which has been churned;
for he is indeed his own being.
He who desires prosperity should approach the deity;
he who would be produced from the fire-pan (ukhā) should indeed be his [deity],
for it is from this that he is produced.
He indeed becomes self-existent (svayambhū) regarding whomever he may desire.
Thinking, "I shall produce a rival for him," he should take [the grain] from elsewhere and pour it down;
thus he directly produces a rival for him.
For one who desires food, he should pour it down from a frying pan.
When food is carried in an ambarīṣa vessel,
one obtains food together with its source.
He places muñja grass down. Muñja grass is indeed strength; verily, he bestows strength upon him.
Agni hid himself from the gods;
he entered the *krumuka* wood.
He places the *krumuka* down.
Whatever of his is deposited there, that very thing he wins.
He mixes it with clarified butter;
for clarified butter is indeed the dear abode of Agni.
He causes him to prosper with his very own dear splendor, and also with his brilliance.
He places one made of *vaikaṅkata* wood; verily he wins splendor. He places one made of *śamī* wood.
With the three verses beginning, "Sit for the sake of peace upon the lap of this mother," he worships the newborn;
these worlds are three.
In these very worlds he attains renown;
moreover, he bestows the vital breaths upon himself.
5.1.10 Anuvāka 10: Holding the Fire-pot (Ukhya).
Formerly, Agni would not burn what had been cut by anything other than an axe; therefore, the seer Prayoga made it palatable for him.

With the verse, "O Agni, whatever [things] there may be," he places a fuel-stick upon the fire. He makes for him that which has not been cut by an axe palatable; everything becomes palatable for him who knows thus.
He places a branch of the Udumbara tree; the Udumbara is indeed strength;
verily, he bestows strength upon him.
Prajāpati created Agni; once he was created, the Rākṣasas sought to destroy him.
He saw this Rākṣoghna [hymn]; with it, indeed, he struck away the Rakṣases.
In that there is a Rākṣoghna [hymn], by means of it one strikes away the Rakṣases from Agni as soon as he is born.
He places one made of *aśvattha* wood;
for the *aśvattha* among trees is the subduer of rivals, [serving] for victory.
He places one made of *vikaṅkata* wood.
Verily he wins radiance;
he places a fuel-stick of *śamī* wood for the sake of pacification.
"Sharpened is my spiritual power (*brahman*); I have extended their arms"—with these words, he makes him recite over the two topmost *audumbara* posts.
By means of the *brahman*, he sharpens the *kṣatra*; by means of the *kṣatra*, the *brahman*.
Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa who possesses a Rājanya surpasses another Brāhmaṇa; therefore, a Rājanya who possesses a Brāhmaṇa surpasses another Rājanya. This Agni is indeed death; gold is immortality.
He puts on a golden plate in between;
verily he places immortality as a barrier against death.
It has twenty-one knobs.
There are indeed twenty-one worlds of the gods: twelve months, five seasons, these three worlds, and yonder sun as the twenty-first. So many indeed are the worlds of the gods;
from them he excludes his rival.
By means of the *nirbādhas*, the gods indeed placed the Asuras under constraint;
that is the reason for the *nirbādha*s being called *nirbādha*s.
He becomes possessed of *nirbādha*s.
He indeed drives away his rivals;
he fastens it with a verse to Sāvitrī for the sake of procreation.
With the next verse, "Night and Dawn," he raises him up by means of day and night;
he says, "The gods supported Agni, the giver of wealth."
The vital breaths are indeed the gods who bestow wealth;
having raised him up by means of day and night, he supports him with the vital breaths.
He puts it on while sitting;
therefore offspring are born sitting.
The black antelope skin is on top.
Gold is indeed brilliance, and the black antelope skin is the Brahman;
thus he encloses him on both sides with brilliance and with the Brahman.
The sling has six suspension-ropes.
There are six seasons; verily by means of the seasons he raises it up. In that it has twelve supports, it is by means of the year.
It is made of muñja grass; muñja grass is indeed strength;
verily, he endows him with strength.
"You are Suparṇa, the Garuḍa," with these words he gazes; he thus proclaims his form and his majesty.
"Go to heaven, fly to the light! he says.
Verily, he causes him to go to the heavenly world.
5.1.11 Anuvāka 11: Designation of the *yājyā* verses for the *prayāja* offerings related to the Aśvamedha sacrifice.

Enkindled, anointing the hollow of our thoughts, O Agni, swelling with honeyed ghee—bearing strength, bring the beloved seat of the gods, O Jātavedas, to the one who possesses strength. Anointing the paths leading to the gods with ghee, may the vigorous steed, knowing the way, go toward the gods. O Steed, let the quarters of space attend upon you; bestow self-sustaining power upon this sacrificer. You are worthy of praise and worthy of adoration, O vigorous one; you are swift and fit for sacrifice, O Steed. May Agni [lead] you...
May Jātavedas, the bearer of oblations, carry him along, being pleased and in harmony with the gods and the Vasus.

The sacrificial grass is strewn; may Aditi, rejoicing in it as well-spread, wide, broad, and first extending upon the earth, joined by the gods and in harmony with them, making it a pleasant seat, establish us in prosperity. May these blessed goddesses, the Doors, possessing all forms, opening wide with their panels and frames, lofty yet bending down as they are adorned—may the divine Doors be easy of access for you. Moving between Mitra and Varuṇa, being in accord at the mouth of the sacrifices, O Dawn and Night, you who are rich in gold and beautiful in form—I place you here in the womb of Cosmic Order (Ṛta).

May the two golden ones, the gods who travel on a single chariot, seeing all beings, come first to you; may they, the two Hotars, bestowing impulsion and measuring it out, point toward the light by their direction. May Bhāratī with the Ādityas desire our sacrifice; may Sarasvatī together with the Rudras protect us. Invoked along with the Vasus, may the goddesses Iḍā, being of one accord, place our sacrifice among the immortals. Tvaṣṭṛ begot the hero who loves the gods; from Tvaṣṭṛ was born the swift horse. Tvaṣṭṛ begot this entire world; O Hotar, worship here the maker of much.

Anointed with ghee by himself, let the horse go to the gods in due season to their place of enjoyment. May the Lord of the Forest, knowing the world of the gods, carry the offerings made savory by Agni. Increasing through the fervor of Prajāpati, as soon as you were born, O Agni, you took possession of the sacrifice; go forth as the leader with the offering consecrated by Svāhā, and let the Sādhyas and the gods eat the oblation.
*Taittirīya Saṃhitā*, Book 5, Praśna 2, Anuvāka 1: Placing the Fire on the Seat and Worship with the Vātsapra Hymn.
The gods, having Viṣṇu as their head, conquered these worlds by means of the meters so as not to be defeated.
When the sacrificer strides the Viṣṇu-strides, he becomes Viṣṇu himself and conquers these worlds by means of the meters so as not to be defeated.
"Thou art the stride of Viṣṇu, the slayer of the adversary," he says; for the earth is the Gāyatrī, and the intermediate space is the Triṣṭubh.
The Jāgatī is the sky;
the Ānuṣṭubh verses are the quarters. By means of the meters, he thus conquers these worlds in their proper order.
Prajāpati created Agni; once created, he went away from him.
He followed him with this [verse]: "He cried out. By means of that, he indeed won for himself Agni's beloved abode.
In that he recites this [verse] after [the others], by it he wins the beloved abode of Agni itself.
He who strides the Viṣṇu-strides is liable to be burnt up from behind;
therefore he turns back with four verses.
There are four meters; indeed, the meters are Agni’s beloved body;
[he approaches] his own beloved body.
The sacrificial fee turns around;
it turns around following its own very vigor.
Therefore, the right half of the self is more vigorous.
Moreover, he turns around following the turning of the sun;
Varuṇa seized Śunaḥśepa, the son of Ajīgarta.
He saw this Vāruṇī [offering];
with it, indeed, he released himself from Varuṇa’s noose.
Varuṇa seizes him who puts on the fire-pan (ukhā).
"Loosen the highest bond from us, O Varuṇa," he says;
by this [verse], he indeed releases himself from the bonds of Varuṇa.
"I have brought you hither," he says,
for he indeed brings him hither;
"Stand firm, do not waver," he says.
"For stability,
let all the people desire you," he says; verily, by means of the people, he causes him to prosper.
"May the kingdom rest upon this one," he says;
thus he makes the kingdom stable for him whom he desires.
Thinking "May there be a kingdom," he should meditate upon him with his mind;
he indeed becomes a kingdom.
"Standing tall at the forefront of the dawns," he says;
verily, he makes him the foremost among his equals.
"He has emerged from the darkness," he says.
"Darkness indeed he drives away from him; 'He has come with light,' he says; verily, he bestows light upon him."
He settles it with four [verses]; there are four meters; thus, by means of the meters themselves.
The *aticchandas* is indeed the highest among the meters; by means of this meter,
he makes him the preeminent one among his peers.
It becomes possessed of essence; it causes him to attain essence itself.
He worships with the Vātsapra hymn. By this, Vatsaprī Bhalandana indeed obtained the dear abode of Agni;
by this, he obtains the dear abode of Agni.
It becomes elevenfold.
Thus he bestows vigor upon the sacrificer in a single unit.
By means of the *stoma*, the gods prospered in this world; by means of the *chandas* meters, they prospered in that world.
The Vātsapra is indeed the very form of the Stoma;
when one worships with the Vātsapra,
he thereby conquers this world.
In that he strides the Viṣṇu-strides, he conquers this very world by means of them.
He strides forward on the previous day and worships on the following day; therefore, the minds of some creatures are set on exertion, while those of others are set on rest.
Therefore, the wanderer is the master of security;
therefore, the wanderer settles in security and makes a firm resolve.
He restrains his speech for the support of the sacrifice.
5.2.2 Anuvāka 2: The Carrying Forth of the Fire in the Pan.
"O Lord of Food, give us food," he says;
for Agni is indeed the Lord of Food.
"He himself bestows food upon us," he says; "of the one who is free from disease and full of vigor," he says; by this, he indeed means "of the one who is free from consumption."
"May you further the giver; bestow strength upon us, bipeds and quadrupeds," he says.
Thus he invokes this very blessing.
"All the gods shall lift you up," he says.
The vital breaths are indeed the All-gods;
verily by means of the vital breaths he raises him up.
"May they bring [him] with their thoughts," he says.
Because he exerts himself for him with that very [mind], by that alone he causes him to prosper; he places [the oblation] down with four [verses],
for there are four meters.
By means of the meters themselves; with the *aticchandas* as the final [meter],
for this *aticchandas* is indeed the height among the meters.
Verily, he makes him the preeminent one among his equals;
it contains the word "sadvatī," for it causes him to attain excellence.
"O Agni, come as one possessing light," he says; verily, he bestows light upon him. Whomever he injures, he injures by means of his own body.
"Do not harm the offspring with your body," he says;
thus he pacifies it for the sake of the offspring.
The Rakṣases indeed attend this sacrifice when one lets out a cry during the pressing.
"He cried out," he says in response,
for the sake of driving away the Rakṣases.
They carry [the cart] with a wagon.
He bestows honor upon him; therefore, among guests, the owner of a wagon and the owner of a chariot are the most honored.
He who knows this becomes possessed of honor.
With the verse, "Honor Agni with fuel," he places a fuel-stick that has been sprinkled with clarified butter once the fire has settled;
this is exactly like the hospitable reception with clarified butter offered to a guest who has arrived.
For a Brāhmaṇa, it is done with a Gāyatrī verse, for the Brāhmaṇa is of the Gāyatra nature.
For the Rājanya, [he offers] with a Triṣṭubh verse, for the Rājanya is of the nature of the Triṣṭubh. He causes the ashes to enter the waters;
for Agni has his origin in the waters.
He causes him to go to his very own womb; he causes him to enter with three verses, for the Trivṛt is indeed [the year].
Agni.
He causes Agni, in his full extent, to attain a firm foundation. Verily, he who casts the ashes into the waters casts away Agni.
He places [the two stones] with two verses containing the word "light";
verily he bestows light upon him; with two [verses], for the sake of stability.
He who casts ashes into the waters sows away his offspring and cattle;
[therefore] he rises up again with the words, "Return with vigor, together with wealth," and thus he places offspring and cattle within himself.
"May the Ādityas, the Rudras, and the Vasus kindle you again," he says;
for these deities indeed kindled him first.
With those very [verses] he kindles him;
he stands near with the words, "Be awake, O thou who art awake," and thus he indeed awakens him.
Therefore, having slept, living beings awaken;
therefore, animals return and settle down each in its proper place.
5.2.3 Anuvāka 3: The Piling of the Gārhapatya Fire-altar As great as the earth is, over it Yama has attained lordship.
Verily, he who piles the fire-altar on this earth without having asked Yama for the sacrificial ground piles it for Yama.
Having resolved, "He has departed," he causes Yama himself to be requested [as the sacrificial ground] for her, and then he piles the fire-altar for himself.
Indeed, those seeking the immortal essence of her at the tip of the arrow did not find it.
Those gods saw this sacrificial formula: "Go away!"— for by means of this, he causes [the enemy] to resolve upon departure.
He piles the fire-altar when it is indeed immortal.
He digs it up; whatever in it is impure, that he strikes away.
He sprinkles water for the sake of peace;
he scatters sand.
This indeed is the form of Agni Vaiśvānara;
by means of its very form, he wins Vaiśvānara.
He scatters saline soil.

These saline soils (ūṣas) are indeed nourishment and procreation; verily, he piles the fire upon nourishment and procreation. Moreover, it is for the sake of recognition; for these saline soils are the means of recognizing cattle.
Heaven and Earth were together.
As they were separating, they said, "Let there indeed be for us both that which is worthy of sacrifice together.
That which was worthy of sacrifice in her (the sky) he placed in this (the earth); those became the saline soil (ūṣāḥ).
Whatever sacrificial element belonged to this [earth], he placed that in yonder [heaven]; that is the black spot in the moon.
While scattering the saline soil, he should meditate on that; thus he piles the fire-altar in the sacrificial portion of both heaven and earth.
"This is that Agni," says Viśvāmitra.
It is well-spoken.
By this, indeed, Viśvāmitra won for himself the beloved abode of Agni;
by this, one wins for oneself the beloved abode of Agni.
By means of the meters, indeed, the gods [reached] the heavenly world; he lays down four facing eastward, for there are four meters.
By means of the meters alone, the sacrificer thus goes to the heavenly world;
as they were proceeding to the heavenly world, the quarters collapsed,
so he placed two bricks facing each other in front and two behind.
Afterwards, they were made firm by those *samīcī* bricks; for when he places two *samīcī* bricks in front and two *samīcī* bricks behind, it is by them that he makes the quarters firm.
For the support of the quarters;
moreover, the meters are indeed cattle;
verily, he bestows cattle upon him in a forward direction.
He places eight [bricks].
The Gāyatrī has eight syllables; Agni is of the nature of the Gāyatrī. As great as Agni is, so much of him he builds.
He places eight [bricks].
The Gāyatrī consists of eight syllables;
the Gāyatrī knows the heavenly world directly.
He places thirteen *lokampṛṇā* bricks for the discernment of the heavenly world.
They amount to twenty-one;
the twenty-onefold is indeed a foundation, and the Gārhapatya fire is a foundation.
Following the foundation of the twenty-onefold, he establishes himself upon the Gārhapatya.
He who knows thus stands facing the fire as it is being piled.
One who is piling for the first time should pile it in five layers; the sacrifice is fivefold.
Cattle are fivefold;
verily he wins both the sacrifice and cattle. One who is building for a second time should pile it with three layers.
There are these three worlds;
they find their support in these very worlds.
One who builds the third [altar] should build it as a single layer;
for the world of heaven is indeed single-fold;
by means of that which is single-fold, he goes to the world of heaven.
He covers it with soil; therefore the bone is covered with flesh.
He who knows this does not become afflicted with skin disease.
There are five layers;
he covers them with five fillings;
they amount to ten.
The Virāj consists of ten syllables; verily, he finds firm support in food and in the power of eating.
5.2.4 Anuvāka 4: Pouring the Fire from the Ukhā Pot.
These two [fires] become hostile toward each other: that which was the fire previously and that which is now in the *ukhā*.
With the four verses beginning "Be united" (*sam itam*), he pours them together.
There are four meters; the meters are indeed the dear body of Agni;
verily, with his own dear body he pacifies them.
"United," he says;
therefore the ruling power (kṣatra) is united with the spiritual power (brahman), since, having mixed them together, he distributes them.
Therefore, the kṣatra departs from the brāhmaṇa;
they indeed consecrate him by means of the seasons.
He is to be released by means of the seasons alone.
"Like a mother her son, the earth [bears] the one who belongs to the soil," he says;
having consecrated him by means of the seasons, he releases him by means of the seasons.
With a verse addressed to Vaiśvānara he takes up the sling; thus he makes it palatable.
There are three black grains parched with husks, dedicated to Nirṛti.
The husks are indeed the share of Nirṛti; black is the form of Nirṛti.
By means of her very form, he makes expiation for Nirṛti.
They go toward this direction; this is [the way].
Verily, he expiates Nirṛti in her own quarter;
he places it on a self-made salt-flat or in a cleft.
This, indeed, is the abode of Nirṛti;
in her own abode he expiates Nirṛti;
he places the sling upon it.
The noose belongs to Nirṛti;
verily, he releases him directly from the noose of Nirṛti;
he places three [bricks] down.
Man is indeed threefold. As great as man is, from him he drives away Nirṛti; he places [the bricks] facing away.
He drives away Nirṛti from him toward the far distance;
they go without looking back for the sake of concealment from Nirṛti.
Having cleansed themselves, they stand near for the sake of purity;
they stand near the Gārhapatya fire.
Having moved about in the world of Nirṛti alone, purified, they return to the world of the gods.
They stand with one [verse];
thus, in a single way, they bestow vigor upon the sacrificer.
"He is the dwelling-place, the gatherer of riches," he says;
for riches are indeed offspring and cattle; thus they cause him to prosper with offspring and cattle.
5.2.5 Anuvāka 5: Ploughing the Field. He measures it out by the length of a man; for the man is measured by the sacrifice.
He measures it out by means of the joints of the sacrifice;
it becomes as large as a man with his arms raised. Indeed, such is the vigor in a man.
By means of vigor alone he measures him out; he becomes winged, for one who is without wings is not able to fly.
The two wings become longer by one cubit;
therefore, birds have long wings.
The two wings and the tail together measure one fathom.
Such indeed is the vigor in a person.
It is commensurate with vigor;
he measures it with a bamboo cane,
for the bamboo cane belongs to Agni.
He yokes with a *yajus* for the sake of easy birth; he plows with a *yajus*.
He ploughs with a team of six oxen for the sake of exclusion; for there are six seasons.

Verily, he ploughs it with the seasons when he uses a team of twelve oxen; [it is] by means of the year. Indeed, this earth was afraid of being over-burned by Agni; she saw this twofold state: that which is ploughed and that which is unploughed.
3. Or else, he did not burn this earth excessively. 4. Since it is both ploughed and unploughed, it is for the sake of its not being burnt excessively;
they say, "One ought to lift up Agni twice [its size]."
That which is ploughed and that which is unploughed;
for the rising of Agni.
So many indeed are the animals—both bipeds and quadrupeds.
If he were to let them go toward the east, he would hand them over to Rudra; if toward the south, he would consign them to the ancestors;
if toward the west, the Rakṣases would slay them.
He releases them toward the north. This direction indeed belongs to the gods and humans; it is toward that very direction he releases them.
Then indeed he releases them toward this direction;
for yonder sun is the breath, and thus he releases them following after the breath itself.
They turn toward the south;
they turn according to their own vigor.
Therefore, the right side of the self is more vigorous.
Moreover, they turn around following the turning of the sun;
therefore, animals disperse facing away and return facing toward [the source].
[They plow] three furrows each.
He ploughs; he thus extends the threefold sacrifice at its opening;
he sows the plants.
Through the *brahman*, he wins food;
on the *arka* altar the *arka* is piled;
with fourteen [verses] he sows.
There are seven cultivated plants and seven wild plants;
for the acquisition of both kinds,
he sows of every kind of food.

For the attainment of every kind of food. He sows on ploughed ground; for on ploughed ground plants find firm support. He sows along the furrows; for the sake of procreation. He sows in twelve furrows; twelve months are a year; by means of the year itself he cooks food for him who piles the fire-altar. This applies to one who piles the fire-altar.
One should eat of what has not been enclosed; by [eating] what is enclosed, one would be deprived.
Those among the trees that bear fruit, those he should also sprinkle upon the kindling wood, for the sake of enclosing what has not been enclosed.
He throws clods of earth together from the quarters; having thus secured the vigor of the quarters, he piles the fire-altar in the vigor of the quarters.
If he should hate anyone, he should bring a clod from the direction in which that person is located.
"From here I take food and strength," he says; thus he wins food and strength from that quarter.
He who is in that quarter becomes hungry.
He scatters [the earth] upon the high altar.
For the fire is piled upon the high altar;
moreover, the high altar is indeed cattle,
so he wins cattle for himself.
And thus, for the sake of not omitting a joint of the sacrifice.
5.2.6 Anuvāka 6:
Sowing Sand and Other Materials in the Field.
With the mantra, "O Agni, yours is fame and vigor," he scatters sand.
This indeed is the hymn of Agni Vaiśvānara;
by means of this very hymn, he wins Vaiśvānara;
with six [verses] he scatters [the grains].
The year consists of six seasons,
and Agni Vaiśvānara is the year;
thus he directly obtains Vaiśvānara.
This metre is indeed called "the ocean";
offspring are born after the pattern of the ocean when he scatters [the seed] having sprinkled it with this.
For the procreation of offspring,
Indra hurled the thunderbolt at Vṛtra.
He divided himself threefold: one third became the wooden sword (*sphyá*), one third the chariot, and one third the sacrificial post (*yūpá*).
Those arrow-shafts that shattered within became pebbles (*śarkará*);
that is the origin of the name "pebble" (*śarkaratva*).
The pebbles are indeed a thunderbolt,
and Agni is an animal;
in that he measures out the fire with pebbles, he encloses the animals for him by means of the thunderbolt itself.
Therefore, animals are encompassed by the thunderbolt;
therefore, one who is more stable does not take away from one who is less stable.
[This rite] with twenty-one [stakes] is for one desiring cattle.
One should measure it around;
for there are seven vital breaths in the head,
and cattle are the vital breaths.
Verily, by means of the vital breaths he wins cattle for him;
for one who has an enemy, [the sacrifice] is performed with the twenty-seven-fold [stomas]; having indeed fashioned the threefold thunderbolt, he hurls it at his enemy.
For the sake of spreading. One should measure with an unlimited number [of bricks] for the attainment of the unlimited.
For one whom he desires, "May he be without cattle," he should scatter pebbles and sand over it without measuring.
His seed, being unrestrained, is indeed poured out in all directions; he becomes truly destitute of cattle.
If he should desire of someone, "May he be rich in cattle," having measured out [the ground] for him, he pours water over the pebbles; thus he pours seed for him in a manner directed toward him.
He indeed becomes possessed of cattle;
he separates them with the Saumya verses, for Soma is the depositor of seed.
Verily, he thereby bestows seed:
with a *gāyatrī* verse for a Brāhmaṇa, for the Brāhmaṇa is connected with the *gāyatrī*; with a *triṣṭubh* verse for a Rājanya, for the Rājanya is connected with the *triṣṭubh*.
Medha did not approach Śaṃyu Bārhaspatya; he entered the fire.
Having assumed the form of a black antelope, he went forth from Agni; he entered the horse,
and he became the intermediate hoof of the horse.
In that he makes the horse step upon [the site], he wins back that very vital essence (medhas) which entered the horse;
"Agni is to be piled by Prajāpati," they say,
for the horse belongs to Prajāpati.
In that he makes the horse step upon [the site], he piles the fire by means of Prajāpati; he places a lotus leaf [upon it],
for the lotus leaf is the womb of Agni.
Verily, he piles the fire in the same manner as [the preceding].
He places it down with the formula, "Thou art the back of the waters.
For the lotus leaf is indeed the back of the waters.
Verily, he places it with its own form.
5.2.7 Anuvāka 7: The Laying Down of the Gold Plate and Other Items.
With the verse "The Brahman was first born," he lays down the gold plate;
for Prajāpati, having the Brahman as his mouth, created offspring.
The sacrificer creates those subjects with the Brahmin as their head;
he says, "The Brahman was born," therefore the Brahmin is preeminent.
He who knows thus becomes preeminent.
The exponents of Brahman say:
"The fire-altar is not to be built on earth, nor in the intermediate space, nor in heaven."
If one were to pile [the fire-altar] upon the earth, he would afflict the earth with pain;
neither herbs nor trees would be able to grow.

If he were to pile it in the intermediate space, he would afflict the intermediate space with pain; the birds would not procreate. If he were to pile it in the sky, he would afflict the sky with pain.
Parjanya would not send rain.
He places a gold plate; gold is indeed immortality.
Verily, he piles the fire in immortality for the sake of procreation;
he places a golden man upon it.
For the separation of the world of the sacrificer:
if one were to place [the brick] upon the perforation of the brick, one would block the breath of both the cattle and the sacrificer.
To the south...
He places it facing forward; he thus supports the world of the sacrificer.
He does not obstruct the breath of either the cattle or the sacrificer.
Then, indeed, he places a blade of grass upon the perforation of the brick for the release of the vital breaths;
he touches it with the formula, "The drop has fallen."
He establishes him in the very *hotrā* offerings;
he places two offering-spoons down:
one made of *kārṣmarya* wood, full of clarified butter, and one made of *udumbara* wood, full of curds.
This one is made of *kārṣmarya* wood, and that one is made of *udumbara* wood;
he places these very two down, and he places them down silently.
For he does not deserve to obtain with the *yajus* the sacrificial fee consisting of the northern post made of *kārṣmarya* wood;
therefore, that one is higher than this.
[He offers] a ladle made of *kārṣmarya* wood, filled with clarified butter.
Clarified butter is indeed a thunderbolt, and the *kārṣmarya* is a thunderbolt;
by means of the thunderbolt, he thus strikes away the Rakṣases from the south of the sacrifice.
A vessel made of udumbara wood filled with curds;
for curds are indeed cattle and the udumbara is vigor; thus he bestows vigor upon the cattle.
He places them when they are full;
verily, he establishes him in that world when it is full.
"Agni is to be piled upon the Virāj," they say;
in that he places two offering-spoons (sruc), he piles Agni upon the Virāj itself.
At every opening of the sacrifice, when it is being performed, the Rakṣases seek to destroy the sacrifice;
the gold plate is the opening of the sacrifice.
In that he sprinkles the gold plate with ghee, he strikes away the Rakṣases from the very opening of the sacrifice.
He sprinkles with five [ladlefuls]; the sacrifice is fivefold; as great as the sacrifice is, from that he drives away the Rakṣases.
He sprinkles transversely; therefore animals move their limbs transversely, for the sake of stability.
5.2.8 Anuvāka 8: The Installation of the *Svayamātṛṇṇā*. He places the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick.
This earth, indeed, is the *svayamātṛṇṇā*.
He places this very [brick] down;
he causes a horse to sniff it, thereby bestowing vital breath upon it.
Moreover, the horse belongs to Prajāpati;
verily, by means of Prajāpati, he piles the fire-altar.
When the first brick is being laid down, he bestows vital breath upon both the cattle and the sacrificer.
The naturally perforated stone is used for the release of the vital breaths and also for the illumination of the heavenly world.
"Fire is to be piled upon fire," they say.
This Brahmin is indeed Agni Vaiśvānara;
to him one should offer the first brick consecrated with a Yajus formula.
A Brāhmaṇa and a [non-Brāhmaṇa] should both lay it down;
thus he piles Agni in Agni itself. For he who, being ignorant, lays down a brick is liable to meet with ruin.
He should grant three boons;
for there are indeed three vital breaths,
[this serves] for the support of the vital breaths.
Only two should be given,
for there are indeed two vital breaths;
only one should be given.
For this Agni is indeed a single vital breath, or rather, a sacrificial animal.
Indeed, cattle do not delight in barren ground;
he lays down a dūrvā-brick for the support of cattle, with two verses for the sake of stability.
"Growing up from joint to joint," he says, for by means of joint after joint this plant is firmly established.
"So do thou, O Dūrvā, extend us with a thousand and a hundred," he says.
The thousandfold Prajāpati [is used] for the attainment of Prajāpati;
the three-lined [brick] is indeed the mark of the gods.
The gods placed that [brick] with the upper marks; the Asuras [placed it] with the lower marks.
Whomever one should desire—
Thinking, "May he become more prosperous," one should place for him a brick marked with upward signs;
he indeed becomes more prosperous, whomever [the priest] so desires.
Thinking, "May he become worse," one should place upon him a lower-marked [brick].
One thus causes him to follow after the womb of the Asuras; he becomes worse.
It is drawn with three lines.
These worlds, indeed, are drawn with three lines.
From these very worlds, he excludes his rival.
When the Aṅgirases were going to the heavenly world, the sacrificial cake, having become a tortoise, crawled after them.

In that he places the tortoise, just as one who knows the terrain leads straight to the goal, even so does the tortoise lead him straight to the heavenly world. The tortoise is indeed the sacrificial essence (*medha*) of animals;
in that he places the tortoise, the animals attend upon it, beholding their own sacrificial essence.
This is indeed made into a cemetery when the heads of dead animals are placed down;
in that he places a living tortoise, it is therefore not built as a cemetery. For this [tortoise] is a dweller in the homestead.
The tortoise.
With the verse, "The winds carry honey for him who observes the cosmic order," he anoints it with curds mixed with honey; thus he makes it palatable.
This food is indeed domestic, namely the curd; the wild is the honey.
When he anoints [the horse] with curd mixed with honey, it is for the attainment of both.
"May the great Heaven and Earth be favorable to us," he says.
With these two very [bricks] he encloses it on both sides;
he places them facing forward;
therefore—
From the east, the animals approach the sacrificial victim facing westward.
He who piles the fire-altar without its navel enters along the sacrificer's own navel;
it is capable of harming him.
He places the mortar down;
this indeed is the navel of Agni; verily, he piles the fire together with its navel for the sake of non-injury.
It is made of Udumbara wood;
the Udumbara is indeed strength; verily, he wins strength.
He places it in the middle;
verily, he bestows strength upon him in the middle;
therefore, they enjoy strength from the middle.
It becomes this much;
he strikes down [the earth] as measured by Prajāpati, the mouth of the sacrifice.
Verily, he makes food itself; he places it down with a verse addressed to Viṣṇu, for the sacrifice is indeed Viṣṇu.
The trees belong to Viṣṇu;
he thus establishes sacrifice upon sacrifice.
5.2.9 Anuvāka 9: The Setting Down of the Fire-pan (Ukhā) and Other Vessels.
This fire-pan is indeed the light gathered from these worlds;
when he places the fire-pan, he wins the light from these very worlds.
He places it in the middle;
verily, he bestows light upon him from the middle;
therefore, we enjoy light from the middle.
He fills it with sand;
this indeed is the form of Agni Vaiśvānara.
By means of that very form, he wins Vaiśvānara.
If one should desire,
"May he be hungry," one should place [the bricks] deficient for him.
He indeed becomes hungry,
whichever [offering] he might desire. If one should desire, "May he eat food without it failing," one should place a full [ladle] for him.
He eats food that does not perish; indeed, for every man he bestows a thousand cattle, while other cattle are [only] in thousands.
He places the human head in the middle.
For the sake of vigor;
he also places it in the fire-pan; verily, he causes it to attain a firm foundation.
This human head is indeed deprived of the vital breaths and is impure;
for the vital breaths are truly immortal.
The immortal is gold;
he throws pieces of gold into the vital breaths.
Having thus caused it to reach a firm foundation, he causes it to prosper through the vital breaths.
He fills it with curd mixed with honey, thinking,
"May I be worthy of sweetness"; and with boiled milk mixed with curd for the sake of purity.
This curd is village food, and honey is wild food;
that he fills [the cups] with curd mixed with honey is for the attainment of both.
He places the heads of animals upon them.
The animal heads are indeed cattle; verily, he wins cattle.
Whomever he may desire—
If he should be without cattle,
he should place those bricks facing in different directions;
thus he bestows cattle upon him from all sides.
He indeed becomes without cattle whom one might desire,
"May he possess cattle"; for him, one should place the bricks so that they face each other.
He bestows cattle upon him in the proper manner, and he indeed becomes possessed of cattle;
he places the horse facing westward in front, and the bull facing eastward behind.
Other animals than cattle and horses are indeed non-animals;
he thus provides him with cattle and horses facing the same way.
So many, indeed, are the animals.
Both bipeds and quadrupeds—
these he indeed places in the fire when he lays down the heads of the sacrificial animals. "I assign that one to you, the wild animal," he says.
From the domestic animals he releases distress upon the wild animals;
therefore, among animals that are born equally, the wild animals are fewer, for they have been struck by distress.
He places a serpent's head; whatever brilliance is in the serpent, that he wins.

If he were to place [the bricks] facing together with the heads of the domestic animals, the biting insects would afflict the domestic animals; if [he places them] facing away, [they would afflict] the wild animals;
therefore, he should simply recite the *yajus* formula.
He secures that brilliance which [resides] in the serpent;
it harms neither domestic animals nor wild ones.
Nevertheless, it should indeed be placed [on the fire].
In that he places [the brick], he thereby wins that brilliance which is in the serpent; in that he recites the *yajus*, it is thereby pacified.
5.2.10 Anuvāka 10: The Laying of the Apasyā Bricks, etc., in the First Layer.
This Agni is indeed an animal;
this womb of the animal is indeed fashioned when the sacrificial formula (yajus) is performed prior to the brick-laying.
The *apasyā* bricks are seed;
he places the *apasyā* bricks;
verily, he places seed in the womb.
He offers five; cattle are fivefold; verily he procreates cattle for him.
There are five on the south;
the waters are indeed a thunderbolt.
By means of the thunderbolt itself, he repels the Rakṣases from the south of the sacrifice.
He places five bricks facing eastward at the back;
for from behind, seed is deposited facing forward.
Thereafter, he places for him the seed facing eastward;
he places five bricks facing westward in front and five facing eastward behind.
Therefore, the seed is placed facing eastward, and offspring are born facing westward.
Five more than that are metrical;
the metrical are indeed cattle;
verily, he piles them around their own abode, [the cattle] already born.
This [earth], indeed, was afraid of being over-burnt by Agni;
she saw these *apasyā* bricks.
He laid them down;
therefore he did not burn this [earth] excessively.
In that he lays down the *apasyā* bricks, it is for the sake of preventing the excessive burning of this [earth].
He said,
"He who has these [bricks] laid down for him, and he who knows them thus, shall eat food with the Brahman. He lays down the Prāṇabhṛt bricks.
Verily, he bestows the vital breaths upon the *retas*;
therefore, an animal is born already endowed with speech, breathing, seeing, and hearing.
This is the first [verse].
With "Bhuvaḥ," he places one in front;
by these [bricks], he indeed sustains the vital breath.
With "Ayaṃ dakṣiṇā viśvakarmā," he places one on the south.
By these [verses], he supported the mind;
with "This one behind, all-encompassing," he supported it from behind;
by these [verses], he supported the eye.
"This is the light from the north," he says toward the north;
by these [verses], he supports the ear.
"This is the thought above," he says from above.
By means of these [bricks], he supports speech itself;
he places them ten by ten for the sake of possessing full vigor; [he places them] crosswise.
He places them on; therefore animals move their limbs crosswise, for the sake of stability.
With those that flow eastward Vasiṣṭha prospered; with those that flow southward Bharadvāja;
with those that flow westward Viśvāmitra.
With those that go northward, Jamadagni;
with those that go upward, Viśvakarman.
He who thus knows the prosperity of these [rays] indeed prospers.
He who thus knows their kinship becomes possessed of kin;
he who thus knows their arrangement finds success.
He who thus knows their abode becomes possessed of an abode; he who thus knows their foundation becomes firmly established.
Having laid down the Prāṇabhṛt bricks, he lays down the Saṃyata bricks.
Having placed the vital breaths within him, he unites them with the *saṃyats* (unifying powers); that is the reason for the name of the *saṃyats*.
Moreover, he thereby places the out-breath (*apāna*) within the in-breath (*prāṇa*).
Therefore, the out-breath and the in-breath move together.
He lays down the bricks facing in different directions;
therefore, the out-breath and the in-breath move in different directions.
Or rather, whatever of Agni’s is unrestrained and does not lead to heaven— that belongs to this [Agni],
for this Agni leads to heaven.
In that he lays them down while restrained, he restrains him; he indeed makes him one who attains the heavenly world.
"The three-year-old is the vigor of the Ayus," he says;
verily, by means of the vital forces, he wins the Ayus.
By means of iron,
they become wind-possessing on all sides; therefore, this [wind] blows from all sides.

5.2.11 Anuvāka 11: The Carving of the Path with Needles May the Gāyatrī, Triṣṭubh, Jagatī, Anuṣṭubh, along with the Paṅkti, the Bṛhatī, Uṣṇihā, and Kakubh—may these, by means of needles, stitch you together. May those that are two-footed, those that are four-footed, those that are three-footed, and those that are six-footed; may those with regular meters and those with irregular meters—by means of needles, stitch you together. May the Mahānāmnīs, the Revatīs, all the quarters that bring forth, the pure lightnings, and the words—by means of needles, stitch you together. The silver ones, the golden ones, and the lead ones are yoked as yokes for the rites.
Let the women stitch you with needles upon the skin of the swift horse.
Let those wives arrange the hair with their wisdom; let the quarters, the wives of the gods, stitch you together with needles.
Surely, just as those possessing barley reap the grain in due order, separating it out, so bring hither the food of those who have not come to the trimming of the sacred grass with their homage.

5.2.12 Anuvāka 12: The Description of the Dissection Who flays you? Who dissects you? Who carves your limbs? And who is your wise immolator? May the Seasons, as your immolators, dissect your joints according to the seasons. May they carve you with the nourishment of the year and with their skillful arts. May the divine Adhvaryu priests flay you and dissect you. Carving your limbs joint by joint, may they perform the work of immolation with skill. May the half-months and the months, performing the immolation, carve your joints. May the Days and Nights and the Maruts prepare whatever in you is disjointed.

May the earth with the intermediate space, and Vāyu, heal your wound; may the sky together with the stars fashion your form perfectly. May there be well-being for your upper limbs, may there be well-being for your lower limbs; may there be well-being for your bones and marrow, and may there be well-being for your body.
5.3 Prapāṭhaka: 3, Anuvāka 1. 5.3.1 Designation of the four bricks, beginning with the Aśvinī, belonging to the second layer:
"This Agni is indeed a ruined sacrifice;
what part of it is performed, and what part is not?"
Whatever part of the sacrifice being performed they omit, that part of it indeed becomes putrid.
He lays down the Ashvini bricks;
the Ashvins are indeed the physicians of the gods.
With those very two he prepares a remedy for him;
he places five [bricks] down, for the sacrifice is fivefold.
To whatever extent the sacrifice extends, for that much he provides a remedy.
He places the seasonal bricks;
this is for the proper ordering of the seasons.
He offers five;
for there are five seasons— just as many as the seasons are.
He arranges them so that they have the same beginning and the same conclusion;
therefore, the seasons are identical.
By means of a single foot they turn back;
therefore the seasons turn back.
He places the Prāṇabhṛts.
Verily, he places the vital breaths in the seasons; therefore, though they are alike, the seasons do not decay.
Moreover, he causes them to be born forth.
This breath is indeed Vāyu;
because he places the Prāṇabhṛts after having placed the Ṛtavyās,
therefore Vāyu revolves throughout all the seasons.
He places [the bricks] that win rain;
verily he wins rain. If he were to place them all at once, it would rain for only one season. He settles them by moving around [the altar]; therefore it rains during all the seasons.
In that he places the *vṛṣṭisani* bricks after having placed the *prāṇabhṛt* bricks, therefore rain, impelled by Vāyu, flows down from heaven.
The *vayasyā* bricks are indeed cattle;
cattle have different minds and different ways of acting, yet they are of one mind toward water alone.
If one should desire,
"May he be without cattle," one should place the vayasyā bricks after laying down the apasyā bricks for him; thus one brings about a lack of harmony with his cattle,
and he indeed becomes without cattle.
If he should desire,
"May he possess cattle," he should place the *apasyā* bricks for him and then place the *vayasyā* bricks; thus he brings about recognition for him by means of cattle,
and he indeed becomes possessed of cattle.
He places four in front;
therefore there are four forms of the eye: two white and two black.
They possess a head;
therefore, the head is in front.
He places five [bricks] on the southern hip and five on the northern one; therefore, an animal is broader behind and slopes forward.
With the words, "The ram is our vigor," he places [a brick] on the right shoulder; with the words, "The bull is our vigor," on the left shoulder;
thus he restores the two shoulders.
With the words, "The tiger is our vigor," he places [a brick] on the right wing; with the words, "The lion is our vigor," on the left.
A man bestows vigor upon the two wings, while the bird places its strength in the middle; therefore, man is the lord of animals.
5.3.2 Anuvāka 2: Designation of the *svayamātṛṇṇā* and others.
With the verse, "O Indra and Agni, [place] the unshaking one," he places the *svayamātṛṇṇā*.
Indeed, these two worlds are held apart by Indra and Agni.
For the separation of these two worlds.
This middle layer is, as it were, unsupported;
it is, as it were, the intermediate space.
"O Indra and Agni," he says. Indra and Agni are indeed the upholders of vigor among the gods;
by means of vigor itself, he piles her in the intermediate space.
He places the naturally perforated brick for support;
the naturally perforated brick is indeed the intermediate space.
He thus places the intermediate space itself;
he causes the horse to smell it.
He bestows vital breath upon this [earth];
moreover, since the horse belongs to Prajāpati, he piles the fire-altar by means of Prajāpati himself.
It is naturally perforated for the release of the vital breaths;
furthermore, it is for the illumination of the heavenly world.
When the gods were going to the heavenly world, the quarters collapsed; they saw these regional bricks (diśyās) and laid them down.
By means of them, they indeed made firm the quarters;
in that he lays down the regional bricks, it is for the support of the quarters.
Ten breath-bearers [are placed] in front, facing toward [the center].
He places [the bricks]; there are indeed nine vital breaths in a person, and the navel is the tenth;
thus he places the vital breaths in front.
Therefore, the vital breaths are in front.
He places the Jyotiṣmatī brick last;
therefore, among the vital breaths, speech is the light that is highest.
He places ten [bricks];
the Virāj consists of ten syllables; it is the light among the meters.
He places light itself in the east; therefore we behold light from the east. The meters ran a race for the cattle; the Bṛhatī won them. Therefore cattle are said to belong to the Bṛhatī.
"The Mā metre," he says, as he places it on the south; therefore the months turn toward the south.
"Earth is the desire," he says at the back, for stability.
"Agni is the deity," he says on the north; Agni is indeed vigor; verily, he bestows vigor on the north. Therefore, one who advances toward the north conquers.
They amount to thirty-six.
The Bṛhatī consists of thirty-six syllables;
cattle are related to the Bṛhatī.
By means of the Bṛhatī, he wins cattle for him.
The Bṛhatī has attained sovereignty over the meters;
he for whom these are laid down attains sovereignty.
He places seven Vālakhilya bricks in front and seven behind.
There are indeed seven vital breaths in the head and two directed downwards; [he does this] for the sake of providing strength to the vital breaths.
With the words, "Thou art the head, the ruler," he places one in front; with the words, "The controller, the ruler," he places one behind.
Verily, he bestows the vital breaths upon him in their proper order.
5.3.3 Anuvāka 3: The Designation of the Akṣṇayāstomīya and Other Chants.
Whatever the gods did at the sacrifice, the Asuras did that too.
Those gods then perceived these Akṣṇayāstomīya chants.
They recited them in one way and laid them down in another;
the Asuras did not follow that, and consequently the gods prevailed while the Asuras were defeated.
In that he lays down the Akṣṇayāstomīya bricks differently from how they are recited, it serves for the overcoming of his rival; he prospers in himself and his rival is defeated.
"The swift Trivṛt," he says, and thus he lays them down in front.
The Trivṛt is indeed the mouth of the sacrifice;
thus he extends the very mouth of the sacrifice in front.
"The sky is the seventeenfold" [he says] from the south.
Food indeed is space;
food is the seventeenfold [stoma].
Verily, he places food on the right side.
Therefore, food is eaten with the right hand;
[the verse says] "the twenty-onefold is the support," for the twenty-onefold is indeed a foundation,
[serving] for the sake of stability.
The Bhānta-stoma consists of fifteen verses; thus on the north side.
Indeed, the Bhānta is vigor, and the fifteenfold stoma is vigor.
He bestows vital essence (*ojas*) from the north;
therefore, one who advances toward the north conquers.
With the words "The onset, eighteenfold," he places it in the east.
He places two threefold [bricks] one after the other at the beginning of the sacrifice;
[the brick] called Abhivarta, consisting of twenty [syllables], he places on the south side.
Food is the *abhivarta*;
food is the *saviṃśa*.
Verily, he places food on the right side.
Therefore, food is eaten with the right hand; "splendor is the twenty-second" refers to the west.
Since there are twenty [syllables] plus two, they thus constitute two *virāj* verses.
In that there are two foundations,
he thereby establishes himself successively in the food-eating power of the Virāj;
"Heat is nineteenfold," [he says] from the north.
Therefore, of the two hands, the left is more ascetic;
he places it in front with the words, "The womb is the twenty-fourth."
The Gāyatrī consists of twenty-four syllables;
the Gāyatrī is the mouth of the sacrifice.
Verily, he extends the mouth of the sacrifice at the beginning.
"The embryos are the twenty-fivefold," [he says] on the south side.
The embryos are indeed food;
the twenty-fivefold is food.
He places food on the right;
therefore food is eaten with the right hand.
"The twenty-sevenfold is vigor," [he says] at the back.
These worlds indeed are the twenty-sevenfold;
he finds firm support in these very worlds.
The twenty-threefold is the gathering.
Therefore, the left hand is more to be honored than the right;
with the words, "The thirty-onefold sacrifice," he places it down in front.
Speech is indeed resolve;
speech is the mouth of the sacrifice.
Thus, he extends the mouth of the sacrifice from the front.
"The thirty-four-fold [stoma] is the summit of the radiant one," he says on the south.
Yonder sun, indeed, is the summit of the radiant one; verily, he bestows spiritual luster upon the south.
Therefore, the southern half is more endowed with spiritual luster (brahmavarcas).
