"The thirty-threefold is the foundation," [he says] at the back, for the sake of stability. "The thirty-sixfold is the firmament (nāka)," [he says] on the north; the firmament is indeed the world of heaven, for the attainment of the world of heaven.
5.3.4 Anuvāka 4: The designation of the Akṣṇayāstomīya and other bricks.
"Thou art the portion of Agni," with these words he places [the brick] in front;
for Agni is indeed the mouth of the sacrifice.
Initiation is the mouth of the sacrifice;
the sacred word is the mouth of the sacrifice;
the Trivṛt is the mouth of the sacrifice.
He extends the very mouth of the sacrifice in the east;
with the words, "Thou art the portion of those who look upon men," he extends it in the south—
for those who have heard [the Vedas] are indeed "those who look upon men."
"The Ordainer [bestows] food upon him as soon as he is born; therefore, once born, he eats food. 'The birthplace is secured, the seventeenfold hymn-form,' he says; for the birthplace is indeed food."
Food is the seventeenth;
he thus places food on the right side,
and therefore food is eaten with the right hand.
With the words, "Thou art the portion of Mitra," [he places it] behind;
Mitra is indeed the out-breath (prāṇa) and Varuṇa is the in-breath (apāna);
thus he bestows both out-breath and in-breath upon him.
"Rain from heaven, winds won over, the twenty-onefold hymn-form," he says;
for the twenty-onefold is a firm foundation,
[and this serves] for stability.
"Thou art the portion of Indra," [he says] on the north. 1. Indra is vigor; 2. Viṣṇu is vigor; 3. the kṣatra is vigor; 4. the fifteenfold [stoma] is vigor.
He bestows vital essence (ojas) from the north;
therefore, one who advances toward the north conquers.
With the words, "Thou art the portion of the Vasus," he places [the brick] in the east.
The Vasus are indeed the mouth of the sacrifice;
the Rudras are the mouth of the sacrifice;
the Caturviṃśa is the mouth of the sacrifice.
He extends the very mouth of the sacrifice in the east.
With the words, "Thou art the portion of the Ādityas," [he extends it] in the south;
for the Ādityas are indeed food.
1. Food, O Maruts; 2. food, the embryos; 3. food, the twenty-fivefold [sacrifice]. 4. He places food on the right side; therefore, food is eaten with the right hand. 5. It is the portion for Aditi.
Eighty [bricks] come after;
Aditi is indeed the foundation, and Pūṣan is the foundation.
The *triṇava* [stoma] is the foundation for the sake of stability; "Thou art the portion of the god Savitṛ," [he says] as he places it to the north.
The god Savitṛ is indeed Brahman; Bṛhaspati is Brahman;
the Catuṣṭoma is Brahman.

Verily, he bestows spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) on the north; therefore, the northern half is more endowed with spiritual luster. It contains the verse addressed to Savitṛ for the sake of impulsion; therefore, the gain of the Brāhmaṇas is impelled toward the north. He places the *dhartra* brick called "the fourfold stoma" in front; for the *dhartra* is indeed the mouth of the sacrifice.
The Catuṣṭoma is the mouth of the sacrifice;
he thus extends the very mouth of the sacrifice from the front with [the formula],
"Thou art the portion of the Yāvānas."
To the south.
The *yāva*s are indeed the months and the *ayāva*s are the half-months;
therefore the months turn toward the south.
The Yavyās are indeed food;
offspring are food.
Thus, he places food on the right side.

Therefore, food is eaten with the right hand. With the words, "Thou art the portion of the Ṛbhus," he places [the cake] behind for stability. With the words, "The turning is the forty-eightfold," he places it on the north for the sake of these two worlds having equal vigor; therefore, these two worlds are of equal vigor.
He for whom the *mukhyavatī* bricks are laid down in the east becomes preeminent;
a preeminent son is born to him.
He for whom the *annavatī* bricks are laid down in the south eats food.
From his mouth food is produced;
he for whom they are well-established stands firm behind him;
he for whom they are vigorous becomes vigorous from the north.
He is born vigorous.
This Agni is indeed the sun;
this [offering] is his very hymn of praise (stotra) and this is his recitation (śastra).
This is its classification.

The sun alone is ordained; after that, the *arkya* is ordained. He who possesses this ordinance ordained for him eats food, becomes an eater of food, and is born [again]; and so too for him who knows it thus.
He places the *sṛṣṭi*-bricks.
Verily, he obtains it exactly as it was created.
Indeed, this world was neither day nor night; it was undifferentiated.
Those gods saw these dawns (vyuṣṭis).
They laid them down;
from that, indeed, this world was illumined.
For whomsoever these are laid down, for him it becomes illumined.
Then indeed, darkness is dispelled.
5.3.5 Anuvāka 5: The Description of the Bricks Named *asapatnavirāj*.
With the mantra, "O Agni, drive away our born enemies," he places [the bricks] in the east;
thus, he drives away his born rivals.
[He recites] "Those born by force" later;
[he recites] "The forty-fourfold hymn-form" on the south side, driving away those very ones yet to be born.
The forty-fourfold [stoma] is indeed spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*). He places spiritual luster on the right side; therefore, the right half is more endowed with spiritual luster.
"The sixteenfold hymn-form" [is recited] on the north; the sixteenfold is indeed vigor;
verily, he bestows vigor on the north.
Therefore,
he who advances from the north is victorious;
for the forty-fourfold [stoma] is indeed a thunderbolt, and the sixteenfold is a thunderbolt.
In that he lays down these two bricks, having driven away both his born and his yet-to-be-born rivals, he hurls the thunderbolt after them for their destruction;
he lays down the one containing loose earth in the middle.
Excrement indeed is the middle of the self;
he who knows this piles the fire with its own self, and he becomes possessed of his own self in yonder world.
These indeed are the bricks named "Without Rivals.
For whomsoever these are laid down,
no rival exists for him.
This Agni is indeed a beast;
he places the Virāj bricks on the uppermost layer; verily, he bestows the Virāj as the highest upon the cattle.
Therefore, one who possesses cattle speaks the most excellent speech.
He places them down ten by ten for the sake of possessing strength;
he places them down transversely.
Therefore, they offer the limbs crosswise for the sake of stability.
Those meters which were conducive to heaven, by means of them the gods went to the heavenly world; by them the seers [did so].
They exerted themselves; they performed austerities;
through austerity, they perceived those [truths].
For them, these bricks were produced:
"The *nirvaś* metre, the *varivaś* metre"—
with these words they laid them down.
By means of them indeed those [ancient seers] went to the heavenly world; when he lays down these bricks,
the sacrificer goes to the heavenly world by means of those very meters which lead to the heavenly world.
By means of sacrifice, Prajāpati indeed created offspring;
he created them by means of the *stomabhāga* verses.
He lays down the *stomabhāgā* bricks; thereby the sacrificer creates progeny.
Bṛhaspati indeed gathered together that brilliance of the sacrifice which is the *stomabhāgā*s.
In that he lays down the *stomabhāgā*s, he piles the fire-altar with its brilliance.
Bṛhaspati indeed perceived this foundation of the sacrifice, which is the Stomabhāgas. In that he lays down the Stomabhāgas, it is for the stability of the sacrifice.
He lays them down seven by seven for the sake of possessing strength.
Three in the middle for the sake of stability.
5.3.6 Anuvāka 6: Designation of the Bricks called Stomabhāgās. With "The Ray" he created the sun; with "The Impulse," the dharma.
"Anviti" is the sky;
"saṃdhi" is the intermediate space;
"pratidhi" is the earth.
"Obstruction": it follows the rain during the day and follows the night.
"Uśij" refers to the Vasus;
"Praketa" refers to the Rudras;
"Sudīti" refers to the Ādityas.
"Ojas" refers to the ancestors;
"tantu" refers to offspring;
"pṛtanāṣāṭ" refers to livestock.
With "Rich indeed are the plants!
You are the victorious one; the pressing-stones are yoked for Indra; for you, for Indra, quicken Indra!"—thus from the south he moved the thunderbolt around for the sake of victory.
He created those creatures without breath; [with the words] "Thou art the overlord," he bestowed breath upon them;
[with the word] "Restrain," he bestowed out-breath.
"Saṃsarpa" is the eye;
"Vayodhā" is the ear.
Those creatures—breathing out and breathing in, seeing and hearing—did not enter into union.
Into them he placed a pair with the words, "Thou art threefold," yet those creatures, though becoming paired, did not procreate.
With the words, "Thou art growth; thou art non-decay," he generated those creatures.
Those creatures, once generated, did not find firm support.
With the words, "Thou art Vasu; thou art Veṣaśrī; thou art Vasyaṣṭi," he established them firmly in these worlds.
When he says,
"Thou art Vasu, thou art the glory of the raiment, thou art the attainment of wealth," he establishes progeny already born in these worlds;
with his self, he ascends to the intermediate region.
Endowed with breath, he finds firm standing in yonder world;
he becomes one who does not fail in his out-breath and in-breath, he who knows thus.

5.3.7 Anuvāka 7: Designation of the Five Kinds of Bricks, beginning with the *nākasad*. By means of the *nākasad* bricks, the gods went to the heavenly world; that is the reason for the *nākasad* nature of the *nākasad* bricks.
In that he lays down the *nākasad* bricks, the sacrificer goes to the heavenly world by means of the *nākasad*s themselves; for the heavenly world is indeed the *nāka*.
For him for whom these are laid down, there is no suffering (*aka*).
The Nākasads are indeed the sacrificial station of the sacrificer.
In that he lays down the Nākasads, the sacrificer thereby prepares his own station.
The Nākasads are the concentrated splendor of the Pṛṣṭha-stotras.
In that he places the nākasads, he wins the splendor of the pṛṣṭhas; he places the five-coiled ones.
These Apsarases, having become these [bricks], lie down by him in yonder world.
Moreover, they are the protectors of the body for the sacrificer;
while laying them down, he should meditate upon whomsoever he hates.
Verily, he cuts him away from these very deities;
swiftly he meets with ruin.
He places the subsequent bricks upon the *nākasad* bricks.
Just as one brings his wife and seats her in the house, such indeed is that.
Thereafter, he places the last brick facing eastward; therefore, from behind, the wife sits facing eastward.
He places the *svayamātṛṇṇā* and the *vikarṇī* as the two uppermost bricks;
for the *svayamātṛṇṇā* is indeed breath, and the *vikarṇī* is life-span.
He bestows both breath and life, the two highest among the vital breaths;
therefore, breath and life are the two highest among the vital breaths.
One should not place any other brick above them.
If one were to place another brick above it, one would place [an obstruction] upon the breath and the life-span of both the cattle and the sacrificer;
therefore, no other brick should be placed above it.
He places the naturally perforated brick. That naturally perforated brick is indeed yonder sky; verily he places yonder sky.
He causes a horse to smell it; verily he bestows vital breath upon it.

Moreover, the horse belongs to Prajāpati; verily, by means of Prajāpati he piles the fire-altar. There is a naturally perforated brick for the release of the vital breaths, and also for the illumination of the world of heaven.
The Vikarṇī brick is indeed the stride of the gods.
In that he lays down the *vikarṇī*, he strides forth following the stride of the gods.
He lays it down on the north;
therefore Agni has his service performed from the north.
The verse containing the word "vāyu" is used for the purpose of kindling.
5.3.8 Anuvāka 8: Designation of the Bricks Representing the Metres. He lays down the metres;
the metres, indeed, are cattle.
Verily, he wins cattle;
for the meters are the desirable wealth of the gods, and cattle are desirable wealth; verily, he wins desirable wealth, namely cattle.
Yajñasena Caitriyāyaṇa indeed discovered this layer; by means of it, he won cattle.
In that one lays down this [layer], one wins cattle.
He places the Gāyatrīs in front;
the Gāyatrī is indeed splendor— verily, splendor itself.
He wears them on his face;
they become possessed of heads; verily he makes him the head of his peers.
He places [bricks] in the *triṣṭubh* meter; the *triṣṭubh* is indeed power; verily, he bestows power in the middle.
He places the Jagatī bricks; cattle are indeed connected with the Jagatī; verily, he wins cattle.
He places them with *anuṣṭubh* verses; for the vital breaths are indeed *anuṣṭubhs*, [he does so] for the release of the vital breaths.
He lays down the *bṛhatī*, the *uṣṇih*, the *paṅkti*, and the *akṣarapaṅkti*— these are the meters of diverse forms;
for cattle are of diverse forms, and cattle are indeed [the bricks].
By means of the *chandāṃsi*,
he wins cattle of various forms;
in the house of him for whom these are laid down, and for him who knows them thus, cattle of various forms are seen.
He places the Aticchandas [verse] upon it;
for the Aticchandas indeed comprises all the meters; thus he piles it with all the meters.
The Atichandas is indeed the summit of the meters;
in that he lays down an Atichandas brick, he makes him the summit among his equals.
He lays them down with two-footed verses.
The sacrificer has two feet for the sake of stability.
5.3.9 Anuvāka 9: Designation of the Three Sayugvat Bricks.
Agni is piled for all the deities;
if one were not to lay down the sayugvat bricks, the deities would exclude him from the fire-altar.
In that he lays down the *sayuj* bricks, he piles him together with his own self as a companion; he is not deprived of the fire-altar.
Moreover, just as a man is held together by his sinews, even so is the fire-altar held together by these bricks.
By means of the fire, the gods went to the heavenly world; they became those Kṛttikās.
He for whom these are laid down goes indeed to the heavenly world; he goes to the light and becomes truly manifold.
He places the maṇḍala-bricks.
These worlds indeed are the maṇḍala-bricks;
these worlds, indeed, are the fortresses of the gods.
He who has piled the fire enters the very city of the gods; he does not suffer distress.
He places the Viśvajyotis bricks.
By means of these, he makes these worlds possessed of light;
moreover, he thereby sustains the vital breaths of the sacrificer.
These indeed are the deities that lead to heaven;
by taking hold of them, he goes to the heavenly world.
5.3.10 Anuvāka 10: Description of the Five Bricks for Obtaining Rain.
He lays down the bricks for obtaining rain;
verily, he wins rain.
If he were to set it down in one place, it would rain for only one season;
he sets it down while moving around it, therefore it rains during all the seasons.
"Thou art the precursor of the east wind," he says.
This indeed is the form of rain;
by its very form he wins rain.
By means of the Saṃyānī verses, the gods went together to these worlds.
That is why they are called *saṃyānīs*.
In that he lays down the *saṃyānīs*, it is just as one travels across the waters by boat;
even so does the sacrificer travel across these worlds by means of them.
The *saṃyānī* bricks are indeed a raft for Agni.
In that he lays down the *saṃyānī*s, he provides this very raft for Agni.
Moreover, even if the waters carry away his fire when these have been laid down, his fire remains uncarried away.
He places the Āditya bricks.
Indeed, the Ādityas push away from prosperity that man who, though capable of prosperity, does not attain it;
[they are] the Ādityas.
Thus they cause him to attain prosperity.
Indeed, the sun takes away the luster of one who, having piled the fire-altar, does not shine;
in that he lays down the Āditya-bricks, the sun itself bestows luster upon him.
Just as he is pleasing to the gods, even so is he pleasing to human beings.
He lays down the ghee-bricks. Ghee, indeed, is the beloved abode of Agni; verily, he causes him to prosper with his own beloved abode.
Then he places it around with splendor; thus he bestows splendor upon it without leaving any part excluded.
Prajāpati piled the fire-altar; he was deprived of glory. He saw these [bricks] that bestow glory.
He deposited them;
by means of them, he indeed placed glory within himself. In that he deposits these "glory-bestowing" bricks, the sacrificer places glory within himself by means of them.
He places five; man is fivefold.
As great as man is, in him he bestows glory.
5.3.11 Anuvāka 11: Designation of the Six Bricks Beginning with the Bhūyaskṛt.
The gods and the asuras were engaged in conflict; the gods were fewer, and the asuras were more numerous.
Those gods saw these bricks;
they laid them down with the formula, "Thou art the maker of abundance," and thus they became more abundant through trees and plants.
With "Thou art the one who honors," they conquered this [earth]; with "Thou art the eastern," they conquered the eastern quarter;
with "Thou art the upward," they conquered yonder [sky].
"You are the one who sits in the intermediate space; sit in the intermediate space!"—thus they conquered the intermediate space; then the gods prospered and the Asuras were defeated.
He for whom these are laid down becomes truly greater;
he conquers these worlds, he prospers in his own person, and his rival is defeated.
"You are seated in the waters; you are seated in the falcon," he says.
This, indeed, is the form of Agni.
By means of this very form, he wins Agni.
"I set you down in the wealth of the earth," he says;
by these [verses], he makes these very worlds possessed of wealth.
He places the life-bestowing bricks;
verily, he bestows life upon him.
"O Agni, that which is your supreme heart-name," he says;
this indeed is the dear abode of Agni; verily, he attains his dear abode.
"Come, let us two clasp hands," he says;
verily, he thus girds him about.
"Be present among the five peoples, O Agni," he says.
This Agni, indeed, belongs to the five peoples—he who consists of five layers;
therefore he speaks thus.
He places the seasonal bricks. The seasonal bricks are indeed the dear abode of the seasons;
verily, he wins the dear abode of the seasons.
"Well-established," he says; the well-established is indeed the year;
verily, he attains the dear abode of the year.
5.3.12 Anuvāka 12: The Ritual of the Horse Sacrifice (Aśvamedha).
The eye of Prajāpati swelled;
it fell away.
That became the horse;
because it moved (*aśvayat*), that is the etymological origin of the horse's name (*aśvatva*).
The gods restored that [power] by means of the Aśvamedha sacrifice itself.
He who performs the Aśvamedha sacrifice indeed makes Prajāpati whole; he himself becomes everything,
for this is the expiation for everything and the remedy for everything.
By means of this, the gods crossed over all evil; indeed,
by means of this, they even crossed over the murder of a Brahmin—
over every evil.
He who performs the horse sacrifice and he who knows this thus both cross over and overcome even the murder of a Brahmin.
That eye of Prajāpati swelled upward;
therefore they cut portions from the horse on the left side, but from the right side of other animals.
The mat is made of reeds;
for the horse has its origin in water,
and the reed is born from water.
He establishes him in his very own womb;
the Stoma is the Catuṣṭoma, for the horse indeed tore out its own thigh-bone.
The gods restored it by means of the Catuṣṭoma itself;
in that the Stoma is the Catuṣṭoma, it is for the sake of the horse's wholeness.
5.4 Prapāṭhaka: 4, Anuvāka 1:
The gods and the Asuras were engaged in conflict; they did not achieve victory.
He, Indra, saw these bodies;
he deposited them,
and by means of them, he placed within himself his own body, sensory power, and vigor.
Thereupon the gods prevailed and the asuras were defeated.
In that he lays down the body of Indra, the sacrificer thereby bestows upon himself body, sensory power, and vigor. Moreover, he builds the fire-altar with Indra and with a body.
He prospers in himself, while his rival is defeated;
for the sacrifice had departed from the gods.
They were unable to restrain him; they saw these sacrificial bodies and deposited them.
By means of them, they indeed secured the sacrifice;
in that he lays down the bodies of the sacrifice, the sacrificer secures the sacrifice itself by means of them.
He lays down thirty-three.
There are indeed thirty-three deities;
verily, he wins the deities themselves.
Moreover, he piles the Agni with its own body and its limbs.
He who knows this becomes possessed of a self in that world.
He places the *jyotiṣmatī* bricks; verily he bestows light upon him.
By means of these, indeed, the piled fire blazes.
With those very [verses] he kindles him;
light comes to him in both worlds.
He lays down the star-bricks;
these indeed are the lights of heaven;
verily, he wins them.
The stars are indeed the lights of those who have performed good deeds;
he attains them.
Moreover, these serve as a mirror for him.
He makes lights for the purpose of illuminating the world of heaven.
If he were to lay them down touching one another, he would enclose the space for rain; Parjanya would not rain.
He lays them down without touching one another; thus he creates the space for rain, and Parjanya becomes a rain-giver.
He places some in front facing westward, and others behind facing eastward;
therefore the constellations revolve both eastward and westward.
5.4.2 Anuvāka 2: Description of the sprinkling of the three *ṛtavyā* bricks and others.
He lays down the *ṛtavyā* bricks for the proper arrangement of the seasons.
He places them in pairs; therefore the seasons are in pairs.
This middle layer, indeed, is as if unstable.
This [layer] is like the intermediate space;
he places the pairs in the other layers, but four in the middle for the sake of stability.
These seasonal bricks (ṛtavyā) are indeed the internal cement of the layers.
In that he lays down the seasonal bricks, it is for the separation of the layers. He places an Avakā plant upon them;
this, indeed, is the womb of Agni.
One who knows thus piles the fire-altar.
Viśvāmitra indeed said this.

"Verily, he shall have food through the sacred word (brahman) for whom these [bricks] are laid down, and also for him who knows them thus. Indeed, the year pushes away from its foundation that man who, having piled the fire-altar, does not find a firm footing.
There are five previous layers; then he piles the sixth layer.
The year consists of six seasons;
verily, he finds support in the seasons, in the year.
These indeed...
These bricks are called *adhipatnī*.
He for whom these are laid down becomes the sovereign (*adhipati*) among his equals.
While laying them down, he should meditate upon whomsoever he hates.
Verily, he cuts him away from these very deities;
swiftly he meets with ruin.
When the Aṅgirases were going to the world of heaven, they pushed back to the seers that which was the expiation of the sacrifice.
That became gold.
In that he sprinkles with chips of gold, it is for the restoration of the sacrifice;
moreover, he thereby provides a remedy for him.
Thus he endows him with form;
and indeed, by means of the golden light, he goes to the heavenly world.
He sprinkles [the horse] with that which possesses a thousandfold power.
Prajāpati is thousandfold;
[this serves] for the attainment of Prajāpati.
"O Agni, may these bricks of mine be milch-cows," he says.
Verily, he makes them into milch-cows; as such, they stand by him as wish-fulfilling cows in yonder world.
5.4.3 Anuvāka 3: Designation of the Śatarudrīya Oblation.
Agni, indeed, is Rudra; he is born at this time when he has been completely piled.
Just as a newborn calf seeks its mother's udder, so does he now seek his portion.
If one were not to offer an oblation to him, it would consume both the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer. Therefore, he offers the Śatarudrīya.
Verily, by means of their own portion he pacifies him;
neither the Adhvaryu nor the sacrificer suffers distress,
provided [he uses] those belonging to domestic animals.

One should offer oblations with milk; [if one does so], one brings calamity upon domestic animals. If [one offers] with the grain-gruel of wild sesame or the grain-gruel of *gavīdhuka*, [one brings calamity] upon wild animals. One should offer either with wild sesame gruel or with *gavīdhuka* gruel.
He does not harm domestic animals nor wild animals;
moreover, they say:
"Indeed, jartila seeds and gavīdhuka grains are not [proper] oblations."
He offers with goat's milk.
For the goat belongs to Agni;
thus he offers by means of an oblation itself.
He does not harm domestic animals, nor those of the forest.
When the Aṅgirases were going to the heavenly world, they poured the Gharma into a goat;
she, burning with heat, cast off her leaf.
He became the *arka*;
that is the essence of the *arka*'s name as *arka*.
One offers with an *arka* leaf for the sake of providing a common origin.
Standing facing north, he offers the oblation;
for this is Rudra’s own quarter, and thus he propitiates Rudra in his own direction.
He offers on the final brick;
thus he propitiates Rudra at the very end.
He offers it divided into three parts.
These are the three worlds;
he makes these very worlds equal in vigor.
He offers at this [point] in front.
"He cools it, he cools it"— these are three worlds;
from these very worlds he pacifies it.
He offers three additional oblations;
they amount to six,
for there are six seasons.
Verily, he pacifies him by means of the seasons.
If he were to offer the oblations while moving around [the fire] in succession, he would make Rudra a wanderer within [the sacrifice].
Moreover, they say:
"In which direction is Rudra, or in which?"—
one should offer while walking around; thus one pacifies him completely, leaving nothing out.
These deities are indeed heavenly; those which are the last,
he makes the sacrificer recite for them,
and by means of them he causes him to go to the heavenly world.
One should set down the animals upon the path of him whom one hates;
whichever animal is the first to step upon it meets with misfortune.
5.4.4 Anuvāka 4: Description of the sprinkling and other rites.
With the verse, "Strength in the stone," he sprinkles around;
he thus purifies him.
Moreover, he indeed satisfies him; satisfied, not hungering, and not grieving, he stands near in yonder world.
He who knows this is satisfied with offspring and cattle.
"O Maruts, being well-disposed, bestow upon us that food and strength," he says;
for food is indeed strength, and the Maruts are food.
Verily, he wins food.
Hunger is yours; thirst is yours.
So-and-so is yours. Śuk.
"May he reach him whom we hate," he says;
verily, he afflicts with hunger and with pain that one whom he hates.
He goes around sprinkling three times.
Agni is indeed threefold;
as great as Agni is, he pacifies his impurity by going around him three times again.
They amount to six; for there are six seasons.
Verily, by means of the seasons, he pacifies his affliction.
The cane is indeed the flower of the waters;
the *śara* reeds and the *avakā* plants are the waters.
He sweeps it away with a branch of the *vetasa* reed and with *avakā* plants;
water is indeed peaceful, and by means of these peaceful things, he pacifies his impurity.
Whosoever, as the first, steps upon the piled fire-altar, is liable to be consumed by its heat;
he draws [the altar] away with a frog,
for this is the animal among animals that cannot be lived upon.
This [sacrificial animal] is neither placed among domestic animals nor among wild ones; he consigns it to sorrow alone.
He ploughs with eight [oxen].
The Gāyatrī has eight syllables, and Agni is of the Gāyatrī nature;
as great as Agni is, he thus pacifies his heat.
With verses containing the word "pāvaka.
Food, indeed, is pāvaka; by means of food, he pacifies his impurity.
The fire is indeed death;
this black antelope skin is the form of Brahman.
He puts on two sandals made of black antelope skin.
"By means of the *brahman* alone he places a barrier against death;
he places a barrier against death," they say. "He places a barrier against the consumption of food. He fastens one [rope] around [the neck], but not another within.
"Thus he places himself beyond death; he secures food for himself when he says, 'Homage to thy heat, to thy flame! For they treat one who is more excellent with reverence after having paid homage."
"May their missiles burn others than us," he says; thus he inflicts pain upon him whom he hates. "Be purifying and auspicious for us," he says.
Food indeed is the purifier; verily, he wins food.
He strides across with two verses for the sake of firm support.
With two verses containing the word "water," for the sake of pacification.

5.4.5 Anuvāka 5: Designation of the sprinkling and other rites. With the formula "To the one sitting among men, vaṭ," he sprinkles; by means of the oblation in the *paṅkti* meter, he takes hold of the beginning of the sacrifice.
He sprinkles transversely;
therefore animals move their limbs transversely, for the sake of stability.
If he were to utter the *vaṣaṭ* call, his *vaṣaṭ* call would become exhausted.
If he were not to utter *vaṣaṭ*, the *rakṣases* would destroy the sacrifice.
He says "vaṭ"; thus he utters *vaṣaṭ* in a cryptic manner.
His *vaṣaṭ*-utterance does not become exhausted, and the *rakṣases* do not destroy his sacrifice.
Some gods are eaters of oblations, others are non-eaters of oblations;
the builder of the fire-altar alone gratifies both of them.
With the mantra "ye devā devānām," he sprinkles [the offering] with curd mixed with honey;
thus the sacrificer gratifies both the gods who eat what has been offered and those who eat what has not been offered,
and they in turn gratify the sacrificer.
With curds alone he gratifies those who eat the oblation, and with honey those who do not eat the oblation.
Curds are indeed village food, while honey is forest food;
when he sprinkles it with curds mixed with honey, it is for the attainment of both.
He sprinkles with a handful of clods; the handful of clods belongs to Prajāpati, for the sake of providing a common womb.
With two [verses], for the sake of stability.
He sprinkles water around [the fire] in succession;
thus he gratifies them completely, without omission.
He who, while piling the fire-altar, steps over it, is deprived of his vital breaths, his offspring, and his cattle;
[therefore] he says, "Giver of out-breath, giver of in-breath," and thus he places the vital breaths within himself.
"Bestower of splendor, bestower of space," he says;
splendor is indeed offspring, and space is cattle; verily, he bestows upon himself both offspring and cattle.
Indra slew Vṛtra;
once slain, Vṛtra bound him with sixteen coils.
He saw this oblation for Agni Anīkavat; he offered it.
Agni Anīkavat, gratified by his own portion, burned away the sixteen coils of Vṛtra.
By means of the offering to Viśvakarman, he was released from evil.
In that he offers an oblation to Agni Anīkavat, Agni himself, as Anīkavat, being gratified by his own portion, burns away his evil;
by means of the offering to Viśvakarman, he is released from evil.
If one should desire,
"May he be released from evil for a long time," he should offer each oblation separately for him.
One is released from evil for a long time; however,
if one should desire that someone be released from evil quickly, one should recite all [the formulas] for him and offer the oblation.
At that very moment, he is released from evil.
Moreover, he indeed offers with two separate hymns;
thus he bestows the power of the two hymns separately.
And also for the sake of firm establishment.
5.4.6 Anuvāka 6: The Rule for Placing the Fuel-Stick and Other Rites.
With the words, "Lead him upward," he places the fuel-sticks;
just as one provides assistance to a person who is traveling, so indeed is that.
He places three [bricks]; for Agni is threefold;
he thus provides a share for Agni as great as he is.
They are made of Udumbara wood;
the Udumbara is indeed strength;
verily, he bestows strength upon him.
"Upward you, O All-Gods," he says;
the All-Gods are indeed the vital breaths; verily, by means of the vital breaths, he raises him up.
"O Agni, may they bring [offerings] with their thoughts," he says;
by that very thought for which he raises him up, he causes him to prosper.
"May the five divine regions, the goddesses, protect the sacrifice," he says.
"For he follows along the quarters," [he says]; "driving away misfortune and ill-will," he says for the sake of striking away the *rakṣases*;
"bestowing upon the lord of the sacrifice an increase of wealth," he says.
Cattle indeed are the increase of wealth;
verily he wins cattle by carrying [the earth] with six [verses].
There are six seasons; verily, by means of the seasons he carries him away. Two [verses] contain the word "enclosing"; this is for the smiting away of the Rakṣases.
"Suryarashmi, Harikesha, from the east," he says for the sake of impulsion.
"Then may the purifying blessings favor us," he says.
Food indeed is the purifier;
verily, he wins food.
The gods and the Asuras were engaged in conflict.
Those gods saw this Apratiratha [hymn];
by it alone they conquered the Asuras without opposition.
That is the "unopposed chariot" nature of the Apratiratha hymn. Because the second Hotṛ recites the Apratiratha, the sacrificer thereby conquers his rivals without opposition;
moreover, he conquers even that which has not yet been conquered.
It consists of ten verses; the Virāj has ten syllables, and these two worlds are held apart by it.
For the separation of these two worlds;
moreover, the ten-syllable [meter] is food.
He indeed becomes sovereign and finds firm support in the eating of food.
The intermediate space is, as it were, non-existent;
the Āgnīdhra shed is, as it were, like the intermediate space.
He places a stone in the Āgnīdhra shed for the sake of stability.
"For stability through both," he says, "this celestial chariot stands in the midst of heaven."
Verily, with this [verse] he measures it out.
"The speckled stone is placed in the midst of heaven," he says;
for the speckled one is indeed food.
Verily, he wins food; he goes as far as the tail with four [verses], for there are four meters.
"By means of the meters indeed.
"All have made Indra grow," he says; thus he turns toward growth.
"The lord of strength, the master of strengths," he says;
for "strength" (vāja) is indeed food.
"Verily, he wins food;
'May the sacrifice, invoking favor, bring the gods hither,' he says; for offspring and cattle are indeed favor."
He bestows offspring and cattle upon himself when he says, "May the god Agni sacrifice for the gods and bring them hither," for the sake of making the *svagā* offering.
"With the impulse of strength, with the upward-grasp, he has grasped me up," he says.
Yonder sun, rising, is the upward-grasp; setting, he is the downward-grasp.
Verily, by means of the *brahman* he raises himself up, and by means of the *brahman* he holds down his rival.
5.4.7 Anuvāka 7: The Procedure for Depositing the Fire on the Altar.
"Go forward along the eastern quarter, O wise one," he says;
by this [verse], he indeed turns toward the world of the gods.
"Step by step with Agni, ascend to the firmament," he says; by this verse, he indeed steps across these worlds. "From the earth, I have ascended to the intermediate space," he says.
"By this [verse], he ascends these very worlds.
"Going to heaven, they look not back," he says; by this [verse], he indeed goes to the heavenly world.
"O Agni, go forward as the first of those seeking the gods," he says;
by this verse, he bestows sight upon both, among gods and men alike.
He steps forward with five; the sacrifice is fivefold;
as great as the sacrifice is, with that he goes to the world of heaven.
He recites the invitatory verse beginning with "Night and Dawn" for the sake of stability;
he says, "O Agni, thousand-eyed."
"Prajāpati is thousandfold;
for the attainment of Prajāpati, we pay homage to you, to that strength—svāhā! he says.
Food indeed is *vāja*;
verily, he wins food.
He offers a vessel full of curds made of udumbara wood upon the naturally perforated stone.
Curds, indeed, are strength;
the udumbara is strength.
This is the naturally perforated brick;
in it he places vigor.
Therefore, from that [brick], we live upon vigor directed hitherward.
He settles it with three [verses]; for Agni is threefold;
he causes Agni, in his full extent, to attain a firm foundation.
"O Agni, shine forth, like a spear-point before us"—with these words he places a piece of Udumbara wood; this indeed is a glowing iron bar with a knob at its end.
With this, they used to [act].

The gods indeed strike down the hundredfold hosts of the Asuras when he places this kindling-stick; verily, the sacrificer hurls this hundred-slaying thunderbolt at his rival for the sake of striking him down, so that there may be no failure.
"May we worship thee in thy highest birth, O Agni"—with these words he places a fuel-stick of *vikaṅkata* wood; thus he wins radiance.
"That wondrous [work] of Savitṛ, the desirable one"—with these words he places a stick of *śamī* wood for the sake of peace.
"Either the fire milks the one who has piled the fire-altar, or the one who has piled the fire-altar milks the fire.
He says, "That wondrous [gift] of Savitṛ, the desirable one..."
This is indeed the milking of Agni;
Kaṇva Śrāyasa alone knew it, and with it he milked him completely.
In that he places a kindling-stick with this [verse], he milks the fire-altar itself;
"Seven, O Agni, are your kindling-sticks, seven your tongues," he says; thus he gratifies his sevenfold sets of seven.
He offers with a full [ladle],
for Prajāpati is, as it were, full;
[it is] of Prajāpati [that he does this].
He offers with a deficient [verse] for the sake of attainment; for from the deficient Prajāpati created offspring.
For the creation of progeny.
Agni hid himself from the gods;
he entered into the quarters.
While offering, he should meditate on the quarters with his mind;
thus he wins them from the very quarters.
He offers curds first and ghee afterwards.
It bestows upon him brilliance and sensory power together;
the cake on twelve potsherds is for Vaiśvānara,
for the year consists of twelve months.
The year is Agni Vaiśvānara; verily,
he directly obtains Vaiśvānara.
If he were to perform the *prayāja* and *anūyāja* offerings, that would be a dismemberment of the sacrifice;
he performs a *darvihoma* for the stability of the sacrifice.
Vaiśvānara is indeed the kingdom, and the Maruts are the people.
Having offered to Vaiśvānara, he offers to the Maruts;
thus he binds the people to the kingdom itself.
He causes the announcement for Vaiśvānara to be made aloud, but he offers to the Maruts in a low voice.
Therefore, the *rāṣṭra* speaks over the *viś*;
they belong to the Maruts, for the Maruts are indeed the *viś* among the gods.
By means of the divine host, he wins for him the human host;
there are seven [verses], for the Maruts consist of seven groups.
Verily, he wins the people by means of groups;
he offers, following one group with another, and thus makes the people follow after him.
5.4.8 Anuvāka 8: The Vasordhārā.
He offers the Vasordhārā with the words, "May the stream of wealth come to me"; indeed, this [offering] is offered as the "stream of wealth."
Or rather, this stream of clarified butter stands by him, swelling for him in yonder world.
He offers with clarified butter;
clarified butter is indeed brilliance, and the stream of wealth is brilliance.
By means of splendor itself, he wins splendor for him;
moreover, the streams of wealth (vasordhārā) are indeed desires,
so he wins desires.
If one should desire,
"May I cut off his vital breaths and his food," he should offer that [oblation] with a pause between the syllables.
He cuts off the very breaths and the food of that person for whom he desires,
"May I extend his breaths and his food. For such a one, he should offer the oblations continuously.
He extends his very vital breaths and his food-eating;
he offers twelve by twelves; the year has twelve months;
verily, by means of the year, he wins food for him.
"May there be food for me and may there be freedom from hunger for me," he says;
for this is indeed the form of food.
By means of form alone, one obtains food.
"Agni and me, and the waters and me," he says;
for this indeed is the source of food.
Verily, he wins food from its own source;
he offers oblations to those dedicated to Indra-Agni;
verily, he wins the deities.

Since Indra receives half of all [the offerings], therefore Indra is the recipient of the largest share among the deities. He pronounces Indra last; he thereby bestows vital power (*indriya*) upon him from above.
He offers the sacrificial implements;
for the sacrificial implements are indeed the sacrifice.
Verily, he wins the sacrifice;
moreover, this is indeed the form of the sacrifice;
by means of its very form, he wins the sacrifice.
"And the final bath for me, and the cry of 'well-done' for me," he says for the sake of making it well-done.
"And Agni for me, and the Gharma for me," he says.
This indeed is the form of spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*);
by means of that very form, he wins spiritual luster.
"May the *ṛc* be mine, and may the *sāman* be mine," he says.
This indeed is the form of the meters;
by means of its very form, he wins the meters.
"And my embryos, and my calves," he says.
This indeed is the form of cattle;
by means of its very form, he wins cattle.
He offers the *kalpa* oblations.
He offers on the even and uneven [days] for the sake of bringing order to what was not yet ordered,
for the sake of pairing.
"May you two be northward-facing. "For the sake of advancing. "And one for me, and three for me," he says; for one and three are indeed the meters of the gods.
He obtains both the meters of men— four and eight— and the meters of the gods;
he offers up to thirty-three.
There are indeed thirty-three deities;
verily, he wins the deities themselves.
He offers forty-eight oblations.
The Jagatī consists of forty-eight syllables;
cattle are of the nature of the Jagatī.
By means of the Jagatī, he wins cattle for him.
With "Vāja and Prasava," he offers the twelfth oblation;
twelve months are a year;
verily, he finds firm support in the year itself.
5.4.9 Anuvāka 9: The Vājaprasavīya.
Agni departed from the gods, seeking his own portion.
The gods said to him:
"Come back to us; carry our oblation," he said.
He replied, "I shall choose a boon: let them offer the *vājaprasavīya* sacrifice to me alone."
Therefore, they offer the *vājaprasavīya* oblation to Agni;
in that he offers the *vājaprasavīya*, he thereby gratifies Agni with his own share.
Moreover, it is indeed his consecration (*abhiṣeka*).
He offers with fourteen [verses]:
seven are cultivated plants and seven are wild.
For the attainment of both kinds,
he offers of every kind of food;
for the attainment of every kind of food.
He offers with a ladle made of Udumbara wood.
The Udumbara is indeed strength; strength is food.
By means of strength, he wins for him strength and food.
Agni is indeed the consecrated one among the gods; the fire-piler is the consecrated one among men.
Therefore, when it rains, the fire-piler should not run, for his food has already been secured.
Rain is indeed like food;
if he were to run, he would run away from food. He should turn back.
Verily, he turns toward food itself.
With the verse, "Night and Dawn," he offers an oblation of milk from a black cow that has a white calf.
By means of the day he causes the night to be bestowed upon him, and by means of the night the day;
thus day and night, being bestowed upon him, milk out for him his desire and food.
He offers the *rāṣṭrabhṛt* oblations.
Verily, he wins the kingdom;
he offers with six [verses],
for there are six seasons.
Verily, he finds firm support in the seasons; with the words "O Lord of the World," he offers five oblations at the front of the chariot,
for the chariot is indeed a thunderbolt.
With the thunderbolt itself he conquers the quarters;
for indeed, in yonder world, the wind blows toward the one who has piled the fire-altar.
He offers oblations with the names of the winds;
thus the wind blows for him in yonder world.
He offers three.
These are the three worlds.
From these very worlds he wins the wind.
"Thou art the ocean, full of mist," he says.
This indeed is the form of Vāta;
by means of its very form, he wins Vāta.
He offers with joined palms.
For in no other way can the oblation of these [beings] be conceived.

5.4.10 Anuvāka 10: The Enjoining of the Fire The chariot of the gods is indeed yoked for the sake of the heavenly world, whereas the chariot of men is yoked for whatever purpose one intends. This fire, indeed, is the chariot of the gods. "I yoke the fire with power and with ghee," he says; thus he truly yokes it. Being thus yoked, it carries him toward the heavenly world.

If one were to yoke with all five [verses], his fire would be yoked but displaced, the oblations would be unsettled, the *stomas* unsettled, and the *ukthas* unsettled. At the morning pressing, he touches it with three verses; Agni is indeed threefold (*trivṛt*);

as great as Agni is, so much of him he yokes. Just as when a yoked horse is placed upon a wagon, even so do the oblations find their support, the *stomas* find their support, and the *ukthas* find their support.

At the *yajñāyajñiya* chant, he touches [the fire] with two verses. This much indeed is the sacrifice—as much as the *agniṣṭoma*—yet its abundance is performed beyond that. Verily, he ascends at the end to the full extent of the sacrifice. He does so with two verses for the sake of stability; with one [verse], it remains unchanted, and then he touches it. Thus the subsequent sacrifice inclines toward him, and also for the sake of continuity. He who piles the fire-altar (*agni*) indeed falls away from this world. No oblation offered by him is properly prepared unless it is upon a brick. Whatever oblation he offers without a brick, [it is not effective].

That [fire] indeed flows away; as it flows away, the sacrifice perishes, and with the sacrifice, the sacrificer. When he piles the *punar-citi* (re-piling), it is for the firm establishment of the oblations;
the oblations become firmly established, the sacrifice does not perish, nor does the sacrificer.

He places eight bricks; the Gāyatrī has eight syllables: by means of the Gāyatrī metre he piles it. If there are eleven, it is by means of the Triṣṭubh; if twelve, by means of the Jagatī; thus, by means of the metres, he piles it.
This Agni, the *punaściti*, is indeed called the "sonless" (*napātka*). He who, knowing this, piles the *punaściti*, eats food through three generations of men.
Just as the re-establishment of the sacred fires (*punarādheya*) is [performed], so is the *punaściti*.

He who does not prosper by means of the establishment of the fires (*agnyādheya*) establishes the fires again; he who, having piled the fire-altar, does not prosper, piles the *punaściti*. In that he piles the *punaściti*, it is for the sake of prosperity.

Now, indeed, they say: "It should not be piled. For this Agni is Rudra; it is just as if one were to wake a sleeping tiger—that is exactly what it would be. Now, indeed, they say: "It should be piled. It is just as if one were to wake a more powerful person with his own share—that is exactly what it would be. Manu piled the fire-altar, but he did not prosper through it. He saw this *punaścit* (re-piling); he piled it, and by means of it he indeed prospered. In that he piles the *punaścit*, it is for prosperity.
5.4.11 Section 11: Designation of the Altars Built for Specific Desires.
One who desires cattle should build the altar of the meters (*chandaściti*). The meters are indeed cattle; thus he becomes possessed of cattle.
One who desires the heavenly world should build the falcon-altar (*śyenaciti*). The falcon is indeed the swiftest of birds; having become a falcon, he flies to the heavenly world.

One who desires, "May I be possessed of a head in yonder world," should pile the Kaṅkacit; he indeed becomes possessed of a head in yonder world. One desiring support should pile the Alajacit in four furrows; he finds firm support in the very quarters, for there are four quarters.
One who has rivals should pile the Praugacit.
In this way, he repels his rivals.
He who desires, "May I repel those rivals already born and those yet to be born," should pile the *ubhayataḥprauga* altar; thus he repels the rivals already born and repels those yet to be born.
One who has rivals should pile the *rathacakracit* altar; the chariot is indeed a thunderbolt (*vajra*), and so he hurls the thunderbolt at his rivals.
One who desires food should pile the Drona-cit; for food is borne in a wooden trough (droṇa), and thus he obtains food from its very source.
One who desires cattle should pile the Samūhya; he indeed becomes possessed of cattle.

One who desires a village should pile the *paricāyya*; he indeed becomes possessed of a village. One who should desire, "May I prosper in the world of the fathers," should pile the *śmaśānacit*; he indeed prospers in the world of the fathers. Viśvāmitra and Jamadagni contended with Vasiṣṭha; Jamadagni saw these *vihavyā* bricks and piled them. By means of them, he appropriated the sensory power and vigor of Vasiṣṭha. In that he piles the *vihavyās*, the sacrificer appropriates the sensory power and vigor of his rival by means of them.
He places it on the hearth of the Hotṛ; for that is indeed the station of the sacrificer.
The Hotṛ wins for himself in his own abode power and vigor.

He places twelve [bricks] as additional layers; the Jagatī meter has twelve syllables, and cattle are of the nature of the Jagatī; verily by means of the Jagatī he wins cattle for him. On the other Dhiṣṇiya hearths he places eight each; cattle have eight hooves; verily he wins cattle.
Six [bricks] on the Mārjālīya; for there are six seasons, and the seasons are indeed the divine ancestors; thus he gratifies the seasons, the gods, and the ancestors.
5.4.12 Anuvāka 12: Enumeration of the Ṛks and other verses related to the Aśvamedha stotra.
"Pavasva vājasātaye" is the opening verse (pratipad), which is an anuṣṭubh;
there are three anuṣṭubhs and four gāyatrīs.
Because there are three *anuṣṭubh*s, therefore the horse stands standing on three [legs];
because there are four *gāyatrī*s, therefore it runs away while replacing all four feet. This [the *anuṣṭubh*] is indeed the supreme among the meters.
The Catuṣṭoma is the highest of the Stomas; the Trirātra is the highest of the sacrifices;
the horse is the highest of animals.
By means of the supreme, he causes him to reach the supreme state.
The day consists of twenty-one [stomas].
In that horse which is sacrificed,
there are twelve months, five seasons, these three worlds, and yonder sun as the twenty-first; this is Prajāpati,
and the horse belongs to Prajāpati.
He prospers directly with that very [Sāman];
the Śakvarī verses constitute the Pṛṣṭha; each is a different metre.
These animals that are sacrificed are various: they are as if domestic, and as if wild.
In that the Śakvarī verses become the *pṛṣṭha* chant, it is for the sake of the horse’s completeness;
the *Pārthuraśma* becomes the *brahmasāman*.
For the horse is controlled by the rein; otherwise,
the uncontrolled horse, being without support, is liable to go to the furthest distance.
That the Pārthuraśma Brahmasāman is performed is for the movement and the support of the horse.
The *acchāvāka*sāman is performed with a *saṃkṛti* [chant].
"This Aśvamedha is indeed a sacrifice that has perished," they say;
"who knows whether it is performed in its entirety or not? they ask.
In that the *acchāvāka-sāman* is performed with a *saṃkṛtī*, it serves for the wholeness of the horse, its completion, and its lack of obstacle;
the final day is an *atirātra* with all the *stomas*, for the attainment of everything and the conquest of everything;
by means of this, he attains everything and conquers everything.
Prapāṭhaka 5, Anuvāka 1: Designation of the Dīkṣaṇīyā Bricks.
That he completes [the rite] with one [verse] is for the continuity and non-interruption of the sacrifice.
The animals dedicated to Indra are those that are castrated.

If those which belong to Indra are offered to the Agnis, one causes discord among the deities. One should employ Triṣṭubh verses addressed to Agni as the invitatory and offering formulas (yājyānuvākyās).
In that they are addressed to Agni, they thereby belong to Agni.
In that they are Triṣṭubhs, they belong to Indra;
this is for prosperity,
so that he does not cause strife among the deities.
One sacrifices a hornless animal to Vāyu accompanied by his team; it is the brilliance of Agni that Vāyu is sacrificed for,
and therefore Vāyu moves horizontally.
The fire blows sideways and burns; that brilliance of his indeed follows after it,
for if it were not possessed by the *niyut* team, the sacrificer would become intoxicated with pride.
There is [a verse] addressed to Niyutvat for the sake of preventing the sacrificer from going mad;
the invitatory and offering verses are addressed to Vāyu and contain the word "white" (śveta) for the sake of providing brilliance.
With the verse, "Hiraṇyagarbha arose in the beginning," he pours the Āghāra libation;
for Hiraṇyagarbha is Prajāpati, and this is done for the sake of conformity with Prajāpati.
Verily, he obtains all the forms of cattle:
that which is the beard is the form of men.
That which is hornless belongs to horses;
that which has teeth on only one side belongs to cattle;
that which has hooves like those of a sheep belongs to sheep.
That which is unborn belongs to the goats.
Vāyu is indeed the dear abode of cattle; when the offering is dedicated to Vāyu, the cattle, recognizing him, attend upon it.
"Should it be dedicated to Vāyu or to Prajāpati? they ask.
"If one were to make it dedicated to Vāyu, he would depart from Prajāpati;
if one were to make it dedicated to Prajāpati, [he would depart] from Vāyu."
In this way he does not depart from Vāyu, since the animal victim belongs to Vāyu;
and in this way he does not depart from Prajāpati, since the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) belongs to Prajāpati.
In that it is on twelve potsherds, he does not depart from Vaiśvānara.
One who is about to be consecrated offers an oblation on eleven potsherds to Agni and Viṣṇu;
Agni is all the deities, and Viṣṇu is the sacrifice.
He undertakes both the deities and the sacrifice.
Agni is the first of the deities, Viṣṇu the last.
In that he offers the cake on eleven potsherds to Agni and Viṣṇu, [he gratifies] the deities.
Thus, by grasping both sides, the sacrificer wins them.
By means of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), the gods prospered in yonder world; by means of the cooked rice oblation (*caru*), [they prospered] in this world.
Whoever should so desire—
Thinking, "May I prosper in that world," he should prepare the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*).
He indeed prospers in that very world; because it is offered on eight potsherds, it belongs to Agni.
That which consists of three potsherds belongs to Viṣṇu for the sake of prosperity,
for one who may desire it.
Thinking, "May I prosper in this world," he should prepare a *caru* offering:
ghee for Agni and rice grains for Viṣṇu; therefore [these are the materials].
A *caru* oblation should be prepared;
he prospers in this very world;
it becomes like the sun.
This earth, indeed, is Aditi;
he finds firm support in her very self, and moreover, it is upon her that he extends the sacrifice.
Verily, for him who piles the fire-altar without having carried the fire in the pan for a year, it is just as if a fetus were to fall prematurely.
He would meet with distress.
He should first offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara;
for Agni Vaiśvānara is the year.
Just as one gives birth after having reached a year when the time has come, even so, having reached a year when the time has come, he piles the fire-altar; he does not meet with misfortune.
Vaiśvānara is indeed the dear body of Agni;
verily, he secures for himself his own dear body.
There are three oblations for these.
These are the three worlds;
for the growth of these worlds.
5.5.2 Anuvāka 2: Description of the Piling and its Fruit.
Having created the creatures, Prajāpati entered into them with his vital breath (praṇa); he was unable to come forth from them again.
He said,
"He who would rebuild me from here would indeed prosper.
The gods rebuilt him.
Verily, they prospered because they piled it together; that is why the piling of the fire-altar is called *citya*. He who, knowing thus, piles the fire-altar, truly prospers.
"For what purpose is Agni piled, and for whom? they ask.
"One piles Agni thinking, 'May I be possessed of fire.'"
"He indeed becomes possessed of fire.
"For what purpose, for whom is the fire piled? they ask.
"It is piled so that the gods may know me," [it is said]. Thus is the fire piled.
The gods know him; they say, "For whom and for what purpose is Agni piled?
Indeed, Agni is piled with the thought, "May I be one who possesses."
"He remains indeed a householder.
"For what purpose is the fire piled? they ask.
"It is for the thought: 'May I possess cattle,' [they say]; Agni is [the means for that]."
It is piled;
he indeed becomes possessed of cattle.
"For what purpose is Agni piled? they ask.
"May seven men live upon me," with these words indeed is the fire piled;
three facing eastward, three facing westward, and the self as the seventh—just so many live upon him in yonder world.
Prajāpati desired to pile the fire.
The Earth said to him:
"If you shall pile the fire upon me, it will burn me excessively; being thus excessively burned, I shall split asunder, and you will become a sinner."
He said,
"I will act in such a way that it will not burn you excessively," and he touched this [earth].
"May Prajāpati settle you; by that deity, sit firm like Aṅgiras!"—
having thus made this very earth into a brick, he placed it down to prevent excessive burning.
Whatever [altar] one should pile facing toward the fire, that he should touch with the formula:
"May Prajāpati settle you; by that deity, sit firm like Aṅgiras!"
Having made this very brick, he lays it down so that there shall be no excessive burning.
Prajāpati desired, "May I procreate."
He saw this fire-pan (ukhya);
he carried it for a year;
from that, indeed, he was born.
Therefore, he should be carried for a year; thus he is indeed born.
The Vasus said to him, "You have been born; let us also be born. He gave him over to the Vasus. They carried him for three days. By means of that—
And they created three hundred and thirty-three;
therefore, one should maintain the wife for three days, for she is thus procreated.
Those Rudras said:
"Come forth! May we be procreated! they said;
they offered him to the Rudras, and they carried him for six days.
From that, they created three hundred and thirty-three;
therefore, the six-day rite (ṣaḍaha) should be performed, for one is indeed born from it.
The Ādityas said to them:
"May you be born forth; may we be born forth," they said,
and they offered him to the Ādityas.
They carried him for twelve days;
by means of him, they created three hundred and thirty-three [beings].
Therefore, one should carry the *dvādaśāha* [sacrifice] for twelve days; thus, one is indeed procreated.
By that very means they created a thousand [cows], with the fire-pan (*ukhā*) as the thousandth;
he who thus knows the thousandfold fire-pan (*ukhya*) obtains a thousand cattle.
5.5.3 Anuvāka 3: Description of the Ukhā-offering and other rites.
"This [Ukhā] is prepared with a Yajus, cooked with a Yajus, and released with a Yajus; yet this very Ukhā is now exhausted in its potency (*yātayāmnī*). They say it cannot be used again."
"O Agni, yoke those [steeds] that are yours; yoke those who are best at summoning the gods"—with these words he offers into the fire-pan (*ukhā*);
by this very means he yokes it again, and by this it becomes unexhausted.
Indeed, he who yokes the fire when the time for yoking has arrived, yokes it among those who are yoking.
"O Agni, yoke those [steeds] that are yours; yoke those who are best at summoning the gods," he says;
for this indeed is the yoking of Agni.
With that very [verse] he yokes it; he yokes among those who are yoking.
The exponents of sacred knowledge (brahmavādinaḥ) say: "Should the fire-altar be piled face down, or face up?"
This Agni is built as a counterpart to birds.
If one were to pile it face downwards, the oblations would strike it from behind;
if one were to pile it face upwards, it would not be able to fly, and he would not attain the heavenly world.
He places the head of a man facing east and turned upward; thus the oblations reach him from the front. He does not pile it face upward; he thereby becomes one who attains the heavenly world.
He offers with a verse addressed to Sūrya; he thereby bestows sight upon him.
He offers twice, for there are two eyes;
he offers with the same [verse], for the eye is one, for the sake of prosperity.
The gods and the asuras were arrayed for battle; they deposited their precious wealth together, and the gods appropriated it by means of the Vāmabhṛt.
That is why the Vāmabhṛt is called Vāmabhṛt.
In that he places the Vāmabhṛt, the sacrificer thereby appropriates the desirable wealth of his rival.
It has a head of gold.
Gold is indeed light, and the desirable is light; by means of light he appropriates for himself his light and his desirable wealth.
There are two *yajus* formulas for the sake of stability.
5.5.4 Anuvāka 4: Designation of the Seed-Sower and Others.

The waters were the wives of Varuṇa; Agni meditated upon them and united with them. His seed fell away; it became this [earth]. That which fell away a second time became that [sky]. This earth is indeed Virāj, and that sky is Virāj. In that he lays down two Virāj bricks, he thus lays down these two very worlds.
Or rather, whatever seed he sheds, that settles in her; that is born, and it becomes these plants.

They become creepers; Agni eats them—he who knows thus is indeed propagated and becomes an eater of food. For one who would be possessed of seed, he should place both [bricks] on the first layer; these two worlds, being joined together, pour seed for him. For one whose seed has been spilled, he should place one [brick] on the first layer and the other on the last layer; thus he encompasses his spilled seed from both sides by means of these two.
For a year, one should not descend toward anyone; for these two do not descend toward anyone—that is their vow.
Verily, he who piles the fire-altar without a head becomes headless in yonder world; he who piles it with a head becomes possessed of a head in yonder world.

"I offer consciousness with mind and clarified butter, so that the gods, who increase the Truth and enjoy the oblation, may come hither. In the path of the ocean, the means of knowledge, I offer the immortal oblation to Viśvakarman, the all-pervading day. Having thus placed the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick, he makes the offering.
This indeed is the head of Agni; he piles the fire with its head. He who knows thus becomes possessed of a head in yonder world.
This fire is piled for the sake of the heavenly world; whatever is done for it out of sequence is not conducive to the heavenly world for him.
Agni is conducive to the heavenly world.
Having laid down the layer, he should touch it with the verse:

"May the wise one distinguish between thought and thoughtlessness; like backs, may he separate the straight and the crooked among mortals. O God, grant us wealth and good offspring; grant us freedom and ward off bondage. Thus he lays it down in its proper order and builds it facing eastward; for him, there is the attainment of heaven.
5.5.5 Anuvāka 5: Designation of the Golden Bricks, etc.

Viśvakarman is the lord of the quarters; may he protect our cattle, may he protect us; homage to him! Prajāpati, Rudra, Varuṇa, and Agni are the lords of the quarters; may they protect our cattle, may they protect us; homage to them!
These deities are indeed the lords of these animals;
he who lays down the heads of the animals is cut off from them.
He lays down golden bricks.
The exponents of the Veda say that he pays homage to these very deities.
He consigns the domestic animals to the fire and strikes the wild animals with heat. "What remains there?
[one asks]. In that he lays down gold bricks—gold being indeed immortality—he provides a remedy for the domestic animals by means of immortality; he does not injure them.
The first naturally perforated brick is indeed the out-breath (*prāṇa*), the second the diffused breath (*vyāna*), and the third the in-breath (*apāna*).
Having laid down the first naturally perforated brick, he should breathe out along it; by means of the out-breath itself, he unites the out-breath; he should breathe out.
Having laid down the second [brick],
he unites the vyāna with the vyāna itself;
having laid down the third, he should exhale.
By means of the downward breath (apāna) he indeed unites the downward breath;
moreover, by means of the vital breaths (prāṇas), he kindles him.
With the words "Bhūḥ! Bhuvaḥ! Suvaḥ! he places the naturally perforated bricks (svayamātṛṇṇās).
These worlds are indeed the naturally perforated bricks.
By means of these very *vyāhṛtis*, Prajāpati was procreated;
therefore, when one lays down the naturally perforated bricks with these *vyāhṛtis*, it is for the purpose of laying down these very worlds within them.
He is born preeminent among the worlds.
For out-breathing, for diffused-breathing, for in-breathing, for speech thee; for sight thee! By that divinity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit thou firm!
By means of Agni, indeed, the gods sought to go to the heavenly world.
Because they were unable to fall [into the pit],
they saw these four naturally perforated stones (svayamātṛṇṇā) and placed them in the quarters.
By means of that all-seeing eye they went to the heavenly world;
in that he places four naturally perforated bricks in the quarters, the sacrificer goes to the heavenly world by means of Agni, who possesses an all-seeing eye.
5.5.6 Anuvāka 6: The Naming of the Forms of the Days and Other Elements. "O Agni, come for the feast!"—thus he says; verily, by this he summons him.
"We choose Agni as the messenger," he says;
by thus offering, he indeed chooses him. "By Agni is Agni kindled."
Thus he says: "Agni has kindled him; may he strike down the Vṛtras. Thus he says: when [the fire] is indeed kindled, he bestows sensory power (*indriya*) upon him.
"O Agni, we meditate upon the hymn," he says;
verily, he causes him to reflect upon these forms of the days.
Day after day he piles it;
he thus secures the forms of the days.
The exponents of sacred knowledge say:
"For what reason is it that while other bricks are exhausted (*yātayāmnī*), the *lokampṛṇā* is not exhausted (*ayātayāmnī*)? One should reply: "Because it belongs to Indra-Agni and Bṛhaspati.
For among the gods, Indra, Agni, and Bṛhaspati are indeed those who are not exhausted. It possesses attendants.
To avoid redundancy, he proceeds with an *anuṣṭubh* verse.
The *lokampṛṇā* is indeed the self, and the *anuṣṭubh* is the vital breath (*prāṇa*); therefore, the vital breath moves along all the limbs.
"Therefore they are his, yielding milk," he says; therefore there is sap in every joint.
"He mixes the Soma with the dappled cows," he says.
The dappled cow is indeed food; verily, he wins food for himself.
Agni is indeed the Arka, and the Arka is food; verily, he wins food for himself.
"Born among the clans of the gods, in the three bright realms of heaven," he says.
Verily, he thus makes these worlds luminous for him.
He who knows the foundation of the bricks stands firm indeed.
"By that deity, sit firm like Aṅgiras," he says.
This indeed is the foundation of the bricks; he who knows thus stands firm.
5.5.7 Anuvāka 7: Designation of the Singleness of the Sacrificial Post, etc.
This Agni is indeed built for the sake of the heavenly world;
the set of eleven [stakes] is a thunderbolt.
If he were to set up the eleven sacrificial posts in the fire-altar, he would exclude him from the heavenly world with the thunderbolt;
if he were not to set them up, he would deprive the animals of their *svaru*-chips.
He sets up a single post.
He does not exclude him from the heavenly world with the thunderbolt, nor does he deprive the cattle of their sacrificial stakes;
indeed, he who steps over the fire while piling it is deprived of power and vigor.
[The verses] belong to Indra.
One should place each brick while ascending with a *ṛc* verse;
thus one is not deprived of sensory power or vigor.
Indeed, this Agni is Rudra.
He has three targets: one facing him, one across from him, and one behind him; he who piles the fire-altar is cut down by these.
Having piled the fire-altar, he should give a bow with three arrows to a Brahmin, unasked for.
He pays homage to them alone;
moreover, he ransoms himself from them with the words,
"O Rudra, that which [is] before thee..."
May the wind blow favorably along that bow of yours; O Rudra, I pay homage to it for you with the passing of a year.
O Rudra, may the wind blow favorably along that bow of yours which is your southern weapon.
To you, O Rudra, I pay homage with a full year;
that bow of yours, O Rudra, which is behind, may the wind blow after it;
to you, O Rudra, I pay homage with a year-and-a-half.
O Rudra, may the wind blow after that bow of yours which is directed upward;
to that bow of yours, O Rudra, I pay homage with a year-long cycle.
O Rudra, may the wind blow after that bow of yours which is above;
to that [bow] of yours, O Rudra, I pay homage for a year.
For this Agni is indeed Rudra.
Just as an enraged tiger stands [ready to spring], so indeed does he now stand; with these prostrations, he approaches him who has been thus accumulated and pacifies him.
Those fires that have entered the earth, dwelling within the soil—
of them you are the highest; impel us toward life.
I have obtained you, O Agni, with the mind; I have obtained you, O Agni, with fervor;
I have obtained you, O Agni, with consecration.
I have won you, O Agni, with the Upasad rites; I have won you, O Agni, with the Soma-pressing; I have won you, O Agni, with the sacrificial gifts.

"O Agni, I have attained you with the *avabhṛtha*," "O Agni, I have attained you with the *vaśā*," "O Agni, I have attained you with the utterance of *svagā*"—so he says. This, indeed, is the attainment of Agni; by means of it, he attains him.
5.5.8 Anuvāka 8: Designation of the Worship and Other Rites.
He worships from the front with the Gāyatra [Sāman]; verily, he bestows breath upon him.
With the Bṛhat and Rathantara [Sāmans], he worships the two wings; verily, he bestows vigor upon him.
Standing in the seasons, he establishes the tail with the *yajñāyajñiya* chant; thus he finds firm support in the seasons.
He worships with the *pṛṣṭha* chants;
the *pṛṣṭhas* are indeed splendor.
He bestows splendor upon him.
Prajāpati created Agni;
once created, he went away from him.
He warded it off with the Vāravantīya; that is the reason for the Vāravantīya’s name "Vāravantīya.
He made it white with the Śyaita; that is the reason for the Śyaita’s name "Śyaita."
In that he worships with the Vāravantīya, he indeed holds him back;
with the Śyaita, he makes him white;
with the Heart of Prajāpati, he worships him limb by limb.

Its measure indeed goes forth: "With the eastern quarter I settle thee; with the Gāyatrī metre, with Agni as the deity; with the head of Agni, I place the head of Agni. "With the southern quarter I settle thee; with the Triṣṭubh metre, with Indra as the deity; with the wing of Agni, I place the wing of Agni."
I settle you with the western quarter.
With the *jagatī* metre, with Savitṛ as the deity, I place the tail of Agni upon the tail of Agni.

With the northern quarter, I settle thee; with the *anuṣṭubh* metre, with Mitra and Varuṇa as the deity, I place the wing of Agni upon the wing of Agni. With the upward quarter, I settle thee; with the *paṅkti* metre, with Bṛhaspati as the deity, I place the back of Agni upon the back of Agni.
He who piles the fire-altar without its self becomes selfless in yonder world;
he who piles it with its self becomes possessed of a self in yonder world.
He places the *ātman*-bricks.
This indeed is the self of Agni; he who knows thus piles Agni with his own self, and he becomes possessed of his own self in yonder world.

5.5.9 Anuvāka 9: Designation of the Oblations, etc. O Agni Udadhi, that arrow of yours which is named Yuvan—with that, be gracious to us! Homage to it! Living under its protection, may we be! O Agni Dudhra, Gahya, Kiṃśila, Vanya, that arrow of yours which is named Yuvan—with that, be gracious to us! Homage to it! Living under its protection, may we be! Indeed, these five fires are the layers; the first is named Udadhi, the second is Dudhra.

The second is Gahya, the third Kiṃśila, the fourth Vanya, and the fifth is [the fifth]. If one were not to offer oblations to them, they would consume both the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer. In that he offers these oblations, he pacifies them with their own respective portions; neither the Adhvaryu nor the sacrificer comes to ruin. May speech be in my mouth, breath in my nostrils, sight in my eyes, hearing in my ears, strength in my arms, and vigor in my thighs. May all my limbs and my body be unharmed. Together with my body, homage be to you; do not harm me.

The vital breaths indeed depart from him who, while piling the fire-altar, steps over it. "May speech be in my mouth; may breath be in my nostrils," he says; thus he places the vital breaths within himself.

"Rudra who is in the fire, who is in the waters, who is in the plants—Rudra who has entered all beings, to that Rudra let there be homage. Some Rudras have the oblations as their portion, others have the sacrificial offerings as their portion."

Others, having offered the Śatarudrīya, should place a *gavīdhuka* pap on the final brick with this *yajus*: "Verily, by means of its own portion, he pacifies it. They say, "The Śatarudrīya has indeed been offered for him by whom this is performed in the fire.

"May the Vasus protect you from the east with the Rudras; may the Fathers, whose king is Yama, protect you from the south with the Fathers; may the Ādityas protect you from the west with all the gods; may Dyutāna Māruta protect you from the north with the Maruts."

May the gods, with Indra as their chief and Varuṇa as their king, protect [the sacrificer] both from below and from above. Indeed, he is neither purified, nor made fit for sacrifice, nor consecrated by that sprinkling which one performs upon him prior to this point; but in that one sprinkles the piled altar with clarified butter, by that it is purified, by that it is made fit for sacrifice, and by that it is consecrated.
5.5.10 Anuvāka 10: Designation of the Oblations to the Serpents and Others.
You are Samīcī, the eastern direction; of you, Agni is the overlord and Asita is the protector.
Homage to him who is the sovereign and him who is the protector; may those two be gracious to us.
Him whom we hate and him who hates us, I place within your jaws.
You are the powerful one by name, the southern quarter.
Indra is its overlord, and the adder is its guardian.
You are the eastern direction, named the western; of you, [that is] yours.
Soma is the overlord, born of itself;
the northern direction is its name,
and Varuṇa is its overlord, the cross-lined one.
You are named Adhipatnī, the great quarter; Bṛhaspati is your overlord, Śvitra.
You are named Vaśinī, this [southern] quarter.
Yama is its overlord; Kalmāṣagrīva is its guardian.
To him who is the overlord and him who is the guardian, homage! May those two be gracious to us. [To] him whom we hate and [him who hates] us...
I do not hate him; I place him within the jaws of you two.
These deities indeed protect the piled fire-altar; if one were not to offer oblations to them, they would consume both the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer.
In that he offers these oblations, he pacifies them with their own portion;
neither the Adhvaryu nor the sacrificer comes to ruin. "You are the darts by name."
Your houses are in front; Agni is your arrows, and you are the Salilas,
called the Nilmipas.
The sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is your abode; O fathers, your arrows are the ocean.
You are named Vajrins;
your dwellings are behind you,
sleep is your arrows, and the abyss is your quiver.
"You are the possessors of stations;
your homes are in the north.
Water is your arrows, and the ocean [is your quiver]."
"You are indeed the overlords; your dwellings are above them.
Like rain, like arrows, you are irresistible."
You are the ones named Kravyād, belonging to the earth;
yours are the dwellings here.
Like food, like arrows, or like the twinkling of eyes, [are] the names of the winds;
homage to you from them! Be gracious to us.
"Whomever we hate and whoever hates us—him I place within your jaws.
Some gods are eaters of oblations, others are non-eaters of oblations;
the fire-piler alone gratifies both of them.
He offers these oblations with curds mixed with honey;
verily, he gratifies them with their own portion.
Now, moreover, they say:
"The bricks are indeed the gods who do not eat oblations";
thus he offers while moving around [the altar],
and so he gratifies them completely, leaving none out.

Suck this vigorous breast, O Agni; drink from it well-filled in the midst of the flood. Enjoy the honeyed fountain, the wide expanse; enter your oceanic dwelling. He who, having yoked the fire, does not release it—just as a yoked horse that is not released perishes through hunger, even so his fire perishes;
and as the fire perishes, the sacrificer perishes after it. Therefore, having piled the fire, he should remain secluded.
It occurs thus: "Suck this vigorous breast, drink of the waters"—with these words, he offers a ladle full of clarified butter;
this indeed is the unyoking of the fire.
Having released it, he indeed provides food for this [horse]; therefore they say: "Whether one knows thus or not, the well-fed steed surely provides nourishment."
Agni indeed is the prize-winner; he thus gratifies him, and being gratified, he in turn gratifies him; he becomes more prosperous.
5.5.11 Anuvāka 11: The Rule for the First Group of Animals Constituting the Remainder of the Aśvamedha Sacrifice.
To Indra the King, a boar;
to Varuṇa the King, a black antelope.
To King Yama, a Rishya; to King Rishabha, a Gavaya;
to King Shardula, a Gaura.
A monkey for a king of men; a quail for a swift hawk; a worm for a blue ox.
The kulunga antelope belongs to King Soma; the porpoise belongs to the Sindhu; the elephant belongs to the Himavat.
5.5.12 Anuvāka 12: The Rule for the Second Group of Animals Constituting the Remainder of the Aśvamedha Sacrifice.
The mayu belongs to Prajāpati;
the ūla, the halīkṣṇa, and the vṛṣadaṁśa belong to Dhātṛ.
To Sarasvatī, a white female śāri bird that speaks like a man; to Sarasvant, a white male śuka parrot that speaks like a man;
a wild goat, a mongoose, and a śakā—these are for Pūṣan.
The curlew [is assigned] to speech.
