5.5.13 Anuvāka 13: The Rule for the Third Group of Animals Constituting the Remnant of the Aśvamedha Sacrifice.
To the grandson of the waters, hail! The crocodile, the makara, and the kulīkāya—these belong to Akūpāra.
The Paiṅgarāja for Vāc;
the Kuṣītaka for Bhaga;
the Ātīvāhasa and the Darvidas are dedicated to Vāyu.
From the quarters comes the ruddy goose.
5.5.14 Anuvāka 14: The Rule for the Fourth Group of Animals Constituting the Remnant of the Aśvamedha Sacrifice.
For Bala, the python;
the mouse, the *sṛjaya*, and the *śayaṇḍaka*—these are dedicated to Mitra.
Asita is for Death;
Svaja,
Kumbhīnasa, Puṣkarasāda, and Lohitāhi— these are the offspring of Tvaṣṭṛ.
Or like an echo for a horse.
5.5.15 Anuvāka 15: The Rule for the Fifth Group of Animals Constituting the Remainder of the Aśvamedha Sacrifice.
The human deer for the Moon;
the monitor lizard and the *kālakā* for the Woodpecker—these are for the Trees.
The female antelope is for the day, the cuckoo is for the night; the woodpecker with the blue head is for Aryaman, and the *katkaṭa* bird is for Dhātṛ.
5.5.16 Anuvāka 16: The ritual for the sixth group of animals forming part of the Aśvamedha sacrifice. The crane belongs to Sūrya; the antelope, the peacock, and the hawk belong to the Gandharvas.
The francolin partridge belongs to the Vasus;
the partridge belongs to the Rudras;
the red deer, the kuṇḍṛṇācī, and the golattikā belong to the Apsarases.
The Sṛmara [goes] to the forest.

5.5.17 Anuvāka 17: The Rule for the Seventh Group of Animals Constituting the Remainder of the Aśvamedha Sacrifice. The spotted deer is for the Viśvedevas; the *pitva* is for the Earth; the *nyaṅku* is for Kaśa; these are for Anumati.
The Anyavāpa, the half-months,
the months, Kaśyapa, Kvayi, Kuṭaru, and Dātyauha— these are for Sinīvālī.
To Bṛhaspati, a vessel with a narrow opening.
5.5.18 Anuvāka 18: The Rule for the Eighth Group of Animals Constituting the Remnant of the Aśvamedha Sacrifice.
The Śakas, the Bhaumas, the Pāṅktas, the Kaśas, and the Mānthīlavas—these belong to the Pitṛs.
The desert lizard belongs to the seasons; the pigeon, the owl, and the hare belong to the Year; these are dedicated to Nirṛti.
The cock belongs to Savitṛ.
5.5.19 Anuvāka 19: The ritual for the ninth group of animals constituting the remainder of the Aśvamedha sacrifice;
the Ruru deer is dedicated to Rudra.
The chameleon, the bird, and the pippakā—these are for the arrow-head;
the antelope is for Māruta;
the śārga is for Brahman.
The black hyena, the four-eyed dog, and the donkey—these belong to the Itarajanas;
for Agni, the *dhūṅkṣṇā* [is offered].
5.5.20 Anuvāka 20: The Rule for the Tenth Group of Animals Constituting the Remainder of the Aśvamedha Sacrifice.
The *alaja* is of the intermediate space;
the *udra*, *madgu*, and *plava* belong to the waters.
The swan-marked [bird] belongs to Aditi;
the vulture with white girdles, the *kīrśā*, and the *vārdhrāṇasa*—these belong to Indrāṇī; they are celestial.
The porcupine belongs to Heaven and Earth.
5.5.21 Anuvāka 21: The ritual rule for the group of eleven sacrificial animals forming part of the Aśvamedha; the Suparṇa is dedicated to Parjanya.
The Haṃsa, Vṛka, and Vṛṣadaṃśa are dedicated to Indra.
The water-owl for Apām Napāt; the fox, lion, mongoose, and tiger for Aryaman; those [animals] for Mahendra.
For the sake of desire, [they seize] the property of others.
5.5.22 Anuvāka 22: The Rule for the First Group of Domestic Animals Constituting the Remnant of the Aśvamedha Sacrifice:
[One] dedicated to Agni with a black neck, and a ewe dedicated to Sarasvatī.
The tawny one belongs to Soma,
the dark one to Pūṣan, and the white-backed one to Bṛhaspati.
The speckled one belongs to the Viśvedevas;
the ruddy one belongs to Indra;
the dappled one belongs to the Maruts.
A bull dedicated to Indra and Agni; a goat with white markings on its lower body dedicated to Savitṛ; a ram dedicated to Varuṇa.

5.5.23 Anuvāka 23: The second rule concerning the herd of domestic animals, which forms part of the Aśvamedha sacrifice. The horse, the hornless goat, and the gayal are dedicated to Prajāpati; those with black necks are dedicated to Agni.
Two with hairy thighs for Tvaṣṭṛ,
two with white backs for Bṛhaspati,
and one with a spotted belly for Dhātṛ.
The white ram belongs to Sūrya.
5.5.24 Anuvāka 24: The Rule for the Third Group of Domestic Animals Constituting a Remnant of the Aśvamedha Sacrifice.
For Agni Anīkavat, a red-marked ox; two [oxen] with dark lower parts, dedicated to Savitṛ.
Two with silver navels are for Pūṣan;
two tawny, hornless ones are for the Viśvedevas;
and one speckled one is for the Maruts.
A black goat is for Agni; a ewe is for Sarasvatī;
and a black ram with one white foot is for Varuṇa.
5.6 Prapāṭhaka: 6, Anuvāka 1: Designation of the mantras for the addressing of the *kumbheṣṭakā* bricks.

Golden-hued, pure, and purifying—those in whom Kaśyapa was born and in whom Indra was born; those of diverse forms who have held Agni as their embryo—may those waters be auspicious and pleasant to us. In whose midst King Varuṇa moves, discerning the truth and falsehood of men; those dripping with sweetness, pure, and purifying—may those waters be auspicious and pleasant to us. Whose portion the gods enjoy in heaven, who exist in many ways in the intermediate space; those bright ones who moisten the earth with milk—may those waters be auspicious and pleasant to us.

Behold me with an auspicious eye, O Waters; touch my skin with your auspicious bodies. I invoke you, all Agnis who dwell within the waters: bestow upon me luster, strength, and vigor. When you were being led forth and cried out at the slaughter of Ahi, from that time you received your name "Nadyas" (Rivers); those are your names, O Sindhus. When, dispatched by Varuṇa, you leaped together swiftly, Indra reached you as you were fleeing; therefore you are called "Āpas" (Waters).

Flowing against your will, you made a loud noise; therefore, O goddesses, Indra with his powers has struck you down, and thus the name "vār" (water) was given to you. One god stood over you as you flowed according to your own desire; because they brought you forth from the great [depths], you are called "udaka. The waters were auspicious; the waters were indeed clarified butter; the waters bear Agni and Soma; such are those waters, possessing a potent essence and mingled with honey.
Come quickly to me, together with breath and splendor!

From the very beginning I see you, or I hear you; the sound of you comes to me, like a voice within my mouth. I think that I have partaken of immortality when I was satiated by you, O golden-colored ones. For you, O Waters, are indeed sources of bliss; grant us strength for great joy and for sight. Grant us a share here of that most auspicious sap of yours, like longing mothers. To him for whose dwelling you quicken us, to him we come readily; O Waters, give us life.
Rest in heaven; strive in the intermediate space; unite with the earth. You are the splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcasa*); for the sake of the splendor of sacred knowledge, I take you.
5.6.2 Anuvāka 2: The Rule for Placing the Water-Jar Bricks (Kumbheṣṭakā).
He draws the cups of water.
Indeed, these cups are the Rājasūya; Agni is the consecration (sava).
The Varuṇasava is the Rājasūya, and the Agnisava is the piling of the fire-altar; by these two alone one is consecrated.
Moreover, he conquers both worlds: that which belongs to one who has performed the Rājasūya and that which belongs to one who has piled the fire-altar.
They become water.
Water, indeed, is the enemy of fire.
In that he places the waters beneath the fire, it is for the sake of overcoming his enemies.
He prospers by himself, while his rival is defeated;
for water is indeed immortality.
Therefore, they sprinkle water upon one who has been exhausted;
he does not meet with distress, he reaches a full lifespan—he for whom these [bricks] are laid down, and he who knows them thus.
Water, indeed, is food.
The waters are cattle;
cattle are food.
He who has these [bricks] laid down becomes an eater of food and possessed of cattle, as does he who knows them thus.
There are twelve;
there are twelve months in a year; by means of the year itself, for him—
He wins food;
there are vessels,
for in a vessel food is eaten.
Verily, he wins food from its own source;
he eats food for twelve generations of men, and moreover, his lineage is not cut off from the sacrificial vessels—he for whom these are laid down, and he who knows them thus.
The *kumbha* jars and the *kumbhī* pots form pairs.
For the procreation of the pair;
he is propagated with offspring, cattle, and pairs, for whom these are laid down and who knows them thus.
Agni is heat; he [the heat] afflicts the Adhvaryu, the sacrificer, and their offspring with pain.
In that he lays down the water-bricks, he pacifies his very heat.
Neither the Adhvaryu nor the sacrificer suffers distress; the offspring become peaceful when these [bricks] are laid down.
These waters are indeed the hearts of the waters;
in that he lays down these waters, he unites them with the celestial waters, and Parjanya becomes bountiful.
Whoever knows the foundation and the arrangement of these [bricks] becomes possessed of a foundation; for him, everything is arranged. He places them following the furrow.
This indeed is their abode, this is their arrangement.
He who knows thus becomes possessed of an abode; it is arranged for him.
He places the others in pairs, four in the middle, for the sake of support.
Or rather, the bricks are food;
for this oblation-pot (caru) is indeed food manifest.
In that he places this oblation-pot, [he places it] manifestly.
In this way he wins food for him;
he places it in the middle,
and thus he bestows food upon him in the very center.
Therefore, food is eaten from the middle;
it belongs to Bṛhaspati,
for Bṛhaspati is indeed the Brahman among the gods.
"By means of the *brahman* alone, he wins food for himself;
'Thou art luster of the *brahman*, for the sake of luster of the *brahman* thee,' he says;
he becomes radiant and possessed of the luster of the *brahman* for whom this [brick] is laid down, and also for whoever knows it thus."
5.6.3 Anuvāka 3: The Rule for Designating the Bhūteṣṭakā Bricks and Others.
He lays down the bhūteṣṭakā bricks.
For death is born here, indeed, in each place.
Wherever death arises, from that very place he sacrifices him away;
therefore, the builder of the fire-altar (agnicit) reaches a full lifespan, for all his deaths have been warded off.
Therefore, the builder of the fire-altar must not practice sorcery; sorcery turns back and strikes down the one who practices it against him.
He who piles the fire-altar is indeed consecrated;
these are the oblations of the Devasū,
for there are just so many consecrations of the gods.
They themselves bestow these consecrations upon him;
they consecrate him.
The Agni [altar] is the Varuṇasava, the Rājasūya; the built [altar] is the Brahmasava.
"At the impulse of the god Savitṛ," he says; thus, impelled by Savitṛ, he consecrates him with the sacred word (brahman) and with the deities.
He sprinkles him with every kind of food for the attainment of every kind of food;
he sprinkles him from the front toward the west.
For food is eaten from the front facing backward;
he sprinkles from the head,
for food is eaten from the head.
He causes it to flow down along the face until the mouth.
Verily, he bestows upon him food from the very mouth.
"I consecrate you with the sovereignty of Agni," he says;
for this indeed is the impulse of Agni.
With that very [substance] he sprinkles him,
saying, "O Bṛhaspati, I sprinkle thee with sovereignty";
for Bṛhaspati is the Brahman among the gods.
He consecrates him with the very Brahman.
"I consecrate you with the sovereignty of Indra," he says;
thus he bestows power upon him from above.
This indeed is the form of the Rājasūya.
He who, knowing thus, piles the fire-altar, conquers both worlds: that of one who has performed the Rājasūya and that of one who has piled the fire-altar.
When Indra was consecrated, his tenfold power and vigor flew away;
the gods gathered it together by means of the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice. Indeed, he who piles the fire-altar is consecrated.
Having piled the fire-altar, he should sacrifice with the Sautrāmaṇī; thus, having gathered sensory power and vigor, he places them within himself.
5.6.4 Anuvāka 4: Designation of the Oblations In harmony with the year and its months; in harmony with the dawn and its ruddy rays.
In harmony with Sūrya and Etaśa, in unison with the Aśvins through their wondrous deeds, may Agni Vaiśvānara be united with the Iḍā invocations.
With ghee, Svāhā! The year is indeed the *abda*;
the months are the *ayāvas*.
Uṣas is ruddy; Sūrya is Etaśa; these two are the Aśvins.
The year is Agni Vaiśvānara;
cattle are the *iḍā*,
and cattle are the clarified butter.
Cattle are born after the year;
verily, by means of the year, he causes cattle to be born for him;
he offers in a clump of darbha grass.
Whatever immortality or whatever vigor belongs to her, that is the *darbha* grass; into it he offers the oblation.
He is indeed born and becomes an eater of food for whom they offer in this manner.
These deities are indeed the portions belonging to Agni’s front; he thus gratifies them.
Moreover, he places the eye itself in front of the fire;
he who knows thus becomes free from blindness.
In the beginning, this world was indeed water, a vast expanse.
That Prajāpati, having become wind, fluttered upon the lotus leaf;
he found no firm support.
He saw this nest of the waters;
upon it he piled the fire-altar,
and that became this earth.
Thereupon he indeed stood firm.
That which he placed in front became his head; that was the eastern direction.
That which he placed on the south became his right wing; that was the southern direction.
That which he placed in the west became the tail; it was the western direction.
That which he placed in the north became the northern wing; it was the northern direction.
That which he placed on top became the back; that is the upward direction.
This Agni consists of five bricks; therefore, when they dig into this earth, they strike against a brick and strike against pebbles.
Indeed, this [earth] shines for all birds to see at night;
therefore, birds do not sit upon it at night.
He who, knowing thus, piles the fire-altar, truly gains [the earth].
He stands firm and conquers the quarters.
The Brāhmaṇa indeed belongs to Agni;
therefore, for a Brāhmaṇa, it is unprosperous in all directions.
He follows that very same direction.
Water, indeed, is the nesting place of Agni;
therefore, water seeks to swallow Agni.
They enter that very womb of their own.
5.6.5. The designation of certain oblations:

Having maintained the fire-pan (ukhya) for one year, in the second year he should offer an eight-potherd cake to Agni, an eleven-potherd cake to Indra, a twelve-potherd cake to the Viśve Devas, a pap (caru) to Bṛhaspati, and a three-potherd cake to Viṣṇu.
In the third year, he should sacrifice with the Abhijit rite.

In that it consists of eight potsherds— the *gāyatrī* has eight syllables, and the morning pressing belongs to Agni and the *gāyatrī*— he thereby supports the morning pressing and the *gāyatrī* metre.

In that it consists of eleven potsherds— the *triṣṭubh* has eleven syllables, and the midday pressing belongs to Indra and the *triṣṭubh*— [he thereby supports the midday pressing and the *triṣṭubh* metre].
By that, he supports the midday pressing and the *triṣṭubh* metre.
In that there is an offering on twelve potsherds— the *jagatī* consists of twelve syllables, and the third pressing belongs to the Viśvedevas and is of the *jagatī* nature— [he thereby supports it].
By that, he indeed supports the third pressing and the *jagatī* metre.
In that there is a pap for Bṛhaspati— Bṛhaspati being the sacred power (*brahman*) among the gods— he thereby supports the sacred power itself.
In that the cake for Viṣṇu consists of three potsherds— Viṣṇu being the sacrifice—
he thereby supports the sacrifice itself; and in that he sacrifices with the Abhijit in the third year, it is for the sake of conquest.
In that he carries the fire-pan for a year, he thereby wins this very world;
in that he piles the fire-altar in the second year, he thereby wins the intermediate space.

In that he sacrifices in the third year, he thereby wins that very world. Para Āṭṇāra, Kakṣīvān Auśija, Vītahavya Śrāyasa, and Trasadasyu Paurukutsya—these, desiring offspring, built this [fire-altar];
thereafter, they indeed obtained a thousand sons each.
He prospers with offspring and cattle; he attains that same measure which those who knew thus attained when they piled the fire.
5.6.6 Anuvāka 6: Praise of the previously mentioned ritual procedure.
Prajāpati piled the fire-altar;
it stood there having become a razor-edged [weapon].
The gods approached him in fear; having covered themselves with the *chandas*, they approached him, and that is the reason for the *chandastva* (the nature of being *chandas*) of the *chandas*.
The meters are indeed Brahman; the black antelope skin is the form of Brahman.
He puts on two sandals made of black antelope skin; having thus covered himself with the meters, he approaches the fire for his own protection.
Agni is indeed deposited as a treasure for the gods.
Others indeed find an unprotected treasure, or he does not recognize it at all. He steps onto the fire-pan; thus he makes himself the guardian for its protection.
Moreover, they say:
"One should not step upon it," [says] Nirṛti;
for if one were to step upon it, one would deliver oneself to Nirṛti. Therefore, one should not step upon it.
He places the human head [on the altar] for protection.
Furthermore, it is just as if one were to say, "Guard this for me"; such indeed is that.
Prajāpati is indeed Atharvan;
Agni himself is Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa, and his bones are the bricks.
Regarding this, the seer indeed spoke thus:
"Indra [repaired] with the bones of Dadhyanc.
When one piles the fire-altar with bricks, one piles the fire as something possessing its very self.
He who knows this becomes possessed of a self in that world.
This altar which is built is indeed the body of Agni; Vaiśvānara is the self.
When one offers to Vaiśvānara upon the built altar, it is as if one has refined the very body.
When the sacrificer piles the fire-altar, he prepares this body;
when he offers the Vaiśvānara oblation upon it having been piled, he mounts that very prepared body by means of his self.
Therefore, they do not cut it away; while still alive, he indeed goes even to the gods.
With a verse addressed to Vaiśvānara, he places the loose soil;
for this earth is indeed Agni Vaiśvānara.
Its layering is this: the loose soil;
verily, he piles Agni Vaiśvānara. Vaiśvānara is indeed this dear body of Agni.
He wins his very dear body.
5.6.7 Anuvāka 7: The Rule for the Options Regarding Consecration (Dīkṣā).
By means of the consecration of Agni, the gods attained the Virāj;
one should remain consecrated for three nights.
One attains the Virāj consisting of three feet;
one should remain consecrated for six nights.
Or, the year consists of six seasons; the year attains the Virāj.
He should remain consecrated for ten nights;

the Virāj consists of ten syllables; he attains the Virāj. He should remain consecrated for twelve nights; twelve months make a year; the year is the Virāj; he attains the Virāj. He should remain consecrated for thirteen nights; thirteen months make a year.
He should remain consecrated for fifteen nights of the year,
for there are indeed fifteen nights in a half-month.
By means of half-months, the year is attained;
the year attains the Virāj.
One should remain consecrated for seventeen nights.
Twelve months and five seasons constitute that year;
[that is] the year.
He attains the Virāj; he should be consecrated for twenty-four nights.
Twenty-four half-months make a year.
The year attains the Virāj;
one who is consecrated should remain so for thirty nights.
One who is consecrated for a month attains the Virāj, which consists of thirty syllables.
That which is the month is the year; the year attains the Virāj.
He should remain consecrated for four months.
For it was the Vasus who bore him for four months; they won the earth and the Gāyatrī metre.
The eight Rudras won the intermediate space and the Triṣṭubh metre.

The twelve Ādityas conquered the sky and the Jagatī metre; from that, they indeed attained distinction and preeminence among the gods. Therefore, one should pile the fire-altar after having observed twelve months.
Twelve months are a year;
the year is the piled fire-altar;
its bricks are the days and nights.
He piles this altar with bricks obtained from trustworthy sources; thus he attains distinction and preeminence among his equals.
5.6.8 Anuvāka 8: Designation of the Anvārohaṇa and other rites.
This Agni is built for the sake of the heavenly world;
if one were not to ascend after it, the sacrificer would be excluded from the heavenly world.
I have stepped upon the earth; may my vital breath not forsake me.
I have stepped upon the intermediate space; may my progeny not forsake me. I have stepped upon the sky; we have gone to the light of heaven.
Thus he says:
"This indeed is the mounting after Agni; by that very means he mounts after him."
For the attainment of the heavenly world:
if one were to erect [the sacrificial post] commensurate with the wingspan,
he would enter upon a lesser sacrificial rite, and his offspring would become more wretched than himself.
He measures it equal to the altar; thus he attains a more excellent sacrificial rite,
and his offspring does not become worse than himself.
One building the altar for the first time should pile it with a thousand bricks;
for this world is measured by a thousand;
verily, he conquers this very world.

One building the second [altar] should pile it with two thousand [bricks]; the intermediate region indeed consists of two thousand; verily, he conquers the intermediate region. One building the third [altar] should pile it with three thousand [bricks].
This world is indeed a triple-thousandfold; he conquers this very world.
One who is building for the first time should pile [the altar] knee-deep;
by means of the Gāyatrī, he ascends to this world.
One building a second altar should not build it reaching up to the navel;
by means of the Triṣṭubh meter, he ascends to the intermediate space.
One building a third altar should build it reaching up to the neck.
By means of the *jagatī* [meter] alone he ascends to this world;
having piled the fire-altar, he should not approach a woman, thinking, "I shall deposit seed in what is not a womb," nor, having piled it a second time, should he approach the wife of another.
He may approach [a woman].
But having piled the third fire-altar, he must not approach any woman at all.
For in piling the fire-altar, he deposits his seed.
If he were to approach [his wife], he would be deprived of semen;
yet, on the other hand, they say that it would lead to childlessness if he were not to approach her.
In that he places two *retaḥsic* bricks, these two indeed sustain the seed of the sacrificer;
therefore, one should approach [his wife] for the sake of preventing the emission of seed.
There are indeed three kinds of seed: the father, the son, and the grandson.
If he were to place two semen-shedders (retaḥsic), he would cut off his semen;
he places three for the continuity of the semen.
This first semen-shedder is indeed this [earth]; this is speech, therefore people see her as visible and hear her as speaking.
The intermediate space is the second; the breath indeed is the intermediate space, therefore they do not see the intermediate space, nor do they see the breath.
That [sky] is the third; the eye indeed is that [sky], therefore they see that [sky], for they see the eye.
And with a *yajus*-formula, these two [earth and sky].
He places this one with the mind;
it is for the establishment of these worlds,
and also for the vital breaths.

"The sacrifice has been offered by the Bhṛgus; may I here partake of the wealth of that sacrifice which has been offered and enjoyed, accompanied by blessings from the Vasus"—thus he says, for by this he milks out both the *stotra* and the *śastra*.
"Pitṛ Mātariśvan has laid down flawless steps; the Uśijs have fashioned flawless steps. "May Soma, the all-knowing leader, lead us; may Bṛhaspati recite the hymns and songs of praise"—thus he says.
This indeed is the hymn (uktha) of Agni;
with that very hymn he recites after him.
5.6.9 Anuvāka 9: Designation of the Seat and Other Implements He who is carried in the fire-pan (ukhā) is indeed consecrated among the fires.
If he were to set it down on the ground, the embryos would be born prematurely.
Moreover, it is just as when one descends from the *sava* sacrifice;
he sets down the stool for the support of embryos and so they do not fall.
Furthermore, he thus makes this very [offering] a *sava*.
The fire-pan (ukhā) is indeed the embryo, and the sling (śikya) is the womb. If one were to pull the pan out from the sling, one would strike the embryo out from the womb.
Therefore, the sling has six suspension-strands.
Man is indeed constituted of six parts: the self, the head, and the four limbs;
he thus sustains him within his own self.
Agni is indeed Prajāpati;
his fire-pan and mortar are his two breasts,
and upon them his offspring subsist.
In that he places both the fire-pan and the mortar, by means of these two the sacrificer milks the fire in yonder world.
This Agni is indeed the year;
its bricks are distributed in three ways: those belonging to Prajāpati and those belonging to Viṣṇu.
They belong to Viśvakarman.
His days and nights are those belonging to Prajāpati. In that he carries the fire in the pan, he thus lays down those very bricks belonging to Prajāpati.
In that he places the fuel-sticks— the trees belong to Viṣṇu—
he thus lays down what belongs to Viṣṇu; and in that he piles the fire-altar with bricks, this earth is indeed Viśvakarman.
Thus he places those bricks belonging to Viśvakarman;
therefore they say, "Agni is threefold."
The sacrificer himself should build that very altar;
for if another were to build it for him, and he were not to satisfy that person with sacrificial gifts, that other person would seize his fire.
Therefore, he should satisfy with sacrificial gifts whoever builds his fire-altar.
Thus, he preserves Agni himself.
5.6.10 Anuvāka 10:
Various Praises of the Piling of the Fire-altar.
Prajāpati piled the fire-altar by means of the seasons for the sake of the year.
With spring alone he built its fore-part;
with summer, the right wing;
with the rainy season, the tail.
The latter fortnight of autumn;
with winter he built its middle part, or rather, with Brahman he built its eastern half.
The right wing with the Kṣatra,
the tail with the Paśus, and the left wing with the Viś.
The middle layer is the intention.
He who, knowing thus, piles the fire, piles it by means of the seasons; moreover, he preserves all this.
They encompass him; they hear him as he has piled the fire-altar; he eats food.
It is pleasing.
This first layer is indeed the plants and the trees; the loose soil is the atmosphere; the second layer is the birds; the loose soil is [the atmosphere].
The third is the lunar mansions; the loose soil is the fourth, the sacrifice; the sacrificial fee is the fifth, the loose soil;
the sacrificer is the sixth, the offspring; the loose soil is the seventh.
If one were to pile [the altar] with three layers, he would exclude the sacrifice, the sacrificial fee, himself, and his offspring; therefore, it should be piled with five layers.
In this way, he secures all of this.
That there are three layers.
For Agni is threefold;
there are two [bricks] for the sacrificer, who has two feet, for the sake of stability; there are five layers.
Man is fivefold; he thus preserves his very self. There are five layers.
He covers it with five layers of soil;
they amount to ten,
for man consists of ten syllables.
As much as a person [is], that much he gains;
moreover, food consists of ten syllables.
Verily, he finds support in the Virāj and in the eating of food; the sixth layer is indeed the year,
and the loose soil is the seasons.
There are six layers and six fillings;
they amount to twelve,
and the year consists of twelve months.
Verily, he finds firm support in the year itself.
5.6.11 Anuvāka 11: Designation of the First Group of Eighteen Animals.
The red, the smoke-colored red, and the jujube-colored red—these belong to Prajāpati.
The brown, the reddish-brown, and the parrot-brown—these belong to Rudra.
A white one with white eyes and a white neck—these three are dedicated to the Pitṛs; three black barren cows are dedicated to Varuṇa; and three white barren cows are dedicated to Sūrya.
The Maitrābārhaspatya animals are hornless oxen with smoke-colored marks on their foreheads.
5.6.12 Anuvāka 12: Designation of the second group of eighteen sacrificial animals.
The speckled, the cross-speckled, and the upward-speckled—these belong to the Maruts.
The pale, the red-wooled, and the white-eyed—these belong to Sarasvatī.

The spotted cow, the large-spotted cow, and the small-spotted cow—these three belong to the Viśvedevas; three dark cows that have not calved belong to Pūṣan; and three red cows that have not calved belong to Mitra.
To Indra and Bṛhaspati are [dedicated] hornless goats with reddish marks on their foreheads.
5.6.13 Anuvāka 13: Designation of the Third Group of Eighteen Animals.
Those with white forelegs, those with white forelegs on one side, and those with white forelegs all around—these are for Indra and Vāyu.
Those with white nostrils, those with white nostrils on one side, and those with white nostrils all around—these are for Mitra and Varuṇa.
Śuddhavāla, Sarvaśuddhavāla, and Maṇivāla are for the Aśvins; three barren cows are for the Śilpas;
and three tawny ones are for Parameṣṭhin.
The animals dedicated to Soma and Pūṣan are dark-spotted, hornless, and shaggy.
5.6.14 Anuvāka 14: The enumeration of groups of four animals with eighteen ribs.
The humpbacked, the bull, and the dwarf—these are for Indra and Varuṇa.
The white-humped, the white-backed, and the white-rumped—these are for Indra and Bṛhaspati.
One with white feet, one with white lips, and one with white eyebrows—these three are for Indra and Viṣṇu;
three speckled barren cows are for Viśvakarman;
and hornless ones with white spots on their foreheads are for Dhātṛ and Pūṣan.
5.6.15 Anuvāka 15: A designation of groups of animals with eighteen parts; three black-eared deer, three *saumya* antelopes, three *śvitiṅga* antelopes for Agni Yaviṣṭha, and three mongooses.
Three ruddy ones with three-year-old calves belong to the Vasus;
three reddish-brown ones with two-year-old calves belong to the Rudras; those with brown spots on their foreheads and hornless are for Soma and Indra.
5.6.16 Anuvāka 16: Designation of the Sixteenth Group of Eighteen Animals.
Three *śuṇṭha* animals are for Viṣṇu;
three *adhīlodhakarṇa* animals are for Viṣṇu Urukrama.
Three years-old calves are for the three Viṣṇus; twenty-five for the wide-striding one; three for the Ādityas; and three yearlings for the Aṅgirases.
To Indra and Viṣṇu belong the white-spotted hornless oxen.
5.6.17 Anuvāka 17: A designation of groups of seven animals with eighteen parts.
Three white-backed animals for Indra the King;
three white-humped animals for Indra the Overlord.
For Indra the self-ruler, three white-bellied cows;
for the Sādhyas, three four-year-old heifers;
for the Viśvedevas, three six-year-old heifers.
Those dedicated to Agni and Indra are black-spotted and hornless.
5.6.18 Anuvāka 18: The Eighteenth Section, Designating the Group of Eight Animals.
Three reddish-brown ones for Aditi;
three black-and-white ones for Indrāṇī.
Three heifers for Aruṇaitā,
three milch-cows for Rākā, and three oxen for Sinīvālī.
For the offering to Agni and Viṣṇu, there are hornless bulls with red marks on their foreheads.
5.6.19 Anuvāka 19: A designation of groups of nine animals with eighteen parts; three tawny ones for Soma;
three dappled ones for King Soma.
Three goats with woolly dewlaps belong to Pārjanya and have the appearance of the sky; three ewes belong to Indrāṇī; [and] the Ādityas [have] three [goats].
The hornless goats for Heaven and Earth.
5.6.20 Anuvāka 20: The enumeration of the group of ten animals with eighteen characteristics.
Three black-spotted on the forehead for Varuṇa;
three red-spotted on the forehead for Varuṇa the King.
Three for Varuṇa, the destroyer of enemies; three with reddish marks on their foreheads for Śilpa; three for the Viśve Devas;
and three speckled ones for all the gods.
To Indra and Sūrya belong hornless rams with white spots on their foreheads.
5.6.21 Anuvāka 21: Designation of Pairs of Animals. For Soma, the self-ruling king, two oxen that draw a cart;
for Indra and Agni, the givers of vigor, two camels.
Two sheep, providers of strength for Indra and Agni;
two milch-cows, belonging to the earth;
a mare from the quarters.
Two cows are from the earth,
belonging to Vairāja; two cows are from the earth, belonging to Puruṣa.
To Vāyu, two oxen for ascending;
to Varuṇa, two black cows that come of their own accord; two divine bulls, Arāḍyas, for Parimarā.
5.6.22 Anuvāka 22:
Designation of the Seasonal Animals.
Eleven bovine animals are offered in the morning.
The spotted goat, the *kikidīvi*, and the *vidīgaya*—these belong to Tvaṣṭṛ; nine white barren cows dedicated to Sūrya are the *anūbandhyā* victims.
A victim for Agni, one for Indra-Agni, and one for the Aśvins are sacrificed at the broad sacrificial post (*viśālayūpa*).
5.6.23 Anuvāka 23: Designation of the Seasonal Animals. Three tawny ones are for the spring; three spotted antelopes are for the summer.
Three spotted ones are for the rainy season;
three speckled ones are for the autumn;
three with speckled thighs are for the winter.
The three Śaiśira [months] are anointed,
with their chests pressed together for the sake of the year.
Prapāṭhaka 5.7, Anuvāka 1: Designation of the Touching of the Citis, etc.
He who piles the fire-altar not according to its deities is cut off from the deities and becomes worse off;
he who piles it according to its deities is not cut off from the deities and becomes more prosperous.
With a *gāyatrī* verse addressed to Agni, he should touch the first layer; with a *triṣṭubh*, the second; with a *jagatī*, the third; with an *anuṣṭubh*, the fourth; and with a *paṅkti*, the fifth.
Thus he piles the fire-altar according to its respective deities; he is not cut off from the deities and becomes more prosperous.
This is indeed the distribution of the *iḍā*.
The sacrificial food is cattle;
with cattle he piles him up.
He who piles the fire-altar after having announced it to Prajāpati does not meet with calamity.
Two horses should stand on either side: a black one to the north and a white one to the south;
having touched them, he should lay down the bricks.
This indeed is the form of Prajāpati; the horse belongs to Prajāpati.
Having thus directly informed Prajāpati, he piles the fire-altar; he does not come to ruin.
Indeed, the white horse is the form of the day, and the black horse is the form of the night;
the brick is the form of the day, and the loose earth is the form of the night.
When about to lay down the bricks, he should touch a white horse; when about to lay down the loose earth, a black one.
Thus he piles it by means of day and night.
He gives a golden vessel filled with honey.
Thinking, "May I be worthy of honey," he gazes at two sun-deities verses containing the word *citra*;
thus, at midday, he indeed becomes variegated.
He causes the horse to smell [the offering].
Yonder sun is indeed Indra; he is Prajāpati, and the horse belongs to Prajāpati.
He prospers directly through that very [person].

5.7.2 Anuvāka 2: Designation of the Bull-Brick and Others O Agni, bull, you who are observant, I have approached you, generating you again as a youth. May our household duties not be deficient; sharpen us with your keen sacred word (*brahman*).
These bricks are indeed cattle; in each layer he places a bull. He thus creates a pair for him in the sacrifice for the sake of procreation; therefore, in every herd there is a bull.
"O Night, you whom they worship as the image of the year—having made [us] rich in offspring and heroes, may we attain a full lifespan."
He places this brick belonging to Prajāpati;
for this Ekāṣṭakā is indeed this earth. Whatever food is prepared on the Ekāṣṭakā, that he wins by means of this [brick].
This is indeed Prajāpati’s wish-fulfilling cow; by means of her, the sacrificer milks Agni in yonder world.
By which path the gods went upward to the light, by which the Ādityas, Vasus, and Rudras [went], and by which the Aṅgirases attained greatness—by that may the sacrificer go in safety.
This Agni is indeed built for the sake of the heavenly world.
With the words, "By which light the gods rose upwards," he kindles the fire-pan (ukhya); he thus places these very bricks made of wood for the attainment of the heavenly world.

To him who has a hundred weapons, a hundred powers, a hundred aids, the overcomer of enemies—may that Indra lead us, unvanquished through a hundred autumns, beyond all difficulties. The four paths leading to the gods which extend between heaven and earth—of these, may he who brings freedom from injury and freedom from defeat grant them to us; O all you gods, entrust us to him here.

May summer, winter, spring, autumn, and the rainy season be auspicious for us. In the shelter and fearlessness of these seasons, which last for a hundred autumns, may we abide. Offer great homage to the *iduvatsara*, the *parivatsara*, and the *saṃvatsara* year. May we long remain unvanquished and unhurt within the benevolent thought of those worthy of sacrifice. O Gods, you have led us from good to better; through your protection, may we attain you. Enter into us, O Food, as a source of bliss; be gracious and gentle to our children and our bodies.
He places these [bricks] with the *ajyāni* formulas; these deities are indeed unconquered, and he enters into them and is never conquered.
The exponents of sacred knowledge (*brahmavādinaḥ*) say:
"Since the half-months, months, seasons, and the year cause the plants to ripen, why then is the *āgrayaṇa* offering set aside for other deities?"
For these deities indeed won that [victory]; if one were to offer [the oblations] for the seasons, he would cause strife among the deities.
Having offered the Āgrayaṇa, he offers these oblations;
thus he gratifies the half-months, the months, the seasons, and the year, and he does not cause strife among the deities.
"O gods, you have led us from good to better," he says for the sake of the sacrificer's eating the oblation and for his non-defeat.

5.7.3 Anuvāka 3: The Rule for the Laying of the Vajriṇī Bricks Thou art the thunderbolt of Indra, the slayer of Vṛtra, our body-protector, our scout. Whoever, seeking to do us harm, assails us from the east, from the south, from the west, or from the north—may he strike against this stone.
The gods and the asuras were arrayed for battle; those asuras oppressed them from all directions, and the gods drove them away with arrows and with the thunderbolt.
In that he lays down the *vajriṇī* bricks, the sacrificer thereby repels his rivals with both the *iṣu* and the *vajra*; he lays them down in the quarters.
Verily, he piles these body-protecting bricks around the divine city:
"O Agni and Viṣṇu, being of one accord, may these songs increase you; come hither with splendors and with strengths!"
The exponents of Brahman say: "Since one does not offer to a deity [in this case], then to which deity does the *vasordhārā* belong?
Agni is the *vasu*; this stream belongs to him."
Viṣṇu is the Vasu; this is his stream.
With a verse addressed to Agni and Viṣṇu, he offers the Vasordhārā; verily, by means of their respective portions, he causes these two to prosper together.
Moreover, he makes this very oblation possessed of a foundation;
whatever desire he offers it with, that very thing he attains.
Agni, indeed, is Rudra;
he has two bodies: one is terrible, the other is auspicious.
When he offers the Śatarudrīya, he pacifies that body of his which is terrible.
In that he offers the stream of wealth (vasordhārā), he thereby gratifies that body of his which is auspicious.
Verily, he who knows the foundation of the stream of wealth stands firm.
Whatever clarified butter remains, in that one should cook the *brahmaudana* (the rice for the Brahman); four Brahmins should consume it.
For the Brahmin is indeed Agni Vaiśvānara.
Indeed, Vaiśvānara is this dear body of Agni;
he thus establishes her in his own dear body.
He should give four milch-cows as a gift.
By means of those very [cows], the sacrificer milks Agni in that world.
5.7.4 Anuvāka 4: The designation of the specific oblations for the *rāṣṭrabhṛt* bricks. "I offer consciousness with mind and ghee," he says.
This oblation for Viśvakarman is indeed called "unassailable" (adābhya);
once it has been piled, no rival can harm him.
Moreover, he wins the very deities themselves.

With the *paṅkti* verse, "O Agni, him today... he offers; by means of the *paṅkti* oblation, he undertakes the beginning of the sacrifice. He says, "Seven are your fuel-sticks, O Agni, seven your tongues."
Verily, he wins the offices of the Hotṛ-priests. Agni departed from the gods, seeking his own portion.
Therefore, they gave this as his portion.
This indeed is Agni’s Agnihotra;
for he is truly born at this time when he has been completely piled.
He provides food for him as soon as he is born; thus, being pleased, he makes him pleased, and he becomes more prosperous.
The exponents of Brahman say: "Since this Gārhapatya fire is piled, then where is its Āhavanīya?
One should reply: "That is the sun (āditya)," for in it they offer oblations to all the deities.

He who, knowing thus, piles the fire-altar, directly prospers through the deities. O glorious Agni, endow this man with glory; bring hither the honor associated with Indra. May he be the head, the supreme lord, full of splendor, and the one of highest renown among his peers.

Beholding what is auspicious, the seers who have found the light of heaven first resorted to fervor and consecration; from that, the ruling power, strength, and vital force were born—may the gods bow down before this for him.

The Ordainer, the Disposer, the Supreme Vision, Prajāpati, Parameṣṭhin, and Virāj; the Stomas, the Metres, and the Nivids—they say these belong to me. Let us bow down together before this sovereignty.
Turn back toward us; come together to us! May this one be your sovereign ruler. Agree with his will; all of you live hereafter following him.
He places these Rāṣṭrabhṛt bricks.
This indeed is the "kingdom-sustaining" piling of the fire-altar; by means of it, he bestows the kingdom upon him.
He indeed becomes the kingdom;
the kingdom does not fall away from him.
5.7.5 Anuvāka 5: A further statement on the rekindling and other rites.
Just as a son who is born dies, so indeed does he die whose *ukhya* fire goes out. If he were to produce a new fire by friction, he would cut off [the continuity] and generate a rival for himself.
That very [fire] is to be girded again;
verily he generates him from his own womb and does not generate a rival for him.
Darkness indeed seizes him whose fire in the pan goes out;
darkness is death.
A black garment and a black cow are the sacrificial fee.
By means of darkness alone he strikes down the darkness that is death;
he gives gold.
Gold is indeed light;
by means of light itself, one strikes away the darkness.
Moreover, gold is indeed splendor.
He bestows splendor upon himself, like the heat of the sun, svāhā! Like the sun, svāhā! Like the bright one, svāhā! Like the light, svāhā! Like the sun, svāhā!
This Agni is indeed the *arka*, and that is Āditya.
The Horse Sacrifice (*aśvamedha*).
In that he offers these oblations, he unites the lights of the *arka* and the *aśvamedha*.
He indeed becomes a performer of the *arka* and *aśvamedha* for whom this is performed in the fire.
In the beginning, this world was indeed water;
Prajāpati beheld this first layer and laid it down, and it became this earth.
Viśvakarman spoke to him.
"I am coming to you," he said;
"There is no world here," he replied.
He saw this second layer; he laid it down, and it became the intermediate space.
That sacrifice said to Prajāpati: "I will come to you."
"There is no world here," he said;
he then spoke to Viśvakarman, "I shall come to you."
"By what means will you approach me?
he asked; "By the quarters," he replied, and so he approached him by means of the quarters.
He deposited them;
they became the quarters.
They came into being.
That Parameṣṭhin said to Prajāpati: "I shall come to you."
"There is no world here," he said;
and he spoke to Viśvakarman and to the sacrifice, saying,
"I shall come to you."
"There is no world here," they said.
He saw this third layer;
he laid it down.
That became he;
he was Āditya. He said to Prajāpati: "Approach you."
"I shall come," he said; "there is no world here," he declared to Viśvakarman and to the sacrifice.
"I would come unto you," he said;
"There is no world here," they replied. He spoke to Parameṣṭhin.
"I shall come to you," he said.
"With what will you approach me? he asked.
"With the *lokampṛṇā* (space-filler) brick," he replied.
He approached it with the *lokampṛṇā* brick; therefore, the *lokampṛṇā* is of unexhausted power (*ayātayāmnī*). For that sun is indeed of unexhausted power.
The seers said to them:
"We approach you"—
"With what will you approach us?"—
"With abundance," they replied.
They approached them with two layers;
thus it became five-layered.
He who, knowing this, piles the fire-altar becomes greater indeed, he conquers these worlds, and the gods take note of him.
Moreover, he attains union with these very deities.
5.7.6 Anuvāka 6: Description of the Performance of Vows, etc.
Agni is indeed the bird; if one who has built the fire-altar (*agnicit*) should eat the flesh of a bird, he would be eating that very Agni and would meet with calamity.
He should observe the vow for a year.
For a year indeed is the vow;
this Agni is indeed an animal,
and an animal surely harms him who attends upon it from the front while facing away.
Therefore, having first performed the service from west to east for the sake of his own non-injury:
"Thou art brilliance; grant me brilliance; grant me the earth;

protect me from the earth. Thou art light; grant me light; grant me the intermediate space; protect me from the intermediate space. Thou art heaven; grant me heaven; grant me the sky; protect me from the sky."
Thus he says; for by these [bricks] indeed these worlds are held apart.
In that he lays them down, it is for the support of these worlds.
Having laid down the *svayamātṛṇṇā* bricks, he lays down the gold bricks; for the *svayamātṛṇṇā* bricks are these worlds, and gold is light.

In that he places the gold bricks after having laid down the naturally perforated stones, he thereby makes these worlds luminous; moreover, by means of these very bricks, these worlds shine forth for him.
O Agni, those splendors of yours which, when you rise as the sun, extend across the sky with your rays—with all of those, grant splendor to our people.
O gods, whatever splendors you possess in the sun, and whatever splendors are in the cattle and in the horses—with all those splendors, O Indra and Agni, and O Bṛhaspati, bestow splendor upon us.
Bestow radiance upon our Brahmins; grant us radiance among the kings. Grant radiance to the Vaiśyas and the Śūdras; through your radiance, bestow radiance upon me.
Or rather, the glory and vital power of one who has piled the fire-altar go in two directions— to the fire that has been piled and to the sacrificer who has performed the sacrifice.
When he offers these oblations,
he places glory and vital power within his own self.
"He who, while piling the fire-altar, steps over it, is indeed liable to misfortune;
therefore, [one should approach it] with this verse addressed to Varuṇa: 'This I implore of thee, adoring thee with a sacred prayer...'"
One should offer oblations; this is indeed peace, a protection for the fire and for oneself.
He who piles the fire-altar is indeed a preparer of the sacrificial offering (havis).

Just as a sacrificial offering spills, so does he spill who, having piled the fire-altar, approaches a woman. He should sacrifice with curdled milk (āmikṣā) dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa; thus he attains the state of Mitra and Varuṇa, to prevent spilling from himself.
He who knows Agni as established in the seasons—for him each season comes in due order—and he stands firm.
Indeed, Agni is the year established in the seasons;

his head is spring, his right wing is summer, his tail is the rainy season, his left wing is autumn, and his middle is winter. The bright fortnights are the layers (*citayaḥ*), the dark fortnights are the loose soil (*purīṣa*), and the days and nights are the bricks. This indeed is Agni established in the seasons; for him who knows thus, each season comes in due order, and he stands firm.
Prajāpati indeed deposited this [fire-altar] when he desired preeminence; from that, he attained preeminence.
He who, knowing thus, piles the fire-altar, attains preeminence.

5.7.7 Anuvāka 7: Designation of the Ākūti-mantras Whatever has flowed forth from intention, or has been gathered from the heart or from the mind, or from the eye—follow that toward the world of the well-done, where the seers are who were first-born and ancient. I entrust this to you, O place of assembly, whom Jātavedas has brought here as a treasure-store. The lord of the sacrifice shall follow you here; recognize him in the highest heaven. Let him recognize him in the highest heaven; O gods, fellow-dwellers, know his form when he arrives.
By the paths traveled by the gods, make his merit from sacrifices and charitable works manifest for him.

Move forward together! Follow along; O Agni, prepare the paths traveled by the gods. In this assembly place, in the highest one, sit down, all you gods and the sacrificer. By means of the sacrificial grass-stalk, the enclosing sticks, the offering-ladle, the altar, and the sacred straw—by means of the *ṛc*, carry this sacrifice of ours to the sun among the gods. Whatever has been sacrificed, whatever has been given away, whatever has been bestowed, and whatever sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) has been given—may Agni Vaiśvakarman establish that for us in the sun among the gods.

O Agni, by that [path] whereby thou carriest a thousand, and by that whereby thou carriest all possessions—by that carry this sacrifice of ours to the world of light (*suvar*) among the gods. O Agni, by that path whereby the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), being harnessed, cause the priests to carry the sacrifice—by that carry this sacrifice of ours to the world of light among the gods. O Agni, by that well-trodden path whereby the streams of honey have pervaded—by that carry this sacrifice of ours to the world of light among the gods. Where the streams of honey and of clarified butter (*ghṛta*) do not fail—that world of light among the gods, Agni Vaiśvakarman shall bestow upon us.

5.7.8 Anuvāka 8: Designation of the Self-Constructed Fire-altar and Other Terms O Agni, those logs of thine, those abodes, those tongues, O Jātavedas, that flame; those ladles of thine, O Agni, those drops—with these, knowing [the way], construct thyself.

This Agni is indeed one whose sacrifice has perished; what part of him is performed, and what is not? When the Adhvaryu passes between while piling the fire, he passes between his own self. [The priest recites: "O Agni, those logs of thine, those abodes... This is indeed Agni’s self-piling; thus it is Agni himself who piles Agni, and the Adhvaryu does not pass between his own self.

[He recites: "Let the four quarters proceed forth; may Agni lead this sacrifice of ours, knowing the way. Let him pour forth the imperishable ghee, rich in heroes; the *brahman* becomes the fuel for the oblations."
The tortoise is indeed laid down for the sake of the heavenly world.

"Let the four quarters proceed; let the fires go forth," he says; by this, he discerns the directions. "May he, knowing, lead this sacrifice of ours," he says, for the purpose of leading toward the heavenly world. "The *brahman* becomes the kindling-stick of the oblations," he says; for by means of the *brahman*, the gods went to the heavenly world. In that he lays it down with a verse containing the word *brahman*, the sacrificer goes to the heavenly world by means of the *brahman*.

This Agni is indeed Prajāpati; his offspring, cattle, and the meters are his form. One should make the bricks of all colors; by means of his very form, he wins offspring, cattle, and the meters. Thus, having won them for the offspring, the cattle, and the meters, he piles him up.
5.7.9 Anuvāka 9: Designation of the Taking of the Fire, etc.
I first take Agni within me for the increase of wealth, for good offspring, and for heroic vigor. I place progeny and luster within me; may we be unharmed in body and possessed of heroic sons.
O Fathers, that immortal Agni who has entered into us mortals within our hearts—him we embrace within ourselves; may he not depart from us, leaving us behind.

If the Adhvaryu were to pile the fire-altar without having taken the fire into himself, he would also pile for the sacrificer that fire which is his own; for cattle indeed follow after the fire, and cattle would be liable to depart from him. Therefore he says, "In me first I take Agni," and thus he establishes his own fire within himself, and cattle do not depart from him.
The exponents of the Veda say: "Since clay and water are not food for the fire, why then is the fire piled with clay and water? [The answer is: because he mixes [the clay] with water.

The waters are indeed all the deities; by means of the deities he unites him when he piles with clay. This earth is indeed Agni Vaiśvānara; it is by means of Agni that he thus piles Agni. The exponents of sacred knowledge say: "Since Agni is piled both with clay and with water, why then is he called 'Agni'? Because he piles with the *chandases* (metres), and the *chandases* are indeed Agnis, therefore he is called Agni. Furthermore, because this earth is Agni Vaiśvānara and he piles with clay, therefore he is called Agni.
He places gold bricks; gold is indeed light, so he places light in him. Moreover, gold is brilliance; he thus bestows brilliance upon himself.

Or, he who piles the fire-altar facing all directions eats food among all creatures and conquers all the quarters. He places a *gāyatrī* verse in the east, a *triṣṭubh* on the south, a *jagatī* in the west, an *anuṣṭubh* on the north, and a *paṅkti* in the middle. This indeed is the fire-altar facing all directions; he who, knowing thus, piles it, eats food among all creatures and conquers all the quarters. Moreover, he weaves quarter upon quarter; therefore, quarter is woven upon quarter.
5.7.10 Anuvāka 10: Designation of the Heads of the Sacrificial Animals.
Prajāpati created Agni;
once created, he ran away from him toward the east. He threw a horse at him.
He turned toward the south; he threw a ram at him.
He turned toward the west; he threw a bull at him.
He turned toward the north; he threw a goat at him.
He ran upwards; he threw a man toward him.
In that he places the heads of the animals, he piles [the fire-altar] having enclosed it on every side.
These animal heads are indeed life-sustaining bricks possessed of sight;
in that he places the animal heads, it is by means of them that the sacrificer breathes in yonder world. Moreover, it is by means of them that these worlds shine forth for him.
He places them after smearing them with clay, for the sake of purity.
Agni is indeed an animal, and animals are food;
for this Agni is indeed the heads of the animals.
Whomever one might desire—
"If his food were to become less," [thinking thus], he should place the animal heads closer together; for him whom [the priest] so desires, his food indeed becomes less.
Thinking, "May his food be equal," he should place [the bricks] in the middle for him; thus his food becomes equal.

If he should desire of someone, "May his food be more," he should place them for him by pushing them out toward the ends; thus he secures food for him from the very ends, and his food becomes more abundant.
5.7.11 Anuvāka 11: Designation of the Mantras Constituting Parts of the Aśvamedha Sacrifice.
With your two tusks, [seize] the *stega* snakes; with your jaws, the frogs.
May water be obtained through the *khāda* fruit; may vigor be obtained through the *saṃsūda* fruit; may the forest be obtained through the *jāmbīla* fruit.
[Cover] the clay with reeds,
the gravel with *avakā* plants,
and the *avakā* plants with gravel.
One should worship Utsāda with the tongue,
Avakranda with the palate, and Sarasvatī with the tip of the tongue.
Anuvāka 12: The recitation of the mantras contained in the previously mentioned second Anuvāka: "May I win strength with my jaws, and water with my mouth."
The Ādityas [are satisfied] by the beard;
the cup is held with the lower lip, and the seat with the upper lip.
The internal by means of the space between,
the external by means of light; the thunder by means of the unobstructed.
The sun and fire [he places] in the two eyes;
lightning in the two temples; the thunderbolt in the brain; and strength in the marrow.
5.7.13 Anuvāka 13: The recitation of the mantras contained in the previously mentioned third anuvāka:
[one should offer] tortoises with their hooves;
[one should offer] francolins with their throats.
Soma with the thumbs;
speed with the shanks;
freedom from disease with the knees.
Vigor from the two elbows;
fear from the two shoulders; the secret place from the two armpits.
The Aśvins with the two shoulders;
Aditi with the head; Nirṛti with the bald head.
5.7.14 Anuvāka 14: The recitation of the mantras contained in the previously mentioned fourth anuvāka; [the rite] with the yoktra and the vultures; [the rite] with the yoke and the bent one.
The mind [is purified] by the neck-tendons,
the vital breaths by the joints,
and the skin by light.
With the outer space as the interior,
with gnats and hair,
with Indra, with the skillful steed.
Bṛhaspati with the Śakunisāda [hymn], and the chariot with the Uṣṇih verses.
5.7.15 Anuvāka 15: The recitation of the mantras contained in the previously mentioned fifth anuvāka:
"Mitra and Varuṇa [are assigned] to the two hips;
Indra and Agni to the two tufts of hair."
Indra and Bṛhaspati from the thighs;
Indra and Viṣṇu from the kneecaps; Savitṛ by means of the tail.
The Gandharvas with the penis;
the Apsarases with the testicles;
Pavamāna with the anus.
The purifier is for the two *potr* [feet];
the stepping forward is for the two *sthūra* [ankles]; the stepping back is for the two *kuṣṭha* [heels].
5.7.16 Anuvāka 16: The mantras contained in the previously mentioned sixth anuvāka are designated as the breast of Indra;
the belly belongs to Aditi.
The clavicles are the quarters;
the clouds [are the body] by means of the heart and the two flanks;
the atmosphere is the skin.
The sky with the stomach;
Indrāṇī with the spleen;
anthills with the lungs.
The mountains with his limbs,
the ocean with his belly,
and Vaiśvānara with his ashes.
5.7.17 Anuvāka 17: A statement of the mantras contained in the previously mentioned seventh anuvāka. The rectum belongs to Pūṣan; the thick intestines belong to Andhāhas.
The serpents with the entrails;
the seasons with the ribs;
the sky with the back.
The first rib belongs to the Vasus, the second to the Rudras,
and the third to the Ādityas.
The fourth belongs to the Aṅgirases, the fifth to the Sādhyas, and the sixth to the Viśvedevas.
5.7.18 Anuvāka 18: Recitation of the mantras contained in the previously mentioned eighth anuvāka. "Vigor with the necks; Nirṛti with the bones."
Indra with his skillful vehicle;
the moving shoulder of Rudra;
the second of day and night.
The third of the half-months;
the fourth of the months;
the fifth of the seasons.
The sixth [month] of the year.
5.7.19 Anuvāka 19: The designation of the mantras contained in the previously mentioned ninth anuvāka, [accompanied] by Ānanda, Nandathu, Kāma, Prati, and Āsā.
I have warded off fear with the two cold ones; I have directed it away with the two directors; [I have warded it off] with the two wolves, [the two] Sūryā and Candramas.
Śyāma and Śabala [are] with the two kidneys;
Vyūṣṭi with form, and Nimrukti with formlessness.
5.7.20 Anuvāka 20: The recitation of the mantras contained in the previously mentioned tenth anuvāka:
"May [the day] come to me with flesh, and the night with fat."
Water with broth,
ghee with meat-broth, and fat with black gram soup.
With his spittle he [overcame] the thunderbolt, with his tears the mist,
and with his form the sky.
The constellations [cover] the earth with their likeness, as a skin covers the hide.
Svāhā to the one brought near;
svāhā to the one seized;
svāhā to the one offered as an oblation.
5.7.21 Anuvāka 21: A statement of the mantras contained in the eleven previously mentioned anuvākas;
[the mantra] for Agni is the wing-tip, and that for Sarasvatī is the inner wing-tip.
The third belongs to Soma;
the fourth to the Waters;
the fifth to the Plants.
The sixth [day] belongs to the Year,
the seventh to the Maruts, and the eighth to Bṛhaspati.
The ninth belongs to Mitra, the tenth to Varuṇa,
and the eleventh to Indra.
The twelfth [digit] belongs to the Viśvedevas; the side belongs to Heaven and Earth;
the rib belongs to Yama.
5.7.22 Anuvāka 22: A statement of the mantras contained in the twelve preceding anuvākas:
"Vāyu is the wing-base; Sarasvatī is the secondary wing."
The third [day] belongs to Candramas,
the fourth to the Nakṣatras, and the fifth to Savitṛ.
The sixth belongs to Rudra, the seventh to the serpents, and the eighth to Aryaman.
The ninth belongs to Tvaṣṭṛ, the tenth to Dhātṛ;
the eleventh belongs to Indrāṇī,
and the twelfth to Aditi.
The side of heaven and earth;
the rib for Yami.
5.7.23 Anuvāka 23: The recitation of the mantras contained in the thirteen preceding anuvākas—
[one] along the path with two verses,
[and] continuity with two [verses] on the sinews.
He turned the parrots yellow with bile, the peacocks green with the liver, and the pigeons grey with the evil wind.
With the entrails of the kūśma-fish for the Śakabhīs,
with the undigested contents for the Śvavartas,
and with the dissected parts for the Śunas.
The serpents [are attracted] by the smell of blood,
the birds by the smell of what is cooked, and the ants by the [sweet] sap.
5.7.24 Anuvāka 24: Enumeration of the mantras contained in the fourteen preceding anuvākas.
The steed has traversed beyond [the worlds] in due order, in harmony with all the gods worthy of sacrifice.
May he lead us to the world of the well-performed deed; may we rejoice in that [world] through your funeral offering (svadhā).
5.7.25 Anuvāka 25: Recitation of the mantras stated in the *Aśvamedha-brāhmaṇa* beginning with "The sky is your back.

The sky is your back, the earth is your seat, and the intermediate space is your self. The ocean is your womb; the sun is your eye; the wind is your breath; the moon is your hearing; the months and half-months are your joints; the seasons are your limbs; and the year is your majesty.
5.7.26 Anuvāka 26: The recitation of the mantras beginning with "Agni was the victim; with him they sacrificed," as spoken in the *Aśvamedha-brāhmaṇa*.
"Agni was the victim; with him they sacrificed."
He conquered this world in which Agni dwells;
that world is yours, and you shall conquer it.
Then indeed they smelled the wind; it was the sacrificial animal, with which they sacrificed.
He conquered this world in which Vāyu dwells;
that is your world,
therefore I shall enter within you if you do not snort at me.
The sun was the sacrificial animal; with it they sacrificed,
and he won this world in which the sun resides.
That world is yours; you shall conquer it if you smell it.
*Taittirīya Saṃhitā*, Book 6, Praśna 6.1, Anuvāka 1: The description of the entry into the *prāgvaṃśa* hall for one consecrated by rites such as shaving.
He makes the *prācīnavaṃśa* hall.
Gods and men divided the quarters among themselves.
The gods [occupy] the east, the ancestors the south, humans the west, and the Rudras the north.
In that he makes the sacrificial shed with its beams facing east, the sacrificer thereby approaches the world of the gods;
he encloses it on all sides.
For the world of the gods is hidden from the world of men;
they say that one should not go away from this world as if it were something familiar,
for who knows whether one exists in that world or not?
He makes openings toward the quarters for the conquest of both worlds; he shaves his hair and beard and clips his nails.
This skin—the hair of the head and the beard—is indeed dead and impure.
Having struck away that dead and impure skin, he becomes fit for sacrifice and approaches the sacrificial essence (*medha*).
When the Aṅgirases were going to the heavenly world, they caused the consecration (*dīkṣā*) and ascetic fervor (*tapas*) to enter into the waters.
He bathes in the waters;
verily, he directly obtains consecration and austerity;
he bathes at a sacred ford.
For they caused her to enter at a sacred ford;
he who bathes at a sacred ford becomes, among his peers, a sacred ford itself.
He drinks water; thus he becomes pure from within. He consecrates him with a garment.
Linen is indeed gentle by its divine nature;
he who undergoes consecration approaches the deity Soma.
"Thou art the body of Soma; protect my body," he says.
He approaches his very own deity;
furthermore, he invokes this very blessing.
The placing of the embers belongs to Agni.
The wind is the draught for the wind;
the girdle is for the ancestors;
the threshing floor is for the plants.
The eastern extension of the Ādityas;
the warp of the Viśvedevas;
the fringes of the Nakṣatras.
Now, this garment indeed belongs to all the deities;
when he consecrates him with a garment, he consecrates him with all the deities.
For man is indeed outside his vital breath.
Its eating is the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
He eats; thus, he undergoes consecration (*dīkṣā*) while indeed possessing the vital breath.
He becomes one who has eaten.
Whatever vital breath he has, with that he attains the sacrificial essence;
the clarified butter belongs to the gods, the whey to the ancestors.
It is fully cooked for human beings.
Indeed, this fresh butter belongs to all the deities.
When he anoints himself with fresh butter, he gratifies all the deities.
For one who is consecrated has departed from this world and has not yet arrived at the world of the gods;
fresh butter is indeed intermediate.
Therefore, he anoints [himself] with fresh butter,
following the natural direction of the hair,
with a sacrificial formula.
For the sake of turning away [evil].
Indra slew Vṛtra; his pupil flew away.
That became collyrium; by applying it, one indeed appropriates the sight of the rival. One applies the right eye first.
For men first anoint the left hand;
they do not wash it, for men indeed do not wash [the left].
He anoints five times;
the *paṅkti* consists of five syllables, and the sacrifice is fivefold.
Verily, he wins the sacrifice;
he anoints a measured amount,
for humans anoint a measured amount.
He anoints with the tufted [branch]; for humans anoint with the tuftless,
for the sake of distinction.
If one were to anoint with a brush without a tuft, it would be like a thunderbolt;
he anoints with a brush that has a tuft for the sake of friendship.
Indra slew Vṛtra.
He died within the waters;
whatever in them was pure, fit for sacrifice, and divine, emerged from the water, and that became *darbha* grass.
In that he purifies him with bunches of *darbha* grass, he purifies him with those very waters which are pure, fit for sacrifice, and accompanied by the gods; he purifies him with two [verses],
and thus he purifies him by means of day and night.
He purifies it with three [strainers];
these worlds are three; verily, by means of these worlds he purifies it.
He purifies with five;
the *paṅkti* consists of five syllables.
The sacrifice is fivefold;
he purifies him for the sake of the sacrifice; he purifies him with six [verses].
There are six seasons;
verily by means of the seasons he purifies him; he purifies him with seven [verses].
There are seven meters;
by means of the meters he purifies him. He purifies him with nine [verses].
There are indeed nine vital breaths in a person;
he thus purifies him together with his vital breath. He purifies him with twenty-one [verses].
There are ten fingers on the hand and ten toes on the feet; the self is the twenty-first.
As large as a person is, he purifies him entirely, leaving nothing behind.
"May Citpati purify you," he says; for Citpati is indeed the mind;
by means of the mind itself, he purifies him.
"May the Lord of Speech purify you," he says;
verily by speech he purifies him.
"May the god Savitṛ purify you," he says.
Impelled by Savitṛ, he purifies him;
"O Lord of the Purifier, with thy purifier, may I be able to accomplish that for which I purify myself," he says;
thus he invokes this very blessing.
6.1.2 Anuvāka 2: Designation of the Consecration Oblations As many gods as purified themselves for the sacrifice, they alone became [successful].
He who, knowing thus, purifies himself for the sacrifice, indeed becomes [successful].
Having purified him externally, he causes him to enter within; having purified him in the world of men, he leads him, purified, into the world of the gods.
"One who is not initiated [is purified] by a single oblation," they say.
He offers four oblations with the *sruva* ladle for the sake of consecration, and the fifth with the *sruc* ladle;
the *paṅkti* meter has five syllables, and the sacrifice is fivefold.
Verily, he wins the sacrifice itself.
"To Ākūti, to Prayuj, to Agni, svāhā! he says.
For with intention a man undertakes the sacrifice,
thinking "May I sacrifice"; he says, "To insight, to mind, to Agni, svāhā!"
"For by means of wisdom and the mind, a person approaches the sacrifice.
He says, "To Sarasvatī, to Pūṣan, to Agni, Svāhā!
Speech indeed is Sarasvatī; Pūṣan is the earth.
With speech alone he sets the sacrifice in motion upon the earth.
"The divine waters, vast, all-beneficent," he says;
for those which are of the rain, they are these.
"The divine waters, vast, bringing welfare to all"—
if he were not to recite this sacrificial formula (*yajus*), the unappeased celestial waters might come to this world.
"The divine waters, vast, bringing welfare to all," he says.
He pacifies them for this very world;
therefore, being pacified, they come to this world.
"O Heaven and Earth," he says.
"For the sacrifice belongs to heaven and earth. "The wide atmosphere," he says;
for the sacrifice is in the atmosphere.
"May Bṛhaspati increase us with the oblation," he says;
for Bṛhaspati is indeed the Brahman among the gods.
By means of the *brahman* alone he secures the sacrifice for him;
if he were to say "vidheḥ," he would strike against the sacrificial post (*yajñasthāṇu*).
"May he grow," he says; thus he avoids the pillar of the sacrifice.
Prajāpati created the sacrifice;
once created, it went away from him.
He pressed out the Yajus; he pressed out the Sāman;
the Ṛc raised it up.
Because the Ṛc raised it up, that is the reason for the name "audgrahaṇa" (the lifting-up).
He offers with a *ṛc* for the elevation of the sacrifice;
"The *anuṣṭubh* elevated among the meters," so they say.
Therefore, one offers with an *anuṣṭubh* verse for the sake of raising up the sacrifice;
"They raised twelve *vatsabandha* [cords] upwards," so they say.
Therefore, those who know the Vātsabandha consecrate with twelve [verses].
This very ṛc is an anuṣṭubh; speech is an anuṣṭubh.
In that he initiates him with this verse, he initiates him with his entire speech.
"Of every god who leads," he says; by this [verse], it belongs to Savitṛ. "A mortal should choose friendship."
Thus he says with this verse addressed to the Pitṛs; "Thou art seeking all riches," he says with this one addressed to the Viśvedevas;
"May he choose glory, may he prosper," he says with this one addressed to Pūṣan.
This very ṛc is dedicated to all the deities;
when he consecrates him with this ṛc, he consecrates him with all the deities.
The first foot has seven syllables, and the [other] three have eight syllables each.
Those which are three become eight;
those which are four become eight; because it consists of eight syllables, by that [it is so].
The Gāyatrī: in that it has eleven syllables, it is the Triṣṭubh;
in that it has twelve syllables, it is the Jagatī. Indeed, this Ṛc is all the meters.
When he consecrates him with this verse, he consecrates him with all the meters;
the first foot has seven syllables,
and the Śakvarī consists of seven feet.
The Śakvarī verses are cattle;
verily he wins cattle.
The first foot is deficient by one syllable.
Therefore, humans subsist on that which is not fully contained in speech;
she offers with a full [ladle], for Prajāpati is, as it were, full.
He offers with a deficient [verse] for the attainment of Prajāpati; for from the deficient Prajāpati created offspring; it is for the creation of offspring.
6.1.3 Anuvāka 3: Description of the performance of the consecration (*dīkṣā*) with the black antelope skin and other implements.
The *Ṛc* and the *Sāman*, while refusing to submit to the sacrifice for the gods, departed and stood apart, having assumed the form of a black antelope.
They thought:

Thinking, "He who shall follow these two will become this," they invited them; having set aside the greatness of day and night, the two followed the gods. That which is white on the black antelope skin is indeed the color of the *Ṛc*;
that which is black is the color of the *Sāman*.
"You two are the crafts of the Ṛk and the Sāman," he says;
thus he wins the Ṛk and the Sāman themselves.
This...

The white color of the day is that of the black antelope skin, and the black is that of the night; whatever is inherent in these two, that he thereby obtains. He consecrates him with a black antelope skin; for the black antelope skin is the form of the Brahman; verily, by means of the Brahman, he consecrates him. "O God, [help] this prayer of one who strives," he says; this is according to the sacrificial formula.
The consecrated one is indeed an embryo; he wraps himself in a garment as if in the chorion. Therefore, embryos are born wrapped.
He should not uncover himself before the purchase of the Soma. If he were to uncover himself before the purchase of the Soma, the embryos of his offspring would be liable to fall away.

When the Soma has been purchased, he unties [the girdle]; that is indeed as when one is born; moreover, it is just as when one unties [his garment] for a superior. When the Aṅgirases were going to the heavenly world, they divided their strength (ūrj); what remained over from that became the reed-grass (śara). The reed-grass is indeed strength; in that the girdle is made of reed-grass, he wins strength.
He girds it in the middle; verily he bestows strength upon him in the middle, and therefore they enjoy strength from the middle.
Indeed, that part of a man above the navel is pure, while that below is impure; in that he girds it in the middle, he separates his purity from his impurity.
Indra hurled the thunderbolt at Vṛtra; it became threefold: one-third became the wooden sword (*sphya*), one-third the chariot, and one-third the sacrificial post (*yūpa*).
Those arrows which were shattered within became *śara* (reeds); that is the reason for the name *śara*.

The *śara* is indeed the thunderbolt (*vajra*). Hunger is truly the enemy of man; in that the girdle is made of *śara*, he directly strikes away the enemy of hunger from the middle with the thunderbolt. It is threefold; the breath is indeed threefold; thus he places the threefold breath in the middle of the sacrificer.
The earth serves as a boundary for the cords; he consecrates the sacrificer with a girdle and the wife with a yoke-halter for the sake of pairing.

The Sacrifice (Yajña) lusted after Dakṣiṇā; he united with her. Indra perceived this and thought, "Whoever shall be born from this will become this [world]. He entered her, and from her, Indra himself was born.

He thought, "Whoever is born after me from this [womb] shall indeed possess this world. Having reflected upon her, he cut off her womb; she became a barren cow that has recently calved. That is the origin of the *sūtavaśā*.

He wound it around his hand; he deposited it among the wild animals, and it became the black antelope horn (*kṛṣṇaviṣāṇā*). He hands over the black antelope horn [with the words]: "Thou art the womb of Indra; do not harm me. Thus he makes the sacrifice co-womb with himself, the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) co-womb, and Indra co-womb, for the sake of co-uterinity.
"For the plowing, thee, for good crops," he says; therefore plants ripen even without being plowed. "For the plants with good fruit, thee," he says; therefore plants bear fruit.
If he were to scratch with his hand, offspring would become afflicted with scabies; if he were to smile, they would become naked.
He scratches with a black antelope horn and smiles while covering his mouth, for the protection of offspring.

One should not remove the black antelope horn before the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) have been led away; for if one were to remove the black antelope horn before the sacrificial fees have been led away, the womb of offspring would be liable to fall away.

When the sacrificial fees have been led away, he throws the black antelope horn into the *cātvāla* pit. The *cātvāla* is indeed the womb of the sacrifice, and the black antelope horn is the womb; thus he places the womb within the womb itself, so that the sacrifice may possess its proper womb.

6.1.4 Anuvāka 4: The Rule for the Performance of Observances Preceded by the Taking of the Staff Speech indeed departed from the gods, refusing to remain for the sacrifice. It entered the trees; that same speech speaks within the trees—that which is in the drum, that which is in the flute, and that which is in the lute.
When he hands over the staff to the consecrated one (*dīkṣita*), he thereby secures speech itself.
It is made of Udumbara wood; the Udumbara is strength, so he wins strength for himself.
It is level with the mouth; thus he bestows strength upon him from the very mouth, and therefore they enjoy strength from the mouth.

When the Soma has been purchased, he hands the staff to the Maitrāvaruṇa; for the Maitrāvaruṇa distributes the speech to the officiating priests beforehand, and the priests establish that speech in the sacrificer.

"Svāhā! To the sacrifice, with the mind! he says, for by means of the mind a person approaches the sacrifice. "Svāhā! To Heaven and Earth! he says, for the sacrifice is in Heaven and Earth. "Svāhā! From the wide atmosphere! he says, for the sacrifice is in the atmosphere. "Svāhā! I take hold of the sacrifice from the wind! he says; this—
He who purifies is indeed the sacrifice; he directly seizes it when he closes his fists and restrains his speech for the support of the sacrifice.
