"This Brahmin has been consecrated," he says three times in a whisper; thus he announces him to the gods. Three times aloud; thus he announces him to both gods and men.
One should not release speech before the stars have risen. If one were to release speech before the stars have risen, he would cut asunder the sacrifice.

When the stars have risen, he releases speech with the words, "Prepare the vow! For the consecrated one is indeed under the vow of the sacrifice; thus, he releases speech directed toward the sacrifice itself.
If he should release [the horse], he should recite a verse addressed to Viṣṇu; for Viṣṇu is the sacrifice, and thus by means of the sacrifice he extends the sacrifice.
He says, "We meditate upon the divine thought"; thereby he softens the sacrifice.
He says, "May our will be easy to cross over"; thereby he wins the dawn.
The exponents of Brahman say:
"Should one offer oblations in the house of the consecrated one, or should one not offer?

For the consecrated one is indeed the sacrificial offering (*havis*). If he were to offer, he would offer having taken a portion from the sacrificer; if he were not to offer, he would omit a joint of the sacrifice. He says: "Those gods born of mind, yoked by mind... [and so on].
The vital breaths are indeed the gods born of mind, yoked by mind; it is into them that he offers in secret.
Thus, it is as if offered, yet not offered.

The Rakṣases seek to slay the consecrated one while he sleeps; Agni, indeed, is the slayer of Rakṣases. By reciting, "O Agni, do thou keep watch well; may we rejoice well," he sleeps having made Agni his guardian, for the purpose of driving away the Rakṣases.

"He who, having been consecrated, sleeps, acts as if he were violating his vow. He says, "O Agni, you are the guardian of vows," for Agni is indeed the lord of vows among the gods; he thus causes him to undertake the vow.
He says, "The god among mortals," [for] he is a god.
"For he, being among mortals, is to be praised at the sacrifices"—thus he says; for they indeed praise him at the sacrifices.
Verily, from one who has been consecrated and has slept, the vital powers (*indriya*) depart to the deities.
"May all the gods turn toward me," he says. By means of this very *yajus*, he leads him together with the deities and with vital power (*indriya*).
If he were not to recite this *yajus*, he would have as many cattle as those for which he was consecrated; [therefore] let there be "as much as this."
"O Soma, be present for my support," he says; thus he wins unlimited cattle. "May they be for my enjoyment in the moon," he says;
thus he receives them according to their respective deities.

If he were not to dedicate these [cows] in this manner with the words, "To Vāyu thee! To Varuṇa thee!", he would cause the sacrificial gift (*dakṣiṇā*) to go to the wrong deity; he would be cut off from the deities. In that he dedicates them in this manner, he causes the sacrificial gift to go to the respective deities, and he is not cut off from the deities.
He says, "O divine waters, O son of the waters..."
"Whatever of yours is pure, worthy of sacrifice, and divine—that may I not step upon," so indeed he says.
"May I follow the unbroken thread of the earth," he says; having thus made a bridge, he passes over.
6.1.5 Anuvāka 5: The Procedure for the Prāyaṇīyā Offering.
The gods, having settled upon the place of sacrifice, did not know the directions. They ran to one another, saying, "By you let us discern it; by you! Then they took counsel together regarding Aditi.
"Let us know [the sacrifice] through you," they said. She replied, "I shall choose a boon: let your sacrifices have me as their beginning and me as their conclusion.
Therefore, the Āditya [offering] is the introductory rite of sacrifices, and the Āditya is the concluding rite.
He sacrifices to five deities for the sake of discerning the five directions.
Moreover, the *paṅkti* consists of five syllables; the sacrifice is fivefold; verily, he wins the sacrifice itself.
They sacrificed to Pathyā Svasti; by her, they discerned the eastern quarter;
with Agni, the southern.
With the Soma [offering] he sacrifices to the western quarter, with the Savitṛ [offering] to the northern, and with the Aditi [offering] to the upward [quarter];
he sacrifices to Pathyā Svasti; by that [offering] he indeed discerns the eastern direction.

Having sacrificed for the sake of a favorable and auspicious path, he sacrifices to Agni and Soma; for these two, Agni and Soma, are the eyes of the sacrifice, and through them he beholds [the sacrifice] accordingly.
Having sacrificed to Agni and Soma, he sacrifices to Savitṛ; impelled by Savitṛ, he indeed looks upon [the world].
Having sacrificed to Savitṛ, he sacrifices to Aditi; Aditi is this earth; on her very foundation he looks upon [the world].
Having sacrificed to Aditi, he recites a verse addressed to the Maruts for the proper ordering of the people.
The exponents of Brahman say:

"The Prāyaṇīya [offering] should be performed like the Prayāja [sacrifices] but without the Anuyāja [sacrifices], and the Udayanīya [offering] should be performed like the Anuyāja [sacrifices] but without the Prayāja [sacrifices]."

These indeed are the *prayāja*s, and those are the *anūyāja*s; that is the continuity of the sacrifice. It should not be done in that way. The *prayāja*s are indeed the self, and the *anūyāja*s are offspring. If he were to omit the *prayāja*s, he would omit his own self; if he were to omit the *anūyāja*s, he would omit his offspring. For whatever part of the sacrifice, once it has been spread out, is not performed, because of that the sacrifice perishes; and following the perishing sacrifice, the sacrificer perishes as well.

The *prāyaṇīya* should be performed with fore-offerings (*prayāja*) and after-offerings (*anūyāja*), and the *udayanīya* likewise with fore-offerings and after-offerings; thus he does not exclude himself, nor his offspring, nor the sacrifice from ruin, nor the sacrificer.
He pours out the *udayanīya* from the scrapings of the *prāyaṇīya*; that indeed is the continuity of the sacrifice.

If one were to make those which are the invitatory verses (*puronuvākyā*) of the *prāyaṇīya* sacrifice the offering verses (*yājyā*) of the *udayanīya*, he would ascend to that world beyond and be liable to perish. By making those which are the invitatory verses of the *prāyaṇīya* the offering verses of the *udayanīya*, he establishes himself firmly in this very world.
6.1.6 Anuvāka 6: The Description of the Purchase of Soma with a Tawny Cow.
Kadrū and Suparṇī indeed vied with each other for their own forms;
Kadrū defeated Suparṇī.
She said, "Soma is in the third heaven from here; fetch him and ransom yourself with him.
This [earth] is indeed Kadrū, and yonder [sky] is Suparṇī.
The Suparṇeyī spoke to the *chandāṃsi*:
"Indeed, the parents support their sons; Soma is in the third heaven from here—fetch him! With him, ransom yourself."
"Thus did Kadrū speak," so saying,
the Jagatī flew up with fourteen syllables;
failing to reach [its goal], it turned back.
Two of its syllables were lost;
she returned with cattle and the consecration (dīkṣā).
Therefore, among the meters (chandas), the Jagatī is the most conducive to cattle.
Therefore, the consecration ceremony favors one who possesses cattle;
the Triṣṭubh flew up while consisting of thirteen syllables, but failing to reach its goal, it turned back.
Two of its syllables were lost;
it recovered them through sacrificial gifts and through austerity.
Therefore, at the midday pressing in the world of the Triṣṭubh, the sacrificial gifts (dakṣiṇās) are led forth.
"This indeed is austerity," they say, "that one gives away one's own property.
Gāyatrī flew up with four syllables, being together with Ajā and Light.
He assigned that [debt] to the goat;
that is the reason for the goat's name.
She brought back the Soma and four syllables.
It became eight-syllabled.
The exponents of Brahman say:
"By what truth does the Gāyatrī, being the smallest of the meters, encompass the mouth of the sacrifice?"
Because he brought that very Soma here, therefore he came to be the beginning of the sacrifice;
therefore he is most brilliant.
With his two feet he gathered two pressings, and with his mouth one.
What he grasped with his mouth, that he sucked;
therefore two pressings contain the *śukra*— the morning pressing and the midday pressing—
and therefore at the third pressing they press the dregs (*ṛjīṣa*).
For they consider it as if it were milked.
He pours in the milk-mixture for the sake of its brilliance; thus he gathers it together.
While that Soma was being brought, the Gandharva Viśvāvasu stole it away; having been stolen, it remained hidden for three nights.
Therefore, the purchased Soma remains for three nights;
the gods said, "The Gandharvas are indeed fond of women; let us redeem it with a woman."
They made Speech into a one-year-old female and bartered for her with it.
Having assumed the form of a red deer, she departed from the Gandharvas and stood aside.
Regarding that, the gods said to Rohita at his birth:
"He has stepped away from you; he does not turn back toward us. Let us call him back."
The Gandharvas spoke the sacred word (brahman) and the gods sang;
that [speech] turned toward the gods because they were singing.
Therefore, women desire a man who sings.
Women desire him who knows thus; and furthermore, he who knows thus becomes one among the people, and they give to him even when they are in great numbers.
He purchases [the Soma] with a one-year-old cow.
He purchases it with his entire speech;
therefore, humans speak speech at the age of one year.
He purchases it with [a cow] that is not hornless, not earless, not one-eyed, not lame, and not seven-hoofed.
He purchases him with all [colors];
if he were to purchase with a white one, the sacrificer would become afflicted with skin disease;
if with a black one, there would be a cow for covering [the dead].
The sacrificer would be short-lived.
If the *vārtraghni* verse were of two forms,
he would either defeat another, or another would defeat him.
He buys [the Soma] with a ruddy, tawny-eyed [cow].
This, indeed, is the form of Soma;
he thus buys it by means of its own deity.
6.1.7 Anuvāka 7: Description of the method of purchasing Soma with a ruddy cow.
That [Soma] became gold;
therefore, they purify gold from the waters.
The exponents of Brahman say:
"By what truth do offspring conceived without bones come to be born with bones?
Because one offers gold, having placed it in clarified butter, therefore offspring conceived without bones are born with bones.
"This indeed is Agni's beloved abode, namely ghee; brilliance is gold.
"This is thy bright body, this is thy luster," he says; thus he endows him with brilliance and a body.
He makes it;
thus he indeed gathers it together.
If he were to place it unbound, the embryos of living beings would be liable to fall away.
He ties it bound for the support of embryos; he ties it with a *niṣṭarkya* knot for the procreation of offspring.
This cow for purchasing Soma is indeed speech;
when he says, "Thou art swift," it is because what one impels with the mind, that one speaks with speech.
"Held by the mind," he says,
for speech is indeed held by the mind; "accepted by Viṣṇu," he says.
Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice;
he thus makes her pleasing for the sacrifice.
"In the impulse of thee, whose impulse is true," he says.
Verily, he wins speech impelled by Savitṛ.
For at every section being performed, the Rakṣases seek to destroy the sacrifice;
this path indeed is not struck down by the Rakṣases, which belongs to both Agni and Sūrya.
"I have mounted the eye of the sun, the pupil of Agni's eye," he says;
thus he ascends that very path which is not struck by the Rakṣases.
This cow for the purchase of Soma is indeed Speech.
"You are consciousness, you are mind," he says;
he thus instructs her, and therefore instructed offspring are born.
"You are consciousness," he says;
for what one perceives with the mind, that one speaks with speech.
"You are the mind," he says.
"For what one approaches with the mind, that one does"—
thus he says, "Thou art the wise one," for what one meditates upon with the mind, that one expresses with speech.
He says, "Sit on the south," for this [direction] is indeed the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
"You are worthy of sacrifice," he says;
thus he makes her indeed worthy of sacrifice.
"You are a Kṣatriya woman," he says.
"For she is a Kṣatriya;
'Aditi, you are double-headed,' he says.
Because the Āditya [oblation] is the introductory (prāyaṇīya) of sacrifices and the Āditya is the concluding (udayanīya), therefore he speaks thus."
If it were unbound, it would be unrestrained;
if the *anustaraṇī* cow were bound by the foot,
the sacrificer would be liable to die prematurely.
If the *vārtraghnī* verse were recited while [the victim] is held by the ear,
he might overcome another, or another might overcome him.
"May Mitra bind you by the foot," he says.
Mitra is indeed the auspicious one among the gods;
with him he binds her by the foot.
"May Pūṣan protect the paths," he says.
This indeed is Pūṣan;
he has made him its guardian for the sake of complete attainment.
"To Indra, the overseer," he says;
thus he makes Indra the overseer of this [earth].
"May your mother consent to you, may your father consent," he says;
it is with their consent that he purchases her. "Go, O goddess, toward the god," he says.
For this goddess is the god Soma;
he says, "Soma for Indra," for Soma is indeed brought for Indra.
If one were not to recite this *yajus*, the cow for purchasing Soma would simply go away.
"May Rudra turn you back," he says;
for Rudra is indeed fierce.
[He recites] "of the gods.
He thus places that very [power] beyond her for the sake of turning back.
Indeed, he does something like a cruel act when he invokes Rudra.
"By the path of Mitra," he says for the sake of peace;
for he who purchases with the Soma-purchase cow indeed sells himself by means of speech.
"May it be well! O friend Soma, come back again with wealth," he says;
having bartered away speech by means of speech itself, he takes speech back into himself.
The speech of one who knows thus does not fail him.
6.1.8 Anuvāka 8: The Enumeration of the Collection of Padas.
He steps down six times;
for six days he does not speak beyond [the prescribed measure].
Moreover, during the course of the year, he wins as much speech as there is;
he offers at the seventh step,
for the Śakvarī consists of seven steps.
The Śakvarī verses are cattle;
verily he wins cattle.
There are seven domestic animals and seven wild animals, and there are seven meters.
He says, "Thou art Vasvī; thou art Rudrā," for the sake of securing both;
this indeed is her form and her greatness.
"Bṛhaspati shall expound you; may he delight you in happiness," he says;
for Bṛhaspati is indeed the Brahman among the gods.
"By means of Brahmā alone he wins cattle for him;
'May Rudra take heed with the Vasus,' he says—
for the sake of turning back."
"I sprinkle you upon the head of the earth, on the place of sacrifice to the gods," he says;
for this place of sacrifice to the gods is indeed the head of the earth.
"On the footprint of Iḍā," he says.
For this is the footprint of Iḍā, that of the Soma-purchase cow; he says, "To the one rich in ghee, Svāhā!"
Because the clarified butter was squeezed from her foot, he speaks thus.
If the Adhvaryu were to offer an oblation where there is no fire, the Adhvaryu would become blind; the Rakṣases do not strike down the sacrifice.
Indeed, at every stage as the rite is being performed, the Rakṣases seek to destroy the sacrifice.

"The *rakṣas* is cut around; the enemies are cut around," he says for the purpose of striking away the *rakṣases*. "Here do I cut off the neck of the *rakṣas*, who hates us and whom we hate," he says.
There are indeed two persons: he whom he hates and he who hates him; it is between these two that he cuts his necks without interval.
The footprint of the Soma-purchase cow is indeed cattle;
as much as is moistened, he strews over it.
Verily, he wins cattle.
With the words, "To us, wealth," he pours it together;
thus the Adhvaryu preserves his own self.
With the words, "He does not depart from cattle, O Tvaṣṭṛ;
[give] wealth," he hands it over to the sacrificer; thus the sacrificer himself bestows wealth.
"Thou art the whole king," [he says] regarding the wife.
For the wife is indeed half of one's own self; it is just as if one were to deposit [the other half] in one's home.
"May you consort with Tvaṣṭṛ's wife," he says;
for Tvaṣṭṛ is the fashioner of the forms of paired animals. Thus, he bestows form upon the animals.
The Gārhapatya fire is established for this world, and the Āhavanīya fire for that world.
If he were to scatter [the seeds] on the Gārhapatya, he would be rich in cattle in this world;
if on the Āhavanīya, he would be rich in cattle in that world.
He scatters [the grains] for both;
thus he makes him possessed of cattle in both worlds.
6.1.9 Anuvāka 9: The Measurement of Soma. The exponents of sacred knowledge (brahmavādinaḥ) say:
"Should the Soma plants be plucked or should they not be plucked?"
Soma is indeed the king of plants; whatever has entered into him is as if swallowed by him.
If one were to sift it, that would be exactly like extracting what has been swallowed from one's mouth.
If he were not to sift it, it would run away just as something that has been eaten runs away; consequently, the Adhvaryu would become hungry and the sacrificer would become hungry.
Therefore, he should simply say, "O Soma-seller, purify the Soma!"
If [he gives] this way or that way, he ruins the Soma-seller by both means;
therefore, the Soma-seller is hungry.
Aruṇa Aupaveśi used to say, "I secure the third pressing by means of the very purchase of the Soma. He measures out [the Soma] on the hide of an animal; verily, he secures cattle.
For cattle are the third pressing. If one should desire of someone,
"May he be without cattle," he should measure out [the Soma] for him by the Ṛks.
A bear is unfavorable to cattle;
he who desires [this] becomes indeed without cattle.
He should possess cattle.
Thus he measures it according to the hair;
for this is the form of cattle.
By means of its very form, he wins cattle for him.
He indeed becomes possessed of cattle;
he purchases it at the edge of the waters;
thus he purchases it as something full of moisture.
"You are a minister," he says; he thus makes him a minister.
"The bright draught is yours," he says.
For Śukra is his cup;
it does not go forth empty,
for it goes forth having attained his very greatness.
He goes with a cart;
therefore, a life that is not to be carried by a cart is possible only on level ground.

Since they indeed carry this [Soma] on the head, therefore it is called "head-carried" (*śīrṣahārya*); while reciting the *aticchandas* verse, "Toward that god Savitṛ," he measures out the living space upon the mountain.
The *aticchandas* indeed contains all the meters; thus he measures it out with all the meters.
The *aticchandas* is the highest of the meters.

In that he measures with verses of the *aticchandas* metre, he makes him the pre-eminent one among his equals. He measures with each verse separately until the completion; thus he measures him with verses that are never exhausted in their power.
Therefore, the fingers have diverse strengths; he draws them all down toward the thumb,
and for that reason it possesses equal strength with the other fingers.
Therefore, he measures along with all [the fingers];
for if he were to measure together with all [of them], the fingers would be joined together.
He measures, releasing [the grain] one by one.
Therefore they are born divided fivefold; he measures with the Yajus five times; the Paṅkti consists of five syllables.
The sacrifice is fivefold;
verily he wins the sacrifice itself by [reciting] five times silently.
They amount to ten;
the Virāj consists of ten syllables, and the Virāj is food.
By means of the Virāj he wins food;
in that he measures with a Yajus, he wins what has been; in that [he measures] silently, [he wins] what is yet to be.
If indeed the Soma were only as much as he measures out, it would belong to the sacrificer alone and not to the members of the assembly (sadasyas).
With the words, "For the offspring," he pushes [the Soma] together;
thus he causes the members of the assembly to share in it as well.
He binds it with a garment; for a garment indeed belongs to all the deities.
Verily, he causes him to prosper with all the deities;
Soma is indeed cattle;
"For breath, thee!"—with these words he ties [the skin] around.
Verily, he places the out-breath (prāṇa) in the animals;
with "For the through-breath (vyāna) thee," he unties it, and thus he places the through-breath in the animals.
Therefore, the vital breaths do not abandon one who is sleeping.
6.1.10 Anuvāka 10, Section 10: The Purchase of Soma by Other Means.

If one should bargain, saying, "I will buy [Soma] from you for a sixteenth part" or "for an eighth part," he would make the Soma worth less than a cow, the sacrificer worth less than a cow, and the Adhvaryu worth less than a cow.
However, he must not diminish the greatness of the cow.
He should simply say, "I will buy it from you with a cow.
Thus he makes the Soma worth a cow, the sacrificer worth a cow, and the Adhvaryu worth a cow;
he does not diminish the greatness of the cow.
He buys him with a goat; verily he buys him who possesses austerity.
He buys him with gold.
He buys him with seed indeed; he buys him with a cow.
Verily, he purchases it with something containing heads;
he purchases it with a bull;
verily, he purchases it together with Indra.
He buys [the Soma] with an ox;
for the ox is a carrier; verily, by means of a carrier, he buys the carrier of the sacrifice.
He purchases [the Soma] with a pair for the sake of obtaining a pair;
he purchases it with a garment.
Clothing indeed belongs to all the deities; he purchases it for all the deities.
They amount to ten;
the Virāj consists of ten syllables, and the Virāj is food. Verily, by means of the Virāj, he wins the eating of food.
"You are the body of austerity, the color of Prajāpati," he says;
thereby the Adhvaryu makes amends for the cattle, so that he himself may not be cut off. He who knows thus goes to prosperity and obtains cattle.
"I buy your bright [soma] with the bright," he says; this is exactly according to the sacrificial formula.
The gods indeed took back by force that gold with which they had purchased the Soma, thinking, "For who would sell away his own brilliance?
Therefore, whatever gold one uses to purchase the Soma, one should take it back by force; thus one places brilliance within oneself.
"Light for us, darkness for the Soma-seller," he says;
thus he bestows light upon the sacrificer and strikes the Soma-seller with darkness.
"If one were to kill [the Soma] without tying it up, those serpents would be equally venomous;
therefore he says, 'I tie this around the necks of the serpents, the biters,' whereby those serpents become non-venomous. He pierces the Soma-seller with darkness."
"Bhrāja," he says. These [deities] indeed guarded Soma in yonder world; from them they brought forth Soma.
If he were not to assign the purchase-offerings to these [deities], his Soma would be un-purchased, and these would not guard his Soma in yonder world.
In that he assigns the purchase-offerings to these, his Soma becomes purchased, and these guard his Soma in yonder world.
6.1.11 Anuvāka 11: The description of the leading away of the purchased Soma by means of a cart.
"The purchased Soma, when bound, belongs indeed to Varuṇa.
[Therefore] he says, "As a friend, come to us, bestowing good friendship."
"For peace! "Enter the right thigh of Indra," he says;
for when the gods purchased Soma, they placed him upon the right thigh of Indra.
He who performs the sacrifice is indeed Indra at this time;
therefore he says thus:
"Up with life, with good life! he says.
He stands up while maintaining contact with the deities,
saying: "Go along the wide mid-region."
For at this time Soma has the intermediate region as his deity.
"Thou art the seat of Aditi; sit on the seat of Aditi," he says;
this is exactly according to the sacrificial formula.
He indeed deprives it of its full power when he makes that which belongs to Varuṇa belong to Mitra;
he restores it to its own deity by setting it down with a verse addressed to Varuṇa;
he encloses it with a cloth.
Clothing indeed belongs to all the deities;
verily, he causes him to prosper through all the deities.
"Furthermore, for the sake of driving away the Rakṣases,
he says, 'In the forests he has stretched out the intermediate space,' for indeed, in the forests he has stretched out the intermediate space."
"Victory in the coursers," he says,
for there is victory in the coursers;
"milk in the cows," he says.
"Indeed, milk is in the cows;
the will is in the hearts," he says, for the will is indeed in the hearts.
"Varuṇa [placed] Agni among the people," he says, for Varuṇa indeed placed Agni among the people;
[he placed] Sūrya in heaven.
Thus he says: "For [he placed] the sun in heaven;
[he placed] Soma on the mountain," so he says.
The pressing-stones are indeed the rocks;
he who sacrifices places the Soma in them,
and for that reason he speaks thus.
With the verse addressed to Sūrya, "Upwards that Jātavedas," he fastens the black antelope skin for the sake of warding off the Rākṣasas;
he says, "O two oxen, come hither, you who bear the yoke."
Just as it is according to the Yajus formula,
he says, "Move forward,
O Lord of the world," for [he belongs] to the beings.
"This is the lord," he says;
"over all abodes," he says,
for he indeed moves over all abodes.
"Lest a thief seize you," he says;
for when the Gandharva Viśvāvasu stole the Soma as it was being brought here, he speaks thus for the sake of preventing theft.
"Thou art the means of well-being for the sacrificer," he says;
this is indeed the sacrificer's taking hold of the sacrifice,
for the sake of non-interruption.
The purchased Soma, when bound up, approaches the sacrificer as Varuṇa;
therefore he says, "Homage to the eye of Mitra and Varuṇa!"
For peace.
They bring Soma;
he stands firm with Agni.
As they come into being, they both come together toward the sacrificer.
Indeed, he who is consecrated moves about having already seized his own self for the sacrifice;
when he immolates the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma, that is his ransom for himself.
Therefore, he should not eat of it,
for it is like the ransom-price of a man.
Furthermore, they say:
"By means of Agni and Soma, Indra indeed slew Vṛtra";
since he offers the animal victim to Agni and Soma, that [offering] of his is truly a slayer of Vṛtra; therefore, it is a lowing [victim].
He attends to it with a verse addressed to Varuṇa;
verily, he attends to it with its own deity.
6.2 Prapāṭhaka: 2, Anuvāka 1: Description of the Guest-Offering (Ātithyeṣṭi) If one were to receive the guest-offering after unyoking both [oxen], he would cut asunder the sacrifice.
If one were to do so without unyoking both, that would be exactly as if the guest-offering were made for one who has not yet arrived.
One ox is unyoked, while the other remains unyoked; then he receives the guest-offering for the continuity of the sacrifice.
The wife takes hold [of him], for the wife has authority over the household goods; with the approval of the wife, he offers the oblation.
Whatever the wife performs in the sacrifice, that constitutes a pair;
moreover, this is the wife’s taking hold of the sacrifice for the sake of its non-interruption.
To as many attendants as the king comes with, hospitality is offered to all of them; for the meters are indeed the attendants of King Soma.

"Thou art the hospitality of Agni; for Viṣṇu, thee! he says; by this, he effects it for the Gāyatrī. "Thou art the hospitality of Soma; for Viṣṇu, thee! he says; by this, he effects it for the Triṣṭubh.
"You are the guest-offering for the guest; for Viṣṇu, you!"—thus he says; by this, he provides for the Jagatī meter.
"For Agni, the giver of increase of wealth; for Viṣṇu, you!"—thus he says; by this, he provides for the Anuṣṭubh meter.
"For you, the falcon, the bearer of Soma; for Viṣṇu, you!"—thus he says; by this, he indeed effects it through the Gāyatrī.
He draws [the cup] five times; the Paṅkti consists of five syllables, and the sacrifice is fivefold; verily, he wins the sacrifice itself.
The exponents of sacred knowledge (brahmavādinaḥ) say:
For what reason is the *gāyatrī* performed on both sides of the *ātithya*?
Because she brought that Soma here; therefore the *gāyatrī* is performed on both sides of the *ātithya*, both before and after.
The guest-offering (ātithya) is indeed the head of the sacrifice; that there is a cake on nine potsherds, therefore the head is split into nine parts.
There is a cake on nine potsherds; these are three sets of three potsherds, commensurate with the *trivṛt* stoma. The *trivṛt* is brilliance; verily he places brilliance at the head of the sacrifice.
There is a cake on nine potsherds; these are three sets of three potsherds, commensurate with the threefold breath. For the *trivṛt* is indeed [the breath].
The *prāṇa* (breath) places the threefold *prāṇa* itself first upon the head of the sacrifice.

These are indeed the eyelashes of Prajāpati: the *aśvavāla* grasses and the crosswise stalk of sugarcane. In that the *prastara* is made of *aśvavāla* grass with a crosswise stalk of sugarcane, he thereby gathers together the eye of Prajāpati himself.
As for those oblations which the gods offered, the Asuras snatched them away in their mouths; the gods saw the *kārṣmarya* tree, for it is fit for ritual action.
Thinking, "One should perform the ritual action with this," they made the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) from *kārṣmarya* wood;
with them, indeed, they struck away the *rakṣases*.
In that the enclosing-sticks are made of *kārṣmarya* wood, it is for the striking away of the *rakṣases*.
He touches [the two fire-sticks] so that the *rakṣases* cannot enter. He does not place them around in front, for the sun, rising in the east, drives away the *rakṣases* from the front.
He places the two fire-sticks upright; thus he drives away the *rakṣases* from above.
He places one with a Yajus formula and the other silently, for the sake of pairing;
he places two, because the sacrificer has two feet, for the sake of stability.
The exponents of sacred knowledge say:
Agni and Soma, indeed, are these two. [The priests ask: "How is it that hospitality is offered to Soma but not to Agni?
When one churns fire and casts it into the fire, by that very act hospitality is offered to Agni.
Furthermore, they say: "Agni is all the deities. When, having set out the oblation, one churns the fire, he thereby generates all the deities for the sake of the oblation that has been set forth.
Anuvāka 2: The description of the Tānūnaptrī sacrifice.
The gods and the Asuras were engaged in conflict; those gods were at variance with one another.

Not yielding to one another in terms of seniority, they divided themselves into five groups: Agni with the Vasus, Soma with the Rudras, Indra with the Maruts, Varuṇa with the Ādityas, and Bṛhaspati with the Viśve Devas.
They reflected:
"We shall surely succumb to the Asuras, our rivals, since we are at variance with one another. Let us offer up those bodies of ours which are dear; he who [harms us] shall be excluded from them."
"May no one among us first betray another"—
therefore, whoever among those who have performed the *tānūnaptra* rite betrays first, he meets with ruin;
in that he portions out the *tānūnaptra* together, it is for the sake of overcoming his rivals.
He prospers by himself, while his rival perishes;
he cuts off five times,
for they divided that [victim] into five parts.
Moreover, the *paṅkti* consists of five syllables, and the sacrifice is fivefold;
verily, he wins the sacrifice.
"I seize you for the Āpati," he says;
the breath indeed is the Āpati.
"He gratifies the vital breath itself," he says;
for the mind is indeed the protector.
"Mind alone gladdens," he says at the *tanūnaptra* offering;
for those [limbs] of his were indeed brought together.
"For power," he says, for they agreed upon those [powers] for the sake of power; "for the most powerful strength," he says.
"For that which is most powerful of your self they have agreed upon. "It is unassailable, it is unassailable," he says;
for this is indeed unassailable and unassailable.
"The vigor of the gods," he says,
for this is indeed the vigor of the gods.
"Protecting from imprecation, not to be imprecated," he says;
for this [sacrifice] protects from imprecation and is not to be imprecated.
"May the Lord of Consecration approve my consecration," he says.
This is just like the sacrificial formula (yajus).
The gods, having made ghee into a thunderbolt, struck Soma.
Indeed, they proceed with the *tānūnaptra* rite as if it were very close to him.
"O divine Soma, may each of your rays swell," he says;
by this, he causes whatever of his has been sucked out and whatever has been measured away to swell once more.
"May Indra swell for you; may you swell for Indra," he says.
Thus he causes both Indra and Soma to swell.
"Swell your friends with gain and wisdom," he says.
The officiating priests are indeed his friends; he causes them to swell.
"O divine Soma, may I attain well-being through thy pressing."
Thus he says;
he indeed invokes this very blessing.
For those who cause the Soma to swell depart from this world.

For Soma, having been made to swell, has the atmosphere as its deity. "Desired riches! Forward for fortune! he says; thus, having paid homage to Heaven and Earth, they find firm support in this world.
The gods and the asuras were arrayed for battle;
those gods, being afraid, entered Agni. Therefore they say:
"Agni is all the deities"— having thus made Agni their protection, they overcame the Asuras.
Verily, he who undergoes the intermediate consecration enters into Agni; it serves for the overcoming of his enemy; he prospers in himself, and his enemy is defeated.
By means of the consecration (dīkṣā), he protects himself; by means of the intermediate consecration (avāntaradīkṣā), he protects his offspring.
He fastens his girdle more tightly, for offspring are indeed closer to oneself.
He has performed his vow with fervor; he purifies himself with the *madantī* waters, for Agni indeed shrinks away from that which is cold.
"For the kindling, that which is your Rudra-natured body, O Agni," he says;
thus he causes him to undertake the vow by means of its own deity.
For the sake of being well-born and for peace.
6.2.3 Anuvāka 3: Designation of the Upasad Oblations.
Those Asuras had three cities: one of iron below, then one of silver, and then one of gold.
The gods were unable to conquer them; they sought to win them by means of the Upasads alone.

Therefore they say: "Whether one knows thus or not, they indeed conquer the great city by means of the Upasads. They fashioned an arrow, with Agni as its point, Soma as its barb, and Viṣṇu as its shaft.
They said,
"Who will suckle her?"
They said, "Rudra!"—for Rudra is indeed cruel; "Let him shoot," they said.
He replied, "I choose a boon: let me alone be the lord of cattle. Therefore, Rudra is the lord of cattle.
Rudra released it; having shattered those three citadels, he drove the Asuras away from these worlds.
Because the Upasad offerings are performed, it is for the purpose of driving away one's rivals.
One should not offer any other oblation beforehand.
If he were to offer another oblation first,
he would make another mouth;
he pours the *āghāra* libation with the *sruva* ladle for the sake of the sacrifice's discernment.
He offers while stepping across;
thus the sacrificer drives away his rivals from these worlds.
Stepping back again, he offers the *upasad* oblation.
Having indeed driven away his rivals from these worlds and having conquered the world of his rivals, he ascends.

For those *upasad* rites which the gods performed in the morning, by means of them they drove away the Asuras from the day; those which they performed in the evening, by means of them [they drove them away] from the night.
In that the *upasads* are performed in the evening and in the morning, the sacrificer thereby drives away his rivals by means of both day and night;
those which would be the *yājyās* in the morning, he should make the *puro'nuvākyās* in the evening, for the sake of non-exhaustion.
He performs three *upasads*; these worlds are three; he thus gratifies these very worlds.

They amount to six; the seasons are six; he thus gratifies the seasons. He performs twelve *upasads* in a *soma*-sacrifice lasting less than a day (*ahīna*); the year has twelve months; he thus gratifies the year.
They amount to twenty-four.
Twenty-four half-months pass; he thus gratifies the half-months themselves.
He who desires [this] should undertake the intermediate consecration that is sharp as the point of an awl.

"May there be prosperity for me in this world"—thinking thus, one should first undergo [the fast] for one day, then two, then three, then four; this indeed is the *ārāgrā* intermediate initiation (*avāntaradīkṣā*). Prosperity comes to him in this very world. He who desires, "May there be prosperity for me in yonder world," should undergo the *parovarīyasī* (progressively longer) intermediate initiation: first for four days, then three, then two, then one; this indeed is the *parovarīyasī* intermediate initiation. Prosperity comes to him in yonder very world.
6.2.4 Anuvāka 4: Designation of the Altar (Vedi) Those who undertake the Upasad rites go to the heavenly world.
Among them, whoever draws [the fire] away is indeed left behind.
"He did not bring it," one should say, as if it were something to be properly carried away.
For he who, striving for his own purpose, becomes exhausted and falls away, dwells together with those who are hostile;
therefore, having drawn once, one should not draw again.
One should stir curds;
this indeed is the form of cattle.
By means of its very form, one wins cattle.
The sacrifice fled from the gods; having assumed the form of Viṣṇu, it entered the earth.
The gods, joining their hands together, sought it.
Indra stepped over him from above;
he said,
"Who is this that has stepped over me from above?"
"I am the slayer in the fortress," he said; "And who are you? [the other] asked;
"I am the retriever from the fortress," he replied.

"You have indeed declared yourself a slayer in difficult places; this boar Vāmamoṣa, beyond the seven mountains, carries the wealth of the Asuras that is to be known. Slay him, if you are a slayer in difficult places!
So saying, he uprooted a bunch of *darbha* grass, pierced the seven mountains, and slew him.
He said, "You have spoken of one who would bring it from a difficult place; let him bring it.
Then the sacrifice itself brought the sacrifice to them.
That wealth which the Asuras found was the Veda; that is the singular state of being known as the Veda of the Asuras, for this earth belonged to the Asuras in the beginning.
As far as one sitting can see, so far [is the range] of the gods.
Those gods said, "Let there be for us a share in this as well."
"How much shall we give you? they asked.
"Give us as much as this female jackal takes three times around," they said.
Then Indra, having assumed the form of a female jackal, took her three times all around.
They found her;
because they found her (imām avindanta), that is the reason for the name "vedī" (the altar).
This earth, indeed, is the entire altar.
Measuring it out with the thought, "I shall be able [to perform the sacrifice] over such a space," they sacrifice upon it:
it is thirty paces wide to the west, thirty-six paces long toward the east, and twenty-four paces wide to the front.
Ten by ten they become complete;
the Virāj consists of ten syllables, and the Virāj is food.
By means of the Virāj, he wins the eating of food.
He digs up; thereby he strikes away whatever in her is impure.
He digs it up; therefore the plants perish.
He strews the sacrificial grass.
Therefore the plants come into being again.
He spreads the *uttarabarhis* over the *barhis*;
the *barhis* is indeed offspring, and the *uttarabarhis* is the sacrificer.
He thus makes the sacrificer superior to the non-sacrificer; therefore, the sacrificer is superior to the non-sacrificer.
6.2.5 Anuvāka 5: Description of the Vow Or rather, when one who is not capable takes up a burden, he surely breaks it under the weight.
If there were twelve *upasads* for a *sāha* sacrifice and three for a *ahīna* sacrifice, the ritual would be performed in a contrary manner.
There are three *upasads* for a one-day sacrifice (*sāhna*) and twelve for a multi-day sacrifice (*ahīna*), for the sake of providing strength and to ensure conformity.

A calf has but one teat, for that is its share; then he approaches the fast-food with one teat, then two, then three, then four. This indeed is the fast-food called "the razor-edged," by which one repels rivals already born and counteracts those yet to be born; thus, by means of something smaller, one attains what is greater.

He undertakes the vow with four teats at first, then three, then two, then one; this indeed is the vow called *sujaghanam*, which is conducive to austerity and leads to heaven; moreover, he is procreated with offspring and cattle.
Barley-gruel is the vow for a Rājanya; for barley-gruel is indeed fierce, and the Rājanya is fierce; it is the form of the thunderbolt, for the sake of success.

Curdled milk (*āmikṣā*) is the form of the *pākayajña* for a Vaiśya; it is for nourishment. Milk is for a Brāhmaṇa; the Brāhmaṇa is indeed brilliance, and milk is brilliance. By means of brilliance, he places brilliance—the milk—within himself. Moreover, embryos grow by means of milk. He who is consecrated (*dīkṣita*) is indeed like an embryo; in that milk becomes his fast-food (*vrata*), he thereby causes himself to grow.
Manu had three observances, the Asuras two, and the gods one.
In the morning, at midday, and in the evening—this was Manu’s observance; it is the form of the *pākayajña*, for the sake of prosperity.
In the morning and in the evening, hunger is the form of the Asuras, being devoid of a center; therefore they were defeated.
At midday and at midnight, it belongs to the gods; therefore they prevailed and went to the heavenly world.
In that his fast-food (vrata) is taken at midday and at midnight—since people eat food from the middle [of their hands]—he thereby places strength in the middle for the sake of overcoming his rival.
He prospers by himself, and his rival is defeated.

This consecrated person is indeed an embryo, and the consecrated hut is the womb. If the consecrated one should depart from the consecrated hut, it is just as when an embryo falls from the womb; therefore, he must not depart for the protection of himself.

This Agni is indeed the tiger, the guardian of the family; therefore, if one who has been consecrated (*dīkṣita*) should go abroad, he is liable to rise up against him and slay him. One must not go abroad for the sake of protecting oneself. He should lie down to the south; this is the station of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), and thus he lies in his own station.
He lies turned toward the fire; he lies having turned toward the deities and the sacrifice.
6.2.6 Anuvāka 6: Designation of the Ground for Optional Sacrifices One should cause him whom one desires to sacrifice on a sacrificial ground with an oblation in front to be consecrated, thinking:
"May the subsequent sacrifice incline toward him; may he conquer the heavenly world."
This indeed is the place for the oblation and the site for sacrificing to the gods, where the Hotṛ, while reciting the Prātaranuvāka, gazes upon Agni, the waters, and the sun.
The higher sacrifice inclines toward him; he conquers the world of heaven.
One who has rivals should cause him to sacrifice on a site where the gods have been won over.
Or he should touch a path or a dug-out pit,
until it is fit for a cart to go upon,
or for a chariot; this indeed is the sacrificial ground obtained.
He surely attains his rival; his rival does not attain him.
One should cause a sacrifice to be performed on a sacrificial ground that is elevated in one place for one who desires cattle;
for from a sacrificial ground elevated in one place, the Aṅgirases created cattle.
If the space between the *sadas* and the *havirdhāna* sheds were to be elevated,
this would be the "one-elevated" sacrificial ground; one who sacrifices there indeed becomes possessed of cattle.
One should cause him who desires heaven to sacrifice on a sacrificial ground that is elevated in three places;
for from a sacrificial ground elevated in three places, the Aṅgirases went to the heavenly world— namely,
between the Āhavanīya fire and the Havirdhāna shed.
The space between the *havirdhāna* shed and the *sadas*, and the space between the *sadas* and the *gārhapatya* fire, should be elevated.
This indeed is the three-elevated sacrificial ground for the gods;
by it, one goes to the heavenly world.
One should cause someone desiring stability to sacrifice on a consecrated sacrificial ground (devayajana); for that sacrificial ground which is level on all sides is indeed stable;
he truly finds firm standing.
One should cause him who desires cattle to sacrifice where various plants are intertwined;
for this is indeed the form of cattle;
by means of that very form, he [obtains] cattle for him.
He secures cattle and indeed becomes possessed of cattle; one should cause him whom he desires to sacrifice on a sacrificial ground seized by Nirṛti.
"May I cause Nirṛti to seize his sacrifice.
That sacrificial ground which is uneven and yet appears level is indeed seized by Nirṛti;
thus, by means of Nirṛti herself, he causes his sacrifice to be seized.

One should cause someone who desires distinction to sacrifice on a sacrificial ground that is separated [from others]. That ground over which they might deliberate regarding either a vessel or a bed—where it slopes eastward from the Āhavanīya fire and westward from the Gārhapatya fire—that indeed is the separated sacrificial ground.
Thus he becomes separated from evil and from his rival.
They do not examine him regarding the sacrificial vessel nor the bed;
one should cause a man who desires prosperity to perform the sacrifice at a place of divine worship where the ritual purpose is fulfilled,
for a man must indeed be made to act.
It indeed exists.
6.2.7 Anuvāka 7: Description of the Uttaravedi.
From among them, the Uttaravedi, having assumed the form of a lioness, stepped aside between both groups and stood there.
Those gods reflected:
"She will turn toward the Yantaras; they shall be this [world]," they said, and they invited her.
She replied:
"Choose a boon; you shall obtain all desires through me, but let the first oblation reach me before reaching the fire.
Therefore, they pour the butter over the *uttaravedi* first, before the fire, for it was chosen as her boon.
He measures it around with a pin; that is its measure. Moreover, by means of what is already yoked, he secures what is to be yoked.
"Thou art my path to wealth," he says.
"For wealth indeed protected them;
'Thou art the bitter-protecting one for me,' he says,
for the bitter ones indeed protected them."
"Protect me, O protectors, from distress," he says,
for he protects these very ones when they are distressed; "protect me, O protectors, from trembling," he says.
He consoles those who are distressed, saying, "May Agni find them; O Agni Aṅgiras, by name Nabhas," and he carries [the fire] three times.
Those very fires that are in these worlds he thereby wins; he carries the fourth silently;
thus he wins what is undefined.
"You are a lioness, you are a buffalo," he says, for she, having assumed the form of a lioness, stood having stepped away between the two.
"Spread wide! May the lord of the sacrifice spread wide for you," he says.
He causes the sacrificer himself to expand with offspring and cattle.

With the words "Thou art firm," he strikes [the earth] for the sake of stability. With the words "Be purified for the gods! Be adorned for the gods! he sprinkles it down and scatters [the dust] for the sake of purification.
"May Indraghoṣa with the Vasus protect you from the east," he says; thus he sprinkles it from all the quarters.
When the high altar turned toward the gods, the Asuras, raising their thunderbolt, advanced against the gods. Indraghoṣa with the Vasus drove them away from the east;
Manojavā with the Pitṛs [drove them] from the south; Pracetas with the Rudras from the west; and Viśvakarman with the Ādityas from the north.
In that he thus sprinkles the *uttaravedi*, the sacrificer thereby drives away his rivals from all the quarters.
Indra gave the Yatis over to the *sālāvṛka* wolves; they devoured them on the south side of the *uttaravedi*.
Whatever remains of the sprinkling water, he should pour down on the south side of the *uttaravedi*.
Whatever is cruel therein, he pacifies with that;
he should meditate upon whomsoever he hates, and thus he strikes him with affliction.
6.2.8 Anuvāka 8: The Procedure for Sprinkling. The Uttaravedi said:
"Through me, you shall attain all desires."
Those gods desired,
"May we overcome our rivals, the Asuras," and they offered oblations.
"You are a lioness, a subduer of rivals; svāhā!
With these words, they overcame their asura rivals, the enemies; having overcome those asura rivals, the enemies, they desired [further success].
"May we obtain offspring," they said, and they offered the oblation:
"Thou art a lioness, winning good offspring; svāhā!"
They found offspring; having found offspring, they desired.
"May we obtain cattle," they said, and they offered the oblation:
"Thou art a lioness, winning the increase of wealth; svāhā!"
They found cattle;
having found cattle, they desired,
"May we find a firm foundation."
They offered, saying, "Thou art a lioness, winning the Ādityas; svāhā! and they found this firm foundation.
Having understood this foundation, those deities desired, "May we attain our blessings," and they offered oblations.
"O lioness, bring the gods hither for the god-seeking sacrificer; Svāhā!"—
thus those deities approached with blessings.
He sprinkles five times;
the *paṅkti* consists of five syllables, and the sacrifice is fivefold.
Verily, he wins the sacrifice itself.
He sprinkles transversely;
therefore animals move their limbs transversely.
For the sake of stability,
he lifts up the offering-spoon with the words, "To the beings, thee!";
those who are the gods, the beings, theirs is that share.
By that very means he gratifies them; he lays around the enclosing-sticks made of *pūtudru* wood.
Of these...
For the support of the worlds. Agni had three elder brothers; while carrying the oblation to the gods, they perished.
That Agni was afraid,
thinking, "In this very way he will surely bring me to ruin," and so he hid himself.
That [power] which he had dwelt among the trees, they found in the *pūtudru*; that which was among the plants, in the *sugandhitejana*; that which was among the cattle, between the horns of the ram;
for that [power], the deities sought a way of access and they found it.
They said to him, "Turn toward us; carry our oblation.
He replied:
"I choose a boon: whatever of the [oblation] that has been taken but not yet offered should fall outside the enclosing sticks, let that be the share of my brothers.
Therefore, whatever of the [oblation] that has been taken but not yet offered falls outside the enclosing sticks, that is their share; he gratifies them with that.
He reflected:
"My ancestors were boneless; let me force my brothers to cast off their bones," he said.
Those bones which he caused to be cast off became *pūtudru* trees.
That flesh which has perished is *gulgulu*; when he collects these materials, he thereby collects Agni himself.
"Thou art the soil (*purīṣa*) of Agni," he says;
for these materials are indeed the soil of Agni.
Moreover, they say:
"These brothers of his, indeed, lie around him—namely, the enclosing-sticks made of *pūtudru* wood."
6.2.9 Anuvāka 9: The Rule for Sprinkling. He unties what is bound; verily he releases them from the noose of Varuṇa.
He washes them; verily he makes them pure.
Having offered with a verse addressed to Savitṛ, he causes the two *havirdhāna* carts to move forward; verily, impelled by Savitṛ, he causes them to move forward.
This axle is indeed Varuṇa, ill-spoken and bound on both sides;
if it were to creak, it would creak toward the house of the sacrificer.
Therefore he says, "O God of fair speech, speak toward the dwellings!"
The house is indeed the dwelling-place;
the wife is for the sake of peace.
He anoints the shoes,
for the wife is the friend of all; it is for the sake of friendship.
Whatever the wife performs at the sacrifice, that constitutes a pairing.
Moreover, this is the wife's taking hold of the sacrifice so that it may not be interrupted.
For the Rakṣases seek to strike down the sacrifice by following along its path.
He offers oblations on the two tracks with two verses addressed to Viṣṇu;
for Viṣṇu is the sacrifice,
and thus he drives away the Rakṣases from the sacrifice itself.
If the Adhvaryu were to offer an oblation in that which is not fire, the Adhvaryu would become blind and the Rakṣases would destroy the sacrifice.
Having placed gold [upon it], he offers;
thus he offers in that which possesses fire.
"The Adhvaryu does not become blind; the Rakṣases do not destroy the sacrifice.
"Going forward, fashioning the sacrifice," he says; thus he causes them to go to the heavenly world.
"Rejoice here on the height of the earth," he says;
for the place of sacrifice is indeed the height of the earth.
The *havirdhāna* shed is indeed the head of the sacrifice.
With the verse containing the word *āśis*, "Whether from heaven, O Viṣṇu, or from earth," he drives in the wedge of the southern *havirdhāna* cart;
thus, from the very head of the sacrifice, the sacrificer secures his blessings.
Or Danda Aupara cut off the axle with the *vaṣaṭ*-call of the third *havirdhāna*.
When the third roof-covering of the two *havirdhānas* is brought forward, it is for the attainment of the third *havirdhāna*; for the *havirdhāna* is indeed the head of the sacrifice.
"Thou art the forehead of Viṣṇu; thou art the back of Viṣṇu," he says; therefore the head is thus expanded.
"Thou art the needle of Viṣṇu; thou art the fixed point of Viṣṇu," he says.
For the Havirdhāna shed has Viṣṇu as its deity.
If one were to tie the first knot and not loosen it, the Adhvaryu would die of urinary retention; therefore, it must be loosened.
6.2.10 Anuvāka 10: Designation of the Sadas.
With the words, "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ," he takes up the spade for the sake of impulsion.
He says, "With the arms of the Aśvins."
"For the Aśvins were the Adhvaryus of the gods. "With the hands of Pūṣan," he says for the sake of restraint.
This spade is indeed like a thunderbolt; "Thou art a spade, thou art a woman," he says for the sake of pacification.

Indeed, while each section of the sacrifice is being performed, the Rakṣases seek to strike down the sacrifice; "The Rakṣas is enclosed, the enemies are enclosed," he says for the purpose of driving away the Rakṣases.

"Here do I cut off the neck of the Rakṣas; him who hates us and whom we hate," he says. There are indeed two persons: him whom one hates and him who hates one. It is of these two alone that he cuts off the necks without interval.
"For the sky thee, for the atmosphere thee, for the earth thee," he says; thus he sprinkles it for these very worlds.
He sprinkles from the farther side toward himself; therefore—
From beyond, men live upon this downward-flowing strength.
Indeed, he does something harsh when he digs; he pours out water for the sake of pacification.
He pours out water mixed with barley; barley is strength, and the Udumbara is strength; thus he unites strength with strength.
The Audumbarī post is equal in height to the sacrificer; as great as the sacrificer is, so much strength does he bestow upon him.
With the words, "Thou art the seat of the Pitṛs," he spreads the sacrificial grass (barhis), for that which is dug in belongs to the Pitṛs.

If he were to set up [the post] without having spread the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), it would be dedicated to the Pitṛs once dug in; he sets it up after spreading the sacrificial grass, so that he sets it up in this very earth, and moreover, he makes it firmly rooted.

"Support the sky, fill the mid-region," he says, for the separation of these worlds. "May Dyutāna Māruta set you up," he says; for Dyutāna Māruta used to set up the Audumbara post for the gods; by that very means [he does so].
He measures this [post] with the words, "Thee, winner of the Brahman; thee, winner of the Kṣatra"—this is exactly according to the sacrificial formula.
With the words, "O Heaven and Earth, be filled with ghee," he offers an oblation upon the Audumbarī post; thus he anoints Heaven and Earth with essence.
He lets it flow down to the edge; verily he anoints the sacrificer with brilliance at the very end.
"Thou art Indra's," [with these words] he lays down a roof-covering, for the Sadas has Indra as its deity.
"The shade of all people," he says, for this Sadas is indeed the shade of all people.
One desiring splendor should have it covered with nine layers; it is commensurate with the Trivṛt Stoma, for the Trivṛt is splendor—he indeed becomes splendid.
One desiring power should have it covered with eleven layers; the Triṣṭubh has eleven syllables and the Triṣṭubh is power—he indeed becomes powerful.
One with fifteen roofs is for one who has rivals; the thunderbolt is fifteenfold, for the overcoming of rivals.
One with seventeen roofs is for one desiring progeny; Prajāpati is seventeenfold, for the attainment of Prajāpati.
One with twenty-one roofs is for one desiring stability; the twenty-one-fold is the foundation of the *stomas*, for the sake of stability.

The belly is indeed always strength, and the udumbara is strength; he fixes the udumbara post in the middle, and thus he bestows strength upon the people in their midst. Therefore, they enjoy strength from the center.

The southern roof-pieces belong to the world of the sacrificer, while the northern ones belong to the world of his rival; he places the southern ones to the north, and thus he makes the sacrificer superior to the non-sacrificer. Therefore, the sacrificer is superior to the non-sacrificer.
He makes the internal partitions for the sake of separation; therefore, living beings subsist upon the forest.
"O lover of songs, may the songs encompass thee," he says; this is according to the sacrificial formula.
"Thou art Indra’s seam; thou art Indra’s firm foundation," he says, for the seat belongs to Indra by deity.
If one were to tie the first knot and not loosen it, the Adhvaryu would die of urinary retention; therefore, it must be loosened.
6.2.11 Anuvāka 11: Designation of the Uparavas. The Havirdhāna cart is indeed the head of the sacrifice; the Uparavas are the vital breaths.
They are dug out in the Havirdhāna.
Therefore, the vital breaths are in the head;
they are hollowed out from below,
therefore the vital breaths are below the head.
"I dig the slayers of Rakṣases, the slayers of Valagas, belonging to Viṣṇu," he says;
for the *uparavas* have Viṣṇu as their deity.
Indeed, when the Asuras were departing, they buried Valagas in the vital breaths of the gods.
They found them at the depth of an arm;
therefore, they are dug out to the depth of an arm.
"Here I dig up that hidden spell."
"Whatever [spell] a kinsman or an alien has buried against us," he says;
for there are indeed two kinds of persons, the one who is a kinsman and the one who is an alien.
Whatever spell those two have buried against him, that very thing he now digs up.
He stitches it together; therefore the vital breaths are joined within. He does not split it apart.
Therefore, the vital breaths are undivided.
He pours out water;
therefore, the vital breaths are moist within.
As many times as he pours down the water.
Barley is indeed strength, and the sounding-holes are the vital breaths; verily, he bestows strength upon the vital breaths.
He spreads the sacrificial grass;
therefore, the vital breaths are hairy within.
He sprinkles it with clarified butter.
Clarified butter is indeed brilliance,
and the sounding-holes are the vital breaths;
verily, he bestows brilliance upon the vital breaths.
The two pressing-boards are indeed the jaws of the sacrifice; he does not join them together, for the jaws are unjoined.
Moreover, in the Dīrghasoma sacrifice, they should be firmly fixed for the sake of stability;
for the oblation-holder (havirdhāna) is indeed the head of the sacrifice.

The vital breaths are the sounding-holes, the two jaws are the pressing-boards, the tongue is the hide, the pressing-stones are the teeth, the mouth is the Āhavanīya fire, the nose is the Uttaravedi, and the belly is the Sadas.
Indeed, when one chews with the tongue upon the teeth, it goes into the mouth;
when it has gone into the mouth, it then goes into the belly.

Therefore, having pressed [the Soma] with the stones upon the hide in the *havirdhāna* shed, and having offered it in the *āhavanīya* fire, they go back westward and consume it in the *sadas*. Verily,
he who knows the milking of the *virāj* at the beginning of the sacrifice, he indeed milks her.
This is indeed Virāj. Her skin is the hide; the two pressing-boards are her udder; the sounding-holes are her teats; the pressing-stones are the calves; the priests milk her; Soma is the milk.
He who knows thus truly milks her.
6.3 Prapāṭhaka: 3, Anuvāka 1, Section 1: The Designation of the Dhiṣṇiya Mounds.
He scatters the dhiṣṇiya mounds from the cātvāla pit; for the cātvāla is indeed the womb of the sacrifice, and this is for the sake of providing the sacrifice with its proper womb.
The gods indeed lost the sacrifice; they won it back from the Āgnīdhra.
That which is the Āgnīdhra is the invincible part of the sacrifice.
When he distributes the hearths from the Āgnīdhra fire-altar, he extends the sacrifice again from that very part of it which is unconquered;
for indeed, those who creep along for the *bahiṣpavamāna* go forth having already been conquered when the *bahiṣpavamāna* has been chanted.
He says: "O Āgnīdh, carry forth the fires, strew the sacrificial grass, and prepare the sacrificial cakes.
Thus, having won the sacrifice, they proceed to perform it once again.
He distributes the coals at two pressings and the sticks at the third,
for the sake of its brilliance;
thus he also gathers it together.
The Dhiṣṇiya fires indeed guarded Soma in yonder world;
from them they brought Soma away;
they followed after him and settled around him.
He who knows thus finds an attendant;
they were deprived of their share of the Soma-drinking.
They desired the drinking of Soma among the gods;
the gods said to them, "Take each two names for yourselves, and then you shall obtain it, or perhaps not."
Now, the hearths (dhiṣṇiyas) are indeed fires; therefore, a Brāhmaṇa who has two names prospers.
Among them, those that were situated closest attained the drinking of Soma: the Āhavanīya, the Āgnīdhrīya, the Hotrīya, and the Mārjālīya.
Therefore, they offer oblations into them; he utters the *vaṣaṭ* call after passing over [the preceding ones], for...
These gods were honored by means of the Soma-drinking. Indeed, those oblations which they offered toward the east, with them they repelled the Asuras who were in the east;
those which they offered toward the west, with them they drove away the Asuras who were in the west.
Other oblations are offered facing eastward, but sitting facing westward, he pours out the libations for the Dhiṣṇiya hearths both from behind and from the front;
thus the sacrificer drives away his rivals from both the rear and the front,
and therefore offspring are born facing backward and facing forward.
These hearth-fires (dhiṣṇiyas) are indeed the vital breaths;
if the Adhvaryu were to pass by the hearth-fires facing westward, he would draw together the vital breaths.
He would be liable to die prematurely.
For the Hotṛ is indeed the navel of the sacrifice;
the out-breath (prāṇa) is indeed directed upward from the navel, while the in-breath (apāna) is directed downward.
If the Adhvaryu were to pass beyond the Hotṛ toward the west, he would place the out-breath into the in-breath, and he would be liable to die.
The Adhvaryu should not sing;
for the Adhvaryu is the very vigor of speech.
If the Adhvaryu should sing along with the chant, he should hand over his speech to the Udgātṛ; his speech would then be liable to fail.
Thus say the exponents of sacred knowledge.

The Adhvaryu should not pass westward toward the Sadas while the Soma has not yet been settled; for how then could he go to offer the Dakṣiṇās? For that is their path. To whom indeed would the gods acknowledge either a path or a non-path?
Having gone around the north of the Āgnīdhra fire, he offers the Dakṣiṇās; thus he does not draw together his vital breaths.
Some *dhiṣṇiya* hearths are sown with seeds while others are not;
by sowing those he gratifies them, and by designating those which he does not sow, he gratifies them.
6.3.2 Anuvāka 2: Designation of the Carrying-forth of Agni and Soma.
These Vaiṣarjana offerings are indeed offered for the sake of the heavenly world;
he offers two with the Gārhapatya fire.
The sacrificer has two feet for the sake of stability;
he offers in the Āgnīdhra fire.
He indeed ascends into the intermediate space;
he offers in the Āhavanīya fire, and thus causes him to go to the heavenly world.
When the gods were going to the heavenly world, the *rakṣases* sought to strike them down;
having struck away the *rakṣases* by means of Soma the King, they went to the heavenly world, making themselves secure so that the *rakṣases* could not seize them.
The Soma has been taken; then he offers the Vaiṣarjana oblations for the smiting away of the Rākṣasas;
"O Soma, you [protect us] from those who harm our bodies," he says.
"For this [sacrifice] thins out the hostilities caused by others," he says;
for the *rakṣas* are indeed caused by others.
"You are the one who extends wide protection," he says;
by this he means, "Make wide space for us.
"May the swift one, being pleased, partake of the clarified butter," he says.
Having indeed made the sacrificer successful, he causes him to go to the heavenly world so that the *rakṣases* may not seize him;
he bestows the *soma*.
They bring forward the pressing-stones, the Vāyu-vessels, and the wooden trough;
they lead up the wife;
they cause the carts to roll forth after them.
Whatever he possesses, with that he goes to the heavenly world;
he offers in the Āgnīdhra fire with a verse containing the word "lead" (nayavatī) for the sake of leading [him] to the heavenly world.
The Āgnīdhra places the pressing-stones and the Vāyavya cups upon the *droṇakalaśa*;
for they draw [the soma] from it by means of those [vessels].
If he were to place them down together, the [soma] would be exhausted.
He causes him to step forward with a gentle verse;
verily, he causes him to step forward by means of his own deity.
"Thou art the seat of Aditi; sit upon the seat of Aditi," he says;
this is according to the sacrificial formula.
Previously, the sacrificer himself was its protector.
"This Soma, O God Savitṛ, [is for you]," he says;
thus, impelled by Savitṛ, he hands him over to the deities.
"O Soma, as a god, you have approached the gods," he says.
"For he, being a god, approaches the gods;
'I am a human, [approaching] humans,' he says."
For this man, being a human, approaches other humans;
if he were not to recite this sacrificial formula (*yajus*), the sacrificer would be without offspring and without cattle.
Therefore he says: "Together with offspring, together with the increase of wealth."
"By offspring and by cattle together, he returns to this world," he says; for "homage to the gods" is indeed the homage due to the gods.
"Self-power to the ancestors," he says, for the utterance "svadhā" belongs to the ancestors.
"Here I am released from the noose of Varuṇa," he says; thus he is indeed released from the noose of Varuṇa. "O Agni, lord of vows..."
"One's own former body should be taken back," they say;
for who knows whether he will give it back again when it has come under his own control, or whether he will not?
The pressing-stones, indeed, are the army of King Soma’s plunderers.
He who, knowing thus, causes the pressing-stones to rest in the Āgnīdhra shed, is not overtaken by the army of thieves.

6.3.3 Anuvāka 3: Designation of the Tree for the Sacrificial Post Having offered an oblation with a verse addressed to Viṣṇu, he approaches the sacrificial post (*yūpa*). For the sacrificial post has Viṣṇu as its deity; thus he approaches it by means of its own deity. He says:

"I have passed others, I have not approached others. For he indeed passes others and does not approach others. He says: "I have found you on this side, not on the far side. For he finds it on this side, not on the far side. "I take pleasure in you."
"Belonging to Viṣṇu, for the sacrifice to the gods," he says, for he delights him for the sake of the sacrifice to the gods.

"May the god Savitṛ anoint you with honey," he says; verily, he anoints him with splendor. "O plant, protect him! O axe, do not harm him! he says; the axe is indeed a thunderbolt, [and he speaks thus] for the sake of pacification.
From the tree that fears the axe, the splendor flies away along with the first chip. The first chip that flies away—one should pick that up as well, so that it may possess splendor.

Thus he brings it [the sacrificial post]. These worlds, indeed, fear one who moves away from the post; [therefore] he says, "Do not scratch the sky with your top; do not injure the mid-air with your middle," thereby appeasing it for these very worlds.

He offers an oblation on the stump with the words, "O Lord of the Forest, grow with a hundred shoots! Therefore, more trees than the stump itself spring up from it. He says, "May we grow with a thousand shoots!"—verily, he invokes this blessing.
If he were to cut one that has no contact with the axle, or if he were to cut one that has contact with the axle, the chariot-pole would be liable to bring about the death of the sacrificer.

If he should desire of someone, "May he be without a firm foundation," he should cut an upward-pointing branch for him; for this among trees is without a firm foundation, and [the sacrificer] indeed becomes without a firm foundation.

If he should desire of someone, "May he be without cattle," he should cut for him [a branch] without leaves and with a dry tip; for this among trees is unfavorable to cattle, and he indeed becomes without cattle.
If he should desire of someone, "May he be rich in cattle," he should cut for him one with many leaves and many branches;
for this among trees is favorable to cattle, and he indeed becomes rich in cattle.

One who desires a firm foundation should cut [a tree] that is firmly established; for among trees, that which grows on level ground from its own natural place is indeed firmly established. He becomes firmly established himself. One should cut that which leans toward the west, for it has leaned toward the sacrificial food (*medha*). For one whom he desires, "May the subsequent sacrifice incline toward him," he should cut one five cubits long; the *paṅkti* meter has five syllables, and the sacrifice is fivefold; thus the subsequent sacrifice inclines toward him.
One who desires a firm foundation should have it six cubits long; for there are six seasons, and thus he finds a firm foundation in the seasons.

One who desires cattle should have it seven cubits long; the Śakvarī verse has seven feet and cattle are the Śakvarī; verily, he wins cattle. One who desires splendor should have it nine cubits long; it is commensurate with the Trivṛt Stoma, and the Trivṛt is splendor; verily, he becomes possessed of splendor.

One eleven-cubit [sacrificial post] for one who desires sensory power; the *triṣṭubh* meter has eleven syllables, and the *triṣṭubh* is sensory power; he thus becomes possessed of sensory power. One fifteen-cubit [post] for one who has rivals; the thunderbolt (*vajra*) is fifteenfold, for the sake of overcoming rivals.
One seventeen-cubit [post] for one who desires offspring; Prajāpati is seventeenfold, for the attainment of Prajāpati.
It is twenty-one cubits long for one who desires a firm foundation; the twenty-one-fold hymn-form (stoma) is the foundation of the stomas, [serving] for the sake of stability.

It has eight corners; the Gāyatrī consists of eight syllables, the Gāyatrī is brilliance, and the Gāyatrī is the mouth of the sacrifice; thus it is commensurate with brilliance, with the Gāyatrī, and with the mouth of the sacrifice.

6.3.4 Anuvāka 4: The Description of the Installation of the Sacrificial Post (Yūpa) "For the earth, for thee; for the intermediate space, for thee; for the sky, for thee," he says; thus he sprinkles it for these very worlds.
He sprinkles it facing away, for the world of heaven is, as it were, turned away.

Verily, he does something cruel when he digs; he pours down water for the sake of pacification. He pours down water containing barley; barley is indeed strength (*ūrj*). The sacrificial post is commensurate with the sacrificer; thus, he bestows upon him as much strength as the sacrificer himself possesses.

With the words, "Thou art the seat of the Fathers," he spreads the sacrificial grass (*barhis*); for that which is dug in has the Fathers as its deity. If he were to set it up without spreading the sacrificial grass, the dug-in post would belong to the Fathers; by spreading the sacrificial grass, he sets it up; he thus sets it up upon this very earth. He throws down a chip of the sacrificial post; verily, he sets it up endowed with its own brilliance.

"May the god Savitṛ anoint you with honey," he says; verily, he anoints him with splendor. "For the plants with fair berries," [he says] as he fastens the top-ring; therefore, the plants bear fruit from the top.

Clarified butter is indeed brilliance. The corner facing the fire (agniṣṭhā) is commensurate with the sacrificer. In that he anoints the corner facing the fire, he anoints the sacrificer himself with brilliance.
He anoints it to the very end; verily, he anoints the sacrificer with brilliance to the very end. He strokes it all around; verily, he bestows brilliance upon him without leaving any part excluded.

"Supporting the sky, fill the mid-region," he says; this is for the separation of these worlds. He prepares it with a verse addressed to Viṣṇu; for the sacrificial post has Viṣṇu as its deity, and thus he prepares it with its own deity.

With two [corner-posts] he fashions them; the sacrificer has two feet for support. If he should desire of someone, "May I deprive him of brilliance, of the gods, and of sensory power," he should cause the corner-post standing nearest the fire (agniṣṭhā) to lean away from the Āhavanīya fire in this way or that way; thus he deprives him of brilliance, of the gods, and of sensory power. If he should desire of someone, "May I endow him with brilliance, with the gods, and with sensory power," [he should do otherwise].
He should measure its corner facing the fire with the Āhavanīya; verily he endows him with splendor, with the deities, and with power.

"Thee, winner of the Brahman, winner of the Kṣatra," he says; this is according to the sacrificial formula. He encircles it with a rope; the rope is indeed strength, and the sacrificial post is measured by the sacrificer; verily he endows the sacrificer himself with strength.
He girds it at the height of the navel; verily he bestows strength upon him at the very height of his navel. Therefore, they enjoy strength from the height of the navel.
If he should desire of someone, "May I deprive him of strength," he should either pull the cord upwards or downwards for that person; verily, he deprives him of strength by means of the cord itself.

If he should desire, "May Parjanya be rainy," he should drive it downward; verily he restrains the rain. If he should desire, "May it be rainless," he should drive it upward; verily he lets loose the rain. That which is buried is for the Pitṛs; that from the point of burial up to the rope is for men; the rope is for plants; that from the rope up to the *caṣāla* (top-ring) is for the Viśve Devas; the *caṣāla* is for Indra; and that which exceeds it is for the Sādhyas. This sacrificial post (*yūpa*) indeed belongs to all the deities; in that he erects the post, he gratifies all the deities.

By means of sacrifice, the gods went to the heavenly world. They thought, "Mankind will follow after us. Having concealed themselves by means of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), they went to the heavenly world. The seers recognized that [world] by means of the sacrificial post alone; that is the reason for the sacrificial post's name.
In that he erects the sacrificial post, it is for the purpose of discerning the heavenly world.

He measures [the post] in front, for that which is in front of the sacrifice is discerned; for that which has passed by is indeed undiscerned, as they say of it, "This was to have been done. The Sādhyas, indeed, overstepped the sacrifice; the sacrifice did not touch them. What was redundant in the sacrifice, that touched them. This is indeed the redundant part of the sacrifice: when one churns fire in the fire and throws it [into the fire], that is the redundant part;
and what of the sacrificial post is above the *caṣāla* (top-ring), that is the redundant part. That is their share; he gratifies them with that.

When the *soma* sacrifice was completed, the gods indeed lifted up the offering-spoons (*sruc*) and the sacrificial post (*yūpa*). They reflected, "We are surely committing a desecration of the sacrifice here. They saw the *prastara* (grass-bundle) as the ransom for the spoons and the *svaru* (wooden chip) as the ransom for the post. When the *soma* sacrifice is completed, he takes away the *prastara* and offers the *svaru*, so that there shall be no desecration of the sacrifice.
6.3.5 Anuvāka 5: Concerning the Churning of the Fire.
The Sādhyas were indeed the gods in this world; nothing else whatsoever stirred.
They offered Agni himself to Agni for the sake of the sacrifice, for they found nothing else fit to be offered;
from that, indeed, these creatures were born.
When one churns fire within the fire and throws it [into the hearth], it is for the procreation of offspring.
This fire is indeed Rudra; the sacrificer is the victim.
If one were to churn the fire after having immolated the victim, he would deliver the sacrificer to Rudra.
If he were to add [it], he would be liable to die prematurely;
however, they also say this.
"Agni is all the deities; this victim is the oblation.
When he churns the fire after having seized the victim, he generates all the deities for the sake of the oblation already set forth. Having merely brought it near, he should churn the fire.
"Therefore he says, 'Thou art neither obtained nor unobtained; thou art the birthplace of Agni,' for this is indeed the birthplace of Agni."
"You two are testicles," he says,
for these two are indeed testicles.
"Thou art Urvaśī; thou art Āyu," he says for the sake of pairing.
