"Anointed with ghee, do ye two bestow virility," he says.
"For these two bear the bull, he who is Agni.
"Be born after the Gāyatrī metre," he says; thus he causes him to be born by means of the metres.
"Recite for the fire being churned," he says;
he recites a verse to Savitṛ;
thus, impelled by Savitṛ, he churns it.
"Recite for her when she has been born; recite for her as she is being struck," he says;
thus, at every single section as it is being performed, he brings him into harmony.
He recites all the Gāyatrīs; for Agni has the Gāyatrī as his metre, and thus he causes him to prosper by means of his own metre.
Agni exists beforehand; having churned the fire, he offers it.
As those two come into being, they come together toward the sacrificer.
"May you two be of one mind for us," he says.
Having offered it for the sake of pacification, he makes an oblation; verily, he bestows food upon him as soon as he is born.
He offers with clarified butter. Clarified butter is indeed the dear abode of Agni; verily, he causes him to prosper through his own dear abode, and also through splendor.
6.3.6 Anuvāka 6: The Binding of the Animal Sacrifice.
"For food, thee!"—with these words he takes the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), for he who sacrifices is indeed like one who desires.
"Thou art the invoker," he says, for he brings them together.
"Near the gods have come the divine clans," he says; for these, being the divine clans, indeed approach the gods.
"The eager bearers," he says; for the priests are indeed the eager bearers; therefore he speaks thus.
"O Bṛhaspati, hold fast the treasures! he says.
He says, "Bṛhaspati is indeed the Brahman among the gods; by means of the Brahman, he wins cattle for him.
He says, "May your oblations be relished"; verily, he makes them relishable.
He says, "O divine Tvaṣṭṛ, make the wealth delightful"; Tvaṣṭṛ is indeed the fashioner of the forms of paired animals; verily, he bestows form upon the cattle.
"O Revatīs, rejoice! he says; for the Revatīs are indeed cattle; verily he causes cattle to rejoice for him.

"At the impulse of the god Savitṛ," [he says] as he takes up the cord; this is for instigation. "With the arms of the Aśvins," he says, for the Aśvins were the two Adhvaryus among the gods. "With the hands of Pūṣan," he says for the sake of restraint.
"O divine oblation, I seize you with the noose of *ṛta*," he says; for *ṛta* is truth, and thus he seizes him with truth by means of *ṛta*.
He carries him around not straight across, for they bind a victim facing backward for the sake of distinction.
"Be bold against men," he says as he fastens him, for the sake of firmness.
"I sprinkle you from the waters and from the plants," he says, for this animal originates from the waters and from the plants.
"Thou art the drinker of the waters," he says, for he who is taken up for sacrifice is indeed a drinker of the waters.
"May the divine waters, having tasted this oblation, make it savory for the gods"—thus he says; verily he makes it savory for him. He sprinkles it from above;
verily he makes it pure from above. He causes it to drink [the water]; verily he makes it pure within. He sprinkles it from below; verily he makes it pure on all sides.
6.3.7 Anuvāka 7: Designation of the Sāmidhenīs and other elements.
By means of Agni as the Hotṛ, the gods indeed overcame the Asuras. [The Adhvaryu] says, "Recite the invitatory verses for Agni being kindled," for the sake of overcoming one's rivals.
He recites seventeen Sāmidhenī verses; Prajāpati consists of seventeen parts; [this is] for the attainment of Prajāpati.
He recites seventeen verses: twelve months and five seasons—that is the year; after the year, creatures are born; it is for the procreation of creatures.
Having recited the *sāmidhenī* verses, the gods did not perceive the sacrifice. Prajāpati then offered the *āghāra* libation silently;
then indeed the gods perceived the sacrifice. In that he offers the *āghāra* libation silently, it is for the illumination of the sacrifice.

The sacrifice was indeed among the Asuras; the gods wrested it away by means of silent oblation (*tūṣṇīṃ homa*). In that he pours the *āghāra* libation silently, he thereby wrests the sacrifice from his rival.

He wipes the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*); verily he purifies them. He wipes each three times; for the sacrifice has a threefold course, and also for the smiting away of the Rakṣases. They amount to twelve; twelve months are a year;
verily he gratifies the year, and also bestows the year upon him for the attainment of the world of heaven.

The *āghāra* libation is indeed the head of the sacrifice, and Agni is all the deities. When he pours the *āghāra*, the sacrificer wins all the deities from the very head of the sacrifice. This *āghāra* is the head of the sacrifice and the animal is the body; having poured the *āghāra*, he anoints the animal, and thus he restores the head of the sacrifice to its own body.

"May your breath unite with the wind," he says; for the breath has Vāyu as its deity; verily, he offers his breath into Vāyu. "May the limbs unite with the sacrificial objects; may the lord of the sacrifice [unite] with the blessing," he says; verily, he causes the lord of the sacrifice to attain the blessing. Viśvarūpa, the son of Tvaṣṭṛ, struck the animal from above; therefore they do not cut portions from the animal from above. In that he anoints the animal from above, he makes it fit for sacrifice.
He chooses the officiating priests; verily he chooses the meters. He chooses seven; there are seven domestic animals and seven wild animals, and there are seven meters—for the attainment of both.

He performs eleven fore-offerings (*prayāja*); ten indeed are the vital breaths of the animal, and the self is the eleventh; as great as the animal is, so much of it he offers. One [priest] lies around the omentum; verily the self lies around the self.

The axe is indeed a thunderbolt, and the splinter from the sacrificial post is a thunderbolt; for the gods, having made ghee into a thunderbolt, slew Soma. "Anointed with ghee, protect the animal! he says; thus, having brought it under control by means of the thunderbolt itself, he seizes it.

6.3.8 Anuvāka 8: Designation of the Slaying of the Animal. He carries fire around it; he thus makes it entirely offered so that nothing may be spilled, for that which spills from what has been offered is not spilled. He carries fire around it three times, for sacrifice is threefold; furthermore, it is for the smiting away of the Rākṣasas.
The exponents of the Veda say:

"Should one touch the victim animals or should one not touch them? [They say: "The victim is indeed led forth for Death; if he were to touch it, the sacrificer would be liable to die. On the other hand, they also say: 'The victim is led forth for the sake of the heavenly world';
if he were not to touch it, the sacrificer would be excluded from the heavenly world. Therefore, he touches it with the two omentum-spits; thus it is both touched and untouched."

"O Hotṛ, give the impulse for the oblations to the gods," he says, for the rite is performed once impelled. "O wealthy ones, enter the lord of the sacrifice with affection," he says; this is exactly according to the sacrificial formula.
He goes forward with Agni at his head to drive away the Rakṣases.

"Protect [the victim] from contact with the earth," he says, as he throws down the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), so that nothing may be spilled; for that which is spilled upon the *barhis* is not truly spilled. Moreover, he thereby establishes it as seated upon the *barhis*.
The Adhvaryu turns away from the victim while it is being slaughtered; he thus withdraws from the cattle, so that there may be no injury to himself.

He who knows this attains glory and obtains cattle. This wife is led forward from the west; when he says, "Homage to your stretchers," it is indeed to the rays of the sun, which are the stretchers, that he pays homage.
"Go forward, unhindered! he says; for the rival is indeed the hinderer, and [he speaks thus] for the removal of the rival.

"Along the stream of ghee, together with offspring, together with the increase of wealth," he says; he thereby invokes this very blessing. "O divine waters, you who purify yourselves," he says; this is according to the sacrificial formula itself.
6.3.9 Anuvāka 9: Designation of the Omentum Oblation.
When the victim has been immolated, pain (śuc) reaches its vital breaths.
"May your speech swell; may your breath swell," he says; thus he pacifies the pain from its very vital breaths.
"From the vital breaths she enters the earth as brilliance;
peace for the days," he says as he leads it down; verily, by means of day and night, he pacifies the heat from the earth.
"O herb, protect him! O axe, do not harm him! he says; the axe is indeed a thunderbolt.
For the sake of peace, he cuts from the side; for humans cut from the middle. He cuts crosswise; for humans cut lengthwise, for the sake of distinction.
With the words, "Thou art the portion of the Rakṣases," having smeared the thick end of the sacrificial grass (barhis), he throws it away; thus he expiates the Rakṣases by means of the fat.

"I lead this lowest darkness, the demon, to him who hates us and whom we hate," he says; for there are indeed two kinds of persons: him whom one hates and him who hates one; both of these he leads to the lowest darkness.
With "For food, thee! he extracts the omentum; for he who sacrifices desires, as it were.

If he were to pierce [the earth], Rudra would be likely to strike down his cattle; if he were not to pierce it, it would be unextended. He pierces with one [blade] and not with another for the sake of stability.
"O Heaven and Earth, clothe yourselves in ghee," he says; thus he anoints Heaven and Earth with essence. Unbroken...
"Riches with good heroes," he says; this is exactly according to the sacrificial formula.
Verily, he does something cruel when he extracts the omentum; "Follow along the wide mid-region," he says for the sake of pacification.
He who takes hold of the animal as it is being led to death falls away from this world; he takes hold again of the two omentum-spits and thus establishes himself firmly in this very world.
He goes forward with fire to strike away the Rakṣases; moreover, he follows the deities with the oblation.
He should not carry the embers beyond the edge; if he were to carry the embers beyond the edge, he would disregard the deities.
"O Vāyu, come to the drops," he says; therefore the drops fall separately.
The omentum is the foremost part of animals, and the *barhis* grass is the foremost part of plants; thus he unites the foremost with the foremost. Moreover, he establishes the animals in the plants.
"Give the command for the offerings consecrated with *svāhā*! he says.

The *pṛṣadājya* is indeed the out-breath and in-breath of the animals for the sake of the completion of the sacrifice; the omentum (*vapā*) is their body. Having sprinkled the *pṛṣadājya*, he sprinkles the omentum;

thus he places the out-breath and in-breath of the animals into its very self. "Svāhā! Go ye to the upward-moving Marut-cloud," he says; for the upward-moving Marut-cloud used to cast away the omentum-spits of the gods; by that very means he casts them away. He casts them away in opposite directions; therefore the out-breath and in-breath move in opposite directions.
6.3.10 Anuvāka 10: Designation of the Portions.
Having immolated the animal, he offers the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*); verily, he immolates it together with its fuel.

Having proceeded with the omentum (*vapā*), he proceeds with the sacrificial cake; for the sacrificial cake is strength (*ūrj*); verily, he bestows strength upon the midst of the cattle. Moreover, he thus mends the breach of the animal.
Having taken up some of the speckled butter, he asks three times, "O slaughterer, is the oblation cooked? For the gods are thrice-true; he who says it is cooked when it is not cooked incurs sin.
These two [breaths] are indeed the out-breath and in-breath of animals.

As for the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*): indeed, when the animal has been immolated, its heart comes together with the self. In that he bastes the heart with speckled butter, he places the out-breath and in-breath of animals within his own self.

By means of the animal, the gods went to the heavenly world; they thought, "Mankind will follow after us. Having cut off its head, they caused the sacrificial essence (*medha*) to flow forth; it became the *plakṣa* tree. That is the origin of the name *plakṣa*. In that the *plakṣa* branch serves as the upper layer of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), it is [the offering] of one who possesses the sacrificial essence.
He cuts off [the omentum] from the victim;
for when the victim is being carried away, the Rakṣases follow after it. He carries it between the sacrificial post and the Āhavanīya fire in order to strike down the Rakṣases.
When the victim has been seized, its mind departs.
"Recite the invitatory prayer for the *manotā* as the oblation is being cut," he says; thus he secures the mind of this [victim].
He cuts eleven portions; ten indeed are the vital breaths of the animal, and the self is the eleventh; as great as the animal is, of that he cuts the portions.

He cuts from the heart first, then from the tongue, then from the chest. For what one perceives with the heart, that one speaks with the tongue; what one speaks with the tongue, that one utters forth from the chest. This indeed is the proper sequence for the animal sacrifice: when he cuts in this manner and then cuts the subsequent parts as he desires, the cutting of this animal becomes truly sequential. He cuts from the middle of the rectum, for the vital breath is in the middle; he cuts from the upper part [of the rectum].

For the vital breath is supreme, whether it be the one or the other; indeed, both are non-violent (*ajāmi*). When being born, a Brāhmaṇa is born with three debts: through studentship to the seers, through sacrifice to the gods, and through offspring to the ancestors. He who has a son, who is a sacrificer, and who has lived as a student—verily he is free from debt. It is by means of these portions that he makes amends; that is why they are called "portions" (*avadāna*). The gods and the Asuras were engaged in conflict. Those gods said to Agni:
"O hero, may we overcome the Asuras through you!

He replied, "I shall choose a boon: let me take the choice portion from the victim. He took this as the choice portion: the fore-arm from the front half, the intestines from the middle, and the hip from the hind half. Thereupon the gods prospered and the Asuras were defeated. In that he cuts portions from these three limbs, it is for the sake of overcoming his rival; he prospers himself, and his rival is defeated.
He cuts crosswise; therefore animals move their limbs crosswise, for the sake of stability.
6.3.11 Anuvāka 11: The Description of the After-offerings (Anūyāja).
He covers the two offering-spoons with fat; for cattle have fat as their form, and thus he bestows form upon the cattle.
Having placed them in the broth, he covers them; for this broth is the essence of cattle, and thus he bestows essence upon the cattle.

He mixes the fat-oblation with the rib. The rib is indeed the middle part of the animal, and the fat is the essence of animals; in that he mixes the fat-oblation with the rib, he places the essence right in the middle of the animals.

Indeed, they kill the animal when they quiet it. The out-breath has Indra as its deity, and the in-breath has Indra as its deity; "May Indra’s breath settle in every limb," he says; thus he bestows both out-breath and in-breath upon the animals.

"O divine Tvaṣṭṛ, let your great abundance come together," he says, for cattle have Tvaṣṭṛ as their deity. "Though you are of diverse forms, you become of one mark," he says, for though they are indeed of diverse forms, they now become of one mark as they go to the gods.

"May the friends follow thee; may the mother and the fathers rejoice after thee," he says; thus, with their approval, he causes him to go to the heavenly world. At the half-verse he offers the *vasā* oblation; yonder [sky] is one half-verse and this [earth] is the other half-verse; verily he anoints these two with sap. He offers to the quarters; verily he anoints the quarters with sap; moreover, from the quarters he wins strength and sap.
This speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*) is indeed the out-breath and in-breath of cattle; they belong to the trees.

Animals indeed have the deity as their essence; when, having taken a portion of the speckled butter, he says, "Recite for Vanaspati! Give the command for Vanaspati! he thereby places out-breath and in-breath within the animals.
He cuts portions from each different part; therefore animals are of diverse forms.
He sprinkles it with broth; for broth is the essence of cattle, and thus he bestows essence upon the cattle.
He invokes the *iḍā*; for the *iḍā* is cattle, and thus he invokes cattle. He invokes four times, for cattle are four-footed.

If one should desire of someone, "May he be without cattle," one should give him [the portion] without fat; for cattle are of the nature of fat. Thus, by means of their very form, he excludes him from cattle, and he indeed becomes without cattle—of whomsoever one should so desire.

Thinking, "May he be possessed of cattle," one should offer him [the oblation] rich in fat; for cattle are indeed of the nature of fat. By means of this very form, he wins cattle for himself and thus becomes possessed of cattle. Prajāpati created the sacrifice;

he created the clarified butter (ājya) in the beginning, the animal (paśu) in the middle, and the speckled butter (pṛṣadājya) at the end. Therefore, the fore-sacrifices (prayāja) are performed with clarified butter, the animal is offered in the middle, and the after-sacrifices (anūyāja) are performed with speckled butter. Thus, this [speckled butter] is as it were mixed, for it was created last.

He performs eleven after-offerings (*anuyāja*). There are indeed ten vital breaths in an animal, and the self is the eleventh; thus he offers in accordance with the entire extent of the animal. Indeed, they kill the animal when they quiet it. Now, the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*) is truly the out-breath and in-breath of animals. In that he performs the after-offerings with speckled butter, he places the out-breath and in-breath back into the animals.

6.4 Prapāṭhaka: 4, Anuvāka 1: The Description of the Offering to the Entrails (Gudayāga). By means of the sacrifice, Prajāpati indeed created offspring; he created them by means of the *upayaṣṭi* offerings.
In that he performs the secondary offerings (upayajas), the sacrificer thereby creates offspring;
he cuts the portions from the hind part,
for from the hind part offspring are born.
He cuts from the thicker part, for from the thicker part offspring are born;
he cuts without piercing, for the non-piercing of the vital breaths.
He does not turn it back;
for if he were to turn it back, there would be a reversal of the people and it would become a snare.
"Go to the ocean, svāhā! he says.
He thus deposits the seed itself.
"Go to the intermediate space, svāhā! he says.
Verily, by means of the intermediate space, he causes offspring to be born for him;
for it is along the intermediate space that offspring are born.
"Go to the god Savitṛ, svāhā! he says.
Impelled by Savitṛ, he procreates offspring for him.
"Go to day and night, svāhā! he says;
verily, through day and night, he procreates offspring for him.
"For indeed, offspring are born according to day and night;
go to Mitra and Varuna, svāhā!"—
thus he says.
"When offspring have been born, he bestows out-breath and in-breath upon them;
'Go to Soma, svāhā! he says, for offspring have Soma as their deity."
"Go to the sacrifice, svāhā! he says;
thus he makes the very creatures worthy of sacrifice.
"Go to the meters, svāhā! he says.
The meters are indeed cattle;
verily, he wins cattle for himself.
"Go to heaven and earth, svāhā! he says.
"Verily, he encompasses on both sides from heaven and earth the offspring that have been born;
'Go to the celestial ether, svāhā! he says."
"He bestows rain upon the very offspring that have been born.
"Go to Agni Vaiśvānara, svāhā! he says;
thus he establishes the very offspring that have been born in this [earth].
He who cuts off a portion of the rectum indeed cuts away the vital breaths;
"Give me mind and heart," he says,
and thus he calls the vital breaths back to their respective places.
When the animal has been immolated, its pain enters the heart;
that [pain] passes into the heart-spike (hṛdayaśūla).
If one were to remove the heart-pain from the earth, one would afflict the earth with grief;
if from the waters, one would afflict the waters with grief.
By removing it at the junction of the dry and the moist, he effects the pacification of both.
One should meditate upon him whom one hates;
thus one strikes him with impurity.
6.4.2 Anuvāka 2: The Description of the Vasatīvarī Waters.
The gods indeed divided the sacrifice at the Āgnīdhra shed; then that which remained over, they spoke of.
"May this indeed dwell with us"— from that [comes] the name *vasatīvarī* for those waters;
they were not able to reach it in the morning.
They caused it to enter the waters;
they became the *vasatīvarī* waters.
He takes the *vasatīvarī* waters.
The Vasatīvarī waters are indeed the sacrifice.
Having commenced and taken hold of the sacrifice itself, he dwells near it; for if they were not taken before sunset, his sacrifice would remain uncommenced.
One should divide the sacrifice;
or one should take [the draught] with the *jyotiṣmatī* verse, or having placed gold [in the ladle], one thus takes [the draught] as accompanied by light (*saśukra*).
Or, one should take it from the vessels of a Brahmin who performs many sacrifices.
For he has taken the *vasatīvarī* waters;
he takes the *vasatīvarī* waters, for the *vasatīvarī* waters are indeed cattle.
Having taken hold of the very cattle, he waits upon them;
if he were to take [the draught] while standing with his face turned along [the line of the herd], the cattle would be liable to stray away from him;
therefore, he takes it while standing with his face turned against [the line].
Having indeed obstructed them for him, he seizes the sacrificial animals.
Indra slew Vṛtra.
He died within the waters;
that which among them was pure, fit for sacrifice, and possessed of the gods, was released,
and they became flowing streams.
He takes from those flowing waters which are pure, fit for sacrifice, and possessed by the gods; he takes from them alone, and he should not pass over the nearest flowing waters.
If he should pass over the waters that flow nearest the end, he would be disregarding the sacrifice;
one should not take water from stagnant sources,
for stagnant waters are seized by Varuṇa.
If he were to take [the water] from stationary sources,
Varuna would cause his sacrifice to be seized.
For when it is day, the night enters into the waters.
Therefore, the waters appear copper-colored by day;
since the day enters the waters at night,
therefore the waters appear bright at night.
He takes [the water] at the junction of shade and sunlight;
thus he takes the color of both day and night for him.
"These waters are rich in oblation," he says.
He takes [the portions] of those who have prepared the oblation;
"May Sūrya be possessed of the oblation," he says.
He draws [the cups] while they still contain the *śukra*.
He draws with an *anuṣṭubh* verse; for the *anuṣṭubh* is speech.
He takes them with the entire speech;
he takes them with a four-footed verse; he sets them down three times.
They amount to seven; the Śakvarī metre has seven feet,
and cattle are the Śakvarī.
Verily, he wins cattle.
For this world the Gārhapatya fire is established, and for yonder world the Āhavanīya.
If he were to place [the oblation] on the Gārhapatya, he would be possessed of cattle in this world.
If one were to place [the oblation] on the Āhavanīya fire, one would possess cattle in that world; therefore, one places it near both fires.
He makes him possessed of cattle in both worlds;
he carries it around on all sides for the sake of driving away the Rakṣases.
"You are the portion of Indra and Agni," he says; this is according to the sacrificial formula itself. The Āgnīdhra causes them to settle down.
The Āgnīdhra shed is indeed the unconquered part of the sacrifice;
he causes them to settle in that very part of the sacrifice which is unconquered.
For wherever in the sacrifice that has been spread out something is not performed, the Rakṣases descend along that [omission].
When he takes [the water] from the flowing streams, that very act of the sacrifice lies ready,
so that the *rakṣases* may not follow after it;
for these [streams] do not slacken.
They lie around until the third pressing for the continuity of the sacrifice.
6.4.3 Anuvāka 3: The Description of the Bringing Down of Soma. The exponents of sacred knowledge say:
"He indeed would be a true *adhvaryu* who, when bringing down the *soma*, brings it down for all the deities."

"For the heart," he says; by this, he prepares it for human beings. "For the mind," he says; by this, he prepares it for the ancestors. "For the sky, for Sūrya," he says; by this, he prepares it for the gods. There are just so many deities; for all of them, he thus brings it down.
He begins the Prātaranuvāka before speech is uttered; thus he wins as much of speech as there is.
He first utters "the waters"; for the waters are the sacrifice—verily, he releases speech directed toward the sacrifice.
He recites all the meters; the meters are indeed cattle, and thus he wins cattle for himself.

He should conclude with a *gāyatrī* for one desiring splendor, with a *triṣṭubh* for one desiring power, with a *jagatī* for one desiring cattle, with an *anuṣṭubh* for one desiring stability, with a *paṅkti* for one desiring the sacrifice, and with a *virāj* for one desiring food. "May Agni hear the call with the kindling-stick!"
He says, "Yes. Impelled by Savitṛ and having announced [the water] to the deities, he goes toward the waters.
He says, "O Hotṛ, seek the waters," for a rite is performed when it has been impelled.
He says, "O Camasādhvaryu of the Maitrāvaruṇa, come hither! Mitra and Varuṇa are indeed the leaders of the waters; through them alone does he go toward them.

"O divine waters, O child of the waters," he says; thus, having ransomed them by means of an oblation, he draws [the water]. Moreover, he draws [them] when they have been prepared as an offering and sprinkled with clarified butter.
"Thou art the furrower," he says; he thus washes away their impurity.
"I take you up for the imperishability of the ocean," he says; therefore, though being consumed and drunk, the waters are not exhausted.

The *cātvāla* pit is indeed the womb of the sacrifice; the *vasatīvarī* waters are the sacrifice. Having touched together the *hotṛ*'s cup and the *maitrāvaruṇa*'s cup, he pours out the *vasatīvarī* waters for the sake of the sacrifice’s having its proper womb.
Moreover, he causes them to be born from their own womb.
"O Adhvaryu, look at the water! (he says).
Thus he says:
"Look at this one, and look at these others!"—
for this is indeed what he says.

If it is an Agniṣṭoma, he offers oblations; if it is an Ukthya, he wipes [the ladle] on the enclosing stick; if it is an Atirātra, he enters while reciting a Yajus formula; this is for the sake of distinguishing between the sacrificial rites.
6.4.4 Anuvāka 4: Description of the Measurement of Soma.
With the formula, "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ," he takes up the pressing-stone for the sake of impulsion.
"With the arms of the Aśvins," he says;
for the Aśvins were the two Adhvaryu priests among the gods.
"With the hands of Pūṣan," he says for the sake of restraint.
Soma is indeed the cattle, and the Upāṃśusavana stone is the vital breath (vyāna).
In that he measures out [the Soma] over the Upāṃśusavana stone, he places the vital breath within the cattle.
He measures it out, saying, "For Indra! For Indra!"
For the Soma is brought for Indra;
five times he measures it with the *yajuṣ* formula.
The *paṅkti* consists of five syllables.
The sacrifice is fivefold;
verily he wins the sacrifice by [repeating] five times silently.
They amount to ten;
the Virāj consists of ten syllables, and the Virāj is food.
By means of the Virāj, he wins food; "Ye are invigorating, O subduers of Vṛtra," he says,
for this indeed is the Soma-drink of the waters.
He who knows thus does not meet with misfortune in the waters;
when he says, "O Soma, that light of thine which is in heaven," it is for these very [beings] that he [offers him].
He gathers [the essence] from the worlds.
King Soma, indeed, desired the quarters;
he entered into the quarters.
"Eastward, westward, northward, southward," he says;
verily from the quarters he gathers him together, and thus he wins the quarters for himself.
"O mother, look down! he says.
Women become desirous of him who knows thus; he says, "O Soma, that name of yours which is invincible and watchful."
This indeed is the Soma-drinking of Soma;
he who knows thus does not meet with any misfortune related to Soma.
For they indeed kill this Soma when they press it.
He takes up the stalks;
verily he protects him.
The stalks are indeed the vital breaths, and Soma is the cattle.
He creates the rays once again;
he places the vital breaths within the animals; he creates them even by twos.
Therefore, there are two breaths each.
6.4.5 Anuvāka 5: The Description of the Upāṃśu Cup The Upāṃśu [cup] is indeed the vital breath (prāṇa).
Since the cups are drawn with the Upāṃśu as the first, they follow after the vital breath itself.
Aruṇa Aupaveśi used to say: "I complete the sacrifice at the morning pressing itself; with it thus completed, I proceed.
He presses [the Soma] eight times first.
The Gāyatrī has eight syllables;
the morning pressing belongs to the Gāyatra;
by this, he indeed obtains the morning pressing.
The second [turn] eleven times;
the *triṣṭubh* consists of eleven syllables;
the midday [pressing] belongs to the *triṣṭubh*.
By that, he obtains the midday pressing;
twelve times [he recites] for the third pressing.
The Jagatī consists of twelve syllables;
the third pressing belongs to the Jagatī.
By this, he obtains the third pressing itself.
He indeed declared this to be the conclusion of the sacrifice,
for the sake of non-splashing; for that which splashes when the sacrifice has reached its conclusion is not truly spilled.
Now, moreover, they say:
"The Gāyatrī indeed is the 'non-excessive speech' at the morning pressing. One's rival does not speak excessively against him who knows thus.
Therefore, the exponents of sacred knowledge say that it should be pressed eight times each.
"The other cups are drawn with purifiers; what is the purifier for the *upāṃśu* cup?
"Speech is the purifier," he should reply.
"Flow pure for the Lord of Speech, O vigorous one," he says.
Verily, by means of speech he purifies him;
"With the two shoots of the bull," he says,
for these two shoots of Soma are indeed the shoots of the bull.
"Purified by rays," he says,
for he purifies him with rays;
"Thou art the god of the gods, the purifier," he says.
"For he is indeed the god of gods, the purifier; 'To those whose portion you are, to them [I give] you,' he says."
For he takes this from those for whom it is a portion;
"Thou art made one's own," he says,
and thus he makes the vital breath his own.
"Make our nourishments honey-sweet," he says; thus he makes all this sweet for him.
"For all thy powers, celestial and terrestrial," he says.
"He bestows life-breaths upon both gods and men," he says, "may the mind enter you."
"Mind alone reaches [everything];
go along the wide mid-region," he says,
for breath has the mid-region as its deity.
"O Svāhā! Thee, O well-born one, to Sūrya! he says;
for the gods who are well-born are indeed the vital breaths (prāṇas); it is into them that he offers in secret.
"For the gods who drink the rays," he says;
for the rays of the sun are indeed the gods who drink the rays;
that is their portion.
If he should desire, "May Parjanya be rainy," he gratifies those very ones by means of that [offering].
Saying "May it be so," he should wipe [it] down with his hand;
thus he brings down the rain itself, if he should so desire.
If he should wish, "May it not rain," he should wipe [the fire] with the palm facing upwards;
thus he holds back the rain itself.
If he should practice sorcery, he should say, "Kill so-and-so, and then I shall offer you."
Seeking to seize him as if he were an oblation, he kills him;
even if he should be far away, he should stand until he faints, for by following after his breath, he kills him.
If he should practice sorcery,
he should set it down with the words, "I set thee down in the breath of so-and-so";
for the breath is indeed unassailable.
He establishes his very breath;
he purifies it with six rays,
for there are six seasons.
Verily, he purifies him by means of the seasons; he purifies him three times,
for these worlds are three.
By these very worlds he purifies him.
The exponents of the Veda say:
"For what reason are three of the sacrificial animals those that take [the offering] from the hand?"
Because he takes it up three times silently with his hand, therefore three among animals take things with their hands: man, the elephant, and the monkey.
6.4.6. Anuvāka 6: The Description of the Internal Sacrificial Vessels.
Whatever the gods did at the sacrifice, the Asuras did that too.
Those gods perceived the sacrifice to be completed within the *upāṃśu* (whispered) offering.
They established it in the *upāṃśu* cup;
those Asuras, having raised their thunderbolt, advanced against the gods,
and the gods, being afraid, ran to Indra for protection.
Indra placed them within himself by means of the Antaryāma cup;
that is the reason for the Antaryāma’s name as "the inner one.
In that the Antaryāma is drawn, the sacrificer places his rivals within himself.
"I place you between heaven and earth, within the wide mid-region," he says;
by means of these very worlds, the sacrificer places his rivals within himself.
Those gods thought,
"Indra has indeed become that which we are," and they said:
"O Maghavan, grant us our share," he said; "in harmony with the gods, both those who are lower and those who are higher"—
referring to both those gods who are higher and those who are lower.
"He shared [the portion] in harmony with the gods, both those who are lower and those who are higher," he says;
thus he shares it with both kinds of gods, those who are higher and those who are lower.
"O Maghavan, rejoice at the Antaryāma," he says;
thus he does not exclude the sacrificer from the sacrifice.
"Thou art taken with a support," he says.
For the support of the out-breath (*apāna*):
if both were taken while unpurified, the out-breath would follow after the in-breath (*prāṇa*), and one would be liable to die.
The Antaryāma cup is drawn with the purifier (pavitra).
This is for the support of the out-breath and the in-breath;
for these two, the Upāṃśu and the Antaryāma, are indeed the out-breath and the in-breath, while the Upāṃśusavana stone is the diffused breath (vyāna).
If one should desire,
"May he be short-lived," one should set down those two for him without touching them;
by means of the *vyāna* alone, one thus cuts off his out-breath and in-breath.
If one should desire of someone,
"May he attain a full lifespan," one should set down those two [cups] for him while they are still in contact.
By means of the vyāna alone, he connects his out-breath and in-breath;
he reaches a full lifespan.
6.4.7 Anuvāka 7: The Explanation of the Aindravāyava Cup This [cup] which is the Aindravāyava is indeed speech.
In that the cups are drawn beginning with the Aindravāyava, they proceed following after speech itself.
The gods said to Vāyu, "Let us slay King Soma. He replied:
"Let me choose a boon: let the cups be drawn beginning with the one for Indra and Vāyu.
Therefore, the cups are drawn beginning with the one for Indra and Vāyu; they struck him down.
It festered; the gods could not overcome it,
so they spoke to Vāyu.
"Make this palatable for us," he said.
And he replied:
"Choose a boon: let your vessels be called after me alone," he said. Therefore, although they belong to various deities, they are called "vāyavya" (dedicated to Vāyu).
Vāyu himself made them palatable for them.
Therefore, that which putrefies they hang out in a windy place,
for the wind is its purifier and its sweetener;
they did not find a means to hold it apart.
Aditi said,
"I choose a boon; let you then take possession [of the Soma] through me, so that the Somas shall have me as their deity."
"You are taken with a support," he says; [these vessels] have Aditi as their deity.
For those vessels of hers which are made of wood are produced from her womb, while those which are made of clay are produced directly from her.
Therefore he spoke thus:
"Speech indeed spoke away, unmanifested;
the gods said to Indra:"
"Interpret this speech of ours," they said.
He replied, "I shall choose a boon: let this [libation] be drawn for me together with Vāyu."
Therefore, the draught for Indra and Vāyu is drawn together;
Indra, having stepped into its midst, separated it,
and therefore this speech is uttered as something distinguished.
Therefore, it is drawn once for Indra from the middle; twice for Vāyu, for he chose two boons.
6.4.8 Anuvāka 8: Explanation of the Maitrāvaruṇa Cup.
The gods said to Mitra,
"Let us slay King Soma.
He replied:
"I am not a friend to everyone," he said;
they replied to him,
"We shall surely kill you."
He said, "I choose this boon: let me mix the Soma with milk.
Therefore, they mix the Maitrāvaruṇa cup with milk.
Therefore the animals departed,
thinking, "Being Mitra, he has done a cruel thing";
for indeed, this [sacrificer] is like one who has done something cruel.
When one who sacrifices with Soma acts [thus], the cattle depart from him;
in that he mixes the offering for Mitra and Varuṇa with milk, he thereby brings Mitra into harmony with cattle and brings the sacrificer into harmony with cattle.
In ancient times, Mitra indeed knew this:
"The cattle will step away from me once I have committed a cruel act.
Therefore, he chose thus.
The gods said to Varuṇa,
"With you as our sharer, let us slay King Soma.
He replied:
"I choose a boon for myself and for Mitra together; let it be drawn up together.
Therefore, the cup for Mitra and Varuṇa (maitrāvaruṇa) is drawn up together.
Therefore, by means of a king born from a portion [of Mitra], they indeed slay a king; by a Vaiśya, a Vaiśya; by a Śūdra, a Śūdra.
At that time, this world was neither day nor night, for it was undifferentiated.
Those gods said to Mitra and Varuṇa:
"May you two cause this to be distributed among us," they said;
"let us choose a boon: let only one cup be drawn first."
Therefore, the draught for Indra and Vāyu is drawn before that for Mitra and Varuṇa,
for these two, the Upāṃśu and Antaryāma, are out-breath and in-breath; Mitra generated the day and Varuṇa the night.
From that indeed did this world dawn;
therefore, when the cup for Mitra and Varuṇa is drawn, it is for the sake of dawning.
6.4.9 Anuvāka 9: The Account of the Āśvina Cup.
The head of the sacrifice was cut off;
the gods said to the two Aśvins:
"You two are indeed physicians; restore this head of the sacrifice," they said.
They replied, "Let us choose a boon: let a cup (graha) be drawn for us here as well."
For them, they drew this cup for the Aśvins;
then indeed those two restored the head of the sacrifice.
In that the cup for the Aśvins is drawn, it is for the restoration of the sacrifice.
The gods said to them, "These two physicians are indeed impure, being men who practice with cooked offerings."
Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa should not practice medicine, for he who is a physician is impure and unholy;
having purified those two by means of the *bahis-pavamāna*, they drew this cup for the Aśvins from them.
Therefore, when the *bahis-pavamāna* has been chanted, the cup for the Aśvins is drawn.
Therefore, one who knows this should approach the *bahiṣpavamāna* chant; for the *bahiṣpavamāna* is a means of purification, and thus he purifies his very self.
They distributed the healing power of those two in three parts:
one third in the fire, one third in the waters, and one third in the Brāhmaṇa.
Therefore, having placed a bowl of water nearby and having seated a Brahmin to the south, one should perform the healing rite.
Whatever healing rite one performs with that [water], it becomes effective for him.
The exponents of Brahman say: "By what truth are the offerings for two deities drawn in a single vessel but offered in two vessels?
Because they are drawn in a single vessel, therefore there is one vital breath within; because they are offered in two vessels, therefore there are two vital breaths on each side."

The offerings to the dual deities are indeed the vital breaths, and the *iḍā* is the cattle. If one were to invoke the *iḍā* before the offerings to the dual deities, he would place the vital breaths within the cattle; he would be liable to die.
Therefore, having consumed the portions of the dual-deity offerings, he invokes the *iḍā*.
Having placed the vital breaths within himself, he invokes the cattle.
The cup for Indra and Vāyu is speech; that for Mitra and Varuṇa is sight; that for the Aśvins is hearing.
He consumes the cup for Indra and Vāyu first; therefore, one speaks with speech from the front.

The cup for Mitra and Varuṇa is placed in front; therefore, one sees with the eye from the front. The cup for the Aśvins is carried around on all sides; therefore, one hears with the ear from all sides.
These cups dedicated to two deities are indeed the vital breaths; he sets them down in vessels that are not empty.
Therefore, the vital breaths (prāṇas) are not empty within; for indeed, wherever a part of the extended sacrifice is left unperformed, the Rakṣases descend upon that sacrifice.
In that he sets down the vessels so they are not empty, that very act of the sacrifice lies performed, so that there may be no descent of the Rakṣases.
He sets them down on the northern track of the southern *havirdhāna* cart; verily, he places speech in speech.
They lie around until the third pressing for the continuity of the sacrifice.
6.4.10 Anuvāka 10: The Description of the Śukra and Manthin Vessels.
Bṛhaspati was the domestic priest of the gods, while Śaṇḍa and Marka were those of the Asuras.
The gods possessed the sacred word (brahman), and the Asuras possessed the sacred word.
They were unable to overcome one another.
Those gods addressed Śaṇḍa and Marka,
and they both said:
"Let us choose a boon; let these two cups alone be drawn for us here as well.
For them they drew these two, the Śukra and the Manthin cups.
Thereupon the gods prospered and the Asuras were defeated.
For one who knows thus, when the Śukra and Manthin cups are drawn, he prospers in his own self and his rival is defeated.
The gods, having driven those two away from themselves, offered them to Indra.
"May Śaṇḍa and Marka be driven away together with that one," he should say, naming whomsoever he hates;
with him whom he hates, he drives them both away.
"He is the first, Saṃkṛti, Viśvakarman"—with these words they offered them to Indra for themselves.
For Indra, repeatedly manifesting these forms, moved about:
yonder sun is the *śukra* cup, and the moon is the *manthin* cup. Having covered [the cups], he went forth toward the east.
Therefore, as he strides, those going eastward do not see him; turning westward, they offer the oblations.
Therefore, these two, the Śukra and the Manthin vessels, are the eyes of the sacrifice, moving toward one another; the high altar is the nose. Moving around on both sides, they offer the oblations.
Therefore, the two eyes are on both sides of the nose;
thus, by means of the nose, the two eyes are held apart as they move all around for the purpose of striking away the Rakṣases.
The gods, indeed, with those oblations which they offered facing eastward, drove away the Asuras who were in the east;
with those which they offered facing westward, they drove away the Asuras who were in the west.
Other oblations are offered facing forward, while the Śukra and Manthin cups are offered facing backward;
thus the sacrificer repels his enemies both from behind and from the front,
and therefore offspring are conceived facing away [from their mothers] and are born facing toward them.
"Indeed, offspring are born after the Śukra and Manthin [cups]; producing offspring who are both eaters and eatable, and possessed of good heroes, go around with the Śukra, with its bright luster;
producing offspring who are well-progeny, go around with the Manthin, with its churning luster," he says.
Truly, those who eat are rich in heroes;
those who are eaten are rich in offspring.
He who knows thus, his offspring is born as eaters, not as those who are eaten.
The eye of Prajāpati swelled;
it fell away and entered the vikaṅkata tree.
It did not find delight in the vikaṅkata;
it entered the barley; it found delight in the barley.
That is the reason for the barley being barley.
In that the stirring-vessel is made of *vaikaṅkata* wood, he mixes it with groats; thus he gathers together the very eye of Prajāpati.
The exponents of Brahman ask: "Why does the *manthipātra* cup, though it is true, not partake of the *sadas*?
One should reply: "Because it is a vessel for those who are afflicted (*ārta*)."
If he were to eat it, the Adhvaryu would become blind and meet with misfortune;
therefore, he does not eat it.
6.4.11 Anuvāka 11: The Exposition of the Āgrayaṇa Cup.
Whatever the gods did at the sacrifice, the Asuras did likewise.
Those gods then beheld the cups preceded by the Āgrayaṇa.
They took them; then indeed they went around as the first.
For whomsoever, knowing thus, the cups are drawn with the Āgrayaṇa as the first, he goes around as the first among his peers.
One who has rivals should draw [the cup] with the verse containing the word *rugṇavat*.
Verily, by causing his rival to break, he passes beyond the summit of his equals.
"O gods, you who are eleven in heaven," he says.
There are indeed so many deities; from all of them he draws it for him.
"This is your womb; for the All-gods you," he says, for this [cup] has the All-gods as its deity.

Speech indeed departed from the gods, refusing to remain for the sacrifice. When Speech had departed, the gods drew the cups in silence. Speech thought, "They are excluding me," and she returned to the Āgrayaṇa cup.
That is why the Āgrayaṇa is called Āgrayaṇa;
therefore, Speech is released at the Āgrayaṇa.

As to why the earlier cups are drawn in silence: it is just as when a hunter stalks a burrow, thinking, "I shall not miss my mark," and then releases his arrow; in the same way, having drawn the Āgrayaṇa cup and commenced the sacrifice, the Adhvaryu releases his speech and utters the sound *hiṃ* three times; thus he chooses the Udgātṛ priests.
The Āgrayaṇa cup is indeed Prajāpati; when, having drawn the Āgrayaṇa, he utters the *hiṃ* syllable, it is Prajāpati himself who thus smells his offspring.
Therefore, a cow smells her newborn calf.
The Āgrayaṇa is indeed the self of the sacrifice; by drawing it at each pressing, he extends the sacrifice within his own self.
He brings it from above; thus he bestows seed. He draws it from below; thus he causes procreation.
The exponents of Brahman ask: "By what truth does the Gāyatrī, being the smallest of the meters, carry all the pressings?
This Āgrayaṇa cup is indeed the calf of the Gāyatrī; returning to it, she thus carries all the pressings.
Therefore, when the calf has been led away, the cow turns back toward it.
Prapāṭhaka 6.5, Anuvāka 1: The Description of the Ukthya Cup.
Indra raised his thunderbolt against Vṛtra;
that Vṛtra was terrified of the raised thunderbolt.
He said, "Do not strike me; there is indeed this vigor in me, and I shall give it to you.
He gave him the Ukthya.
He held out a second [spear] to him; he said, "Do not hurl it at me! There is this vigor within me; I shall give that to you."
Therefore, he gave him the Ukthya alone; he raised the third [libation] for him,
and Viṣṇu stood by him.
"Kill it," he said.
"Do not strike me; there is indeed this vigor within me, and I shall give that to you."
Therefore, he gave him the Ukthya alone;
he struck it down when it had become devoid of magic,
for the sacrifice was its magic.
In that the Ukthya cup is drawn, the sacrificer thereby seizes the power and vigor of his rival.
"For Indra, thee, the great and vigorous," he says.
For he gave it to Indra;
"To thee for him, to Viṣṇu thee," he says,
because Viṣṇu indeed stood by it.
He said, "Kill him! Therefore, he causes Viṣṇu to participate;
he draws [the portions] three times, for thrice did he give that to him.
"This is your womb; you are the oblation again," he says,
for he takes it out from us again and again.
The Ukthya is indeed the eye of the sacrifice;
therefore, the other Soma offerings follow the Ukthya when it has been offered,
and for that reason the body follows after the eye.
Therefore, many follow after one who leads; therefore, one among many becomes preeminent;
therefore, one finds many wives.
If the Adhvaryu should desire,
"May I endow myself with the glory of the sacrifice," he should pour [the water] down while standing between the Āhavanīya fire and the Havirdhāna shed;
thus he endows himself with the glory of the sacrifice.
If he should desire,
"May I endow the sacrificer with the glory of the sacrifice," he should pour [the water] down while standing between the *sadas* and the *havirdhāna*;
thus he endows the sacrificer himself with the glory of the sacrifice.
If he should desire,
"May I endow the members of the assembly with the glory of the sacrifice," he should lead [the victim] down after touching the *sadas*;
thus he endows the members of the assembly themselves with the glory of the sacrifice.
6.5.2 Anuvāka 2: The Description of the Dhruva-vessel.
The Dhruva is indeed the life-span of the sacrifice; it is drawn as the last of the vessels. Therefore, life is the last of the vital breaths.
"The head of heaven, the messenger of earth," he says;
verily, he makes him the head of his equals.
"Agni Vaiśvānara, born for the sake of Truth," he says.
For Vaiśvānara is life itself by virtue of his divinity. Vaiśvānara is drawn from both sides;
therefore, the vital breaths are on both sides.
Below and above,
other cups are drawn as halves; the *dhruva* cup is [the whole], therefore it is a half.
The *ardhya* cup has its breath directed downwards;
other cups are set down on the strewn ground, while the *dhruva* is set down on ground not strewn.
Therefore, some creatures are established through bone, and others through flesh.
The Asuras indeed sought to overturn the earth from the north; the gods made it firm with the Dhruva [offering], and that is the reason for the Dhruva's name "the Firm."
That the *dhruva* is set down to the north is for the sake of stability.
The *dhruva* is indeed the life-span of the sacrifice, and the *hotṛ* is its self;
when he pours the *dhruva* into the *hotṛ*-cup, he places it within the very self of the sacrifice.
"He bestows life at the beginning of the hymn, for he is one who must be poured out," they say; for he enjoys [the world] from the very beginning of his life.
"One should pour it out in the middle," they say,
"for one enjoys the middle of life.
"One should pour it out in the northern half," they say.
For he enjoys the very best of his lifespan;
when the verse addressed to the Viśvedevas is being recited, he pours [the water] down,
for offspring belong to the Viśvedevas.
He bestows life-span upon the subjects themselves.
6.5.3 Anuvāka 3: The Description of the Seasonal Cup (Ṛtugraha).
By means of the sacrifice, the gods indeed went to the heavenly world;
they reflected:
Thinking, "May humans follow after us," they waited for a year and then went to the heavenly world;
the seers recognized that [world] by means of the seasonal cups (ṛtugraha).
In that the seasonal cups are drawn, it is for the discernment of the heavenly world; twelve are drawn,
for the year consists of twelve months.
For the sake of discerning the year, the first two cups are drawn together and the last two are drawn together;
therefore, there are two seasons each.
The vessel for the seasons has openings on both sides;
for who indeed knows from where the mouth of the seasons comes?
"Prompt with the season," he says six times; for there are six seasons. Thus, he gratifies the seasons themselves.
"By the seasons," he says four times;
thus he gratifies the four-footed cattle.
He says "by the season" twice again.
He gratifies only the bipeds;
he says "Prompt with the season" six times, and "With the seasons" four times.
Therefore, four-footed cattle live dependent upon the seasons.
Twice more he speaks by means of the season;
therefore, bipeds subsist upon four-footed cattle.
He says, "Prompt with the season! six times; four times with "With the seasons"; twice again he says "With the season.
Thereby the sacrificer makes a stepping-stone, a bridge, for the attainment of the world of heaven.
One should not follow after the other;
for if one were to follow after the other, season would follow upon season, and the seasons would become confounded.
The Adhvaryu enters by the south in the established manner, and the Pratiprasthātṛ enters by the north in the established manner.
Therefore, the sun moves southward for six months and northward for six. "You are taken with a support; you are the gliding one; for Aṃhaspatya, you! he says.
"There is a thirteenth month," they say.
It gratifies that very one.
6.5.4 Anuvāka 4:
These seasonal cups (ṛtugrahas) are drawn for the sake of the heavenly world;
Indra and Agni are the light.
In that he draws the cup for Indra and Agni with the ṛtupātra, he places light above him for the illumination of the world of heaven;
for Indra and Agni are indeed the two bearers of vigor among the gods.
In that the cup for Indra and Agni is drawn, he wins strength;
he draws the cup for the Viśvedevas with the Śukra vessel,
for offspring belong to the Viśvedevas.
That Āditya is the Śukra;
because he draws the Vaiśvadeva cup with the Śukra vessel, therefore that Āditya rises facing all creatures.
Therefore, everyone thinks,
"It has risen toward me";
thus he draws the Vaiśvadeva cup with the Śukra vessel.
Offspring indeed belong to the Viśvedevas;
Śukra is brilliance.
In that he draws the Vaiśvadeva cup with the Śukra vessel, he bestows brilliance upon the offspring.
6.5.5 Anuvāka 5: Explanation of the Marutvatīya and Mahendra Cups.

Indra, together with the Maruts through their shared knowledge, slew Vṛtra at the midday pressing. Since the Marutvatīya cups are drawn at the midday pressing, they are drawn for the sacrificer as slayers of Vṛtra.
When he had slain Vṛtra, the seasons became confused; he drew the Marutvatīya cups with the Ṛtu-vessel, and thereby he discerned the seasons.
In that the Marutvatīya cups are drawn with the Ṛtu-vessel, it is for the discernment of the seasons.
The sacrificer hurls this very thunderbolt at his rival when he recites the Marutvatīya hymns: with the first he restrains it, with the second he hurls it, and with the third he lays him low.
Indeed, the sacrificer prepares this very weapon when he recites the Marutvatīyas: the first is the bow, the second is the string, and the third is the arrow.
With the first [verse] he takes it up; with the second he releases it; with the third he pierces it.
Having slain Vṛtra, Indra went to the farthest distance, thinking, "I have committed a transgression."
He became green;
he saw these Marutvatīya cups as means for protecting himself,
and he took them.

By the first [cup] he secured the out-breathing (*prāṇa*), by the second the in-breathing (*apāna*), and by the third the self (*ātman*). For these Marutvatīya cups are drawn for the sacrificer as means of securing the self; indeed, by the first he secures the out-breathing, by the second the in-breathing, and by the third the self.
Indra slew Vṛtra.
The gods said of him, "Great indeed has he become, who slew Vṛtra";
that is the reason for Mahendra's name, Mahendra.
Having slain Vṛtra, he extracted this Mahendra as a special portion for himself among the other deities;
therefore, when the Mahendra cup is drawn, the sacrificer extracts that same special portion for himself among the other subjects.
He draws it with the Śukra vessel.
Mahendra indeed has the sacrificer as his deity; the *śukra* is brilliance. When he draws the *māhendra* cup with the *śukra* vessel, he bestows brilliance upon the sacrificer himself.
6.5.6 Anuvāka 6: The Discourse on the Āditya Planet.
Aditi, desiring sons, cooked a *brahmaudana* (sacrificial rice) for the Sādhyas, the gods;
they gave her the remnants.
He ate it; she conceived seed, and from it the four Ādityas were born.
She cooked a second [offering].
She thought:
"These [gods] have known from the remnants; if I eat first, those who will be born from me will be more prosperous than I."
She ate it whole; she conceived seed, and from her was born a defective egg.
She cooked a third [offering] for the Ādityas,
thinking, "May this toil of mine be for their enjoyment."
They said, "Let us choose a boon: whoever is born from this [seed] shall be our one [representative], and whoever prospers in his offspring shall belong for our enjoyment.
Thereupon, Vivasvat Āditya was born.
Or rather, these human beings are his offspring;
among them, he alone who performs sacrifice prospers and becomes a source of enjoyment for the gods.
The gods indeed excluded Rudra from the sacrifice;
he then pursued the Ādityas.
They sought refuge with the deities of the dual-divinity cups,
but they did not surrender them;
therefore, even today, one does not surrender a person who has sought refuge, even if he is deserving of death.
Therefore, the Āditya cup is drawn from the remains of the offerings to the dual deities;
since they were born from the remnant, it is drawn from the remnant.
He draws it with three verses.
The mother, the father, and the son— that is that very couple;
the amnion, the embryo, and the placenta— that is that very couple.
These Ādityas are indeed cattle; curds are vigor.
He mixes [the offering] with curds in the middle; verily, he places vigor in the midst of the cattle with the boiled milk for the Ātaṅkya.
For the sake of purity,
therefore the raw milk yields the cooked;
these Ādityas are indeed the cattle.
Having enclosed it, he draws [the cup]; verily, by hemming them in, he secures cattle for him;
for these Ādityas are indeed cattle, and this Agni is Rudra.
Having enclosed it, he draws [the cup]; verily, he hides the cattle away from Rudra.
This Upāṃśusavana stone is indeed Vivasvat Āditya; he lies around this very draught of Soma until the third pressing.
"O Vivasvat Āditya, this is your draught of Soma," he says.
He causes Vivasvat Āditya himself to participate in the Soma-drinking.
With the words, "I mix you with that which is divine rain," he should mix [the offering] for one who desires rain;
thus he wins rain itself.
If it falls quickly, Parjanya will be rainy;
if for a long time, he will not rain.
He does not set it down.
For from non-being indeed offspring are born;
he does not utter the *anuvaṣaṭ* call,
for if he were to utter the *anuvaṣaṭ* call, he would let Rudra loose upon the offspring.
Having offered the oblation, he should not look back;
for if he were to look back, his eye would be liable to perish.
Therefore, he must not look back.
6.5.7 Anuvāka 7: The Description of the Sāvitra and Vaiśvadeva Cups.
He draws the Sāvitra cup from the Āgrayaṇa vessel using the Antaryāma cup;
for this Āgrayaṇa is indeed Prajāpati.
He does not set it down for the procreation of offspring;
for from that which is not set down, offspring are produced.
He does not pronounce the *anuvaṣaṭ* call;
for were he to pronounce the *anuvaṣaṭ*, he would let Rudra loose upon his offspring.
Savitṛ, indeed, is the one among the gods who belongs to the *gāyatrī* metre.
This Āgrayaṇa cup is drawn in the world of the Gāyatrī.
In that he draws the Sāvitra cup from the Āgrayaṇa using the Antaryāma vessel, he draws it forth from its own womb. All...
The gods could not secure the third pressing.
They led Savitṛ—who was entitled to a share in the morning pressing—to the third pressing;
then indeed they secured the third pressing.
In that the Sāvitra cup is drawn at the third pressing, it is for the elevation of the third pressing;
he draws the Vaiśvadeva cup from the pitcher with the Sāvitra vessel,
for offspring belong to the Viśve Devas.
The *vaiśvadeva* jar belongs to Savitṛ, who is the lord of instigations;
in that he draws from the jar for the *vaiśvadeva* cup with the *savitṛ* vessel, it is indeed by the instigation of Savitṛ that he bestows offspring upon him.
He produces Soma from Soma; he thus deposits seed.
"You are well-protected, you are well-established," he says; for he draws Soma over Soma for the sake of stability.
Moreover, in this very cup, [the offering] is made for humans, for the gods, and for the ancestors;
"Thou art a good refuge, a good support," he says— by this,
he indeed makes [the offering] for humans.
"Great," he says;
by this he pays homage to the gods.
"Homage," he says.
By this he acts for the fathers;
for so many indeed are the deities,
and from all of them he takes it for him.
"This is your womb; for all the gods you," he says, for this [cup] belongs to the Viśvedevas.
6.5.8 Anuvāka 8: The Description of the Pātnīvata Cup-offering.
The Upāṃśu cup is indeed the vital breath (*prāṇa*).

In that the first and the last cups are drawn with the Upāṃśu vessel, they follow after the vital breath and they rise up after the vital breath. The Āgrayaṇa cup is Prajāpati, and the Upāṃśu is the vital breath; [thus] they procreate offspring as wives.
In that he draws the Pātnīvata cup from the Āgrayaṇa vessel with the Upāṃśu vessel, it is for the procreation of offspring;
therefore, offspring are born after the vital breath.
The gods indeed went from here to the heavenly world with their wives.
Desiring to conquer the world,
they did not know the heavenly world;
they saw this offering to the wives' husband (pātnīvata).
They took it; then indeed they discerned the world of heaven.
In that the cup for the wives (pātnīvata) is drawn, it is for the discernment of the world of heaven.
That Soma did not submit while being drawn for the women; making clarified butter into a thunderbolt, they struck him, and having deprived him of his power, they took him.
Therefore, women are powerless and do not inherit; yet they speak more intimately than a sinful man.
In that he mixes the Pātnīvata offering with clarified butter, he takes hold of him [the sacrificer] after having brought him under control by means of the thunderbolt.
"You are taken with a support," he says.
This earth, indeed, is the support;
therefore, offspring are born after this earth.
"Of you, the son of Bṛhaspati," he says;
Bṛhaspati is indeed the sacred power (brahman) of the gods. By means of the sacred power, he causes offspring to be born for him.
"Indu," he says; Indu is indeed semen; thus he bestows semen.
"Indriyāva," he says;
offspring, indeed, is *indriya*.
Verily, he procreates offspring for him.
"O Agni! he says;
for Agni is the depositor of seed.
"Like a wife," he says, for the sake of pairing;
"In harmony with the god Tvaṣṭṛ, drink the Soma," he says.
Tvaṣṭṛ is indeed the fashioner of the forms of paired animals;
he bestows form upon the animals.
The gods, indeed, sought to slay Tvaṣṭṛ.
He entered his wives;
they did not hand him back to him,
and for that reason also—
They do not hand back one who has fallen into the power of the executioner; therefore, for Tvaṣṭṛ accompanied by the wives (pātnīvata), [the cup] is drawn,
but he does not set it down.
For from non-existence indeed offspring are born;
he does not utter the secondary *vaṣaṭ* call, for if he were to utter the secondary *vaṣaṭ*, he would let Rudra loose upon the offspring.
If one were not to perform the *anuvaṣaṭ* call, the *agnīdh* would consume the Soma while it is unappeased.
He performs the *anuvaṣaṭ* call in a whisper;
he does not release Rudra upon the offspring, and the *agnīdh* consumes the Soma while it is appeased.
O Agnis, sit upon the lap of the Neṣṭṛ.
"O Neṣṭṛ, lead the wife forward," he says.
Thus the Agnīdh places seed in the Neṣṭṛ, and the Neṣṭṛ causes it to be united with the wife by means of the Udgātṛ.
The Udgātṛ is indeed Prajāpati; he causes the waters to flow forth for the procreation of offspring.
He thus pours forth semen;
he causes it to flow forward with the thigh,
for by the thigh semen is poured forth.
He causes the thigh to be uncovered;
for when the thigh is naked, then they become a couple,
and then the seed is emitted.
Then offspring are born.
6.5.9 Anuvāka 9: The Description of the Hāriyojana Cup.
Indra slew Vṛtra;
he split open his skull.
He became the *droṇakalaśa* vessel; from him the Soma flowed forth,
and he became the *hāriyojana*.
He hesitated over it, thinking, "Should I offer it?
Or should I not offer it?
Then he reflected.
Thinking, "What I shall offer, what I shall burn, and what I shall not offer— I shall cause a disturbance to the sacrifice," he resolved to offer it. Then Agni said:
Thinking, "You shall not offer raw [milk] to me," he mixed it with parched grains.
He offered that which had become cooked;
when he mixes the *hāriyojana* with parched grains, it is for the sake of its being cooked; thus he offers it as something that has indeed become cooked.
He mixes [the offering] with many [verses].
Thus many indeed become for him milch-cows yielding desires in yonder world.
Now, moreover, they say:
"These indeed are Indra's dappled, wish-fulfilling cows, namely the *hāriyojanī* verses";
therefore, one should mix [the soma] with many [verses].
The *ṛc* and the *sāman* are indeed Indra’s two bay steeds, the drinkers of soma.
The enclosing-sticks (paridhi) are the placement for those two.
If one were to offer the oblation without having cast down the enclosing-sticks, one would be offering fodder between the two jaws.
Having struck the enclosing-sticks, he offers; by means of the two "without support" [offerings], he indeed provides fodder.
The Unnetṛ offers, for at this point the Adhvaryu has become exhausted once the *svagā* has been uttered.
Whatever the Adhvaryu might offer, it is just like unyoking [the chariot] and then yoking it again.
Having placed it upon the head, he offers;
for from the head indeed did he come into being.
He offers while stepping forward; for Indra slew Vṛtra while stepping forward,
for the sake of prosperity.
The cups for the yoking-horse (hāriyojanī) are indeed cattle;
if he were to break them, cattle would attend him while consuming only a small amount.
If he were not to break it, many animals would approach it while grazing;
[the sacrificer] distresses them mentally;
thus he effects both.
Many cattle, while feeding, attend upon him;
by seeking an invitation from the Unnetṛ, they obtain whatever Soma-drinking there may be.
He scatters [the grains] on the high altar;
the high altar is indeed cattle,
and the Hāriyojanī offerings are cattle.
They establish the cattle among the cattle themselves.
6.5.10 Anuvāka 10: A further explanation of the drawing of the cups, beginning with the Āgrayaṇa.
Along with the cups, offspring and cattle are produced:
goats and sheep [are produced] from the Upāṃśu and Antaryāma cups.
Men are the Śukra and Manthin cups;
one-hoofed animals are the seasonal cups (Ṛtugrahas);
cows are the Āditya cup.
The Āditya cup is drawn with the greatest number of ṛg-verses;
therefore, among animals, cows are the most numerous.
As for the fact that he draws it three times in a low voice with his hand:
Therefore, the unborn one gives birth to two or three, and then to many more; for this Āgrayaṇa is the father and the pitcher is the son.
If the Āgrayaṇa should fail, one should draw [the Soma] from the pitcher.
Just as a father runs to his son when he is in distress, so it is with this:
if the *kalaśa* should fail, one should draw [the draught] from the *āgrayaṇa*.
Just as a son, when exhausted, runs to his father for refuge, so indeed is that.
The Āgrayaṇa is indeed the self of the sacrifice.
If either the cup or the jar should leak, one should draw [the juice] from the Āgrayaṇa.
He prepares the sacrifice from his very self.
For this Āgrayaṇa cup is drawn while unmanifest;
he draws it with a vessel and offers it with a Vāyu-vessel, therefore—
One who kills a Brahmin [is purified] by [carrying] an embryo that is not yet known; they descend for the final bath (avabhṛtha),
they throw away the cooking pots, and they carry out the vessels dedicated to Vāyu.
Therefore, they cast out a female child at birth, but they carry off a male.
When he recites the *puroruca*, it is just as if he were bringing [wealth] to one who is more prosperous;
when he draws the cup (*graha*), it is just as if, having brought [wealth] to one who is more prosperous, he announces it.
In that he sets it down, it is just as when one departs after leaving something deposited with a superior.
Whatever is performed in the sacrifice by means of the *sāman* or the *yajus* is loose; whatever is performed by means of the *ṛc*, that is firm.
Those with the *upayāma* formula at the beginning are taken with a *yajus*; those with the *upayāma* formula at the end are taken with a *ṛc*, for the support of the sacrifice.
6.5.11 Anuvāka 11: Praise of the Soma Vessels.
Some vessels are joined together, while others are not;
those which are joined face away from one another—by means of them, he conquers that very world.
For that world is, as it were, turned away;
but those [rites] which are performed again and again, by them one conquers this very world,
for this world is, as it were, repeated.
Other vessels are employed;
those which are employed facing away, along with them the plants perish, whereas those which are [employed] again...
After those [vessels] have been employed, the plants come into being again; other vessels are employed, while others that were used previously are not.
After those which are employed once and for all, the wild animals depart to the forest.
Furthermore, those [vessels] which are employed, after them the domestic animals follow toward the village. He who knows the foundation of the cups becomes possessed of a foundation.
"Clarified butter" is the hymn; that indeed is the foundation of the cups.
That which he recites in a whisper belongs to the Upāṃśu and Antaryāma cups; that which he recites aloud belongs to the other cups.
This indeed is the fundamental cause of the *grahas*.
He who knows this becomes possessed of that fundamental cause.
He who knows the pairing of the *grahas* is procreated with offspring, cattle, and pairings.
Some cups are drawn with bowls, others with Vāyu-vessels;
this indeed is the pairing of the cups.
He who knows thus is procreated with offspring, cattle, and pairings.
Indra drank Tvaṣṭṛ’s Soma by force; he was shattered in every limb.
He found no delight in himself;
he saw these sacrificial cakes at each pressing and offered them.
With them, he indeed created for himself a place of rest;
therefore, sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśas) are offered at each pressing.
Therefore, one should eat of the sacrificial cakes at each pressing; thus he creates a place of rest for himself, and Soma does not flow past him.
The exponents of Brahman say:
"Neither by the Ṛg-verse nor by the Yajus-formula is the fivefold nature (pañktitva) attained; what then constitutes the fivefold character of the sacrifice?
[It is: parched grains (dhānā), groats (karambha), parched rice (parivāpa), the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa), and the curd-mixture (payasyā).
By that, the fivefold sequence is obtained;
such is the fivefold nature of the sacrifice.
6.6 Prapāṭhaka: 6, Anuvāka 1: The Description of the Dakṣiṇā Offerings.
These offerings of the sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā*) are indeed offered for the sake of the heavenly world;
he offers with two verses in the *gārhapatya* fire.
The sacrificer has two feet for the sake of stability;
he offers in the Āgnīdhra fire-shed.
He indeed steps into the intermediate space;
he approaches the seat; verily, he causes him to go to the heavenly world.
He offers on the Gārhapatya fire with two verses addressed to Sūrya;
he thus causes him to ascend to that very world.
He offers on the Āgnīdhra fire with a verse containing the word "lead."
For the attainment of the heavenly world, he says, "Go to heaven, fly to the light! and having offered the gold, he takes it up.
Verily, he causes him to go to the heavenly world.
"By means of form I approach your form," he says;
for by means of form he approaches their form, since [he does so] with gold.
"May Tutha, the all-knowing, distribute to you," he says;
for Tutha, the all-knowing, used indeed to distribute the sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā*) of the gods; by that very means he distributes them.
"This gift of thine, O Agni, comes flowing with Soma," he says,
for his gift indeed comes flowing with Soma.
"Lead them by the path of Mitra," he says for the sake of peace.
"Go forth by the path of Ṛta, O you whose sacrificial fee is a moon," he says.
"Truth or Right.
Verily by truth and by right he distributes them, saying: "Leading us on the path of sacrifice toward prosperity."
"For these sacrificial gifts go by the path of the sacrifice.
"Today may I win over a Brāhmaṇa, a seer, the descendant of seers," he says.
This is indeed the Brāhmaṇa seer, the descendant of seers, who has heard [the sacred tradition];
therefore he says thus:
"Behold the light! Behold the atmosphere!"—so he says.
He causes him to go to the heavenly world itself;
"Exert yourself with the members of the assembly," he says for the sake of friendship.
"Go among the gods as given by us; full of sweetness, enter the giver," he says.
"We here are the givers; full of sweetness, enter us there," that is indeed what he says.
He gives gold;
gold is indeed light;
verily he places light in front.
For the illumination of the heavenly world,
he gives to the Āgnīdhra;
thus he gratifies the seasons, which have Agni as their mouth.
He gives to the Brahman for the sake of procreation;
he gives to the Hotṛ.
The Hotṛ is indeed the self of the sacrifice;
he thus causes the self of the sacrifice to prosper through the sacrificial gifts (dakṣiṇās).
6.6.2 Anuvāka 2: Exposition of the Samiṣṭayajus Oblations.
He offers the samiṣṭayajus oblations for the completion of the sacrifice.

Whatever in the sacrifice is cruel, whatever is impaired, whatever it oversteps, whatever it does not overstep, whatever it does in excess, and whatever it does not do—that very thing he propitiates with these.
He offers nine oblations; for there are nine vital breaths in a person.
The sacrifice is commensurate with man;
he gratifies the sacrifice in its entirety by offering six verses containing the word *ṛk*.
There are six seasons;
verily he gratifies the seasons with three sacrificial formulas.
These are the three worlds. It is these very worlds that he gratifies when he says, "O sacrifice, go to the sacrifice; go to the lord of the sacrifice."
Verily, he causes him to go to the lord of the sacrifice;
"Go to your own womb," he says; verily, he causes him to go to his own womb.
"This is your sacrifice, O lord of the sacrifice, accompanied by the *sūktavāka* and rich in heroic sons," he says;
thus the sacrificer himself bestows vigor.
Vāsiṣṭha Sātyahavya questioned Devabhāga.
"Since you caused me, who have performed many sacrifices, to sacrifice for the Sṛñjayas,
did you establish sacrifice upon sacrifice, or did you establish it upon the lord of sacrifice?"—
thus he spoke.
"In the lord of the sacrifice"—it was because of truth that the Sṛñjayas perished, so he said; "the sacrifice was indeed established in the sacrifice so that the sacrificer would not suffer defeat.
"O gods who know the way, having found the way, go on the way," he says.
He establishes the sacrifice within the sacrifice itself,
for the sake of the sacrificer’s non-defeat.
6.6.3 Anuvāka 3: Explanation of the Avabhṛtha-yajus Offerings.
He offers the Avabhṛtha-yajus oblations;
whatever sin he commits that is prior to one year of age, he expiates that very thing by means of them.
He goes down to the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) in the waters;
for Varuṇa is indeed in the waters—
thus he directly propitiates Varuṇa.
Following along the path of the sacrifice, the *rakṣases* seek to destroy it;
the *prastotṛ* follows along with the *sāman*, for the *sāman* is indeed the slayer of *rakṣases*.
For the sake of driving away the Rākṣasas, he approaches the finale three times;
for these worlds are three.
From these very worlds he drives away the *rakṣas* demons;
man after man attains the *nidhana*.
"Man, for man is a protector, for the warding off of demons.
"The King Varuṇa has indeed made wide space," he says.
"For stability," he says, "a hundred physicians are yours, O King, a thousand. Thus he provides healing for him.
"The noose of Varuṇa has been stepped upon," he says;
thus he steps directly upon the noose of Varuṇa, and he offers an oblation over the sacrificial grass (barhis).
For the firm establishment of the oblations;
moreover, he offers in that which possesses fire.
[He performs] the fore-offerings without the *barhis* grass.
He sacrifices;
the sacrificial grass (barhis) is indeed offspring;
verily, he releases offspring from the nooses of Varuṇa.
He offers the two portions of clarified butter;
he does not exclude the two eyes of the sacrifice.
He sacrifices to Varuṇa.
Verily, he releases him from Varuna’s noose.
He sacrifices to Agni and Varuna;
thus he directly releases him from Varuna’s noose.
He performs two after-offerings (anūyāja) excluding the *barhis*;
the *barhis* is indeed offspring;
thus he releases offspring from Varuna’s noose.
He performs four fore-offerings and two after-offerings;
they amount to six,
for there are six seasons.
Verily, he finds firm support in the seasons.
"O bath, O you who plunge down," he says;
thus he propitiates Varuna exactly as prescribed.
"In the ocean is your heart, within the waters," he says, for Varuṇa is indeed within the ocean. "May the plants and the waters enter you," he says.
Verily, by means of water and plants, he makes him harmonious.
"O divine waters, this is your offspring," he says;
this is exactly according to the sacrificial formula.
Soma is indeed cattle.
If he were to consume the drops, he would possess cattle, but Varuṇa would seize him.
If he were not to eat it, he would be without cattle and Varuṇa would seize him;
by merely touching it, he becomes possessed of cattle and Varuṇa does not seize him.
"The noose of Varuṇa is cast off," he says.
Thus he is released from Varuna’s noose.
They return without looking back, for the sake of concealment from Varuna.
"Fuel art thou; may we prosper," he says.
Approaching the fire while paying homage with the kindling-stick, he says, "Thou art brilliance; bestow brilliance upon me";
verily, he bestows brilliance upon himself.

6.6.4 Anuvāka 4: The Description of the Set of Eleven Sacrificial Posts (Yūpaikādaśinī) He digs up the altar with the wooden sword (sphya) and measures out [the site] with the axle of a chariot; he erects the sacrificial post.
