Having thus prepared the threefold thunderbolt, he hurls it at his rival for his destruction.

If he were to erect it within the altar, he would conquer the world of the gods; if outside the altar, the world of men. He erects it at the junction of the edge of the altar, for the conquest of both worlds.

One should measure [the sacrificial post] to the height of the *upara* for one desiring the world of the ancestors; to the height of the *raśanā* (girdle) for one desiring the world of men; to the height of the *caṣāla* (top-ring) for one desiring sensory power; all of equal height for one desiring a firm foundation. Those three which are middle-sized should be equal for one desiring cattle;
along these indeed cattle attend; he becomes possessed of cattle. He should interlace the others; verily, by means of offspring he interlaces him with cattle.

If he should desire of someone, "May he be short-lived," he should erect for him a *gartamit* (pit-measured) post, making the northern one the tallest and the other shorter; for this is indeed the *gartamit*, and he for whom he erects it in this manner dies quickly.
He should erect the southern one as the tallest for one who desires heaven, and the other as shorter; thus the sacrificer makes a staircase and a bridge for the attainment of the heavenly world.

Because he winds two girdles around a single sacrificial post, therefore one man wins two wives; because he does not wind a single girdle around two posts, therefore one woman does not win two husbands. If he should desire of someone, "May a female child be born to him," he should intertwine the two girdles near the ends; a female child is indeed born to him.
If he should desire of someone, "May a male child be born to him," he should wrap them right to the ends; a male child is indeed born to him.

It is born. Indeed, the Asuras drove the gods from the south; the gods repelled them by means of the *upaśaya* (the leaning post) alone. That is why it is called the *upaśaya*. Because it leans (*upaśaye*) toward the south, it serves for the repelling of the enemy. All other sacrificial posts possess cattle, but the *upaśaya* alone is without cattle; therefore, the sacrificer is its "cattle. If he were not to designate it, the sacrificer would meet with ruin. He should designate it, saying: "This one is your cattle," referring to whomsoever he hates. It is him [whom he hates] that he [destroys].
He hates him; he assigns that animal to him.
If he should not hate anyone, he should say, "The mouse is your animal. Thus he harms neither domestic animals nor wild animals.

Prajāpati created offspring; he was deprived of food. He saw this set of eleven [animals], and by it he indeed obtained food. In that there are ten sacrificial posts—the Virāj consists of ten syllables, and the Virāj is food—he obtains food through the Virāj itself.
The eleventh post is indeed her breast; with it he milks her.

This set of eleven posts is measured out as a thunderbolt; it is capable of crushing the sacrifice from the front toward the west. In that he erects the post for the wives (*pātnīvata*), it is for the support and stabilization of the sacrifice.

6.6.5 Anuvāka 5: The Exposition of the Eleven Animal Victims (Paśvekādaśinī) Prajāpati created offspring; he felt himself depleted. He perceived this set of eleven victims; by means of it, he placed life-span, sensory power, and vigor within himself. Indeed, he who sacrifices creates offspring just like Prajāpati; at this point, he is as if depleted. In that there is this set of eleven victims, the sacrificer thereby places life-span, sensory power, and vigor within himself.
By the victim for Agni, he causes [the sacrificer] to propagate; by the victim for Sarasvatī, he effects union; [by the victim for Pūṣan,] he places seed.

With the [offering] to Soma he bestows and brings forth; with that to Pūṣan he causes procreation. There is one for Bṛhaspati; Bṛhaspati is indeed the *brahman* among the gods; verily, by means of the *brahman*, he brings forth offspring for him. There is one for the Viśvedevas; offspring belong to the Viśvedevas; verily, he brings forth offspring for him. By the [offering] to Indra, he wins power (*indriya*); by that to the Maruts, the people (*viś*); by that to Indra and Agni, vigor and strength. There is one for Savitṛ for instigation; one for Varuṇa for freedom from Varuṇa’s noose. He offers the [victim] for Indra in the middle; verily, he places power in the midst of the sacrificer.

Before the offering to Indra, he sacrifices an animal for the Viśvedevas; food indeed belongs to the Viśvedevas, and thus he places food at the very beginning. Therefore, food is eaten first. Having sacrificed to Indra, he sacrifices to the Maruts; the Maruts are the people (viś), and thus he binds the people to him from behind.

If he should desire, "May he who has attained power be excluded, and may he who is excluded attain power," he should sacrifice a victim to Varuṇa in the place of Indra, and one to Indra in the place of Varuṇa.
He who had attained power is excluded, and he who was excluded attains power.
If he should desire, "May the offspring become bewildered," he should intermingle the animals; thus he indeed bewilders the offspring.

If he were to offer the animal to Varuṇa with the flow of the waters directed toward him, Varuṇa would seize the offspring; he offers it from the south, facing north, with the flow of the waters directed away from him, so that Varuṇa does not seize the offspring.

6.6.6 Anuvāka 6: Indra caused Manu to sacrifice with his wife; he released her after she had been encircled by fire. Through her, Manu attained prosperity. In that he releases the offering for the wives (*pātnīvata*) once it has been encircled by fire, the sacrificer attains that very prosperity which Manu attained.

From the non-establishment of the sacrifice, the sacrifice perishes; following the perishing of the sacrifice, the sacrificer perishes. In that he completes the *pātnīvata* offering with clarified butter (*ājya*), it is for the establishment of the sacrifice; following the establishment of the sacrifice, the sacrificer establishes himself.
The sacrifice is accomplished with the omentum;

it is not yet accomplished with the *vaśā* cow. Then he proceeds with the offering to the wives of the gods (*pātnīvata*); thus he proceeds at a proper ford. Moreover, at this very point his journey belongs to Tvaṣṭṛ.
Tvaṣṭṛ indeed transforms the forms of the seed once it has been shed; he releases that bull among the wives, and he (Tvaṣṭṛ) creates various forms for him.
6.6.7 Anuvāka 7: The Description of the Soma-Offering of Cooked Rice (Saumyacaru).
Indeed, they kill the Soma when they press it; in that there is an offering of cooked rice for Soma, it is just as if one were to kill a cow to accompany a dead man to the funeral pyre.

If one were to offer it in the northern half or in the middle, one would cause strife among the deities; he offers it in the southern half. This is indeed the quarter of the ancestors; thus, in its own quarter, he satisfies the ancestors. They carry it to the Udgātṛs. The Soma-cup belongs to the Sāman-deities; whatever they do incorrectly regarding the Sāman, this [offering] is the atonement for that. He lowers it...

They gaze at the filter; indeed, O gentle one, they purify themselves. He who does not look upon himself would be as one whose life has departed. Having made a reflection [of himself], he should gaze into it, for in that he beholds himself; thus he purifies himself. He whose mind has wandered away should gaze, saying: "That mind of mine which has gone afar, or that which has not gone afar—by means of King Soma, we establish that within ourselves. Thus he establishes his mind within himself.

He does not become dejected. Indeed, at the third pressing, the sacrifice departs from one who has sacrificed toward one who has not sacrificed. He offers with a verse addressed to Agni and Viṣṇu: "Of the ghee... Agni is all the deities, and Viṣṇu is the sacrifice; thus he sustains both the deities and the sacrifice.
He sacrifices in a low voice for the sake of forming a pair.

The exponents of Brahman say: "Mitra takes charge of the well-offered part of the sacrifice, and Varuṇa of the ill-offered part. Where, then, is the sacrifice, and where is the sacrificer? When he offers a barren cow to Mitra and Varuṇa, he pacifies the well-offered part of the sacrifice with Mitra and the ill-offered part with Varuṇa; thus the sacrificer does not come to ruin.

Just as they cleave the soil with a plough, so do the *ṛc* and the *sāman* cleave the sacrifice. When he offers a barren cow to Mitra and Varuṇa, he provides a means of sustenance for the cleaved sacrifice, for the sake of peace.

The meters of one who has sacrificed become exhausted; the essence of the meters is the barren cow. When he offers a barren cow to Mitra and Varuṇa, he thereby gratifies the meters once more so that they may not be exhausted, and he places essence back into the meters.
6.6.8 Anuvāka 8: The Description of the Atigrāhya Cups.
The gods, indeed, divided among themselves their sensory power and vigor;
what remained over from that became the Atigrāhyas.
That is why the *atigrāhya* cups are called "exceeding-graspers. Because the *atigrāhya*s are drawn, the sacrificer places within himself sensory power (*indriya*) and vigor (*vīrya*):
brilliance through the cup for Agni, sensory power through the cup for Indra, and spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) through the cup for Sūrya.
The *atigrāhya* cups are indeed the support of the sacrifice, as are the *pṛṣṭha* chants.
If one were not to draw them during the *pṛṣṭhya* day, the *pṛṣṭha* chants would crush the forward-moving sacrifice.
If [one does not draw them] during the *ukthya*...
One should take them facing westward; the *atigrāhya* cups should be drawn together.
They are to be taken in the *Viśvajit* sacrifice when it is performed with all the *pṛṣṭha* stotras, for the sake of providing the sacrifice with full vigor.
Prajāpati assigned the sacrifices to the gods.
He cast off his dear bodies;
they became the *atigrāhya* cups.
"His sacrifice is bodiless," they say, "for whom the *atigrāhya* cups are not drawn."
They should also be drawn at the Agniṣṭoma for the sake of the continuity of the sacrifice.
Indeed, all the deities were once alike; they did not attain distinction from one another.
Those gods saw these cups; they drew them.
Agni [attained] that which belongs to Agni, Indra that which belongs to Indra, and Sūrya that which belongs to Sūrya;
from that, indeed, they attained distinction from other deities.
For him who, knowing thus, these cups are drawn, he attains distinction from his evil rival.
"These worlds must be made luminous and equal in power," they say.
"One places light in this world with the [oblation] to Agni; one places light in the intermediate space with the [oblation] to Indra; for Indra and Vāyu are yoked together."
By means of the offering to Sūrya, he establishes light in yonder world; these worlds become luminous for him; he makes them equal in strength.
Bamba and Viśvavayas indeed discovered these cups;
through them, these worlds—both those turned away and those turned toward—became manifest.
For him who knows thus and for whom these cups are drawn, these worlds, both turned away and turned toward, shine forth for him.
6.6.9 Anuvāka 9: The Description of the Adābhya Cup. Whatever the gods did at the sacrifice, the Asuras did that too.
Those gods established the meters and the pressings within the Adābhya cup.
Then the gods prospered and the Asuras were defeated.
For him who, knowing thus, has the Adābhya cup drawn, he prospers in his own person and his rival is defeated.
Indeed, because the gods overcame the Asuras with the Adābhya, that is the reason for the Adābhya’s name "unassailable."
He who knows thus indeed overcomes his rival; his rival does not overcome him.
This body of Prajāpati is indeed called "the deliverer," namely the Adābhya cup.
He draws it while it is still bound for the sake of deliverance.
He who knows thus is delivered beyond evil and his rival.
They indeed slay this Soma when they press it; when the Soma is slain, the sacrifice is slain; when the sacrifice is slain, the sacrificer is slain.
Thus say the exponents of the Veda.
"What does the sacrificer perform at the sacrifice by which he goes to the heavenly world while still living?
This Adābhya cup is indeed a 'living-draught';
he draws it from [Soma] that has not yet been pressed."
He causes him to go to the heavenly world while still alive.
They indeed tear the sacrifice asunder when they conclude it at the Adābhya cup.
He pours out the stalks for the continuity of the sacrifice.
6.6.10 Anuvāka 10: The Description of the Aṃśu Cup.
The gods indeed drew their cups simultaneously;
then Prajāpati beheld this Aṃśu cup.
They took it; by that indeed he prospered.
For whomsoever, knowing thus, the *aṃśu* cup is drawn, he indeed prospers.
He draws from that which has been pressed once, for he prospered by it once;
he draws with the mind.
For Prajāpati is like the mind; he takes [the milk] with a vessel made of udumbara wood for the attainment of Prajāpati.
The Udumbara is indeed strength;
verily he wins strength.
It has four corners.
He who knows the abode of the *aṃśu* cup becomes possessed of an abode; he indeed finds firm standing in the very quarters.
The *vāmadevya* is the *sāman*; that indeed is its abode. Singing it with the mind, he draws [the cup]; thus he becomes possessed of an abode.
If the *adhvaryu*, while drawing the *aṃśu* cup, should fail to succeed, he would fail for both the *adhvaryu* and the sacrificer.
If he were to prosper by means of both, he would indeed prosper;
he draws [the cup] without taking breath—this is his prosperity. He breathes over the gold.
Gold is indeed immortality, and breath is life; by means of life, he thus bestows immortality upon him.
It is a hundred mānas in weight, for man has a lifespan of a hundred years and possesses a hundredfold power.
One becomes established in life-span and in the sense-faculties.
6.6.11 Anuvāka 11: The Description of the Ṣoḍaśin Cup.
Prajāpati assigned the sacrifices to the gods; he felt himself depleted.
He drew out for himself the sixteenfold power of the senses from the sacrifices;
that became the *ṣoḍaśin*.
Indeed, there is no sacrifice named the *ṣoḍaśin*.
In that there is indeed a sixteenfold stotra and a sixteenfold śastra, by that it is the Ṣoḍaśin; that is the reason for the Ṣoḍaśin’s name.
When the Ṣoḍaśin cup is drawn, the sacrificer thereby places within himself sensory power and vigor.
The heavenly world, indeed, did not suffice for the gods; they saw this *ṣoḍaśin* sacrifice.
They took it from them, and then indeed the world of heaven became available to them;
therefore, when the *ṣoḍaśin* is taken, it is for the conquest of the world of heaven.
Indra was indeed the youngest among the gods;
he ran to Prajāpati,
who gave this *ṣoḍaśin* (sixteenfold cup) to him.
He took it;
therefore, he indeed went before the gods.
For whomsoever, knowing thus, the *ṣoḍaśī* cup is drawn, [he likewise goes before].
He goes to the very summit among his equals;
he draws [the cup] at the morning pressing,
for the *ṣoḍaśin* is indeed a thunderbolt.
The Vajra is the morning pressing;
he draws it from its own womb; he draws it at each pressing.
Verily, from each pressing he brings him forth;
one who desires cattle should draw [the cup] at the third pressing.
The *ṣoḍaśin* is indeed a thunderbolt, and cattle belong to the third pressing.
By means of the *vajra* itself, he wins cattle for him from the third pressing; however,
he should not draw [the cup] at the *ukthya*,
for cattle are indeed the *ukthas*.
If one were to draw it at the Ukthya, he would burn away his offspring and cattle;
one who desires cattle should draw it at the Atirātra.
The sixteenth [stotra] is indeed a thunderbolt;
by means of that very thunderbolt, he secures cattle for him and pacifies them with the night at the end.
He may also take [the draught] for a Rājanya even at the Agniṣṭoma.
For a Kṣatriya who desires distinction performs the sacrifice;
on that very day, he grasps the thunderbolt for him,
and that thunderbolt either kindles him toward prosperity or consumes him.
The twenty-first hymn serves for firm establishment;
it is recited as containing the word "harivat," the beloved abode of Indra.
The meters among the gods were fewer, while those among the Asuras were greater.
Those gods, by means of a lesser meter, overcame a greater meter.
Thereby they indeed deprived the Asuras of their world.
In that one recites a larger metre over a smaller metre, one deprives the rival of his world;
thus they cause six syllables to be redundant.
There are six seasons;
he thus gratifies the seasons.
They prepare four of the former [verses].
By means of four-footed [verses] he wins quadrupeds; by two further [verses] he wins bipeds.
They bring them together into the *anuṣṭubh*;
for the *anuṣṭubh* is speech.
Therefore, speech is the highest of the vital breaths.
When the sun has half-risen, he begins the Stotra of the Ṣoḍaśin.
For it was in this very world that Indra slew Vṛtra.
He hurls the thunderbolt directly at his rival.
A reddish-brown horse is the sacrificial fee;
that indeed is the form of the thunderbolt.
For prosperity.

Taittirīya Saṃhitā, Kāṇḍa 7, Prapāṭhaka 1, Anuvāka 1: The Description of the Jyotiṣṭoma and its First Form, the Agniṣṭoma. Agni is the procreative light; he is the light among the deities, the Virāj among the meters, and the light of speech. The Virāj is established in Agni.
He attains the Virāj;
therefore it is called light.
Two *stomas* carry the morning pressing, just as the out-breath and the in-breath do.
Two [verses] are for the midday pressing, corresponding to sight and hearing;
two are for the third pressing, corresponding to speech and the foundation.
This sacrifice is commensurate with man and is not one-sided.
Whatever desire one desires, that one attains by means of this;
for by means of the *asthūri* one attains everything.
Indeed, Prajāpati created offspring by means of the Agniṣṭoma.
He enclosed them by means of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice;
from among those thus enclosed, a mule escaped, and having pursued it, he took its seed.
He wiped it on a donkey;
of those [semen] taken up, a mule surpassed them all.
Having pursued it, he took its semen.
He wiped it on a donkey;
therefore the donkey has double seed.
Moreover, they say:
"He struck her upon the mare";
therefore the mare has double seed.
Moreover, they say:
"He has rubbed [it] into the plants," they say; therefore, the plants, though unanointed, hum.
Moreover, they say that he has struck down among the offspring;
therefore twins are born.
Therefore, the mule does not procreate, for its seed has been taken;
therefore it is not fit for the sacrificial grass (barhis), but it is fit for the gift of all one's possessions or for a thousand [cows].
For he who, knowing thus, sacrifices with the Agniṣṭoma passes over the unprocreated offspring; he procreates those offspring that have been born, and he takes hold of those already born.
Therefore they say:
"The Jyeṣṭhayajña."
Prajāpati, indeed, is the eldest; for he was the first to sacrifice with this.
Prajāpati desired.
Thinking, "May I procreate," he measured out the Trivṛt from his mouth.
After it was measured out, Agni was emitted as its deity, the Gāyatrī as its metre, the Rathantara as its Sāman, the Brāhmaṇa among men, and the goat among animals.
Therefore they are the principal ones,
for they were created from the mouth;
from the chest and the two arms he measured out the fifteenfold [stoma].
Indra was created after him, along with the Triṣṭubh metre, the Bṛhat Sāman,
the Rājanya among men, and the sheep among animals;
therefore, they are full of vigor.
From vigor they were emitted;
from the middle he measured out the seventeenfold [stoma];
after it all the gods were emitted as deities, the *jagatī* metre, the *vairūpa* sāman, the Vaiśya among men, and cattle among animals.
Therefore they are the first;
for they were created from food,
and therefore they are more numerous than others.
For the majority of the deities were created after him; he measured out the twenty-first [day], and the Anuṣṭubh meter followed it.
The Vairāja Sāman was created after [the other Sāmans]; among humans, the Śūdra; among animals, the horse.
Therefore, both the horse and the Śūdra are capable of passing over into other states of being.
Therefore, the Śūdra is not entitled to sacrifice;
for he was not created alongside the deities; therefore, he lives by serving [the other castes] with his feet.
For the two worlds were produced; the Trivṛt is indeed the vital breaths,
and the Pañcadaśa is the half-months.
Prajāpati is seventeenfold; these three worlds are [the first seventeen],
and yonder sun is the twenty-first.
In this, indeed, these are supported; in this, they are established.
He who knows thus is supported in this very thing; he is established in this very thing.
7.1.2 Anuvāka 2: A Statement on the Collective Action of the Stomas.
At the morning pressing, indeed, he goes forward bestowing light upon the threefold stoma by means of the *gāyatrī* metre;
with the threefold [stoma], which is spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), he goes forward bestowing light upon the fifteenfold stoma.
Bestowing light upon the seventeenfold [stoma] by means of the fifteenfold [stoma] with its vigor and strength, he goes forth;
bestowing light upon the twenty-onefold [stoma] by means of the seventeenfold [stoma] belonging to Prajāpati, which is generative, he goes forth;
thus, the stoma itself, bestowing light upon the stoma, goes forth.
Moreover, one leads the Stoma forward toward the Stoma;
for as many as are the Stomas, so many are the desires, and so many are the worlds.
So many are the lights.
He wins just as many stomas, as many desires, as many worlds, and as many lights.
7.1.3 Anuvāka 3: The Drawing Out for the Atirātra Rite. The exponents of sacred knowledge say:
"He indeed should sacrifice who, having sacrificed with the Agniṣṭoma, then sacrifices with the Sarvastoma."

He whose threefold [stoma] they exclude, his vital breaths they exclude; "May there also be for me [a share] in the vital breaths," thinking thus indeed does the sacrificer sacrifice with the sacrifice.
He whose fifteenfold [stoma] they exclude, his vigor they exclude.
"Indeed, thinking 'may there be no lack of vigor in me,' one performs sacrifice with the sacrifice; for him from whose [sacrifice] they exclude the seventeenfold [stoma],
they exclude his offspring."
"May there also be offspring for me"—with this thought, indeed, the sacrificer performs the sacrifice;
if they omit the twenty-first [stotra], they omit his foundation. "May there also be a foundation for me"—with this thought, indeed, the sacrificer performs the sacrifice.
For him whose Triṇava stoma they omit, they omit both the seasonal *ṛtus* and the stellar *virāj*.
"May the seasonal *ṛtus* and the stellar *virāj* be mine," with this thought indeed the sacrificer performs the sacrifice by means of the sacrifice.
"The deities pass within him whose thirty-three [stomas] pass within;
may there also be for me a place among the deities"—with this thought, indeed, does the sacrificer sacrifice by means of the sacrifice.
He who knows the lowest of the *stomas* as reaching the highest point, reaches the highest point itself.
The Trivṛt is indeed the lowest of the Stomas, and the Trivṛt is the highest;
he who knows thus attains the highest state.
7.1.4 Anuvāka 4: Exposition of the Rules for the Two-Night Ahīna Sacrifice of the Aṅgirases.
The Aṅgirases indeed performed a sacrificial session (sattra);
they went to the heavenly world.
Among them, both Haviṣmān and Haviṣkṛt were left behind. They desired:
"May we go to the heavenly world."
The two of them saw this two-night rite; they took it up and sacrificed with it.
Thereupon, indeed, those two went to the heavenly world.
He who, knowing thus, sacrifices with the Dvirātra, goes to the heavenly world. They arrived having come by means of the first day and reaching it by means of the second.
The Abhiplava is the first day; the Gati is the subsequent one.
The Jyotiṣṭoma Agniṣṭoma is the first day; by it he wins brilliance.
The Sarvastoma Atirātra is the subsequent one, for the attainment of everything and for the securing of everything.
On the first day, the Gāyatra Sāman is used;
the Gāyatrī is indeed brilliance,
and the Gāyatrī is spiritual luster.
He places splendor itself, as Brahman-splendor, within himself;
the latter [verse] is in the Triṣṭubh meter.
The Triṣṭubh is indeed force and vigor.
He places vigor itself as strength within himself;
on the first day, the Rathantara becomes the Sāman.
This [earth] is indeed the Rathantara;
he finds firm support on this very [earth],
while the Bṛhat is in the higher [region].
That [sun] is indeed the Bṛhat; he thus finds firm support in that very [sun]. Regarding this, they say:
"Where are both the Jagatī and the Anuṣṭubh?
"The Vaikhānasa Sāman is on the preceding day; by that he does not depart from the Jagatī.
The Ṣoḍaśin is on the following day; by that [he does not depart] from the Anuṣṭubh."
Then they say:
"If these two were to occur in the same half-month, the vigor of one day would be lost.
The first day occurs on the new moon (amāvāsyā), and the second on the following day.
The two half-months are distinct;
they possess distinct powers.
The day with the *haviṣmat* finale is the first, and the day with the *haviṣkṛt* finale is the latter.
For stability.
7.1.5 Anuvāka 5: The Description of the Garga-trirātra Sacrifice.
In the beginning, this world was indeed water, a mere ocean;
therein Prajāpati, having become Vāyu (the wind), moved about.
He saw her;
becoming a boar, he seized her,
and becoming Viśvakarman, he wiped her clean.
She expanded;
she became the earth (pṛthivī); that is the essence of the earth's name.
In that [state], Prajāpati exerted himself;
he created the gods— the Vasus, the Rudras, and the Ādityas—
and those gods said to Prajāpati:
"Let us procreate," they said.
He replied,
"Just as I have created you through austerity, so do you seek procreation through austerity."
He gave fire as their abode, saying,
"Exert yourselves with this abode.
They exerted themselves with fire as their abode.
For a year they created a single cow;
they presented it to the Vasus, the Rudras, and the Ādityas,
saying, "Guard this!"
The Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas protected her;
she brought forth offspring for the Vasus, the Rudras, and the Ādityas—three and... [thirty-three].
And there were thirty-three hundred; they became the thousandth,
and those gods spoke to Prajāpati.
"Perform the sacrifice for us with a thousand [cows]," he said;
he performed the Agniṣṭoma for the Vasus,
and they conquered this world.
They gave that to him;
he sacrificed for the Rudras with the Ukthya,
and they conquered the intermediate space.
They gave it to him;
he caused the Ādityas to sacrifice with the Atirātra,
and they conquered that world.
And as they gave it,
that intermediate space became separated.
Therefore, the Rudras are destroyers;
for they have no abode,
therefore so it is said.
"The middle day of the three-night rite is indeed loose, for it has become relaxed"; thus,
the *ājya* litany of the middle day is in the *triṣṭubh* metre, and he recites the *saṃyāna* hymns.
He recites the Ṣoḍaśin chant for the support of the day and to prevent it from becoming slack;
therefore, of the three-night rite, the first day should be an Agniṣṭoma, then an Ukthya, and then an Atirātra.
For the support of these worlds,
he gives three hundred [cows] each day for three days in succession, without interruption,
for the continuity of these worlds.
One should not divide the ten;
[one thinks], "Lest I divide the Virāj.
Then, regarding that which was the thousandth [cow], Indra and Viṣṇu contended for it.
Indra thought:
"By means of this [cow], Viṣṇu will surely consume this thousandfold [offering]. Then they two were formed within her.
Indra has two shares and Viṣṇu the third; concerning this, the following verse is recited:
"Both of you have conquered."
The Acchāvāka indeed recites this [verse];
then, that which is the thousandth [cow] is to be given to the Hotṛ.
Or rather, it exceeds the Hotṛ;
that which exceeds is the Hotṛ’s means of attaining what has not yet been attained.
Now, they say:
"O Unnetṛ, you have gone beyond!
This [offering] is indeed the surplus of the thousand;
the Unnetṛ is the surplus among the officiating priests.
Then they say:
"One should give it to all the members of the assembly.
Then they say:
"Having made her an offering, she should act according to his will," they say;
then they further say,
"She should be given to both the Brahman and the Āgnīdhra."
Two parts for the Brahman and a third for the Agnīdh;
for the Brahman belongs to Indra and the Agnīdh to Viṣṇu. Thus it was that those two were properly constituted.
Then they say:
"She who is beautiful and multiformed, she is the deity.
Then they say:
That cow which is two-colored and brindled on both sides is the *devī* (divine one); she is for the securing of a thousand.
This, indeed, is the course of the thousand;
there are a thousand *stotrīyā* verses.
The sacrificial fees are a thousand;
the heavenly world is measured by a thousand;
this is for the conquest of the heavenly world.
7.1.6 Anuvāka 6: The Naming of the Thousandth.
Soma indeed found the thousand;
Indra found it after him.
Yama approached them and said to them,
"Let there be for me a share here as well."
"So be it," they both said.
Yama perceived the creative power (*vīrya*) in one of them, thinking, "This [earth] indeed possesses the creative power of this thousand. He said to them, "Let this be mine; let that be yours two."
The two of them said,
"We all see this entire vigor contained within it; let us take our respective shares."
They took a portion from it and cast it into the waters, saying, "O Soma, come forth!"
That Rohiṇī, having assumed the form of a reddish-brown one-year-old cow, came forth together with three hundred and thirty-three [cows].
Therefore, one should purchase the Soma with a reddish-brown one-year-old cow;
for he who, knowing thus, purchases the Soma with a reddish-brown one-year-old cow, [obtains it] together with three hundred and thirty-three for him.
Soma becomes purchased for hundreds; he sacrifices with that which has been well-purchased;
they caused it to enter into the waters.
"Come forth for Indra!"— saying this, she,
having assumed the form of a red, marked, four-year-old cow that slays Vṛtra, rose up together with three hundred and thirty-three [gods].
Therefore, one should give away a red, marked, four-year-old cow that slays Vṛtra.
He who, knowing thus, gives a red, marked, four-year-old cow that slays the enemy— she becomes as if three hundred and thirty-three have been given by him;
they caused her to enter into the waters.
"Give me one for Yama!
said she; then that old, foolish woman, having assumed the form of the most wretched among them, rose up together with three hundred and thirty-three [gods].
Therefore, one should make an old, foolish, and most wretched woman the sacrificial animal to be slaughtered in place of the victim.

He who, knowing this, makes an old, foolish cow the most inferior of its kind serve as the *anustaraṇī* (the cow to be strangled at the funeral), for him there are three hundred and thirty-three [cows] in that world;
speech itself is the thousandth.
Therefore...
A boon should be given;
for she is indeed a boon, and thus she becomes bestowed upon him by the thousands.
Therefore, the boon should not be accepted; for that boon, once accepted, becomes a thousandfold for him.
He should say, "This one is the prize. Then he should say to another,
"This one is mine."
In this way, his thousand remains unappropriated.
It should be a cow of two-colored stripes;
regarding this, they say:
There should be a female with variegated legs; "a thousand beyond this"—
that should be a bride who is beautiful and perfected in form.
For she is indeed the boon for prosperity;
having led her around the north of the Āgnīdhra fire, one should cause her to smell the Droṇakalaśa at the edge of the Āhavanīya fire.
"Smell the jar for me; may you, who possess a wide stream of milk, be full of nourishment. May the drops enter you as rivers enter the ocean.
Grant me a share of a thousandfold wealth, together with offspring and cattle; may riches enter me again.
Thus, he unites him with offspring, cattle, and wealth.
He prospers, becoming possessed of offspring, cattle, and wealth— he who knows thus.
Having gone with her to the Āgnīdhra shed, he should offer the oblation while she stands in front, facing westward.
"Both of you have conquered; you are not defeated; neither of these two has been defeated. O Indra and Viṣṇu, when you strove together, you distributed a thousandfold in three ways.
For in the three-night sacrifice, a thousand is indeed divided into three parts.
Verily, he makes it thousandfold;
he makes its measure equal to a thousand.
He offers forms;
verily by means of forms he causes her to prosper.
Having approached her, he should whisper into her ear:
"O Iḍā, Rantī, Aditi, Sarasvatī, Priyā, Preyasi, Mahī, Viśrutī—these are your names, O inviolable one; declare me as a doer of good deeds among the gods.
Thus he makes him known to the gods.
The gods perceive him following after him.
7.1.7 Anuvāka 7: The Rule for the Thousandth [Soma-pressing].
By means of the thousandth, the sacrificer indeed goes to the heavenly world;
it causes him to go to the heavenly world.
"Lead me to the heavenly world," he says;
verily, he leads him to the heavenly world.
"Lead me to the luminous world," he says.
"He leads him indeed to the world of light.
"May she lead me to all the worlds of merit," he says;
thus he leads him indeed to all the worlds of merit.
"Lead me to a firm foundation together with offspring and cattle; may wealth enter into me again"—with these words, he establishes him upon wealth through offspring and cattle;
he who knows thus becomes possessed of offspring, cattle, and wealth.
One should give it to the Āgnīdhra, or to the Brahman, or to the Hotṛ, or to the Udgātṛ, or to the Adhvaryu;
for him who gives it without knowing this, it becomes as if a thousand have been given by him, and a thousand have been accepted by him.
If he accepts it, he should accept it [with these words]:
"Thou art one, not a thousand."
"I accept you as one being, not as a thousand; enter me as one being, not as a thousand.
He who knows thus accepts her as one being, not as a thousand.
"Thou art pleasant, well-seated, and very gracious; as the pleasant one, enter me; as the well-seated one, enter me; as the very gracious one, enter me," he says.
Having thus become pleasant, well-seated, and very gracious, she enters him and does not harm him.
The exponents of Brahman say:
"Does the thousandth follow the thousand? Does the thousand follow the thousandth?
If he were to let it go toward the east, the thousand would follow the thousandth.
That thousand would be unknown;
one would not know the heavenly world.
He releases it toward the west.
A thousand follow after her;
she, knowing it, goes to the heavenly world.
He releases it toward the sacrificer; quickly a thousand offspring are born.
Led as the last, it goes as the first to the gods.
7.1.8 Anuvāka 8: The Description of Atri’s Four-Night Rite.
Atri gave his progeny to Aurva, who desired offspring;
he, feeling depleted, thought himself devoid of vigor, relaxed, and exhausted.
He saw this four-night rite; he took it up and sacrificed with it.
From that, indeed, four heroes were born to him: a skilled Hotṛ, a skilled Udgātṛ, a skilled Adhvaryu, and one who is successful in the assembly.
He who, knowing thus, sacrifices with the Catūrātra, to him are born four heroes: a skilled Hotṛ, a skilled Udgātṛ, a skilled Adhvaryu, and one who is successful in the assembly.
Those Pavamāna chants which consist of twenty-four [verses] constitute spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*).
Whatever hymns arise, that is Śrī.
Four powers did not come to Atri, the sacrificer whose deity was Faith: brilliance, sensory power, spiritual luster, and the food of nourishment.
He beheld these four Soma sacrifices consisting of fourfold Stomas.
He brought them; he sacrificed with them.
By the first, he won splendor (*tejas*); by the second, sensory power (*indriya*); by the third, spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*); and by the fourth, the enjoyment of food (*annādya*).

He who, knowing thus, brings four *catuṣṭoma* Soma sacrifices and sacrifices with them, wins splendor by the first, sensory power by the second, spiritual luster by the third, and the enjoyment of food by the fourth.
Whatever prosperity Atri attained, that very same prosperity the sacrificer attains.
7.1.9 Anuvāka 9: Designation of the Four-night Sacrifice of Jamadagni.
Jamadagni, desiring prosperity, sacrificed with the four-night rite; he thereby attained these prosperities.
Therefore, the two descendants of Jamadagni who had turned grey did not recognize one another;
he who, knowing thus, sacrifices with the four-night rite, prospers with these very nourishments.
The Upasad days consist of sacrificial cakes.
The sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) is indeed cattle; verily, he wins cattle for himself. The sacrificial cake is indeed food.
He indeed secures food;
he becomes an eater of food and possessed of cattle, who, knowing thus, sacrifices with the four-night rite.
7.1.10 Anuvāka 10: The Designation of the Five Nights.
This [universe] was indeed one, the year;
it desired.
Thinking, "May I create the seasons," he saw this five-night rite;
he took it up and sacrificed with it.
From that, he indeed created the seasons;
he who, knowing thus, sacrifices with the five-night rite, is truly propagated.
Those seasons, once created, did not turn away from one another.
They saw this five-night rite;
they brought it and sacrificed with it.
Then indeed they turned away from him;
he who, knowing thus, sacrifices with the Pañcarātra, turns away from evil and from his rival.
Sārvaseni Śauceya desired [this].
Thinking, "May I possess cattle," he brought this five-night sacrifice and performed it with it.
Verily, he who, knowing thus, performs the Pañcarātra sacrifice obtains a thousand cattle; he indeed attains a thousand cattle. Babara Prāvāhaṇi desired [this].
"May I be a speaker of speech," [thinking thus], he performed this five-night rite.
He took it and sacrificed with it;
from that, he indeed became a speaker of speech.
He who, knowing thus, performs the sacrifice with five nights, becomes indeed a master of speech;
moreover, they call him "the Lord of Speech.
The four-night rite is incomplete, and the six-night rite is excessive; therefore, this five-night rite is the sacrifice that is perfectly proportioned.
He who, knowing thus, sacrifices with the Pañcarātra, truly sacrifices with the sacrifice;
it becomes a five-night rite,
for the year consists of five seasons.
Verily, he finds firm support in the seasons and in the year;
moreover, the *paṅkti* consists of five syllables, and the sacrifice is fivefold.
Verily, he wins the sacrifice;
it becomes a threefold Agniṣṭoma, and thus he wins brilliance.
It becomes fifteenfold;
thus he wins the sense-faculties.
It becomes seventeenfold.
It is for the attainment of food; moreover, one is propagated by means of it. The Agniṣṭoma becomes twenty-fivefold for the fulfillment of Prajāpati.
One who observes the great vows performs the Viśvajit Atirātra sacrifice with all the Pṛṣṭha-stotras for the attainment of food;
it serves for the conquest of everything.

7.1.11 Anuvāka 11: Recitation of the Mantras for the Aśvamedha Sacrifice I take you up at the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins and the hands of Pūṣan. The seers grasped this rein of Cosmic Order (ṛta) in the assemblies during former times. By means of it, the gods attained the pressed [Soma]; it is the flowing stream of the navel of Cosmic Order.

Thou art the designator; thou art the world; thou art the restrainer; thou art the supporter. Go thou to Agni Vaiśvānara, the far-extending, consecrated by *svāhā* upon the earth. Thou art the restrainer, the sovereign; thou art the restrainer, the controller; thou art the supporter, the sustainer. For agriculture thee! For security thee! For wealth thee! For prosperity thee! For the earth thee! For the intermediate space thee! For the sky thee! For the existent thee! For the non-existent thee! For the waters thee! For the plants thee! For all beings thee!

7.1.12 Anuvāka 12: Exposition of the Mantras for the Aśvamedha Sacrifice Vast through your mother, powerful through your father—you are a horse; you are a steed; you are a racer; you are a man; you are a courser; you are a prize-winner; you are a bull; you are one whose mind is directed toward men; your name is "The Swift"; follow the flight of the Ādityas! Svāhā to Agni! Svāhā to Indra and Agni! Svāhā to Prajāpati! Svāhā to the Viśvedevas! Svāhā to all the divine powers!

Here is steadfastness, Svāhā! Here is support, Svāhā! Here is delight, Svāhā! Here is enjoyment, Svāhā! You are the earth; for the past I offer you, for the present I offer you, for the future I offer you; for all beings I offer you. O gods, guardians of the quarters, protect this horse, consecrated for the sacrifice to the gods.
7.1.13 Anuvāka 13: Recitation of the Mantras for the Aśvamedha Sacrifice.
Hail to the coming! Hail to the departure!
Svāhā to the one who causes to run away!
Svāhā to the one who has run away!
Svāhā to the snorting one!
Hail to the one who has made the sound "śū! hail to the one who has fled;
hail to the one who has not fled!
Svāhā to him as he comes toward us! Svāhā to him as he goes away from us! Svāhā to him as he approaches!
To the one who exerts himself, svāhā!
To everything, svāhā!
7.1.14 Anuvāka 14: Exposition of the Mantras for the Aśvamedha Sacrifice.
To Agni, svāhā! To Soma, svāhā!
Svāhā to Vāyu!
Svāhā to the Delight of the Waters!
Svāhā to Savitṛ!
Svāhā to Sarasvatī!
Svāhā to Indra! Svāhā to Bṛhaspati!
Hail to Mitra!
Hail to Varuṇa!
Hail to the All!
7.1.15 Anuvāka 15: Recitation of the Mantras for the Aśvamedha Sacrifice To the earth, svāhā! To the intermediate space, svāhā!
Hail to the day! Hail to the sun! Hail to the moon!
Hail to the lunar mansions!
Hail to the eastern quarter!
Hail to the southern quarter!
Hail to the western quarter!
Hail to the northern quarter!
Hail to the upward quarter!
Svāhā to the quarters!
Svāhā to the intermediate quarters!
Svāhā to the years!
Svāhā to the autumns! Svāhā to the days and nights!
Svāhā to the half-months!
Svāhā to the months! Svāhā to the seasons! Svāhā to the year!
Svāhā to all!
7.1.16 Anuvāka 16: Recitation of the Mantras for the Aśvamedha Sacrifice.
To Agni, Svāhā! To Soma, Svāhā!
Svāhā to Savitṛ; svāhā to Sarasvatī; svāhā to Pūṣan.
Svāhā to Bṛhaspati!
Svāhā to Apām modā! Svāhā to Vāyu!
Svāhā to Mitra! Svāhā to Varuṇa!
Svāhā to the All!
7.1.17 Anuvāka 17: Recitation of the Aśvamedha Mantras To the earth, svāhā! To the intermediate space, svāhā!
To the day, svāhā!
To Agni, svāhā! To Soma, svāhā!
Svāhā to the Sun! Svāhā to the Moon!
Svāhā to the Day!
Hail to the Night!
Hail to the Upright! Hail to the Righteous!
Hail to good dwelling! Hail to hunger!
Hail to the act of eating!
Hail to disease! Hail to cold! Hail to chill!
To the heat, svāhā!
To the forest, svāhā!
To heaven, svāhā!
Svāhā to the world! Svāhā to everything!

7.1.18 Anuvāka 18: Exposition of the Mantras for the Aśvamedha Sacrifice "O Earth, you are the path of the gods through their ritual action; you are the path of the moving world. With the Vasus as deities, with the Gāyatrī metre, I yoke you; with the spring season, with the oblation, I consecrate you. With the Rudras as deities, with the Triṣṭubh metre, I yoke you; with the summer season, with the oblation, I consecrate you."

With the Ādityas as deities, with the gods, with the Jagatī metre, I yoke you; with the rains as the season, with the oblation, I consecrate you; with the Viśvedevas as deities, with the gods, with the Anuṣṭubh metre, I yoke you.

With the season of autumn, with the oblation, I consecrate you. With the Aṅgirases as deities, with the Pāṅkta metre, I yoke you. With the seasons of winter and the cool season, with the oblation, I consecrate you. I have ascended to consecration, the consort of Cosmic Order (Ṛta), with the Gāyatrī metre and with the sacred word (Brahman). I have established Cosmic Order in Truth; I have established Truth in Cosmic Order. To the great, well-protecting Earth—here is stability, Svāhā! Here is support, Svāhā! Here is delight, Svāhā! Here is rest, Svāhā!
7.1.19 Anuvāka 19: Exposition of the Mantras for the Aśvamedha Sacrifice. Svāhā to the sound *īm*;
svāhā to that which has been uttered as *īm*.
To the one who cries out, svāhā!
To the one who cries down, svāhā! To the one who snorts, svāhā!
To the snorting, svāhā! To the smell, svāhā!
To the one who smells, svāhā!
Svāhā to the out-breath!
Svāhā to the diffused breath! Svāhā to the in-breath!
Hail to him being bound! Hail to him bound!
Hail to him being loosened!
Hail to the one being torn apart! Hail to the one about to flee! Hail to the one who has fled!
He will cease, svāhā!
To him who has ceased, svāhā! He will enter, svāhā!
Hail to him as he is settling down! Hail to him as he has settled down! Hail to him as he is about to sit down!
Svāhā to him as he sits down; svāhā to him who has sat down; svāhā to him as he is about to sit.
Hail to him who is sitting! Hail to him who has sat down!
Hail to him who will lie down!
Hail to him as he is sitting down! Hail to him as he has sat down! Hail to him as he is about to lie down!
Hail to him who is lying down! Hail to him who has lain down! Hail to him who is about to close his eyes!

1. Svāhā to him who is closing his eyes; 2. Svāhā to him who has closed his eyes; 3. Svāhā to him who will sleep; 4. Svāhā to him who is sleeping; 5. Svāhā to him who has slept; 6. Svāhā to him who will wake up; 7. Svāhā to him who is waking up; 8. Svāhā to him who has woken up; 9. Svāhā to him who will become watchful; 10. Svāhā to him who is being watchful; 1. Svāhā to him who has become watchful; 2. Svāhā to him who is desiring to hear; 3. Svāhā to him who is hearing; 4. Svāhā to him who has heard; 5. Svāhā to him who will look; Svāhā to him who is looking; Svāhā to him who has looked.
To him as he is about to yawn, svāhā!
To him as he is yawning, svāhā!
To him as he has yawned, svāhā!
Hail to him who is about to turn; hail to him who is turning;
hail to him who has turned!
To him who is about to rise, svāhā!
To him who is rising, svāhā!
To him who has risen, svāhā!
To the one who shall shake off [evil], svāhā!
To the one who is shaking off, svāhā!
To the one who has shaken it off, svāhā!
To him who is about to ascend, svāhā! To him who is ascending, svāhā!
To him who has ascended, svāhā!
Svāhā to him who will walk; svāhā to him who is walking;
svāhā to him who has walked.
Svāhā to the one who will scratch;
svāhā to the one who is scratching; svāhā to the one who has scratched.
To the one who will be rubbed, svāhā!
To the one being rubbed, svāhā! To the one already rubbed, svāhā!
To that which he eats, svāhā; to that which he drinks, svāhā; to that which he urinates, svāhā.
To that which he makes into dung, svāhā!
To semen, svāhā! To offspring, svāhā!
Hail to procreation!
Hail to everything!

7.1.20 Anuvāka 20: Recitation of the Aśvamedha Mantras To Agni, Svāhā! To Vāyu, Svāhā! To Sūrya, Svāhā! You are the Cosmic Order (*ṛta*), you are the Order of the Order; you are Truth (*satya*), you are the Truth of Truth. You are the path of the Order, the shadow of the gods. That which is the name of the Order—that is Truth, that you are Prajāpati. As the beautiful ones vie for the prize upon this [chariot], so do the people vie with the Sun of heaven. Choosing the waters, the wise one flows, like a watchful herdsman guarding his cattle, he who moves all around.
7.2 Prapāṭhaka: 2, Anuvāka 1: The Description of the Six-Day Rite (Ṣaḍrātra).
The Sādhyas, the gods who desired heaven, perceived this six-day rite; they took it up.
With that they sacrificed; then indeed they went to the heavenly world.
Those who, knowing thus, perform the six-night rite, go to the heavenly world.
The six-night rite is indeed a sacrifice for the gods, for these *pṛṣṭha* chants are manifest.
Those who, knowing this, perform the six-night rite, directly ascend to the deities.
It is a six-night rite;
for there are six seasons and six *pṛṣṭha* chants.
By means of the *pṛṣṭha* chants they ascend after the seasons, and by means of the seasons they ascend after the year; they find firm support in the year itself,
and they proceed with the *Bṛhat* and *Rathantara* chants.
This [earth] indeed is the Rathantara, and yonder [sky] is the Bṛhat. By means of these two alone they proceed;
moreover, in these two alone they find firm support.
These indeed are the two direct paths of the sacrifice; by these very paths they go to the heavenly world.
The Agniṣṭoma becomes the Trivṛt.
They indeed obtain splendor;
it consists of fifteen [stotras],
and they thereby obtain sensory power.
It consists of seventeen [verses],
for the attainment of food.
Moreover, they are indeed propagated by means of it.
It consists of twenty-one [verses] for the sake of stability;
moreover, they place radiance within themselves.
There is a Triṇava [Stoma] for victory;
there is a Trayastriṃśa [Stoma] for stability.
Those who possess both the *sadas* and the *havirdhāna* sheds should sacrifice with this six-night rite.
The *havirdhāna* and the *āgnīdhra* shed are made of *aśvattha* wood, for that leads to heaven.
The sacrificial post has rings for the attainment of the heavenly world;
it has a mortar-base.
They go eastward for the sake of firm establishment, for heaven, as it were, lies in the east.
The world goes by means of Sarasvatī;
this indeed is the path leading to the gods.
They mount after him alone;
they go on crying out. Having fastened misfortune upon another, they attain a firm foundation.
When they perform ten hundred [stomas], then there is a single rising.
A man has a life-span of a hundred years and a hundred powers; thus they find firm standing in both life-span and power.
When they perform a hundred or a thousand [repetitions], it is a single rising. That world is measured by a thousand;
they thus conquer that very world.
If among them one should die, or if they should be defeated, then there is a single rising;
for that indeed is the sacred ford.
7.2.2 Anuvāka 2: The Description of the Seven-Night Rite.
Kusurubinda Auḍālaki desired, "May I be possessed of cattle."
He performed this seven-night sacrifice;
he sacrificed with it, and by means of it, he indeed obtained as many domestic animals as there were.

He who, knowing thus, sacrifices with the seven-night rite, wins as many domestic animals as there are; it consists of seven nights because there are seven domestic animals, seven wild animals, and seven meters.
The Agniṣṭoma is threefold for the attainment of both; it is brilliance.
Thus he wins it;
it consists of fifteen parts; verily, he wins sensory power.
It consists of seventeen [verses].
This is for the attainment of food;
moreover, by means of it, one is indeed procreated.
It becomes twenty-onefold for the sake of stability;
moreover, one bestows radiance upon oneself.
There is a Triṇava [Stoma] for victory;
there is a Pañcaviṃśa Agniṣṭoma for the attainment of Prajāpati.
One who observes the great vows performs the Viśvajit Atirātra sacrifice with all the Pṛṣṭha-stotras for the attainment of food;
it serves for the conquest of everything.

If they were to perform the *pṛṣṭha* chants directly on the preceding days, then the *viśvajit* would be performed directly; it would be like approaching a cow that has already been milked— thus the final day would be [useless],
and there would not even be a single night [of the sacrifice].
They approach the Bṛhat and Rathantara [Sāmans] on the preceding days;
this earth is indeed the Rathantara and yonder sky is the Bṛhat.
Thus they do not depart from these two, and moreover, they find firm support in them.
That they employ the *pṛṣṭha* chants in the Viśvajit sacrifice which are directly perceived is exactly like milking a cow that has already been milked.
7.2.3 Anuvāka 3: The Description of the Eight-Night Rite.
Bṛhaspati desired, "May I be possessed of spiritual luster."
He saw this eight-night rite; he took it up and sacrificed with it.
Thereupon he indeed became possessed of spiritual luster (*brahmavarcas*).
He who, knowing thus, sacrifices with the eight-night rite, becomes possessed of spiritual luster.
It consists of eight nights.
The Gāyatrī has eight syllables;
the Gāyatrī is spiritual luster.
By means of the Gāyatrī itself, one wins spiritual luster.
It lasts for eight nights.
There are four quarters and four intermediate quarters; verily, from the quarters he wins spiritual luster.
The Agniṣṭoma is threefold; verily, he wins brilliance. It is fifteenfold.
Verily, he wins the sense-faculties;
it consists of seventeen parts for the attainment of food;
moreover, by means of it, he is indeed propagated.
It consists of twenty-one [verses] for the sake of firm establishment;
moreover, he bestows radiance upon himself.
There is a Triṇava [stoma] for victory; there is a Trayastriṃśa [stoma].
The twenty-five-fold Agniṣṭoma is for stability; it possesses the Mahāvrata for the attainment of Prajāpati and for the acquisition of food.
The Viśvajit Atirātra sacrifice, characterized by all the Pṛṣṭha-stotras,
takes place for the sake of conquering everything.
7.2.4 Anuvāka 4: The Exposition of the Nine Nights. Prajāpati created offspring; once they were created, they fell into hunger.
He saw this nine-night rite;
he took it up and sacrificed with it.
Then indeed, it was prepared for the creatures;
whenever the creatures should fall into hunger, then one should sacrifice with the nine-night rite.
For these worlds were unprepared for them, and thus they fell into hunger.
He fashions these very worlds for them; as they are being fashioned, he fashions himself after them,
and they are fashioned.
Through this, he places vigor in these worlds and in offspring.
By means of the three-night rite, he prepares this world; by the three-night rite, the intermediate space; and by the three-night rite, yonder world.
Just as one strings a string upon a string, even so does he string world upon world for the sake of stability and to prevent looseness.
The *stomas* known as Jyotis, Gauḥ, and Āyus come into being.
This [earth] indeed is Jyotis, the intermediate space is Gauḥ, and yonder [sky] is Āyus.
In these very worlds they find firm support.
The knowledge of the people departs;
it becomes a nine-night [sacrifice].
He bestows radiance upon him in successive order;
he who has been long ill should sacrifice with the nine-night rite,
for his vital breaths have indeed become unsteady.
Now, if he suffers from a long-lasting illness, it is indeed his vital breaths that he sustains;
even if his life-force has departed, he yet lives.
7.2.5 Anuvāka 5: Exposition of the Ten-night Rite. Prajāpati desired, "May I procreate."
He saw this Daśahotṛ; he offered it, and by means of it, he created the ten-night sacrifice.
By means of that ten-night rite he was procreated;
one who is about to undergo initiation for the ten-night rite should offer the Daśahotṛ formula.
By means of the Daśahotṛ itself, he creates the ten-night rite.
By means of that ten-night rite one is procreated;
for this sacrifice which is the ten-night rite is indeed the Virāj.
He who, knowing thus, sacrifices with the ten-night rite, attains the Virāj itself.
This ten-night sacrifice belongs indeed to Prajāpati.
He who, knowing thus, sacrifices with the ten-night rite is indeed propagated.
Indra, indeed, was once equal to the other deities; he did not attain distinction.
He ran to Prajāpati;
he gave this ten-night rite to him,
and he took it.
With that he sacrificed; then indeed he attained distinction from other deities.
He who, knowing thus, sacrifices with the ten-night rite, attains distinction from his evil rival.
This ten-night sacrifice is indeed three-peaked: the fifteen-fold [stoma] is one peak, the twenty-one-fold is the central peak, and the thirty-three-fold is the other peak.
He who, knowing thus, sacrifices with the ten-night rite becomes a three-peaked mountain among his equals:
the sacrificer is the fifteen-fold one, the sacrificer is the twenty-one-fold one, the sacrificer is the thirty-three-fold one, while the others are the foothills.
One who is being practiced against by sorcery should sacrifice with the ten-night rite.
He piles [the altar] right upon the gods' city;
for him there is no affliction from any quarter, and the one practicing sorcery against him does not strike him down.
The gods and the asuras were arrayed for battle;
those gods saw these divine citadels, which are the ten-night rite.
They carried them around;
for them, there was no injury from any quarter whatsoever.
Thereupon the gods prospered and the asuras were defeated.
He who has rivals should sacrifice with the ten-night rite;
he thus encloses himself within divine fortresses,
and no affliction from any quarter shall befall him.
He prospers by himself, his rival is defeated;
the *stoma* becomes the underlayer for the *stoma*, and thus he makes his rival an underlayer.
Verily, they commit a repetition when, having approached a larger stoma, they approach a smaller one;
in that the Agniṣṭoma-sāmans occur both before and after, it is for the sake of avoiding repetition.
The Agniṣṭoma is a Trivṛt; it takes place with verses addressed to Agni in the Agniṣṭut, whereby he wins brilliance.
The Ukthya is a Pañcadaśa; it takes place with verses addressed to Indra.
Verily, he wins the sense-faculties;
with the threefold Agniṣṭoma on verses addressed to the Viśve Devas,
he wins nourishment.
The seventeenth [day] is the Agniṣṭoma with the Tīvrasoma offering for the Prājāpatya verses;
it is for the attainment of food,
and furthermore, by means of it, one is indeed procreated.
The Ukthya with twenty-one [stotras] is performed on verses addressed to Sūrya for the sake of stability;
thus he places radiance within himself.
The Agniṣṭoma with seventeen [stotras] is the Upahavya sacrifice, belonging to Prajāpati.
He indeed goes to the invitation; there are two Triṇava Agniṣṭomas on either side with verses addressed to Indra for the sake of victory.
The Trayastriṃśa Ukthya with the Vaiśvadeva verses is for the sake of stability; it becomes a Viśvajit Atirātra with all the Pṛṣṭha-stotras.
For the conquest of everything.
7.2.6 Anuvāka 6: The Exposition of the Eleven-Night Rite.
The Seasons, desiring offspring, did not find offspring;
they desired [it].
"May we create offspring; may we obtain offspring; may we find offspring; may we possess offspring"—thinking thus, they beheld this eleven-night rite and performed it.
With that they sacrificed; from that indeed they created offspring, they won offspring, they obtained offspring, they became possessed of offspring—
they became the seasons.
That is why they are called *ārtava*;
for these are indeed the sons of the seasons (*ṛtu*).
Therefore...
The Ārtava sacrifices are so called because those who, knowing thus, perform the eleven-night rite, create progeny, win progeny, obtain progeny, and become possessed of progeny;
it includes an Atirātra of light.
They place light in front for the illumination of the heavenly world;
there is a *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period.
There are six seasons and six *pṛṣṭha* chants; by means of the *pṛṣṭhas*, they ascend after the seasons, and by means of the seasons, after the year.
Thus, they find firm support in the year itself.
It consists of twenty-four [verses]; the Gāyatrī has twenty-four syllables, and the Gāyatra is spiritual luster.
Verily, they find firm support in the Gāyatrī for the sake of spiritual luster;
it consists of forty-four syllables,
for the Triṣṭubh has forty-four syllables.
The *indriya* [stoma] is the *triṣṭubh*;
verily, they find firm support in the *triṣṭubh*, in the *indriya*.
It consists of forty-eight [verses].
The Jagatī consists of forty-eight syllables;
cattle are of the Jagatī nature. Thus, they find firm support in the Jagatī, that is, in cattle.
It lasts for eleven nights;
there are five seasons and five seasonal periods.
Having established themselves in the seasons and the seasonal periods within the year, they obtain offspring.
There are Atirātra sacrifices on both sides for the sake of securing progeny.

7.2.7 Anuvāka 7: The Description of the Twelve-Day Rite (Dvādaśarātra) One who desires, "May offspring be arranged in their proper order," should draw the cups beginning with those for Indra and Vāyu.

Indeed, according to the arrangement of the sacrifice, offspring are arranged; according to the lack of arrangement of the sacrifice, they are not arranged. He arranges the offspring in their proper order; the younger does not overstep the elder.
One should draw the cups beginning with that for Indra and Vāyu for one who is ill; for he whose illness afflicts him is deprived of his vital breath (prāṇa),
and the cup for Indra and Vāyu is the vital breath.
He causes him to prosper by means of the vital breath itself.
Those whose consecrated companion dies should draw the cups beginning with that for Mitra and Varuṇa;
for those whose consecrated companion dies are deprived of both out-breath and in-breath.
Mitra and Varuṇa are the out-breath and the in-breath;
verily, they preserve the out-breath and the in-breath at the beginning.
One who is younger than his elder brother should draw the cups beginning with those for the Aśvins.
The Aśvins were indeed the youngest of the gods; like cattle, they went around to the front.
The Aśvins belong to this deity for one who is younger than his elder brother; they alone lead him to the front.
One who has lost his fortune but desires stability should draw the first portions of the *śukra*.
Yonder sun is indeed the *śukra*, and he is within [the vessel]; man reaches the end by means of the end.
Having gone for the sake of prosperity, he returns;
from end to end he grasps,
and he does not become worse off because of it.
One practicing exorcism should take the foremost *manthin* cups; for this *manthin* cup is a vessel of affliction—
it causes him to be seized by death itself.
He quickly incurs misfortune. One whose father and grandfather were virtuous, yet who does not attain that [status], should draw the cups beginning with the Āgrayaṇa.
He whose father and grandfather were virtuous is indeed deprived of speech and of sensory power.
But if he does not obtain it, then [he fails].
The Āgrayaṇa is like the breast of the sacrifice, like speech.
By means of speech itself, he causes him to prosper with power.
He does not become worse because of that.
One who is being subjected to malevolent magic should draw the Ukthya cups first;
for the Ukthya cup is the sensory power of all the vessels.
He impels him with his entire vital power (*indriya*). He should use "O Sarasvatī, lead us toward what is better" as the *puroruc*.
Speech, indeed, is...
By means of Sarasvatī, he impels him with speech itself.
"May we not go from you to alien fields," he says;
for the fields of death are indeed alien.
By that very [means], one does not go to the fields of death;
one should seize the full planets. For him who is ill, the pain reaches his vital breaths.
The vital breaths are the seizers;
he releases his very breaths from distress.
Even if his life-force has departed, he indeed lives.
One should draw the full cups when Parjanya does not rain;
for at that time, pain reaches the vital breaths of creatures when Parjanya does not rain,
and the vital breaths are the cups.
He releases the breaths of living beings from their afflictions and swiftly sends down rain.
7.2.8 Anuvāka 8: Exposition of the Twelve-Night Rite.
The cup for Indra and Vāyu is indeed of the Gāyatrī metre;
the introductory day is of the Gāyatrī metre.
Therefore, on the Prāyaṇīya day, the cup for Indra and Vāyu is drawn;
he draws it in its own proper place,
for the Śukra cup is indeed of the Triṣṭubh metre.
The second day belongs to the Triṣṭubh;
therefore, on the second day the Śukra cup is drawn,
for he draws it in its own proper abode.
The Āgrayaṇa cup belongs to the Jagatī metre;
the third day is of the Jagatī metre.
Therefore, the Āgrayaṇa is drawn on the third day.
He seizes him in his very own abode.
Indeed,
one reaches the sacrifice when one reaches the meters.
When the Āgrayaṇa is drawn on the following day, he joins that sacrifice again from the very point where they first beheld it;
for the second three-night period has the Jagatī as its opening,
and the Āgrayaṇa is of the nature of the Jagatī.
In that the Āgrayaṇa is drawn on the fourth day, he draws it in its own proper abode;
moreover, they turn back toward their own respective meters, for the cup for Indra and Vāyu is connected with the Rathantara.
The fifth day belongs to the Rathaṃtara;
therefore, on the fifth day, the draught for Indra and Vāyu is drawn.
He takes him in his own abode;
for the *śukra* cup belongs to the *bṛhatī*,
and the sixth day belongs to the *bṛhatī*.
Therefore, on the sixth day, the Śukra cup is drawn;
he draws it in its own proper abode.
Indeed, this is the second sacrifice one encounters when one attains the metres.
Because the *śukra* cup is drawn on the following day, he joins that very sacrifice again from the very point where they first beheld it;
for the third three-night period has the *triṣṭubh* as its opening and is of *traiṣṭubha* nature.
The Śukra: in that the Śukra is drawn on the seventh day, he draws it in its own abode;
moreover, they turn back according to their own metre.
The Āgrayaṇa is indeed speech;
the eighth day is speech.
Therefore, on the eighth day, the Āgrayaṇa is drawn.
He takes it in its own abode;
for the cup for Indra and Vāyu is the breath, and the ninth day is the breath.
Therefore, on the ninth day the cup for Indra and Vāyu is drawn; he draws it in its own proper place.
This is so.
Verily, he reaches the third sacrifice when he obtains the meters;
since the cup for Indra and Vāyu is drawn on the following day, he joins the sacrifice again from the very point where they first beheld it. Moreover, they return to their own respective meters.
Those who proceed by another [path] than the Aindravāyava cup go astray from the path;
for this tenth day is indeed the interior of the sacrifice,
and on the tenth day the Aindravāyava is drawn.
Having indeed reached the end of the sacrifice, they go from one path to another; moreover,
it is just as when they carry back the offering with a more ample vehicle.
The *chandases* (metres) meditated upon one another's world;
the gods separated them by means of this very [rite]. This fourth day is indeed the station of the *aindravāyava* cup.
In that [cup] the Āgrayaṇa is drawn;
therefore, on the ninth day, the Aindravāyava is drawn in the place of the Āgrayaṇa,
for that which is the fifth [cup] is indeed the place of the Śukra.
On that day, the draught for Indra and Vāyu is drawn;
therefore, on the seventh day, the Śukra draught is drawn in the place of the draught for Indra and Vāyu.
The sixth day is indeed the proper place for the Āgrayaṇa;
on that day the Śukra cup is drawn. Therefore, on the eighth day, which is the proper place of the Śukra, the Āgrayaṇa is drawn.
Verily, he causes the meters to intermingle; he who knows thus attains an ever more excellent intermingling. Moreover, he establishes concord among the deities at the sacrifice.
Therefore, this one gives it to the other.
7.2.9 Anuvāka 9: The Exposition of the Twelve-Night Rite.
Prajāpati desired, "May I be propagated."
He saw this twelve-night rite; he took it up and sacrificed with it.
From that indeed he was procreated;
he who should desire, "May I be procreated," [should do so].
He should sacrifice with the twelve-night rite;
he is indeed procreated.
The exponents of sacred knowledge say:
The Agniṣṭoma sacrifices have the Agniṣṭoma as their beginning; now, why is the Atirātra employed first?
These two Atirātras are indeed the eyes of the sacrifice, and the two Agniṣṭomas are the pupils.
If they were to perform the Agniṣṭoma first, they would place the pupils outside;
therefore, the Atirātra is performed first.
Having thus established the two eyes in the sacrifice, they place the pupils in their proper positions in the middle.
He who knows the Gāyatrī with light as its wings goes to the heavenly world by means of light and splendor; those two Agniṣṭomas are the wings,
and the eight Ukthyas that are between them constitute the body.
This Gāyatrī indeed has light for its wings;
he who knows thus goes to the heavenly world with light and radiance.
This twelve-night rite is indeed Prajāpati divided twelvefold:
the two Atirātras are the two wings,
and the eight Ukthyas in between are the body.
This [sacrifice] is indeed Prajāpati; being real (sat), he truly rescues (spṛṇoti) by means of the sacrificial session (sattram).
The vital breaths (prāṇāḥ) are indeed the real; verily, he rescues the vital breaths.
Indeed, those who sit for a sacrificial session (sattra) subsist on the vital breaths of all these creatures;
therefore, people ask,
"Are these men performers of a sattra?"
He who knows thus becomes beloved by his subjects and rises to eminence.
7.2.10 Anuvāka 10: The Exposition of the Twelve-Night Sacrifice (Dvādaśarātra) Verily, this [Agni Vaiśvānara], being otherwise, was not capable of reaching the heavenly world.
Indeed, he was stretched out upwards.
Those gods drew this Vaiśvānara around for the attainment of the world of heaven.
Indeed, the seasons caused Prajāpati to sacrifice with this; he prospered among them, and so did it.
He indeed prospers among the officiating priests who, knowing thus, performs the twelve-day sacrifice;
they desired him,
and he bestowed essence upon the spring.
Barley for the summer, herbs for the rainy season, rice for the autumn, and beans and sesame for the winter and cool seasons—
with that, Prajāpati caused Indra to sacrifice;
from that, indeed, Indra became Indra.
Therefore they say,
"The sacrifice of one who is younger," for he indeed sacrificed with this first.
He who accepts a gift at a *sattra* sacrifice indeed eats a corpse— either a human corpse, a horse corpse, or food as a cow.
From that vessel with which they carry food, if he does not wash it clean, [he partakes of that].
Impurity arises.
One alone should sacrifice;
for Prajāpati alone attained prosperity.
One should be consecrated for twelve nights;
twelve months are a year,
and the year is Prajāpati.
This [sacrifice] is indeed Prajāpati;
he truly comes into being who is born from austerity.
These twelve Upasad nights are fourfold, consisting of three sets of three nights each.
With those which are first, he brings together the sacrifice;
with those which are second, he undertakes the sacrifice;
with those which are third, he cleanses the vessels.
With those which are the fourth [offerings], he purifies himself internally;
for whoever eats his animal, he eats its flesh; whoever eats the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), he eats its brain.
That which is the outer husk is the feces;
that which is the clarified butter is the marrow;
that which is the Soma is the sweat.
Indeed, he who accepts gifts at the twelve-day sacrifice (dvādaśāha) receives even the secret excretions from the head;
therefore, one should not officiate for another at the twelve-day sacrifice, for the sake of warding off evil.
7.2.11 Anuvāka 11: Recitation of the Mantras for the Aśvamedha Sacrifice. Svāhā to one; svāhā to two.
Svāhā to three; svāhā to four; svāhā to five.
Hail to the six!
Hail to the seven!
Hail to the eight!
Hail to the nine!
Hail to the ten!
Hail to the eleven!
Svāhā to twelve! Svāhā to thirteen! Svāhā to fourteen!
Hail to fifteen!
Hail to sixteen!
Hail to seventeen!
Hail to eighteen!
Hail to nineteen! Hail to twenty-nine!
Svāhā to thirty-nine! Svāhā to forty-nine!
Svāhā to fifty-nine!

7.3 Prapāṭhaka: 3, Anuvāka 1. Explanation of the specific details remaining from the previously mentioned twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*).
"By means of this tenth day, they indeed go with speed;
by means of this tenth day, they become free from evil."
He who indeed takes a wrong path when others are traveling straight, he who strikes a stump, or he who falls into error—he is defeated.
He who is struck down on the tenth day, the *avivākya*, is defeated;
but he who speaks for that one who has been struck down, by taking hold of him, attains success.
Now, he who speaks out is defeated;
therefore, on the tenth day, the Avivākya, one should not speak to one who has been struck down.
Now, moreover, they say:
"By the success of the sacrifice, the gods went to the heavenly world; by the failure of the sacrifice, they brought about the destruction of the Asuras.
Indeed, whatever part of the sacrifice is successful belongs to the sacrificer, and whatever part is unsuccessful belongs to his rival.
If one is struck down on the tenth day, which is the *avivākya*, he indeed causes an excess; those who are outsiders, the *dṛśīkas*, should deliberate upon this.
If they do not find [the verses] there, they should recite them from within the assembly;
that indeed is the recitation. Or rather, they praise with the verses of the Queen of Serpents (Sarparājñī).
This [earth] is indeed the Queen of Serpents (sarparājñī);
whatever they have praised in her or whatever they have praised beyond her, by that she is the Queen of Serpents— whatever they have praised with speech, and whatever they shall praise hereafter.
"Having attained and secured both of these, let us rise up"—
with these words they praise with the mind;
for neither a horse-chariot nor a mule-chariot is able to traverse this earth in a single day.
The mind alone is able to encompass this [Brahman] instantly; it is the mind that one must master when they speak of Brahman.
For the *ṛg*-verses are limited, the *sāman*-chants are limited, and the *yajus*-formulas are limited; but of this Brahman, there is no end.
He should announce that to the one who responds;
that is the response.
Anuvāka 2: Exposition of the Ahīna Twelve-Day Sacrifice.
The exponents of sacred knowledge say:
"Does the sacrificer, by means of the first day of the twelve-day sacrifice, choose for himself the officiating priests?"
If it is said that "the sense-faculty is splendor," what is the purpose of the second [syllable]?
It is for the sake of the vital breaths and food.
"What is the purpose of the third? "These three worlds.
"What is the purpose of the fourth?"
Regarding "four-footed cattle," why [is it said] "with the fifth"?
It is because the *paṅkti* consists of five syllables.
"What is the use of the sixth?
"The six seasons.
"What is the use of the seventh?"
"If it is the *śakvarī* consisting of seven feet, what then of the eighth?
[He replied: "It is the *gāyatrī* consisting of eight syllables."
"What by the ninth?
"The *trivṛt* hymn-form.
"What by the tenth?"
Regarding the statement "the ten-syllabled *virāj*," why is it not [called] the eleven-syllabled?
It is the eleven-syllabled *triṣṭubh*.
"What is the use of the twelfth?
[He replied: "The Jagatī has twelve syllables.
"Indeed, there is only as much as this."
Whatever exists, that he takes away from them.
7.3.3 Anuvāka 3: The Description of the Thirteen-Night Rite.
This thirteen-night rite is indeed the perfected twelve-day rite;
for that day which is the introductory day is identical to that which is the concluding day.
There is a Tryatirātra; these are the three worlds;
it is for the attainment of these worlds.

The first *atirātra* is indeed the *prāṇa*, the second is the *vyāna*, and the third is the *apāna*. They find firm support in the *prāṇa*, *apāna*, and *udāna*, and they attain a full lifespan—those who, knowing thus, perform the thirteen-night rite.
Regarding this, they say:

This twelve-day rite is indeed speech stretched out; if they were to place an *atirātra* in the middle, they would cut that speech asunder, and the speech of the householder would be liable to perish.
They perform the Mahāvrata after the Chandomas; thus he secures speech that is continuous, and the speech of the householder becomes free from failure.
The Chandomas are indeed cattle, and the Mahāvrata is food.
In that they perform the Mahāvrata after the Chandomas, they find firm support both in cattle and in the enjoyment of food.
7.3.4 Anuvāka 4: The Description of the Fourteen-Night Sacrifice. The Ādityas desired:
"May we prosper in both worlds."
They saw this fourteen-night rite; they took it up and sacrificed with it.
Thereby indeed those who,
knowing thus, perform the fourteen-night rite prosper in both worlds, both in this one and in yonder one;
the rite consists of fourteen nights.
There are seven cultivated plants and seven wild plants; for the attainment of both kinds, the *pṛṣṭha* chants are performed in a forward direction;
by means of them, they conquer that very world yonder.
In that the *pṛṣṭha* stotras are performed in reverse order, they conquer this very world by means of them.
There are two *triṇava* stomas in the middle; they attain sovereign rule (*sāmrājya*). They are *adhirāja* stomas; they become *adhirāja*s among their equals.
There are Atirātra rites on both sides for the sake of complete enclosure.
7.3.5 Anuvāka 5: Another Account of the Fourteen-Night Rite.
Prajāpati went to the heavenly world;
the gods followed after him.
The Ādityas and the cattle followed after them;
those gods said,
"Those very cattle upon which we have depended for our livelihood have come after us."
For them, they prepared this fourteen-night rite.

Those Ādityas ascended to the heavenly world by means of the *pṛṣṭha* chants; by means of two three-day periods (*tryaha*), they secured cattle in this world. By the *pṛṣṭha* chants the Ādityas prospered in yonder world, and by the two three-day periods, in this one.
In this world there are cattle.
Those who, knowing thus, perform the fourteen-night sacrifice, prosper in both worlds—both in this one and in that one.
By means of the *pṛṣṭha* chants they prosper in that world; by means of the two three-day periods they prosper in this world.
The three-day rite consists of Jyotis, Gauḥ, and Āyus;
for this world is indeed Jyotis, the intermediate space is Gauḥ, and yonder world is Āyus.
Thus they ascend these very worlds.
If the back-ribs were on one side, there would be a separation;
the back-ribs are in the middle for the sake of non-separation.
The *pṛṣṭha* chants are indeed vigor and strength;
they place vigor and strength in the very middle by means of the *bṛhat* and *rathaṃtara*.
They proceed with the *bṛhat* and *rathaṃtara*.
This [earth] indeed is the Rathantara, and yonder [sky] is the Bṛhat.
By means of these two they proceed;
moreover, they find firm support in these two.
These indeed are the two direct paths of the sacrifice;
by them alone they go to the heavenly world. Those who perform the *pṛṣṭha* chants in a forward direction are, as it were, ascending to the heavenly world from behind.
The three-day period is reversed for the sake of descending again and for stability;
having prospered in both worlds, they stand firm.
These [days] are fourteen.
