Of these, those which are ten consist of ten syllables; the *virāj* is food, and by means of the *virāj*, they obtain food.
Those which are four are the four quarters; thus they find firm support in the quarters.
There are *atirātra* rites on both sides for the sake of complete enclosure.
7.3.6 Anuvāka 6: The Exposition of the Fifteen-Night Rite.
Indra was indeed equal to the other deities; he did not attain distinction.
He ran to Prajāpati;
he gave this fifteen-night rite to him,
and he performed it.
With that he sacrificed; then indeed he attained distinction from the other deities.
Those who, knowing thus, perform the fifteen-night rite, attain distinction from evil and from their rival.
The three-day period consists of Jyotis, Gauḥ, and Āyus;
this earth indeed is Jyotis, the intermediate space is Gauḥ, and yonder sky is Āyus.
They find firm support in these very worlds. That which is without the Chandomas is indeed not a sacrificial session (*sattra*);
in that the Chandomas are performed, it thereby becomes a sacrificial session.
By means of the *pṛṣṭha* chants they win the deities; by means of the *chandomas* they win cattle.
They find firm support in strength, in heroism, and in cattle.
There is a fifteen-night rite.
The fifteenth day is the vajra;
they strike the vajra at their rivals.
There are Atirātra rites on both sides.
For the sake of the mastery of the sense faculty.
7.3.7 Anuvāka 7: Explanation of the Second Fifteen-Night Rite.
Indra, indeed, was as if loose and without support; he was afraid of the Asuras.
He ran to Prajāpati;
he gave him this fifteen-night sacrifice as a thunderbolt.
With it, having overcome and conquered the Asuras, he attained prosperity.
By means of the Agniṣṭut, he burned away evil; by means of the fifteen-night rite, he placed vigor, strength, sensory power, and heroism within himself.
Those who, knowing thus, perform the fifteen-night rite, having utterly defeated their rivals and conquered, attain prosperity.
By means of the Agniṣṭut, they burn away evil.
They burn away [impurities] during fifteen nights; they place vigor, strength, sensory power, and heroism within themselves.
These very [days] are favorable to cattle, for there are fifteen nights in a half-month.
The year is obtained by means of half-months;
cattle are born following the year; therefore, it is conducive to cattle.
These very fifteen nights of the half-month are heavenly;
by means of the half-months, the year is attained.
The year is the world of heaven;
therefore, they lead to heaven.
There is a three-day period consisting of Jyotis, Gauḥ, and Āyus.
This [earth] indeed is the light, the intermediate space is the cow, and yonder [sky] is life;
they thus ascend these very worlds.
If the *pṛṣṭha* stotras were elsewhere, there would be a separation;
they are in the middle for the sake of continuity. The *pṛṣṭhas* are indeed vigor and strength.
They place vigor and strength in the middle;
they proceed with the Bṛhat and Rathantara [Sāmans].
This earth is indeed the Rathantara, and yonder sky is the Bṛhat.
By these two alone they go;
moreover, in these two alone they find firm support.
These indeed are the two direct paths of the sacrifice.
By means of those two alone they go to the heavenly world;
for those who employ the *pṛṣṭha* chants in a forward direction indeed ascend to the heavenly world in a forward direction.
The three-day period is directed backward for the sake of descending again and for stability;
having prospered in both worlds, they stand firm—
these are fifteen [days].
Of those [verses], those which consist of ten syllables each are the *virāj*; the *virāj* is food; thus, by means of the *virāj*, they obtain food.
Those which consist of five each are the quarters; thus, they find firm support in the quarters.
There are *atirātra* sacrifices on both sides.
For the grasping of the senses, of vigor, of progeny, and of cattle.
7.3.8 Anuvāka 8: Exposition of the Seventeen-Night Sacrifice.
Prajāpati desired:
"May I be an eater of food."
He saw this seventeen-night rite; he took it up and sacrificed with it.
From that, indeed, he became an eater of food;
those who, knowing thus, perform the seventeen-night rite, become eaters of food.
There is a five-day period.
Or the year consists of five seasons;
they find firm support in the seasons, that is, in the year.
Moreover, the *paṅkti* meter has five syllables.
The sacrifice is fivefold;
they thus obtain the sacrifice itself.
This, indeed, is not a sacrificial session (asattra).
That which is without the *chandomas*—in that they perform the *chandomas*, it becomes a *sattra*.
By means of the *pṛṣṭhas*, they win the deities; by means of the *chandomas*, they win cattle.
They find firm support in vigor, in heroism, and in cattle;
there is a seventeen-night rite, for Prajāpati is seventeenfold.
For the attainment of Prajāpati;
there are Atirātra rites on both sides for the securing of food.
7.3.9 Anuvāka 9: The Description of the Twenty-Night Sacrifice.
That Virāj, having stepped forth, stood among the gods by means of the sacred word (*brahman*) and among the Asuras by means of food (*anna*).
Those gods desired: [to become superior].
"May we win both: the sacred word and food.
They saw these twenty nights;
then indeed they won both—the sacred word and food—and they became possessed of spiritual luster and eaters of food.
Those who, knowing thus, sit for these [days], win both: the sacred word (brahman) and food. They become radiant with the splendor of the sacred word and eaters of food.
For these two are indeed Virāṭ verses.
They find support separately in those two alone;
for man consists of twenty parts: ten fingers of the hands and ten toes of the feet.
Having obtained the man in his full extent, they emerge.
The *jyotis*, *go*, and *āyus* are three-day periods.
This world indeed is the *jyotis*, the intermediate space is the *go*, and yonder world is the *āyus*.
Thus they ascend these very worlds.
The three-day periods come in ascending order;
indeed, they ascend to the heavenly world in ascending order.
That the *pṛṣṭha* stotras which follow from another [set] become the middle *pṛṣṭhas* is for the sake of continuity.
The *pṛṣṭha* chants are indeed vital force and vigor;
they place vital force and vigor in the very middle by means of the *bṛhat* and *rathantara*. They proceed with these two.
This [earth] indeed is the Rathantara, and yonder [sky] is the Bṛhat.
By means of these two they proceed;
moreover, in these two they find firm support.
These indeed are the two direct paths of the sacrifice;
by them alone they go to the world of heaven.
Those who perform the *pṛṣṭha* chants in a forward direction are, as it were, ascending to the world of heaven with their faces turned away.
The three-day period is reversed for the sake of descending again and for stability;
having prospered in both worlds, they stand firm.
There are Atirātra rites on both sides.
For the complete grasping of spiritual luster and the eating of food.
7.3.10 Anuvāka 10: The Description of the Twenty-one Night Rite.
Yonder sun was in this world;
the gods, having enclosed it with the *pṛṣṭha* chants, caused it to go to the heavenly world.
With the *parastobha* chants they enclosed it from below; with the *divākīrtya* chant they established it in the world of heaven.
With the *para* chants they enclosed it from above; with the *pṛṣṭha* chants they descended.
Indeed, that sun in yonder world is enclosed on both sides by the *para* chants.
In that there are *pṛṣṭha* chants, by them the sacrificers go to the heavenly world;
with the subsequent ones they enclose it from below, and with the *divākīrtya* chant they find firm footing in the heavenly world.
They enclose [the fire] from behind with the backs [of their hands], and they descend [to the earth] from above;
for if there were no [enclosure] beyond from behind, they would fall away from the heavenly worlds while facing away; and if there were none below, they would consume the offspring.
The Paraḥsāman chants are on both sides of the Divākīrtya;
thus they enclose it on both sides in the heavenly world.
The Divākīrtya, indeed, is the sacrificers themselves.
The *paraḥsāman* chants are the year;
they are on both sides of the *divākīrtya*,
for the year is on both sides.
They find firm support:
the *divākīrtya* is indeed the back, and the *paraḥsāman*s are the two sides;
the *paraḥsāman*s are on both sides of the *divākīrtya*.
Therefore, on both sides and at the back,
the largest vessels are drawn;
it is most highly praised [to do so].
They tie a knot in the middle of the sacrifice itself to prevent it from slipping;
seven [cups] are drawn, for there are indeed seven vital breaths in the head.
Verily, they bestow the vital breaths upon the sacrificers;
in that the *pṛṣṭha* chants are performed in a forward direction, they ascend to that world,
but not to this world.
The sacrificers might descend back, or they might become intoxicated, or they might perish, if the *pṛṣṭha* chants were performed facing westward;
by means of these [chants], they descend back to this very world.
Thus, they find firm support in this very world, so as not to go mad.
Indra, indeed, was without support;
he ran to Prajāpati for help.
He gave this twenty-one-night rite to him; he took it and sacrificed with it.
From that, indeed, he established himself.
Those who are frequent sacrificers but lack a firm foundation should perform the twenty-one-night sacrifice.
There are twelve months, five seasons, these three worlds, and yonder sun as the twenty-first.
So many indeed are the worlds of the gods;
in them they find firm support, each in its proper order.
That Āditya did not shine;
he ran to Prajāpati,
and he gave him this twenty-one-night sacrifice.
He brought it; with it he sacrificed; then indeed he shone forth.
Those who, knowing thus, perform the twenty-one-night sacrifice, truly shine.
There is a twenty-one-night sacrifice;
the twenty-first is indeed splendor.
Verily, they go to brilliance and also to a firm foundation,
for the twenty-one-fold [stoma] is a firm foundation.
There are two Atirātra rites on both sides for the securing of spiritual luster.

7.3.11 Anuvāka 11: Recitation of Mantras Pertaining to the Aśvamedha Sacrifice May the sacrifice pass over to me from that [enemy], he who is the domestic priest (*purohita*) of the seers (*ṛṣi*). Having rendered him godless and heroless, let the *viṣkandha* (the wasting disease) be cast upon him who hates us; let the impurity of the sacrifice and his debt sink into the body of him who hates us. O Sacrifice, with that splendor which belongs to the sacrifice, come over to me! I invoke the Brahmins, the officiating priests, and the gods of the sacrifice by means of this fervor; may you be satisfied by what is offered and cooked.
I summon you with the *svāhā*! I gather for you the well-performed rite, as well as offspring and cattle.

I gather for you the *praisha*s, the *sāmidhenī* verses, the two *āghāra* libations, the two *ājyabhāga* portions, the *āśruta*, and the *pratyāśruta*. I gather for you the *prayāja*s and *anuyāja*s, the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, the *iḍā*, and the blessings; I gather the light of heaven. With Agni, Indra, Soma, Sarasvatī, Viṣṇu, and the deities—with the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses—I summon you with the *svāhā*; I take hold of your sacrifice, your *vaṣaṭ*-utterance, the hymn, the recitation, the response, the cup, the *iḍā*, and the blessings.
I turn toward heaven; I call upon you for the Patnīsaṃyāja offerings. With the Svāhā-call, I take for myself your Samiṣṭayajus.

I invoke for you the animals, the pressed soma, the sacrificial cakes, the libations, and indeed the sacrifice itself—the gods together with Indra, those who have Agni as their mouth and Soma as their portion, and all others.
7.3.12 Anuvāka 12: Recitation of the Mantras Pertaining to the Aśvamedha Sacrifice That which has been, that which is, and that which will be—vaṣaṭ, svāhā, namaḥ!
The Ṛg, Sāman, and Yajus—vaṣaṭ, svāhā, namaḥ!
Gāyatrī, Triṣṭubh, Jagatī; Vaṣaṭ, Svāhā, Namaḥ!
Earth, Atmosphere, Heaven; Vaṣaṭ, Svāhā, Namaḥ! Agni, Vāyu, Sūrya; Vaṣaṭ, Svāhā, Namaḥ!
Prāṇa, vyāna, apāna—vaṣaṭ! Svāhā! Reverence!
Food, agriculture, rain—vaṣaṭ! Svāhā! Reverence! Father, son, grandson—vaṣaṭ! Svāhā! Reverence!
Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ vaṣaṭ svāhā namaḥ.

7.3.13 Anuvāka 13: Recitation of the Mantras Pertaining to the Aśvamedha Sacrifice May my house prosper; may my progeny prosper; may the heroic sacrifice enter me. May the divine, worshipful waters enter me; may the abundance of a thousandfold [prosperity] not forsake me. May my *graha* (libation) be present; may the *puroruc* and the *stotra-śastra* (hymns and recitations) enter me together. May the Ādityas, Rudras, and Vasus be my fellow-sacrificers in the assembly; may the abundance of a thousandfold [prosperity] not forsake me. May the *agniṣṭoma* enter me; may the *ukthya*, the *atirātra*, and the *apiśarvara* enter me.
May the well-offered oblations of the day before enter me; may the abundance of the thousandfold not forsake me.
7.3.14 Anuvāka 14: Exposition of the Mantras Pertaining to the Aśvamedha.
By means of fire, austerity was attained;
by means of speech, the Brahman.
Through the jewel, [he wins] forms;
through Indra, the gods; through Vāta, the vital breaths.
By means of the sun, [he attains] the sky;
by means of the moon, the constellations; by means of Yama, the ancestors.
A king [should not take] men who cannot be won over by rewards,
nor snakes from a python.
With a tiger [he subdues] wild beasts;
with a hawk, birds; with a stallion, horses.
With a bull, the cows; with a goat, the goats; with a ram, the ewes.
Through rice, [he obtains] grains; through barley, medicinal herbs; through the Nyagrodha tree, forest trees.
From the udumbara tree, vigor;
from the gāyatrī meter, the meters;
from the trivṛt stoma, the stomas.
Or by a Brahmin, [he utters] speech.
7.3.15 Anuvāka 15: Recitation of the Mantras Pertaining to the Aśvamedha Sacrifice.
Svāhā to the resolve, to that which is resolved;
svāhā to the resolved, to the mind; svāhā to the mind.
Svāhā to Prajāpati!
Svāhā to Ka!
Svāhā to Kasmai!
To whom [is it] svāhā?
To Aditi svāhā! To Great Aditi svāhā!
Svāhā to Aditi the benevolent; svāhā to Sarasvatī;
svāhā to Sarasvatī the Great.
Svāhā to Sarasvatī the Purifier; svāhā to Pūṣan;
svāhā to Pūṣan the Guardian of Paths.
Svāhā to Pūṣan, the protector of men; svāhā to Tvaṣṭṛ;
svāhā to Tvaṣṭṛ, the bestower of seed.
Svāhā to Tvaṣṭṛ of many forms! Svāhā to Viṣṇu! Svāhā to Viṣṇu, the protector of the furrows! Svāhā!
To Viṣṇu, the protector from invisibility, svāhā!
7.3.16 Anuvāka 16: Recitation of the Mantras pertaining to the Aśvamedha Sacrifice.
Svāhā to the teeth;
svāhā to the jaws.
Svāhā to the two lips;
svāhā to the mouth; svāhā to the two nostrils.
Svāhā to the two eyes! Svāhā to the two ears!
Svāhā to the eyelashes that look outward and those that look inward!
Hail to the eyelashes of the near side for the sake of the eyelashes of the far side; hail to the head;
hail to the two eyebrows.
Svāhā to the forehead! Svāhā to the head! Svāhā to the brain!
Hail to the hair! Hail to the neck! Hail to the vertebrae! Hail!
Svāhā to the shoulders! Svāhā to the ribs!
Svāhā to the vertebrae!
Svāhā to the belly;
svāhā to the two sides; svāhā to the two shoulders.
To the two arms, svāhā!
To the two forearms, svāhā! To the two shanks, svāhā!
Hail to the hips! Hail to the thighs! Hail to the knees!
To the two shanks, svāhā! To the ashes, svāhā!
To the tufts of hair, svāhā!
To the tail, svāhā!
To the testicles, svāhā! To the penis, svāhā!
Hail to the seed! Hail to the offspring! Hail to procreation!
Hail to the feet!
Hail to the hooves!
Hail to the hair!
Hail to the skin! Hail to the blood! Hail to the flesh!
Hail to the sinews!
Hail to the bones!
Hail to the marrow!
Svāhā to the limbs!
Svāhā to the self!
Svāhā to the whole!
7.3.17 Anuvāka 17: Recitation of the Mantras Pertaining to the Aśvamedha Sacrifice.
Hail to the one with anointed forehead!
Hail to the one with anointed thighs!
Svāhā to the white-footed one!
Svāhā to the white-humped one! Svāhā to the white-orificed one!
Hail to the white-backed one! Hail to the white-shouldered one!
Hail to the flower-eared one!
Hail to the one with white lips! Hail to the one with a white brow!
Hail to the one who sits upon what is white!
Hail to the white, shining one!
Hail to the ointment!
Hail to the spotted one!
Svāhā to the one with dark knees; svāhā to the one with black-spotted [skin]; svāhā to the one with red-spotted [skin].
Hail to the ruddy-white one!
Hail to the such-like one! Hail to the what-like one!
Svāhā to such a one; svāhā to a similar one; svāhā to a dissimilar one.
Hail to the well-formed!
Hail to beauty!
Hail to everything!
7.3.18 Anuvāka 18: Recitation of the Mantras Pertaining to the Aśvamedha Sacrifice. To the black one, Svāhā!
To the white one, Svāhā!
Hail to the tawny one!
Hail to the dappled one!
Hail to the ruddy one!
Hail to Gaura! Hail to Babhru!
Hail to Nakula!
Hail to the ruddy one! Hail to the crimson one! Hail to the dark-brown one!
Hail to Śyāma! Hail to Pākala! Hail to Surūpa!
Svāhā to the one who is conformable; svāhā to the one who is deformed; svāhā to the one who is uniform.
Svāhā to Pratirūpa, svāhā to Śabala, svāhā to Kamala.
Hail to Pṛśni!
Hail to Pṛśnisaktha!
Hail to the All!
7.3.19 Anuvāka 19: Recitation of the Mantras pertaining to the Aśvamedha Sacrifice.
To the plants, Svāhā!
To the roots, Svāhā!
Hail to the tufts! Hail to the stalks! Hail to the shoots!
Svāhā to the flowers! Svāhā to the fruits!
Svāhā to those that have been gathered!
Hail to those who have not been seized!
Hail to those who have fallen away!
Hail to those who are lying down!
Hail to all!
7.3.20 Anuvāka 20: Recitation of the Mantras pertaining to the Aśvamedha Sacrifice.
Svāhā to the lords of the forest; svāhā to their roots.
Hail to the tufts! Hail to the trunks! Hail to the branches!
Hail to the leaves! Hail to the flowers! Hail to the fruits!
Svāhā to those that have been taken up! Svāhā to those that have not been taken up!
Svāhā to those that have fallen away!
Hail to those who lie down!
Hail to the remainder!
Hail to the over-remainder!
Svāhā to the remnant; svāhā to that which has been gathered together; svāhā to the leavings.
Hail to the empty!
Hail to the not-empty!
Hail to the overflowing!
To the emptied one, svāhā!
To the overflowing one, svāhā! To everything, svāhā!
Prapāṭhaka 7.4, Anuvāka 1: Exposition of the First Caturviṃśarātra Sacrifice.
Bṛhaspati desired: "May the gods grant me their ear; may I attain the office of domestic priest."
He saw this twenty-four-night rite; he took it up and sacrificed with it.
Then indeed, the gods granted faith to him; he attained the office of domestic priest.
Those who, knowing thus, perform the twenty-four-night rite—for them men grant faith, and they attain the office of domestic priest.
There are three-day periods consisting of Jyotis, Go, and Āyus.
This [earth] indeed is Jyotis, the intermediate space is Gauḥ, and yonder [heaven] is Āyus.
They thus ascend these very worlds.
The Tryahas occur in successive order.
They ascend to the heavenly world in regular succession.
That which is without the *chandomas* is not a *sattra*;
in that the *chandomas* are performed, it becomes a *sattra*.
By means of the *pṛṣṭha* chants they win the deities, and by means of the *chandomas* they win cattle;
for the *pṛṣṭhas* are indeed vigor and heroism, and the *chandomas* are cattle.
Thus, they find firm support in vigor, in heroism, and in cattle.
They proceed with the Bṛhat and the Rathantara;
this [earth] is indeed the Rathantara and that [sky] is the Bṛhat;
it is by means of these two alone.
They go [by these],
and furthermore, they find firm support in these very two;
for these are indeed the straight paths of the sacrifice.
By means of these two alone they go to the heavenly world;
there is a twenty-four-night rite,
for the year consists of twenty-four half-months.
The year is the world of heaven;
they find firm support in the world of heaven, which is the year.
Moreover, the Gāyatrī consists of twenty-four syllables.
The Gāyatrī is spiritual luster.
By means of the Gāyatrī itself, they obtain spiritual luster.
There are Atirātra rites on both sides.
For the securing of spiritual luster.
7.4.2 Anuvāka 2: Second Exposition on the Caturviṃśarātra Sacrifice.
Just as humans were, so indeed were the gods in the beginning; they desired.
"Having struck away misfortune, evil, and death, may we go to the assembly of the gods"—
thinking thus, they saw this twenty-four-night rite and performed it.
With that they sacrificed; then indeed, having struck away misfortune, evil, and death, they went to the assembly of the gods.
Those who, knowing thus, perform the twenty-four-night rite, having likewise struck away misfortune and evil, attain prosperity.
For prosperity is indeed the divine assembly of man;
it becomes the Jyotir Atirātra.
The Pṛṣṭhya Ṣaḍaha is for the manifestation of the heavenly world;
for there are six seasons in a year.
Having entered it, the months, the half-months, and the seasons went to the divine assembly;
those who, knowing thus, perform the twenty-four-night rite, having entered the year itself, go to a more excellent assembly.
There are three [sets] of thirty-three below, and three [sets] of thirty-three above.
By means of the Trayastrimsha stomas alone, they drive away misfortune and evil from both sides and proceed to the divine assembly in the middle;
for the Prishtha-stotras are indeed the divine assembly.
They indeed commit a repetition when three sets of thirty-three [stotras] follow one after another. The central [day] is undefined (anirukta); thereby it is not a repetition.
The Pṛṣṭha-stotras are ascending, and the Chandomas are ascending.
By means of both forms they go to the heavenly world.
That which is without the *chandomas* is indeed not a sacrificial session (*sattra*);
in that the *chandomas* are performed, it becomes a sacrificial session.
By means of the *pṛṣṭha* chants they win the deities, and by means of the *chandomas* they win cattle;
for the *pṛṣṭhas* are indeed vigor and strength, and the *chandomas* are cattle.
They find firm support in vital force, in heroism, and in cattle.
There are three sets of thirty-three [stomas] below, three sets of thirty-three above, and the *pṛṣṭha* chants in the middle.
The thirty-three are indeed the chest, and the *pṛṣṭhas* are the self.
The sacrificers bind that very armor upon themselves for protection from injury;
they proceed with the Bṛhat and the Rathantara.
This earth is indeed the Rathantara, and yonder sky is the Bṛhat.
By these two alone they go;
moreover, they find firm support in these two.
These indeed are the straight paths of the sacrifice.
By means of those two alone they go to the heavenly world;
for those who employ the *pṛṣṭha* chants in a forward direction indeed ascend to the heavenly world in a forward direction.
The six-day period is directed backward for the sake of descending again and also for stability;
having prospered in both worlds, they stand firm.
From the *trivṛt* they proceed to the *trivṛt*, for the attainment and mastery of the *stomas*.
The Agniṣṭoma is a light; this indeed is that dwelling-place. By means of it, they do not depart from this very dwelling-place.
It consists of twenty-four nights;
there are twenty-four half-months in a year,
and the year is the world of heaven.
They find firm support in the world of heaven for a year;
moreover, the Gāyatrī consists of twenty-four syllables,
and the Gāyatrī is spiritual luster (brahmavarcasa).
By means of the Gāyatrī itself, they obtain spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*).
There are Atirātra rites on both sides,
for the sake of encompassing spiritual luster.
7.4.3 Anuvāka 3: Exposition of the Thirty-Night Rite.
This earth was indeed hairless;
she desired.
"May I be propagated by means of herbs and trees"— thinking thus, she beheld these thirty nights;
from that, indeed, this [earth] was propagated by means of herbs and trees.
Those who desire offspring and cattle should perform these [rites]; they are indeed procreated with offspring and cattle.
This earth, indeed, was hungry.
He saw that Virāj; having placed her within himself, he obtained food-eating, as well as plants,
trees, offspring, and cattle.
By that he grew;
he attained preeminence and greatness.
Those who, knowing thus, sit upon these [bricks], having placed the Virāj within themselves, obtain food.
They increase in progeny and cattle;
they attain victory and greatness.
The Atirātra becomes the light for the manifestation of the heavenly world.
There is a Pṛṣṭhya Ṣaḍaha; for there are six seasons and six Pṛṣṭhas; by means of the Pṛṣṭhas they ascend the seasons, and by means of the seasons, the year.
They find firm support in the year itself; they proceed from one set of thirty-three to another set of thirty-three for the continuity of the sacrifice.
Now, Prajāpati is indeed the thirty-threefold; they take hold of Prajāpati himself for stability. There is a twenty-sevenfold [stoma] for victory. There is a twenty-onefold [stoma] for stability.
Moreover, they place radiance within themselves.
The Agniṣṭut sacrifice consists of the Trivṛt stoma;
by it they burn away evil. Furthermore, the Trivṛt is indeed splendor; they place splendor within themselves.
There is a fifteen-fold Stoma for Indra;
they thus obtain power itself.
It consists of seventeen [verses],
for the attainment of food;
moreover, by means of it they are indeed propagated.
It becomes twenty-onefold for the sake of firm foundation;
moreover, they place radiance within themselves.
It becomes twenty-four; there are twenty-four half-months in a year,
and the year is the world of heaven.
They find firm support in the heavenly world for a year.
Moreover, this [day] is indeed the Viṣūvān;
they become possessed of the Viṣūvān who, knowing thus, perform these [rites].
They proceed with the twenty-four *pṛṣṭha* chants, having established themselves upon the year itself as their foundation.
The deities ascend;
from the thirty-three they go unto the thirty-three,
for there are indeed thirty-three deities.
They find firm support in the deities themselves;
there is a twenty-sevenfold [stoma],
for these worlds are indeed the twenty-sevenfold.
They find firm support in these very worlds;
there are two sets of twenty-one [stomas] for the sake of stability.
Moreover, they place radiance within themselves;
there are many *ṣoḍaśin* cups, therefore among offspring there are many males.
Because these *stomas* are interwoven, therefore this earth is interwoven with herbs and trees;
those who, knowing thus, perform these [rites], become interwoven with offspring and cattle.
Otherwise, these [stomas] go to the heavenly world unprepared;
for they approach various high and low stomas. Since these stomas are upright and prepared, they go to the heavenly world prepared; thus it is made fit for them in both worlds.
These are thirty;
the Virāj consists of thirty syllables, and the Virāj is food.
By means of the Virāj they obtain food;
there are Atirātra rites on both sides for the sake of securing food.
7.4.4 Anuvāka 4: The Designation of the Thirty-Two-Night Rite.
Prajāpati went to the heavenly world;
the gods, however, did not reach it by means of whichever metre they employed.
They saw these thirty-two nights;
the Anuṣṭubh consists of thirty-two syllables,
and Prajāpati is of the nature of the Anuṣṭubh.
Having reached Prajāpati by means of their own meters and having ascended, they went to the heavenly world; those who, knowing thus, perform these [days], there are thirty-two of them.
The Anuṣṭubh consists of thirty-two syllables.
The *anuṣṭubh* is Prajāpati;
having attained Prajāpati by means of its own meter, they attain prosperity.
For prosperity is the heavenly world for a human being.
These are thirty-two;
speech is the *anuṣṭubh*, for the *anuṣṭubh* consists of thirty-two syllables.
They attain every speech;
they all become speakers of speech;
for indeed, they all go to prosperity.
The *jyotis*, *go*, and *āyus* constitute three-day periods (*tryaha*).
This world is indeed the *jyotis*, the intermediate space is the *go*, and yonder world is the *āyus*; thus they ascend these very worlds in succession.
These three-day periods occur in forward order.
They ascend to the heavenly world in due order;
they proceed with the Bṛhat and the Rathantara.
This [earth] is indeed the Rathantara, and that [heaven] is the Bṛhat.
By these two alone they go;
moreover, they find firm support in these two.
These indeed are the direct paths of the sacrifice.
By means of these two alone they go to the heavenly world.

Those who undertake three-day periods in forward succession indeed ascend to the heavenly world in a forward direction; there is a three-day period in reverse order for the sake of descending back down and also for the sake of stability.
Having prospered in both worlds, they stand firm;
these [bricks] are thirty-two.
Of these, those which are thirty are the Virāj of thirty syllables; the Virāj is food, and by means of the Virāj, they obtain food.
Those two days and nights—by means of both these forms they go to the heavenly world;
there are Atirātra rites on both sides for the sake of complete enclosure.
7.4.5 Anuvāka 5: The Description of the Thirty-three-Day Rite There are indeed two sacrificial sessions for the gods: the twelve-day rite and the thirty-three-day rite.
Those who, knowing this, perform the thirty-three-day rite, directly ascend to the very deities.
Just as one who has ascended to a superior position acts according to his desires, so it is:
if he pierces [the target], he becomes worse;
if he does not pierce it, he remains equal.
Those who, knowing thus, sit for thirty-three days, turn away from evil and from their rival. For these gods were the first to take possession of the day;
one took possession of the day, another took possession of the day.
By means of them, they indeed prospered in all directions.
Those who, knowing thus, perform the Trayastriṃśadaha for thirty-three days, all indeed prosper together and all attain the status of village leaders;
there are five five-day periods.
Or the year consists of five seasons;
they find firm support in the seasons, that is, in the year.
Moreover, the *paṅkti* meter has five syllables.
The sacrifice is fivefold;
they thus obtain the sacrifice itself.
There are three offerings for the Aśvins.
There are these three worlds;
in these very worlds they find their support.
Moreover, there are indeed three powers of the sacrifice; these they obtain.
There is a Viśvajit [offering] for the attainment of food.
It stands at the back of everything for the sake of conquering everything; the twelve-day rite is indeed speech.

If they were to enter upon the twelve-day rite beforehand, they would approach speech that is unattained; their speech would be liable to fail. They enter upon it after the twelve-day rite; thus they approach speech that is already attained. Therefore, we speak with speech from above.
[The intermediate...]
By means of the ten-night rite, Prajāpati created offspring; in that there is a ten-night rite, the sacrificers thereby create offspring.
Udanka Śaulbāyana declared this to be the prosperity of the sacrificial session: namely, the ten-night rite.
That there is a ten-night period is for the sake of completing the sacrificial session (*sattra*);
furthermore, it serves as the pacification of whatever was done incorrectly during the preceding days.
These nights constitute two opposing ranks; the *viśvajit* is the sacrificer.
The first sixteen days are together with an *atirātra* on either side; the latter sixteen days are together with an *atirātra* on either side.
For those who, knowing thus, perform the thirty-three-day rite, their offspring are born in two ranks.
There are *atirātras* on both sides.
For the sake of grasping.
7.4.6 Anuvāka 6: The Description of the Thirty-Six Night Rite. The Ādityas desired, "May we go to the heavenly world."
They did not know the world of heaven, nor did they go to the world of heaven;
they saw this thirty-six-night rite and performed it.
With that they sacrificed; thereby indeed they discerned the world of heaven and went to the world of heaven.
Those who, knowing thus, perform the thirty-six-night rite, discern the world of heaven and go to the world of heaven.
The Atirātra sacrifice is the light;
they thus place light in front.
The six-day periods exist for the manifestation of the heavenly world; for there are six seasons.
They find firm support in the seasons;
there are four [of them], for there are four directions.
They find firm support in the very quarters. That which lacks the *chandomas* is indeed not a *sattra*; in that the *chandomas* are performed, it becomes a *sattra*.
By means of the *pṛṣṭha* chants they win the deities, and by means of the *chandomas* they win cattle;
for the *pṛṣṭhas* are indeed vigor and heroism, while the *chandomas* are cattle. Thus, they find themselves in vigor itself.
They establish themselves in vigor;
the rite consists of thirty-six nights,
for the Bṛhatī meter has thirty-six syllables.
The cattle belong to the Bṛhatī;
by means of the Bṛhatī itself, they win cattle;
the Bṛhatī attained sovereignty among the meters.
Those who, knowing thus, perform the thirty-six-night rite, attain self-sovereignty; they go indeed to the heavenly world.
There are Atirātra rites on both sides for the securing of the heavenly world.
7.4.7 Anuvāka 7: The Exposition of the Forty-nine Night Rite.
Vasiṣṭha, whose sons had been slain, desired:
"May I obtain offspring; may I prevail over the Saudāsas."
He saw this forty-ninth [offering];
he took it and sacrificed with it.
Thereupon he indeed found offspring and surpassed the Saudāsas.
Those who, knowing thus, perform the forty-nine-fold [sacrifice], find offspring and surpass their rivals.
There are three Agniṣṭomas consisting of the Trivṛt-stoma.
They sharpen the very face of the vajra;
there are ten and fifteen,
and the fifteenth is the vajra.
They hurl the thunderbolt itself at their rivals;
the tenth day is possessed of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup; they thus bestow the thunderbolt as vigor.
There are twelve and seventeen;
this is for the attainment of food. Moreover, by means of them, they are indeed propagated.
There is a Pṛṣṭhya Ṣaḍaha; for there are six seasons and six Pṛṣṭha-stotras.
By means of the *pṛṣṭha* chants they ascend after the seasons, and by means of the seasons they ascend after the year; thus they find firm support in the year itself.
There are twelve *ekaviṃśa* stomas.
For stability; and thus they place radiance within themselves.
There are many *ṣoḍaśin* cups for the sake of victory;
there are six *āśvina* cups.
There are six seasons;
they find firm support in the seasons.
These nights are indeed deficient or redundant.
In that there are not fifty for one [verse], they are deficient; in that there are more than forty-eight, they are redundant.
From both the deficient and the redundant, indeed, Prajāpati was born.
Those who desire offspring and desire cattle should employ these [verses].
They are indeed procreated with offspring and cattle.
This sacrifice consisting of forty-nine [verses] belongs to Virāj.
Those who, knowing thus, perform the forty-nine-fold [rite], attain Virāj and become eaters of food.
There are Atirātra sacrifices on both sides;
this is for the sake of securing food.

7.4.8 Anuvāka 8: The Time for Initiation into the Year-long Sattra Sacrifice. Those intending to undergo initiation for the year-long sacrifice (*saṃvatsara-sattra*) should undergo initiation on the Ekāṣṭakā day. For this Ekāṣṭakā is indeed the wife of the year.
On this very night, he dwells within her;
thus they undergo initiation by directly grasping the year itself.
Those who undergo initiation on the Ekāṣṭakā day indeed initiate themselves against the afflicted part of the year; for those two seasons become the "End-named" ones.
Those who undergo consecration on the Ekāṣṭakā day undergo it by setting aside parts of the year; they fall upon two seasons named "End.
They should undergo consecration on the full moon of Phalgunī, for that is indeed the beginning.
The full moon of Phalguna is the beginning of the year; having thus commenced the year at its very mouth, they undergo initiation,
and its single exit occurs when the Viṣuvant day coincides with the Sākamedha sacrifice.
They should undergo initiation on the full moon of Citrā;
for the full moon of Citrā is indeed the mouth of the year.
Thus, they undertake initiation by beginning the year from its very mouth.
For him there is no departure whatsoever;
they should undergo initiation four days before the full moon,
for them the purchase of the Soma falls on the Ekāṣṭakā.
Therefore, they do not perform the Ekāṣṭakā rite in vain;
for them,
the Soma-pressing falls during the bright fortnight.
The months join together with the fortnights of the waxing moon; they rise up with the fortnights of the waxing moon,
and as they rise up, the plants and the trees rise up after them.
Auspicious fame follows after them:
"These sacrificers have succeeded," and accordingly, everyone prospers.
7.4.9 Anuvāka 9: Discourse on the Dīkṣā and Upasad Initiations Those who enter upon a sacrificial session (sattra) go indeed to the heavenly world.
They kindle themselves with the Dīkṣās and cook themselves with the Upasads.
With two [verses] they shave the hair; with two, the skin;
with two, the blood;
with two, the flesh.
With two [verses] he offers for the bone,
with two for the marrow; indeed,
this sacrificial session has the self as its sacrificial fee.
Having offered themselves as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), they go to the heavenly world;
they shave their topknots for the sake of prosperity.
"Moreover, being more vigorous, may we go to the heavenly world."
7.4.10 Anuvāka 10: The designation of the first day called the Prāyaṇīya.
The exponents of sacred knowledge (brahmavādinaḥ) say:
"The Atirātra is the highest of the sacrificial rites (yajñakratu); why do they perform it first?"
Indeed, they first enter upon the Agniṣṭoma, then the Ukthya, then the Ṣoḍaśin, and then the Atirātra;
thus, having entered upon these sacrificial rites in their proper order, having taken hold of them and encompassed them, they sit drinking the Soma itself.
They enter upon the Jyotiṣṭoma first.
The Jyotiṣṭoma is indeed the mouth of the Stomas;
verily, they employ the Stomas from the very mouth.
When the verses have been fully recited, they amount to the Virāj;
two *ṛc*s remain in excess:
by one the Gāyatrī is in excess, and by one the Āyuṣmatī is deficient.
The heavenly world is indeed light, vigor, and the Virāj; by this [sāman], they go to the heavenly world itself.
"The Rathantara is for the day, the Rathantara is for the night," so say the exponents of sacred knowledge (brahmavādinaḥ). "By what means is there non-repetition (ajāmi) in that? [They reply:
the Saubhara is the Brahmasāman at the third pressing, and the Bṛhat [is used].
They place it in the middle for the sake of separation;
thereby it is not a repetition.
7.4.11 Anuvāka 11: The Statement of the Days within the Month.
They perform the Jyotiṣṭoma first;
by means of it, they find firm footing in this very world.
They undertake the Goṣṭoma as the second; by it they find firm support in the intermediate space. They undertake the Āyuṣṭoma as the third.
In that very world they find firm standing.
This [earth] indeed is the light; the intermediate space is the cow;
yonder [sky] is life.

In that they perform these Stomas, the performers of the sacrificial session proceed while finding firm support in these very worlds; when they have been chanted together, they culminate in the Virāj.
Two *carcā*s are left over:
by one the *gāyatrī* is in excess, and by one the *anuṣṭubh* is deficient.
The world of heaven is indeed light; the *virāj* is vigor. Verily, they win vigor.
They do not suffer from the pain of hunger;
they become free from hunger, for those engaged in sacrificial sessions (sattrins) are as if oppressed by hunger.
The two Agniṣṭomas on either side are the two fellies, the Ukthyas in the middle are the nave;
that is this revolving wheel of the gods.
In that they proceed by means of this six-day rite, they indeed ascend the wheel of the gods for safety;
they attain well-being.
They proceed by means of a six-day period; for there are six seasons; they thus find firm support in the seasons.
They proceed with the Ubhayatojyotis [Sāman];
thus they proceed while firmly establishing themselves on both sides in the heavenly world.
There are two six-day periods.
These amount to twelve days.
Man indeed consists of twelve parts: two thighs, two arms, the trunk, and the head; four limbs, and the two breasts as the twelfth.
Thus they revolve around the person.
There are three six-day periods;
these amount to eighteen days,
nine of one kind and nine of another.
There are indeed nine vital breaths in a person;
thus they turn around following the vital breaths.
There are four six-day periods.
Those amount to twenty-four days;
there are twenty-four half-months in a year;
thus they revolve in accordance with the year.
"Indeed, they say that the year is without foundation, for it is greater than a foundation. The Brāhmaṇa of the year is indeed as much as a month;
thus, establishing themselves month by month, they proceed.

7.4.12 Anuvāka 12: Statement of the Mantras for the Limbs of the Aśvamedha Sacrifice May the ram protect you with cooked offerings; may the red-necked goat [protect you] with goats; may the *śalmali* tree [protect you] with growth; the *parṇa* tree with sacred knowledge (*brahman*); the *plakṣa* tree with wisdom (*medha*); the *nyagrodha* tree with cups (*camasa*); the *udumbara* tree with strength (*ūrj*); the *gāyatrī* with meters (*chandas*); and the *trivṛt* with hymns (*stoma*). You are the protectors; may the protectors protect you. You are the beloved of the beloved; we invoke you, the most excellent among the dear, the lord of treasures among treasures—O Vasu, mine!
7.4.13 Anuvāka 13: Recitation of the Mantras for the Limbs of the Aśvamedha Sacrifice.
Svāhā to the waters of the wells;
svāhā to the waters of the riverbanks.
Hail to those that are dug out! Hail to those that are scooped out! Hail to those that are excavated! Hail!
Hail to the waters of the pools!
Hail to the waters of the wells!
Hail to the waters of the lakes!
Hail to the waters of the Vaiśantī lakes! Hail to the waters of the pools!
Hail to the waters of the rain!
Hail to the non-raining ones,
hail to the hailstones,
hail to the dappled ones!
Hail to the flowing ones! Hail to the stationary ones! Hail to those of the rivers! Hail!
Hail to those from Sindh! Hail to those from the ocean! Hail to all!
7.4.14 Anuvāka 14: Recitation of the Mantras for the Aśvamedha Ritual.
Svāhā to the waters;
svāhā to the flowing waters.
Svāhā to those flowing around; svāhā to those flowing all about;
svāhā to those flowing swiftly!
Svāhā to those carrying swiftly!
Svāhā to those carrying fiercely! Svāhā to those carrying dreadfully!
Svāhā to the waters! Svāhā to the skies!
Svāhā to the great realms!
Hail to all!

7.4.15 Anuvāka 15: Recitation of the Mantras for the Aśvamedha Sacrifice He who seeks to strike down the courser—him Varuṇa strikes down; further off is the mortal, further off the dog. O slayer of Vṛtra, both I and you have come together for the sake of gains. Even the ill-disposed, O wielder of the stone, shall acknowledge us, O Hero; auspicious are the gifts of Indra. O Indra, you have surpassed all in wisdom upon the earth; the mid-worlds cannot contain your greatness. For with your own power you slew Vṛtra; no enemy has found the limit of your might in battle.
7.4.16 Anuvāka 16: Exposition of the Mantras Constituting Parts of the Aśvamedha Sacrifice. Homage to the King; homage to Varuṇa.
Homage to the horse;
homage to Prajāpati; homage to the sovereign lord.
He is the sovereign; do not make him the sovereign; may I become the sovereign of creatures; place him in me, place me in myself.
Svāhā to the one brought near;
svāhā to the one seized;
svāhā to the one offered as an oblation.

7.4.17 Anuvāka 17: Recitation of the Mantras for the Aśvamedha Sacrifice May the wind blow pleasantly upon the cows; may they graze upon herbs rich in nourishment. May they drink from waters abundant in fatness, which bring prosperity to living beings. O Rudra, be gracious to our four-footed cattle! O Parjanya, grant great protection to those cows who are uniform, diverse, or of a single form, whose names Agni knows through sacrifice, and whom the Aṅgirases produced here through their ascetic heat. Those who have offered their bodies among the gods, and whose every form Soma knows—may they swell for us with milk, O Indra, bringing us progeny.
Bestow them upon the cow-pen!

Prajāpati, bestowing these upon me, in harmony with all the gods and the ancestors, has brought them into our cow-pen as auspicious and true ones. May we abide together with their progeny. Here is stability, svāhā! Here is support, svāhā! Here is delight, svāhā! Here is pleasure, svāhā! [And] the great, well-protecting... (Ṛgveda 10.63.10).

7.4.18 Anuvāka 18: Recitation of the Mantras Constituting Parts of the Aśvamedha Sacrifice What was the first thought? What was the great bird? What was Piśaṅgilā? What was Pilippilā? The sky was the first thought; the horse was the great bird; the night was Piśaṅgilā; the sheep was Pilippilā. Who indeed wanders alone? Who indeed is born again? What is the remedy for cold? What is the great vessel? The sun wanders alone.

The moon is born again; fire is the remedy for cold; the earth is the great vessel for sowing. I ask you about the furthest limit of the earth; I ask you about the navel of the world. I ask you about the seed of the stallion; I ask you about the highest heaven of speech. They call the altar the furthest limit of the earth; they call the sacrifice the navel of the world. They call Soma the seed of the stallion; the Brahman is indeed the highest heaven of speech.

7.4.19 Anuvāka 19: Recitation of the Mantras for the Horse Sacrifice (Aśvamedha) “O Mother! O Ambālī! O Ambikā! No one leads me away. The little horse sleeps. O fortunate one, dweller of Kāmpīla, in the heavenly world, may you two cover me together. I have become a bearer of the embryo; you too have become a bearer of the embryo. May we two together stretch out our four feet. May the bull, the bestower of seed, bestow seed upon you both. Place a support between your thighs; anoint the joint, follow the anointing. He who is the consumer of women while they live, he who belongs to them...”
He who cleanses the beehives; he who is lovely even to women, and who has struck away their dark mark with a blow.

"O Mother, O little mother, O dear mother! No one at all excites my desire. My little horse sleeps. Raise her up like a load of bamboo upon a mountain; then let her waist swell, like one purifying herself in the cold wind. "O Mother, O little mother, O dear mother! No one at all excites my desire. My little horse sleeps. When the doe eats barley, she does not consider the fodder nourishing; when the *śūdrā* woman has a noble lover, she does not care for nourishment or wealth.

O Ambā, O Ambālī, O Ambikā! No one at all desires me. The little horse sleeps; this little bird that crawls about saying "Ahala" has struck the womb; the little creature gurgles within the belly. O Ambā, O Ambālī, O Ambikā! No one at all desires me. The little horse sleeps. Both your mother and your father climb to the top of the tree.

Your father stretched out his fist toward the womb, saying, "I shall impel you. I have celebrated Dadhikrāvan, the victorious, the spirited steed. May he make our mouths fragrant; may he prolong our lives.

O Waters, you are indeed the sources of bliss; grant us strength so that we may behold great joy. Grant us a share here of that most auspicious essence of yours, like longing mothers. We come to you for that [essence] for whose dwelling you quicken us; O Waters, give us life.

7.4.20 Anuvāka 20: Recitation of the Mantras for the Horse Sacrifice (Aśvamedha) Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ! May the Vasus anoint you with the Gāyatrī metre; may the Rudras anoint you with the Triṣṭubh metre; may the Ādityas anoint you with the Jagatī metre. Since the wind has gone to the waters, the beloved body of Indra—O singer, by this path bring back to us this horse! Lājīñ chācīñ yaśo mamā3m! (The parcher and the scatterer: my glory!)

For the sake of barley and for the sake of cattle—O Gods, eat this food; O Prajāpati, eat this food! They harness the ruddy, bright one as he moves about those who stand still; the luminaries shine in the sky. They harness his two beloved bay horses to the chariot, on opposite sides—the two red, bold steeds that carry the hero. Creating a signal for the signal-less, a form for the formless, O men—you were born together with the dawns.
7.4.21 Anuvāka 21: Recitation of the mantras belonging to the Aśvamedha sacrifice. *Svāhā* to the out-breath (*prāṇa*).
Hail to the diffused breath!
Hail to the downward breath!
Hail to the sinews!
Hail to the continuities! Hail to the surrounding continuities!
Hail to the joints!
Hail to the joints! Hail to the bodies!
Hail to the sacrifice!
Hail to the sacrificial fees! Hail to the heavenly world! Hail to the world! Hail!
Hail to all!
7.4.22 Anuvāka 22: Recitation of the Mantras Constituting Parts of the Aśvamedha Sacrifice. To the white one, svāhā! To the black one, svāhā!
To the one addressed, svāhā!
To the one not addressed, svāhā! To the one joined, svāhā!
Hail to the unyoked! Hail to the well-yoked!
Hail to the one who has exerted himself!
Svāhā to the liberated one! Svāhā to the completely liberated one!
Svāhā to the one who deceives!
To the one who deceives, svāhā! To the one who deceives completely, svāhā!
To the one who deceives after, svāhā!
To him who rises up, svāhā!
To him who goes, svāhā! To him who runs, svāhā!
To him who stands, svāhā!
To everything, svāhā!
Prapāṭhaka 7.5: Anuvāka 1. The Description of the Saṃvatsara-sattra.
Cows indeed performed this sacrificial session (sattra) with the desire: "Though we are hornless, may horns grow for us."
They remained seated for ten months; then their horns grew, and they stood up, saying,
"We have succeeded!"
Then those whose [calves] were not born stood waiting for a year.
Those whose [calves] were born and those whose were not— both these groups stood up, saying, "We have succeeded!"
"We have succeeded," they said;
for the Gosattra is indeed the year.
Those who, knowing thus, undertake the year-long rite, indeed prosper; therefore, even a hornless cow grazes during the two months of the rainy season,
for she has already achieved victory through that sacrificial session.
Therefore, whatever is performed in the house of one who sits for a year-long session (*saṃvatsarasad*) is performed as something attained, secured, and conquered.
Those who undertake the year-long session float away upon the ocean;
indeed, he who does not see the further shore of the ocean does not emerge from it.
The year is indeed the ocean;
its further shore is these two Atirātra rites.
Those who, knowing thus, undertake the year-long rite, go to the highest goal unharmed.
This [earth] indeed is the first Atirātra, and yonder [heaven] is the latter;
the mind is the first, and speech is the latter.
The out-breath is the first, the in-breath is the latter;
the former is the obstruction, the latter is the rising.
The Jyotiṣṭoma Vaiśvānara Atirātra takes place.
They place light in front for the illumination of the world of heaven;
the opening sacrifice consists of twenty-four [verses].
Twenty-four half-months make a year; indeed,
they find firm support in the year as it proceeds.
It has three hundred and sixty stotriya verses;
there are as many nights in the year.
Thus they attain both forms of the year.
Having established themselves for safety, they proceed with the subsequent days;
there are six-day periods, for the year consists of six seasons.
Verily, they find firm support in the seasons and in the year;
the *go* and the *āyus* chants as *stomas* are placed in the middle,
for that constitutes a productive pair in the very midst of the year.
They bear light for the sake of procreation; it comes into being on all sides.
That is indeed liberation;
the *chandasyas* themselves attain that liberation.
Moreover, by means of the six-day rite (*ṣaḍaha*) which has light on both sides, they go to the heavenly world.
The exponents of Brahman say:
"By what do they proceed? One should reply: "By the path of the gods."
The meters are indeed the path leading to the gods: the Gāyatrī, the Triṣṭubh, and the Jagatī.
The Gāyatrī is light, the Triṣṭubh is the cow, and the Jagatī is life; when these Stomas are employed, [the sacrificer gains] these very things.
They go by that very path which is the way of the gods;
the Sāman remains the same.
The Sāman is indeed the world of the gods;
thus they do not depart from the world of the gods.
The *ṛc*s become one after another.
The *ṛc*s belong to the world of men;
thus, ascending from the world of men to one divine world after another, they proceed.
The *abhivarta* becomes the *brahmasāman*.
It serves for the attainment of the heavenly world;
it is the Abhijit,
for the conquest of the heavenly world.
There is the Viśvajit sacrifice for the conquest of all; they perform the Pṛṣṭha-lauds month by month,
and the Atigrāhya cups are drawn month by month.
Month by month indeed they bestow vigor for the stability of the months;
after the months, they proceed with the *pṛṣṭha* chants.
Therefore, above that, the plants bear fruit.
7.5.2 Anuvāka 2: An Exposition of the Alternative Performance of the Saṃvatsara-sattra by Means of a Ten-Month Rite.
"The cows indeed performed this sacrificial session (*sattra*). Being hornless, they desired to obtain horns.
For them, ten months passed while they were seated [in session]."
Then the horns were produced;
they said, "We have succeeded! Let us stand up! We have accomplished that desire for which we sat down."
Of them, some said, "Whether it be half [of us] or as many as there are of us,
let us stay here until we have completed these two twelve-month periods and the year.
Of them...
In the twelfth month, horns grew out, whether through faith or lack of faith;
these are those that are hornless.
Both indeed prospered: those that grew horns and those that secured nourishment.
He prospers if he departs in ten months; he prospers if he departs in twelve, he who knows thus.
Indeed, they go by means of a footprint; indeed, one finds by means of a footprint.
This very journey is prosperous.
Therefore, this is a winner of cattle.
7.5.3 Anuvāka 3: Description of the Variations of the Pṛṣṭhya-Ṣaḍaha.
They perform the Pṛṣṭha days in the first month, they perform them in the middle [month], and they perform them in the last month;
regarding this, they say:
"That which they approach three times on a single day yields but little through its two subsequent milkings; so from where will it yield that which they approach twelve times?
Having completed the year, they should perform the *pṛṣṭha* days once in the final month; thus the sacrificers obtain the sacrifice and cattle.
Those who undertake the year-long rite float upon the ocean that is indeed without a shore and without a limit;
if they were to cast aside the *bṛhat* and *rathaṃtara* [sāmans], it would be just as if they were to cast aside their boat in the middle of the ocean.
Having proceeded with the Bṛhat and Rathantara [Sāmans] without relinquishing them, they attain a firm foundation;
for the *sandhi* (junction) milks all desires,
and thus the sacrificers obtain all their desires.
7.5.4 Anuvāka 4: A statement regarding the specific types of the northern wing.
The *ṛc* verses are common;
indeed, the *ṛc*s belong to the world of men.
They do not depart from the world of men;
for the *sāman* is one thing and the world of the gods is another.
The *sāman* is indeed the world of the gods.

Descending from the world of the gods to various other worlds of men, they go; first they approach the *jagatī*. For the meters descend; the *āgrayaṇa* cup [descends], the *bṛhat* *pṛṣṭha* chants, and the thirty-threefold hymn-form (*stoma*).
Therefore, the younger one descends after the elder;
the cup for Viśvakarman is drawn,
and by that, the sacrificers obtain all ritual acts.
The Āditya cup is drawn;
Aditi, indeed, is this earth.
In this very [state] they find firm support. They are taken up one after another for the sake of pairing and procreation.
Indeed, it was by means of the ten-night rite that Prajāpati created offspring in the intermediate space.
In that there is a ten-night rite, the sacrificers thereby create progeny.
Indeed, Udaṅka Śaulbāyana declared this ten-night rite to be the prosperity of the sacrificial session;
in that there is a ten-night rite, it is for the sake of the prosperity of the session.
Moreover, whatever is done contrary to the proper order on the preceding days, this [rite] is the pacification of that very thing.

7.5.5 Anuvāka 5: Specification of the Distinctions between the Two Gavāmayana-rites Undertaken out of Envy. If two Soma-sacrifices should coincide, one should commence the Prātaranuvāka at the latter part of the night;

[for] the one who begins first appropriates the speech, the one who begins first appropriates the deities, and the one who begins first appropriates the meters. One should employ as the introductory verse (*pratipad*) one containing the word "bull" (*vṛṣan*).
By means of the morning pressing, he excludes Indra from them;
moreover, they say that it should be performed at each opening of the pressing.
From the opening of each pressing, he indeed appropriates Indra for them;
for the lying down and the sitting, for the Gāyatrī, the Triṣṭubh, the Jagatī, the Anuṣṭubh, and the Paṅkti, for supremacy, Svāhā!
The meters indeed are the lying down and the sitting.
By means of the meters themselves, he appropriates their meters;
the *sajanīya* hymn is to be recited.
The Vihavya hymn is to be recited;
the hymn of Agastya beginning with "Kayā śubhīyā" is to be recited;
indeed, this much is all that there is.
Whatever exists, that he seizes from them;

if the pitcher should break at the morning pressing, they should chant verses addressed to Viṣṇu containing the word *śipiviṣṭa*. For whatever is redundant in the sacrifice, that is redundant with respect to Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa.
Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa is indeed the redundant; he bestows the redundant. Thus, having obtained the redundant by means of the redundant itself, they win it.
If it should break at midday, they should perform the Sāman with the *vaṣaṭ*-call as its finale (*nidhana*).
The *vaṣaṭ*-call is indeed the foundation of the sacrifice;
they cause it to reach that very foundation, even if this occurs at the third pressing.
Anuvāka 6: The description of the *utsarga* (suspension) as a modification of the qualities of the *gavāmayana*.
Having completed the months by means of six-day periods (*ṣaḍaha*), they suspend the day, for they perceive the completion of the months by means of six-day periods.
Having completed the months by means of half-months, they release a day;
for by means of half-months they perceive the ends of the months. Having completed the months by means of the new moon day, they release a day.
For by means of the new moon (amāvāsyā), they perceive the ends of the months;
having completed the month by means of the full moon (paurṇamāsī), they release the day.
For indeed, by means of the full moon, they perceive the ends of the months.
He who pours out from what is full pours it away;
he who draws up from what is full bestows vital breath upon it.
When they omit a day after completing the month at the full moon, they thereby bestow vital breath upon the year;
accordingly, the performers of the sacrificial session (satrin) breathe.
If they were not to omit a day, the year would fall apart, just as a leather water-skin falls apart when it is overfilled.
They would meet with distress.
When they omit a day after completing the months at the full moon, they thereby provide an upward breath for the year; following that, the performers of the sacrificial session [proceed].
They do not suffer,
they do not come to grief;
for at the full moon, the Soma is pressed for the gods.

When they conclude the month with the full-moon sacrifice and omit a day, they thereby descend from one sacrifice to another by means of the sacrifice of the gods. Indeed, they cut the sacrifice asunder when, after it has been continuous for six days, they omit a day;
therefore, they immolate an animal dedicated to Prajāpati.
Prajāpati is all the deities.
It is by means of the deities that they extend the sacrifice;
indeed, those who [omit] the day fall away from the pressing.
The *sāṃnāyya* is indeed the fourth pressing;
since there is the *sāṃnāyya*, they do not depart from the pressings by means of it.

Having summoned them together, they consume [the remains]. For these are indeed the Soma-drinkers even now; for those who omit a day, the deities entitled to the pressings go to their respective places.
They offer the sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśa) at each pressing;
thus they win for themselves the deities who partake in the pressings according to their proper place:
cakes on eight potsherds at the morning pressing, on eleven potsherds at the midday pressing, and on twelve potsherds at the third pressing.
Having obtained the meters, they win them;
at the third pressing, they offer a pap for the Viśvedevas,
for the third pressing belongs to the Viśvedevas.
By that very means, they do not depart from the third pressing.
7.5.7 Anuvāka 7: A Description of the Specific Rules for the Suspension of the Day.
"Should one suspend [the ritual] or should one not suspend it? thus do the exponents of the Veda deliberate.
Regarding this, they say:
"It should indeed be suspended.
"It should be suspended on the new moon day and on the full moon day," they say,
"for these two carry the sacrifice."
"But they say that those two who have shared in the intermediate sacrifice must not be released; rather,
one should release them on the first *vyaṣṭakā* day,
for this month is indeed the point of dissolution."
It has not been enjoined.
They should release [the ritual].

If they should release it as prescribed, then at whatever point during the subsequent repetition of the flood (paryāplāva) it might coincide with the middle of the six-day period—having completed the months by means of the six-day periods—they should release it on that seventh day. On that day, they should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Vāsumat, curd to Indra, a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra Marutvat, and a cake on twelve potsherds to the Viśvedevas.
The morning pressing belongs indeed to Agni accompanied by the Vasus.
In that he offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni accompanied by the Vasus, they thereby make the deity a sharer in it;
they approach the pressing with eight [verses].
In that there is curd for Indra, they do not deprive Indra of his share.
The midday pressing belongs to Indra accompanied by the Maruts.
In that they offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra accompanied by the Maruts, they make the deity a sharer; with the eleven potsherds, they approach the pressing.

The third pressing belongs to all the gods accompanied by the Ṛbhus. When they offer the cake on twelve potsherds for the Viśve Devas, they thereby make the deities sharers in it; with twelve potsherds they approach the pressing.
They immolate an animal dedicated to Prajāpati;
Prajāpati is indeed the sacrifice, [this is done] so that the sacrifice may not be abandoned.
For six months from here, the *brahmasāman* is the *abhivarta*.
The *abhivarta* is indeed the Brahman.
It is by means of the Brahman that they go forth, turning toward the heavenly world;
for the heavenly world is, as it were, turned away from here.

"O Indra, bring us wisdom, just as a father provides for his sons; teach us, O much-invoked one, on this journey, so that we may live and attain the light"—this is the *brahmasāman* performed during the six months when [the sun] is moving away from there. This world is indeed the light, and progeny is the light.
Beholding this very world, they come forward addressing one another.
7.5.8 Anuvāka 8: Description of Specific Sāmans.
When the gods had reached the end [of their journey], their sensory power and vigor departed;
they recovered it by means of the *krośa* chant.
That is the reason for the *krośa* being called a *krośa*.

Because they chant at the edge of the *cātvāla* pit with the *krośa*, having reached the very end of the sacrifice, they obtain sensory power and vigor through the success of the sacrificial session (*sattra*).
They chant at the edge of the *āhavanīya* fire.
Having made Agni their witness, they approach him with prosperity;
they chant within the two oblation-holders with the *Hṛdaya* of Prajāpati;
thus they attain his very love.
They praise in front of the assembly with a *śloka*, and behind it with an *anuśloka*;
having thus reached the end of the sacrifice, they become partakers of the *śloka*.
The Adhvaryu priest chants the *udgītha* with nine [verses]; for there are indeed nine vital breaths (*prāṇa*) in a person; thus he bestows the vital breaths upon the sacrificers.
All [the verses] belong to Indra; they place the sense-faculty in the vital breaths.
He sings the *udgītha* with unimpeded [verses].
Therefore, a man draws all other limbs toward the head;
the head alone becomes the fifteenfold Rathantara, and thus they obtain sensory power.
The seventeenth [stotra] is the Bṛhat, for the attainment of food;
moreover, by means of it they are indeed propagated.
The wives sing toward the twenty-first auspicious verse for the sake of stability among bipeds,
for the sake of pairing and procreation.
Prajāpati created living beings;
he desired,
"May I attain sovereignty over them."
The kingdom of those [deities] was encompassed by the Rājan alone;
that is the reason for the Rājan’s name as "Rājan.
When there is a Rājan, the sacrificers thereby encompass the kingdom for the sake of the subjects.
The twenty-fifth [stotra] belongs to Prajāpati for his attainment;
they chant while standing with five [verses], and thus they conquer the world of the gods.
With five [stomas], when seated, they conquer the world of men;
they become ten; the Virāj consists of ten syllables, and the Virāj is food.
By means of the Virāj they obtain food;
sitting down in five groups, they chant praise for the sake of the five directions.
They find firm support in the very quarters; they come together with each one as it has not yet been chanted; from the quarters themselves they gather food;
with those [verses], the Udgātṛ sings the *udgītha*.
Having gathered the food-eating power from all directions, they place radiance within themselves;
therefore, the single vital breath protects all the limbs.

Moreover, just as a bird about to fly up raises its head highest, even so do the sacrificers become the highest among their offspring. The Udgātṛ ascends the throne-seat; they attain sovereignty itself.
The Hotṛ ascends the swing; they ascend to the very back of the firmament.
The Adhvaryu takes two bundles of grass; they go to the very summit of the radiant realm.
So many indeed are the worlds of the gods; in them they find firm footing in due order.
Moreover, the sacrificers thereby construct a staircase and a bridge for the attainment of the heavenly world.

7.5.9 Anuvāka 9: Description of the Lute with a Thousand Strings, etc. By means of the *arkya* hymn, Prajāpati created offspring by the thousands; through the *ilāndas*, he obtained for them sustenance (*irā*) and thread (*lūtā*).
In that there is an *arkya* chant, the sacrificers thereby create offspring. In that there is an *ilāda*, they obtain nourishment (*irā*) for the offspring once created;
therefore, in whatever year a sacrificial session (*sattra*) is successful, the offspring in that year become hungry, for they have taken away their food and their strength.
In whatever year [the rain] has failed, in that same year the offspring do not suffer from hunger;
for they do not take away their food or strength, but rather they raise a cry of joy.
Just as those being released from bonds cry out aloud, even so do the sacrificers, being released from the bonds of the gods, cry out aloud, placing nourishment and vigor within themselves.
The lute has a hundred strings;
man has a lifespan of a hundred years and possesses a hundred faculties.
They establish themselves in life and the vital powers;
they run the race for the sake of winning what has not yet been won;
they beat the drums together.
This speech in the drum is indeed supreme;
they thus obtain supreme speech.
They beat the earth-drum;
whatever speech has entered this [earth], that they win, and thus they conquer this very [earth].
They utter all speech for the attainment of all speech;
they strive upon the moist hide.
For the restraint of the senses.
One cries out, another recites;
he who cries out purifies them indeed.
He who praises [the sacrificer] bestows food upon those who are purified;
for by means of the previous months, they obtain both what is performed by the seers and what is performed by the gods.
Since the *sāman*s consist of the "desire of beings," they serve for the attainment of both.
Those who undertake the year-long rite depart from the state of union;
therefore, two couples unite within the sacrificial altar.
For that very reason, they do not go with pairs.
7.5.10 Anuvāka 10: Statement of the Mantras for the Limbs of the Aśvamedha Sacrifice. They split open the hide;
they split open the evil of these [sacrificers].
"Do not fail, do not overstep," he says; thus they truly shatter the evil of these [vessels].
Having set down the water-pitchers, the female slaves dance around the Mārjālīya fire, stamping their feet and singing, "This is honey."
Honey is indeed the supreme food of the gods;
they obtain the supreme food itself when they strike down the footprints.
They bestow greatness upon these very ones.
7.5.11 Anuvāka 11: Recitation of the Mantras for the Aśvamedha Subsidiary Rite To the earth, svāhā! To the intermediate space, svāhā! To the sky, svāhā!
To that which is about to be submerged, svāhā! To that which is being submerged, svāhā! To that which has been submerged, svāhā!

To the one who will become a cloud, svāhā! To the one becoming a cloud, svāhā! To the one who has become a cloud, svāhā! To the cloud, svāhā! To the mist, svāhā! To the frost, svāhā! To the lightning-flash, svāhā! To the female lightning-flash, svāhā!

To the one about to flash forth lightning, Svāhā! To the one flashing forth lightning, Svāhā! To the one flashing forth together, Svāhā! To the one about to thunder, Svāhā! To the one thundering, Svāhā! To the one thundering fiercely, Svāhā! To the one about to rain, Svāhā! To the one raining, Svāhā! To the one raining down upon, Svāhā! To the one raining all around, Svāhā! To the one raining together, Svāhā!

Svāhā to him who is about to rain; svāhā to him who will sprinkle; svāhā to him who sprinkles; svāhā to him who has sprinkled; svāhā to him who is about to flow; svāhā to him who flows; svāhā to him who flows all around!
To him who will take up, svāhā; to him who is taking up, svāhā; to him who has taken up, svāhā; to him who will be overwhelmed, svāhā; to him who is being overwhelmed, svāhā;
to him who has been overwhelmed, svāhā; to him who will be heated, svāhā; to him who is being heated, svāhā; to him who is intensely heated, svāhā.

Hail to the Ṛg-verses! Hail to the Yajus-formulas! Hail to the Sāman-chants! Hail to the Aṅgirases! Hail to the Vedas! Hail to the Gāthās! Hail to the Nārāśaṃsīs! Hail to the Raibhīs! Hail to the All! Hail!
7.5.12 Anuvāka 12: Statement of the Mantras Constituting Parts of the Aśvamedha Sacrifice.
To the one with teeth, Svāhā! To the toothless one, Svāhā!
To the breathing one, Svāhā! To the breathless one, Svāhā!
Hail to the one possessing a mouth, hail to the mouthless; hail to the one possessing a nose, hail to the noseless;
hail to the one possessing eyes, hail to the eyeless.
Hail to the one with ears, hail to the earless;
hail to the one with a head, hail to the headless; hail to the one with feet, hail to the footless.
Svāhā to the one who breathes, svāhā to the one who does not breathe;
svāhā to the one who speaks, svāhā to the one who does not speak; svāhā to the one who sees, svāhā to the one who does not see.
Hail to the one who hears! Hail to the one who does not hear! Hail to the one possessed of mind! Hail to the one without mind!
Hail to the one possessing seed! Hail to the seedless! Hail to offspring! Hail to procreation!
Hail to the hairy! Hail to the hairless!
Svāhā to the skin; svāhā to that which is skinless; svāhā to the one possessing hide; svāhā to the one without hide;
svāhā to the one possessing blood; svāhā to the one without blood.
Hail to the one possessing flesh, hail to the one without flesh; hail to the sinews, hail to the one without sinews;
hail to the one possessing bones, hail to the one without bones.
Hail to the marrow, hail to that which is without marrow!
Hail to the limb, hail to that which is without limb!
Hail to the self, hail to that which is not the self!
Hail to all!
7.5.13 Anuvāka 13: Exposition of the Mantras for the Limbs of the Aśvamedha Sacrifice.
Who yokes you? May he yoke you. May Viṣṇu yoke you.
For the success of this sacrifice, for my own submissiveness, for such-and-such a desire—for you, for long life; for you, for out-breath; for you, for in-breath; for you, for diffused breath.
For prosperity thee, for wealth thee, for gain thee,
for fame thee, for nourishment thee, for renown from afar thee.
For falling away, thee!
7.5.14 Anuvāka 14: Statement of the Mantras as Subsidiaries of the Aśvamedha Sacrifice.
An offering on eight potsherds for Agni—associated with the Gāyatrī metre, the Trivṛt stoma, the Rathantara sāman, and the spring season;
and an offering on eleven potsherds for Indra—associated with the Triṣṭubh metre, the Pañcadaśa stoma, the Bṛhat sāman, and the summer season.
To the Viśve Devas, who are connected with the Jagatī metre, the Saptadaśa stoma, the Vairūpa sāman, and the rainy season, there is an offering on twelve potsherds.
To Mitra and Varuṇa, who are connected with the Anuṣṭubh metre, the Ekaviṃśa stoma, the Vairāja sāman, and the autumn, there is an offering of curd-mixture (payasyā).
To Bṛhaspati, who is connected with the Paṅkti metre, the Triṇava stoma, the Śākvara sāman, and the winter, there is an oblation of cooked rice (caru).
To Savitṛ, for the Aticchandas meter, for the thirty-three gods, for the Raivata Sāman, and for the Śaiśira season, there is an offering on twelve potsherds; to Aditi, the wife of Viṣṇu, a pap;
to Agni Vaiśvānara, an offering on twelve potsherds.
A pap offering for Anumati;
a cake on one potsherd for Ka.

7.5.15 Anuvāka 15: Exposition of the Mantras Constituting Parts of the Aśvamedha Sacrifice That fire which is cast into the fire, and that which is King Soma—for these two, this [offering] to Agni and Soma is the guest-reception (*ātithya*).
Now, this [altar] that is being built is Rudra.

If one were not to offer these oblations when the fire has been piled, this very Rudra, being unappeased, might rise up and strike down the progeny and cattle of the sacrificer. In that he offers these oblations when the fire has been piled, he appeases him with his own share; thus Rudra does not remain unappeased toward him.
Having risen, he looks upon his offspring and cattle;
there are ten oblations,
for there are nine vital breaths in a person, and the navel is the tenth.
He places the vital breaths indeed within the sacrificer; moreover, the Virāj consists of ten syllables,
and the Virāj is food.
He indeed shines and finds firm support in the eating of food. "He is to be built with the seasons, the meters, the *stomas*, and the *pṛṣṭhas*," they say;
in that he offers these oblations, he builds him up with the seasons, the meters, the *stomas*, and the *pṛṣṭhas*.
"They say that by means of the oblation being offered, the quarters are conquered;
when he offers these oblations, it is for the conquest of the quarters."
By means of this [offering], the gods caused Indra to sacrifice; therefore it is called the *Indrasava*. By means of this, men caused Manu to sacrifice; therefore it is called the *Manusava*.
Just as Indra is among the gods and Manu among men, so does he become who, knowing thus, sacrifices with this offering.
The invitatory verses (puro'nuvākyā) correspond to the quarters;
this is for the conquest of all the quarters.

7.5.16 Anuvāka 16: Recitation of the Mantras for the Aśvamedha Sacrifice He who by his greatness alone became the sole king of the breathing and blinking world; he who rules over these bipeds and quadrupeds—to what god shall we offer worship with our oblation? You are taken with a support; I take you, acceptable to Prajāpati. The sky is your greatness, the stars are your form, and the sun is your splendor. To that greatness, to Prajāpati, svāhā!

7.5.17 Anuvāka 17: Recitation of the Mantras Constituting Parts of the Aśvamedha Sacrifice He who gives self, who gives strength, whose command all the worlds and the gods revere; whose shadow is immortality, whose [other aspect] is death—to what god shall we offer worship with our oblation? You are taken with a support; I take you, acceptable to Prajāpati. The earth is your greatness; the plants and the trees are your form; fire is your splendor. To that greatness, to Prajāpati, svāhā!
7.5.18 Anuvāka 18: Statement of the Mantras Constituting Parts of the Aśvamedha Sacrifice.
"O Brahman, may a Brāhmaṇa endowed with Vedic luster be born;
in this kingdom, may a Kṣatriya be born who is skilled in archery, a hero, and a great chariot-warrior."
A cow that milks is a *dhenu*; a bull that draws is an *anaḍvān*; a swift steed is an *āśu-sapti*.
A woman of noble form, victorious, standing upon the chariot, a youth fit for the assembly hall.
May a heroic son be born to this sacrificer;
may Parjanya rain for us according to our every desire, and may our plants ripen with fruit.
May our security and well-being be provided for.

7.5.19 Anuvāka 19: Recitation of the Mantras for the Limbs of the Aśvamedha Sacrifice The vigorous steed has stepped upon the earth; he has made Agni his companion, O vigorous steed, O courser. The vigorous steed has stepped into the intermediate space; he has made Vāyu his companion, O vigorous steed, O courser. The vigorous steed has ascended to heaven; he has made Sūrya his companion, O vigorous steed, O courser. O vigorous steed, Agni is your companion; I take hold of you; carry me safely across. O vigorous steed, Vāyu is your companion; I take hold of you; carry me safely across.

Carry me across, O Āditya; you are the swift steed, I grasp onto you for well-being—carry me safely across! You are the sustainer of the out-breath (*prāṇa*), make my out-breath firm. You are the sustainer of the diffused breath (*vyāna*), make my diffused breath firm. You are the sustainer of the in-breath (*apāna*), make my in-breath firm. You are sight, bestow sight upon me. You are hearing, bestow hearing upon me. You are life, bestow life upon me.
7.5.20 Anuvāka 20: Exposition of the Mantras Constituting Parts of the Aśvamedha Sacrifice.
The seed is born;
Parjanya is the rain-giver.
