May he ripen the grain; may the plants bear good fruit;
may this earth be easy to traverse.
Agni is easy of access; the intermediate space has a good overseer; the purifying wind is well-purifying.
May the sky be well-established; may that sun shine auspiciously, and may day and night be as they were before.
The half-months consist of fifteen days,
the months consist of thirty days; thus are the seasons ordained.
The year is peaceful.
7.5.21 Anuvāka 21: Statement of the Mantras for the Subsidiary Rites of the Aśvamedha.
[The offering] to Agni is a cake on eight potsherds; that to Soma is a pap.
A cake on eight potsherds for Savitṛ,
a pap for Pūṣan,
and a pap for Rudra.
If [the victim] does not come, there is a cake on twelve potsherds for Agni Vaiśvānara at the deer’s den;
[and] a cake on eight potsherds for Agni Aṃhomuc, and milk for Sūrya.
The portion of clarified butter belongs to Vāyu.
7.5.22 Anuvāka 22: Exposition of the Mantras for the Subsidiary Rites of the Aśvamedha.
An offering on eight potsherds for Agni, the Deliverer from Distress; an offering on eleven potsherds for Indra, the Deliverer from Distress.
A curd-mixture for Mitra and Varuṇa as the dispellers of the cow;
a pap for Vāyu and Savitṛ as the dispellers of the cow;
parched grains for the Aśvins as the dispellers of the cow.
To the Maruts, the deliverers from sin, an offering on seven potsherds; to the Viśvedevas, the deliverers from sin, an offering on twelve potsherds;
a pap for Anumati.
A cake on twelve potsherds for Agni Vaiśvānara;
a cake on two potsherds for Heaven and Earth, the deliverers from distress.
7.5.23 Anuvāka 23: Statement of the Mantras Constituting Parts of the Aśvamedha Sacrifice I have bowed down to Agni; I have bowed down to Pṛthivī.
Just as Agni has bowed down to Pṛthivī, so may auspicious conciliations bow down to me.
He concurred with Vāyu; he concurred with the intermediate space.
As Vāyu concurred with the intermediate space, so he concurred with Sūrya; he concurred with the sky.
Just as the sun bowed down to the day, so did it bow down to the moon and the constellations;
just as the moon [bowed down] to the constellations.
He has conciliated Varuṇa; he has conciliated the waters,
just as Varuṇa [is conciliated] by the waters.
He brought the *sāman* into harmony with the *sāman*; he brought the *sāman* into harmony with the *ṛc*.
Just as the *sāman* was brought into harmony with the *ṛc*, so was it brought into harmony with the *brahman* and brought into harmony with the *kṣatra*.
Just as the Brahmin concurred with the Kṣatriya for the sake of the King, and concurred with the Vaiśya;
just as the King [concurred] with the Vaiśya.
It was prepared for the chariot; it was prepared for the horses.
Just as the chariot was prepared with the horses, so was it prepared for Prajāpati; it was prepared for all beings.
Just as Prajāpati made peace with all beings, so may auspicious inclinations be inclined toward me.

7.5.24 Anuvāka 24: Recitation of the Mantras Constituting Parts of the Aśvamedha Sacrifice O Savitṛ, those paths of yours which are ancient, dustless, and spread across the mid-air—by those easy-to-traverse paths, protect us today, O God, and speak for us. Homage to Agni, who dwells on earth and fills the world; grant a world to this sacrificer. Homage to Vāyu, who dwells in the mid-air and fills the world; grant a world to this sacrificer. Homage to Sūrya, who dwells in heaven and fills the world; grant a world to this sacrificer.
7.5.25 Anuvāka 25: Recitation of the Mantras Constituting Parts of the Aśvamedha Sacrifice He who knows the head of the sacrificial horse becomes possessed of a head and fit for sacrifice.
Dawn, indeed, is the head of the sacrificial horse.
The sun is the eye;
the wind is the breath;
the moon is the ear.
The quarters are his feet;
the intermediate quarters are his ribs;
day and night are his winking.
The half-months are its joints,
the months are its connections,
and the seasons are its limbs.
The year is his body; the rays are his hair;
the constellations are his form.
The stars are the bones, the sky is the flesh,
and the herbs are the body hair.
The trees are the hair;
Agni is the mouth;
Vaiśvānara is the gaping maw.
The ocean is his belly,
the atmosphere is his anus,
and heaven and earth are his testicles.
The pressing-stone is the penis; Soma is the semen.
When one gnaws [the wood], that is the lightning-flash.
What it shakes is its thundering; what it urinates is its raining;
its speech is indeed its voice.
Verily, when the horse is being born, its greatness is born first as day; its greatness is born after it as night.
These two great powers have indeed come together on both sides of the horse:
as a *haya* it carried the gods, as an *arvan* the Asuras, as a *vājī* the Gandharvas, and as a *aśva* human beings.
The ocean is the source of the horse; the ocean is its kin.
